*Johannes Trithemius*

A sect was founded in these times, in the year 40 of Samael, or thereabouts. Hence, for the rest, it is that all things happen by providence. The Saracens waged many battles against the Christians in Asia and Africa. Constantinople was taken by the Germans, and Baldwin, Count of Flanders, was made emperor. From Germany more than 26,000 children were drowned at sea by pirates; seduced by a vain spirit, they said that they were going to recover the Holy Land. From Spain, herdsmen gathered together, admitting no one to Paris, seized the goods of the clergy, while the people rejoiced. But when they stretched out their hands to the goods of the laymen, they were killed. In the year of the Christians 1212 Frederick II was elected; he ruled for 33 years, and did much against the Church.

In the year 1238 an eclipse and earthquakes continually crushed many thousands of people. Frisia too was almost submerged by sea-floods, and more than 100,000 people perished. The Tartars devastated Hungary and Poland, after first overcoming Greater Armenia and many regions. In the year of the Christians 1244, a certain Jew at Toledo, while digging, found a book in which it was written: “In the third world Christ will be born of the Virgin Mary and will suffer for the salvation of men.” Believing at once, he was baptized. The third world was the third revolution of the spirit of Saturn, of which mention was made above; at its beginning Christ was born of the Virgin. The Roman pontiffs, removing Frederick from the empire, declared that it had been vacant for 28 years, until the election of Rudolf, Count of Habsburg, whom they set among the kings. By election of the princes, first Henry, Count of Schwarzburg, a Thuringian; William, Count of Holland; [Conrad?], son of Frederick; Alfonso, King of Castile; and Richard, Earl of Cornwall, brother of the King of England; and evils were multiplied on the earth. At this time, around the year of the Lord 1260, the confederation of the Swiss first began: a people small in number, which grew with time and killed many of the nobles, driving others from their borders; warlike men, whose commonwealth is known to all the peoples of Germany. In the year of the Christians 1273 Rudolf of Habsburg was made emperor by election of the princes, and ruled for 18 years, a man in all respects prudent and excellent, from whom all the later dukes of Austria descended. The Tartars, invading the lands of the Christians, Constantinople, and Greece, inflicted much damage on the Christians. The Saracens occupied many cities in Asia and killed more than four hundred thousand Christians. When Rudolf died, Adolf of Nassau was elected king and ruled for 6 years; afterward Albert, son of Rudolf, defeated him in battle near Worms, killed him, and was elected emperor in the year 1298; he ruled for 10 years and was killed by his brother’s son. The order of the Templars was destroyed by Pope Clement V. The island of Rhodes was taken by Christians from the hands of the Saracens in the fourth year of the siege and of continuous war against them. After Albert was killed by his nephew, Henry VIII, Count of Luxembourg, was made emperor, and ruled for five years. When he died, Louis IV of Bavaria ruled for [12?] years, beginning in the year [1315?]; the Roman pontiffs gave him the crown. Frederick, Duke [unclear]. Charles IV, King of Bohemia, emperor. Earthquake. Tolls. [Charles’s?] son Wenceslaus, emperor. [The Duke] of Austria opposed him, but was defeated by him. After Louis, Charles IV, King of Bohemia, was made emperor; he raised the bishopric of Prague to an archbishopric and ruled for 31 years. There were very great earthquakes. This Charles newly instituted many things concerning tolls in favor of the prince-electors. Günther, Count of Schwarzburg, calling himself king, opposed Emperor Charles, but prevailed in nothing against him. After Charles, his son Wenceslaus ruled for [112?] years; after him Jodocus, Margrave of Moravia, succeeded Sigismund, brother of Wenceslaus. Leopold, Duke of Austria, with 8 counts and more than 4,000 men, was killed fighting in battle by the Swiss. Under Wenceslaus, king and emperor of the Bohemians, the teaching of the Hussites took its beginning. Wenceslaus was deposed; after his deposition, Rupert, Count Palatine of the Rhine and Duke of Bavaria, was elected, and ruled for 10 years. In the year of the Lord [1369?], the Christians brought war upon the Saracens, but it went badly because of the arrogance of the French, since they killed more than 100,000 of our men, besides the captives, among whom was John, Duke of the Burgundians. There were many wars in these times. In the year [1407?] Sigismund became emperor for 27 years. He tried to lay waste Bohemia for the extirpation of heresies, but made little progress. The kingdom of France was cruelly laid waste and afflicted by the English and the Burgundians. When Sigismund departed this life, Albert, Duke of Austria, his son-in-law, succeeded him in the year of the Christians 1438; and he ruled for [56?] years, a man divine in intellect and peaceful in spirit. In the year of the Lord 1440 he began to reign. In the year of the Christians 1453 Constantinople was taken by the Turks through the betrayal of a certain Genoese, and gradually all Greece fell away from the Christian faith. For thereafter in time many *Mystical Chronology.*

The kingdoms and provinces of the Christians are devastated and captured by the Turks. At this time Christians had many very grave wars among themselves in Gaul, England, Saxony, Westphalia, Prussia, Flanders, Swabia, and other places. In these times the art of printing was newly invented at Mainz, the metropolis of Germany, by wondrous industry, a gift of divinity. In the year of the Christians 1456, the Turks were overthrown in Hungary by the faithful, and many perished. The pilgrimage of children to Saint Michael was remarkable. There were earthquakes in the kingdom of Naples; more than 4,000 men perished. In the year of the Lord 1462, Mainz, the metropolis of the Franks, was captured and plundered. Charles, duke of Burgundy, defeated the French in the year 1465. Afterwards, in the year 67, he destroyed Dinant and Liège. In the year 1473 he entered Guelders and powerfully obtained it, likewise the whole duchy of Lorraine. A comet appeared through the month of January in the year of the Lord 1472. Charles, duke of Burgundy, besieged the town of Neuss for the space of a year, in the year 74; afterwards, in 1477, he was killed in battle, a magnanimous prince.

In these times the Turks took many cities of the Christians: Negroponte in Euboea, also the Bosnian kingdom, the duchy of the [Despot?], Achaia, Mitylene, and several kingdoms in the East. In 1476 a gathering of fools took place at Niklashausen in the Franconia of Germany, full of errors. In the year 1480 the Turks besieged the Rhodians with a great army, but did not prevail. In the same year, departing from Rhodes, they took Hydruntum, more than 12,500 Christians being killed and only 22 escaping by flight. And in the following year the emperor of the Turks, Mehmed, died; Bayezid, his first-born, succeeded him in the kingdom, now ruling into his twenty-seventh year. In the year of the Christians 1486, Maximilian, son of Frederick, was established king of the Romans at Frankfurt; he was greeted as Caesar by Pope Julius in the year 1508. He founded the military order of Saint George against the heretical Turks; he subdued the Swiss in war; he attacks the rebellious Sicambri in war even to this day, and will prosper against all treaty-breakers. The king of the French, persecutor of the Empire in his usual manner, has been found to be devising new plots. May the Almighty protect those assigned to the dominion of Samael in the year [1508?]. The Venetians, rebels against Caesar’s empire, have been marked by ban and war. There will be punishment for obstinacy, and reward for prudent satisfaction.

Around the end of this third revolution of Samael, the image of alteration will pass to the first; it will be the destruction of many. For unless Y., with God ministering, is brought back to Algos, there will be the monarchy of someone, or the transfer of some great kingdom. A great sect of religion will arise, the destruction of old religions. It is to be feared lest the fourth beast lose one head. In Samael, Mars first foretold the Flood, in the second the destruction of Troy; in the third, near the end, there will be great damage to unity. For from preceding things let the future things that follow be judged. This third revolution of Mars will not be completed without the prophecy of some new institution of religion. From here, in the year of the Christians 1508, there remain years up to the year of the world 7086, the eighth month; but of the Lord’s nativity, 1879, likewise two months. The future sequence of this revolution requires prophecy.

I have not written these things assertively, most sacred Caesar; they are by no means to be believed with any injury to the orthodox faith. There are, however, those who have reckoned the months in these matters as lunar; if you decide that they should be agreed with, those things which I have written otherwise must be changed. With my own hand also I protest, and with my mouth I confess, that in all these things I believe nothing, admit nothing, except what the Catholic Church believes; the rest I reject and despise as vain, fabricated, and superstitious.

Praise to almighty God.

*[unclear]*

*A compendium or breviary of the first volume of the Annals or Histories, concerning the origin of the kings and people of the Franks, addressed to the most reverend father and prince in Christ, Lord Laurentius, Bishop of Würzburg and Duke of eastern Francia, by Johannes Trithemius, Abbot.*

*Epi-* *Letter of Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of St James, formerly of Spanheim, to the most reverend father in Christ and prince, Lord Laurentius, of the noble and very ancient family of the Bibras, bishop of the distinguished Church of Würzburg and sole duke of Eastern Francia, concerning the compendium of the first volume of the annals on the origin of the Franks.*

To the most reverend father in Christ, most excellent prince and lord, Lord Laurentius, bishop of the noble Church of Würzburg and sole duke of Eastern Francia, Johannes Trithemius, unprofitable, and abbot in name alone of the poor little monastery of St James the Apostle in the suburbs of the aforementioned city of Würzburg, offers ready service in all things, no less voluntary than owed by right.

Most reverend father, illustrious prince, and gracious lord, I have written, as your Most Reverend Lordship knows, three great volumes, the work of no small labor, on the origin, course, and particular deeds of the kings, dukes, princes, and people of the Franks, taking the beginning of my narration and of the succession of the kings from the four hundred and fortieth year before the birth of Christ, at which time, after Antenor, the great king of the people, had been killed by enemies, his son Marcomer succeeded to the kingdom and led out his people, namely our forebears, from Scythia, from the borders to the borders of Germany and Saxony, to the mouths of the Rhine, where Guelders now is. In these three volumes I have embraced a period of one thousand nine hundred fifty-four years, in which the kings of the Franks, succeeding one another in proper order, from that same Marcomer already named down to the twentieth year of Maximilian Augustus, emperor of the Romans and Caesar, are counted as one hundred and three. There were many collateral kings, outside the direct line of genealogy, who are excluded from this number of kings. Through the whole first volume, moreover, I continue the successions of the kings of the Franks and their deeds down to King Pippin, exclusively, over one thousand one hundred ninety years, in which there were sixty-one kings succeeding one another in a direct line. Pippin was succeeded by his son Charles, surnamed the Great. After him came his son, Louis the Pious. When he died, his sons divided the kingdom of the Franks into very many parts. When they too had departed this life, their grandsons again the kingdom of the Franco[unclear] in such a manner divided principally into two kingdoms; of these one is to be called, to be, and to remain Germanic, the other Gallic, and neither is to be subject to the other. And this division is such as follows.

The kingdom of the Franks, Germany, is to have perpetually by itself its own king, subject to no mortal whatsoever, not even to the Roman Empire, but, according to the ancient custom of the Franks, most free. To this kingdom, in the aforesaid division, fell the subject nations, cities, peoples, and races: namely the whole kingdom of Germany, with the Saxons, Thuringians, Marcomanni, Danes, Frisians, Hessians, [Westphalians?], East Franks, Bavarians, Swabians, Bohemians, Sorbs, southern Germans, and all the nations, peoples, and races that lie among those named above.

Likewise the whole kingdom of Austrasia, with these cities: Metz, the whole of what is now called Lorraine, Trier, with the Mosellans, the Eifel people, and the [Cinonotes?], Cologne, Aachen, Liege, and both lower and upper Utrecht, with Holland, Zeeland, Brabant, Hainaut, the entire region from the river Rhine westward as far as the sea; with the Tongrians, Flemings, Morini, and the whole land that either adjoins or lies between the aforesaid regions and cities.

Finally, the kingdom of Arles, with its eight counties in Gaul, is considered from ancient times subject to the rule of the king of the Germans. For this reason the archbishop of Trier, whoever he may be at the time, is afterwards known to have been appointed archchancellor of the German kingdom throughout Gaul, for the aforesaid kingdom of Arles. The kingdom of Burgundy also, with all its counties, was assigned in the same division to the kingdom of the Germans. All Alemannia as well, with its cities and peoples, in which are the cities of Chur, Sion, and [Valais?], fell by lot to the kingdom of the Germans, together with the Swiss, Alsatians, [Caurici?], Savoyards, people of Constance, Basel, Strasbourg, Speyer, Worms, Mainz, and all peoples from the rising of the river Rhine as far as the sea, into which it flows by three mouths.

But the Roman Empire, together with Italy, Lombardy, and all those subject to it by ancient right, except Greece, the Eastern Empire, was, and today remains, annexed and subject to the kingdom of the Germans. Nevertheless, over time many disputes, invasions, and changes arose between the kings of the Germans and the Gauls concerning certain boundaries of the kingdom; of these matters it has been written more fully in the second volume.

The kingdom of the Franks of Gaul also, now divided from ours already mentioned, is in like manner, as the constitution declares, to have its own free king, who is no less free than the king of Germany and is subject to no one at all. For it is manifest that the Franks from their origin have always been had been very free, and never served the Romans nor any other nation whatsoever, nor existed as subjects, but rather they themselves destroyed the empire of the Romans and made it subject to themselves. And for this reason both kings, in the division of the kingdom, determined that each should preserve everywhere the ancient liberty of the other unimpaired.

But the king of Gallic France, in the division of the monarchy, received as his portion the kingdom of Neustria, or Paris, and also the kingdom of Orléans, the kingdom of Aquitaine, the kingdom of [Toulouse?], the kingdom of Armorica, or New Britain, with all the provinces and peoples of inner Gaul, as far as Spain: from the river Rhône as far as the western sea.

After that division of the kingdom of the Franks, I too compressed the history, henceforth leaving aside the Gallic Franks; in the second and third volumes of the Annals I continued the narrative concerning only the German Franks. But since, in so long a course of years, reckoning first from the entrance of the people into Germany, the history became rather lengthy, I judged it worth the effort if from those three volumes of annals I should draw out as many shorter books, which would contain in summary the names, successions, and deeds more worthy of remembrance of the kingdom of the Franks of Germany. For I know that your most reverend Lordship both delights in ancient histories and, by reason of administering your principality, is continually occupied in many affairs. Since, therefore, no prince lives today among mortals to whom, after God, I am by right more bound and more ready, with the most submissive will, to serve and please according to my strength and beyond, than to your most excellent and most reverend Lordship, I judge no one more worthy to whose name I either ought or wish to dedicate these lucubrations of mine concerning the origin of the Franks. Therefore, I pray, may your gracious Lordship kindly receive the work of compendium which I offer, and hold me, your humble servant, commended.

In the year 1515.

*** 4 *A Compendium or Abridgment of the First Volume of the Chronicles or Annals of Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Saint James the Greater, Apostle, in the suburb of the city of Würzburg, concerning the origin of the nation and kings of the Franks, addressed to the most reverend father and prince in Christ, Lord Laurentius, Bishop of Würzburg and Duke of Eastern Francia, begins.*

With the aid of our Lord Jesus Christ, we have written, not without very great labors, three volumes of our annals, of by no means small size. In them, from the origin of the nation of the Franks down to the twenty-eighth year of Caesar Maximilian Augustus, we have set forth a fuller history, distinguished in the following order of division. For in the first volume we described both the origin and the kings of the aforesaid nation of the Franks, beginning from Marcomitus, who began to reign in the four hundred thirty-ninth year before the birth of Christ. After the death of his father, whom the Goths had killed in war, he reigned twenty-eight years, and was the first to lead the nation from the mouths of the Danube into Germany, to the mouths of the Rhine. This people, once sprung from Trojan fugitives, while they were still among their own fellow-citizens, had the Trojan name; afterward, scattered among various nations and wandering, they very often changed their name together with their settlements. For at first, when they were called Trojans, they were Trojans; afterward, among the Scythians, they too were named Scythians; but when they came into the borders of Germany, for a time they were called Sicambri; finally, from Francus their king, they were called Franks. Nevertheless the Sicambri could not at once obtain from the neighboring peoples, especially from the Roman Gauls, to whom their power was always suspect, that they should be called Franks, until at last, expanding their kingdom and name, they powerfully subjected to themselves the Romans, together with Italy and all Gaul. And because they lived with the Germans, they were more often named Germans than Franks by the writers of deeds. Thus the whole period of the first volume of our annals contains 1,189 years, from Marcomirus down to King Pippin.

The second volume of the annals takes its beginning from the year of the Lord's nativity 750, when Pippin, mayor of the palace, was elected king of the Franks, Hilderic having been shorn as a monk. From there down to the eighth year of Richard, king of Germany, who succeeded William amid the dissension of the princes, it contains a period of 515 years, as is clear to one who counts the sequence of the order; in these years the history of the German kingdom is woven together.

The third volume of annalistic notes takes its beginning from the eighth year of King Richard, which was the 1266th year of the Lord's nativity. This we have continued to the twenty-eighth year of King Maximilian, namely the 1514th year of the Lord's nativity, containing 248 years. And thus the whole period of the three volumes makes 1,953 years, whose deeds we have embraced.

*Compendium, Book I.*

And so, intending from a fixed consideration of our mind to write an epitome of the first volume of our Annals, a compendium or breviary, we warn the reader not to censure the work before he has prudently examined it. It is the manifest mark of a rash man to judge what he does not know, and to think that no one can know what he himself perhaps does not know. I know that many have written various and divergent things about the origin of the Franks: some of them maintain that the people was native-born, while others that it was immigrant from I know not what city of the Sicambri. We believe that no one can either distinguish or reconcile their diverse opinions unless Hunibald’s compilation enlightens him. For that sound historian of the Franks flourished in human life in the times of King Clodoceus, whom Saint Remigius, prelate of the Romans, baptized, in the five-hundredth year of the Lord’s nativity; after Doracus the philosopher, Wasthald the historian, and many other very ancient writers of deeds, he wrote a distinguished work, which he divided into eighteen books. In the first six he traces the earliest origin of the people of the Franks from the Trojan destruction down to the death of King Antenor, whom the Scanzians, Goths, and Sueci or Suedi killed near the mouths of the Danube, namely in the four-hundred-fortieth year before Christ’s nativity. In the other six books he embraces the time from the death of the aforementioned King Antenor down to Faramund, king of the Franks, the forty-third of the second order. From Faramund the remaining six books are continued down to the last year of Clodoceus, the first Christian among the kings, who died in the five-hundred-fourteenth year of the Lord’s nativity. And because I have written about all these things in the first volume of our Annals, the rationale of the name Breviary requires that we here pursue brevity. Here ends the Proem.

*The breviary of the first volume of his Annals, by Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Saint James at Würzburg, of the Order of Saint Benedict, happily begins.*

Indeed, in the four-hundred-fortieth year before the nativity of the Lord, our Savior Jesus Christ, from Mary ever an untouched virgin, when the peoples who were afterward called Franks, but previously Scythians, and still earlier Trojans, were settled by the maritime borders of Scythia, not far from the mouths of the Danube, King Antenor ruled. Against him a most fierce people, numerous beyond number, having come forth from the Scanzian islands, which are now called Gothic, wore down his people by repeated attack, bringing arms against arms, hands against hands. Antenor, now defeated, now [unclear], was at last killed by the Goths in battle with many of his men, in the year noted above, before Christ’s nativity, as we have said, 440; his son Marcomir succeeded him in the kingdom.

*The First King.*

Marcomir, the elder son of the slain King Antenor, placed in his father’s stead, reigned twenty-eight years; and he began in almost the same year in which his father was killed. He was a magnanimous, strong, bold, warlike man, who avenged his father’s death upon the nearer Goths by repeated attacks, although he seemed far inferior to the Goths in number of fighters and in strength. Moreover, in the fourth year of his reign he held counsel with the chief men of the kingdom as to how either the Goths might be kept away from the kingdom, or, if this could not be done, provision might be made for the people in some other way, lest it perish.

At last it pleased all who judged rightly that, since they could in no way resist so immense a multitude of Goths, they should change their settlements by the will of the gods. Therefore, after the ministers of the gods had been summoned, the elders commanded that inquiry be made of the divine powers in which direction they ordered them to go. The rites suited to prophecies are prepared; sacrifices are offered by an art composed for summoning infernal powers. In the midst, before the altar of Jove, stands a frenzied priest; he twists his head about, utters songs in a murmur, gnashes tightly with his teeth, with his fingers bent back twists and shakes his arms with his hands, and, darting about, bends backward in like manner, appearing to a sane beholder like a foolish, insane man. At last, after the divine power had been summoned by song, the priest Menolpor, asked for a prophecy, gave response and began to thunder thus: “Marcomir, prince of Jove, the divinity bids itself be tranquil, and not to fear the hazards of the long journey, because he tends westward after his brothers to the mouths of the Rhine, where [unclear] Brutus, [unclear].”

*Counsel of the Franks concerning transmontane Germany. They seek the response of Jove through the priests. Jove’s prophet [unclear] that counsel should be made in the temple.*

*Marcomir ruled in Germany for twenty-eight years.* *Annals of Trithemius.*

[unclear]. And each of you is by nature a brother to you and by nation a faithful friend. Go, with swift course take possession of the seats prepared, to be enlarged, by the will of the father, into a third part of the world.

That same night King Marcomirus summoned the ancestral deity by an incantation, with a murmured chant, and brought before him as prophetess one whom, because of her sagacity, they named Aliruna. He prepared a portent and confirmed the prophecy of the priestess by the authority of the Sibyl, and at once ordered the people to be led across, so that their offspring, multiplied exceedingly as the vision foretold, might remain stronger forever.

Marcomirus saw a three-headed deity standing there, and heard the separate prediction of each head; and he saw a distinct diadem placed high above each one. The first head was that of a toad; the second, of a lion; the third, in the form of an eagle, as if standing above with wings spread, holding and cherishing the lion on the right and the toad on the left. And the eagle said: “Marcomirus, your progeny shall subject my head to itself; it shall trample the lion and at the same time slay the toad.” And the toad itself added: “Do not think me to be despised, handsome king, because I appear foul. My outward form is suited to future events. Your generation will first destroy me far away; after this it will keep the lion captive by the sword. Take care to hear from his mouth what remains further.”

Afterward the lion’s head said to King Marcomirus: “Guest about to come into my [land], most valiant king, with your people, you will soon conquer the toad by toil; after much time, then my rights will everywhere yield to their own, of their own accord in wars [unclear]. Afterward the eagle on the right will crown me when conquered, having at the left the toad bound by your seed. What will happen afterward is shown to you by our conjunction.”

When the lion-shaped apparition had uttered these words, the three heads were suddenly changed into one, and the three-headed portent stood transformed into the image of a man, not of lowly condition, but of a king crowned with a golden diadem, holding a scepter in his left hand and a sword in his right. Muttering in a harsh voice, in speech taught by spells, to summon up the shades and to bring down the highest gods from heaven, it answered: “Let them bear with your enchantments, so that the future may be as future: understand, lest we speak in vain. As the transformation of our image confirms the form, so this very voice of prophecy makes certain that a kingdom, varied in condition, is promised in the future to this people; a long time will vary it, and the multitude of the ruling stock, so that it will neither always be one nor divided into very many. Now one, then two, now three, then four; beyond that, now it returns into one; at last it will stand divided into two, when the eagle has been joined as friend to the lion, and the toad, plotting against the eagle, has held the left side.” When all these things had been said, the vision disappeared.

King Marcomirus asked Aliruna what the meaning of the prophecy was. She said to him: “It is the ancestral god, O king, who accompanies you and your people; by his predictions you have been instructed about the future for your people and for the kings who will be born from you. From here you must know that you are to migrate as quickly as possible to the farthest lands of the lion toward the west. The lion designates the people who dwell on this side of the river Rhine, sprung from the ancient stock of the Trojans. On the other side of the river lives the people of the toad, inhabiting a broad and fruitful region. The third people, which is designated by the eagle, are the Romans, whose pride strives to subject the whole world to its dominion. Therefore go with your people toward the west. They will dwell between those two peoples, of the lion and of the toad, between the sea and the Rhine. For it will come to pass that many battles will be waged between your people and the people of the toad, and very many on both sides will fall slain by the sword.”

On the following day, when the nobles had again been summoned to him, he commended the plan and by public edict warned them that their settlements must altogether be transferred. And so an embassy was sent to the Saxons in Germany, who themselves are recorded as descended from the Trojans, and they asked them as brothers to allow the Scythians places to remain in some corner of their land. The Saxons readily gave consent to their petition, promising that they would give them excellent settlements, and nevertheless adding that they should hasten to come as quickly as possible. A cause pressed the Saxons on account of which they willingly agreed to the Scythians their brothers: namely, they very much desired to place them as a wall and bulwark between themselves and the Gauls.

*On the arrival of the Scythians into the borders of Germany, to the parts [unclear], with their king Marcomirus: they were first Trojans, then Scythians, afterward Sicambri, and in the last generation were called Franks.*

Therefore in the four hundred thirty-third year before the birth of Christ, which was the beginning of the seventh year of King Marcomirus, around the middle of the month Hecatombaeon, which the Romphaei, Saxons [unclear].

Saxons. [Bentius?] designates the Angles. Aliruna, that is, a wise-woman, [unclear]. A monstrous three-headed deity appeared. Words of the toad, that is [unclear], to the king. Galicia is designated as first to be overcome. Germany designates the lion to be conquered. Interpretation of the portent by Aliruna [unclear]. The varied change of the kingdom of the Franks. That the Franks would overcome the Romans. An embassy of the Franks is sent to the Saxons. The Saxons willingly admit the Trojan brothers. *Compendium, Book I.*

... which we call April, King Marcomir himself, with Sunno, Panthenor, and Priam, his brothers, the leaders left beyond the Danubian sea, circling for a long distance through the borders of Scythia and toward the north, and then turning their route toward the region of the Teutons, began his migration westward with the whole people of the kingdom, their wives, children, and all their goods, with great labor, difficult and long-lasting.

There were, apart from women and little children, 175,658 men most ready for war. The names of the princes who were with Marcomir and had descended from his lineage were: Duke Nicanor, uncle of King Marcomir; Sunno, Panthenor, Priam, brothers of Marcomir, the aforesaid king; Duke Helenus, Duke Antenor, Duke Menander, Duke Edrasius, Duke Gethenus, Duke Priamus, Duke Marenus, Duke Ermon, Duke Nicanor, Duke Pyndari, Duke Helam, Duke Marcomir, Duke Colam, Duke Masan, Duke Antenor, Duke Ancreasius, Duke Bengoth, Duke Calomer, Duke Rodanus, Duke Malda, Duke Kylan, Duke Solas, Duke Colo, Duke Bremus, Duke Sunno, Duke Melanus, Duke Nicamor, Duke Thaphon, Duke Salon, Duke Meodarus.

The number of the whole people, as Hunibald bears witness, men, women, and little children of both sexes together, was 489,360, not counting the servants attending them. But if anyone desires to know fully what great difficulties they had on the journey, what wars they waged with the peoples opposing them, and what great dangers they either fell into or escaped, let him read the writer mentioned in the book of histories of the people of the Franks. Just as its beginnings are remarkable, so they seem to me, saving the judgment of those who judge better, to be fabulous in many respects.

At length, after many labors and countless difficulties, King Marcomir came into Germany with his leaders and the whole people. They were kindly received by the Saxons as brothers, and among them received the desired settlements by the Rhine, namely that province in which those now dwelling there are called the West Frisians, and also the Gelderlanders and Hollanders: that is, around that region where the Rhine flows into the sea by three mouths, although at first they received rather narrow settlements, which in a short time they made wider westward by force of arms.

Indeed, in the twentieth year of his reign, King Marcomir, provoked by an injury from the Transrhenane Gauls, gathered an army and, after crossing the river, subjected to his rule that land which, enclosed by islands of the Rhine, is nearest to the sea, expelling its inhabitants; and he entrusted it to his brother Sunno to guard. He brought in by ship people of his own nation to inhabit and cultivate it.

But when the Gauls took ill the incursion of the new foreign people into the borders of the Hollanders, and were provoking it with various attempts, King Marcomir, in the twenty-fourth year of his reign, having gathered a great army both of his own people and of the Saxons, crossed the Rhine by ship, entered western Gaul, devastating everything with sword and fire, and reached as far as the Meuse. Thereafter he fought many battles with the Gauls, triumphing everywhere as victor, and his name was terrible to the conquered Gallic peoples; all who heard of Marcomir feared him. He made a treaty with the Britons dwelling on the island.

From that time, for almost nine hundred years, the kings of the aforesaid people of the Scythians never ceased from harrying the Romans and the Gauls, sometimes defeated, yet more often victors, until at last they compelled by arms into their power not only all Gaul, but also all Alemannia, Swabia, Bavaria, Burgundy, Italy, Sclavonia, Thuringia, Austria, Saxony, the Teutons, Cimbri, Danes, Cisrhenanes, Mosellans, Treveri, Metz people, Austrasians, Liege people, Morini, Tournai people, people of the Meuse, Atrebates, Cologne people, Mainz people, Vangiones, Nemetes, Strasbourg people, Helvetii, Rauraci, Bohemians, and Sorbs, together with the Spaniards, all the Germans, and almost all Europe.

After this King Marcomir died, when the twenty-eighth year of his reign had been completed, namely in the year 412 before the birth of Christ, in the twenty-first year from the entry of the people into the borders of Saxony at the Rhine. He left three sons, dukes, Antenor, Priam, and Nicanor, and twelve daughters.

Down to this year Wasthald the Scythian, or Sicamber in his native speech, carried down, as it were, the historical work of the people, through more or less 758 years, beginning from the fall of Troy. In it he describes the various dwellings of his race, their settlements, and also their leaders, wars, kings, and the different deeds of the Pori in order. After him Hunnibald the Frank, from the written songs of the flamens, continued the history of the people of the Franks for 1,426 years, down to the last year of King Clovis, who, first of the kings, received Christ, baptized by Saint Remigius, in the year of the Lord 498. *Second—* *The Second of the Annals of Trithemius.*

Antenor, the elder son of King Marcomir, raised to the kingship in the same year, reigned after his father for thirty years. He was held in the highest honor among his people; he secured for himself the very firm friendship of the Saxons, with whose help, as victor, he engaged in many battles with the Romans and the Gauls. His brothers Priamus and Nicanor assisted him, together with the rest of the dukes, with steadfast loyalty; after crossing the river, they often inflicted many troubles upon the Gauls. Sunno too, the king's uncle, with his sons, always adhered to Antenor himself with the utmost fidelity in all things, and instructed him in government as his own son, while nevertheless venerating him as lord.

King Antenor had a wife named Cambra, who was the daughter of Belinus, king of Britain. She was a woman of surpassing beauty above all the daughters of the whole kingdom, and of such great prudence that the king was always accustomed to obey her counsel in all matters, no otherwise than that of some deity, before the princes of the Franks. The manners of the people, still excessively rude with Scythian savagery, she rendered more cultivated by laws; she taught the nobles to build cities and castles. There she introduced adornment of the forehead, gave women likewise the practice of sowing flax, committing hemp to the earth, and weaving and preparing it for clothing and various uses. She composed laws, pronounced judgment, and presented herself as a prophetess and priestess of Diana, an Aliruna.

And since, though a woman in sex, she bore in mind the character of a king and priest, it came among the Saxons from laughter into a proverb that, whenever they heard someone exulting or speaking with more than customary prudence, as if wishing to imitate the prudence of Cambra, they would say reproachfully: "Behold Cambra." This in their language is said thus: "Si Camber," as though they were saying, "Do you understand the prudence of Cambra?" Thus in time the proverb became established, because the last two words, that is, the adverb and the name, "Si Camber," made one word, which as a whole makes "Sicambrus."

After the queen had died years later, the Sicambrians, by a decree of the kings and nobles, counted her among the goddesses in her memory. They had formerly been called by their Saxon friends Novimagi, that is, Neumagi, as it were "new kinsmen"; thereafter they were called Sicambrians for almost four hundred years, until at last, from a certain king of theirs named Franco, as we shall say, they were called Franks, down to the present day, although with an admixture of peoples.

Meanwhile, however, because they were with their Trojans, they were also called Trojans; with Armenians, Armenians; with Scythians, Scythians; with Germans, Germans; with Gauls, Gauls. Frequently acquiring one name after another from others, they often changed their customs, language, idiom of speech, and name along with their settlements.

In the twelfth year of Antenor, his uncle Sunno died, leaving two sons, Marcomir and Hector. The first of these afterwards, while riding on horseback over the ice, was drowned in the Rhine; the younger governed his father's duchy in Holland under the king's authority. He left four other sons, begotten by four other concubines, who are not counted among the dukes, since the law of the Sicambrians forbade it; this law prohibited, while children by the first wife survived, the sons of subsequent women from being or being called princes. Queen Cambra enacted that law so that the kingdom would not be thrown into confusion.

Priamus, brother of King Antenor, held the duchy among the Gruni, namely in that region bounded by the sea which is now called Frisia. In it the duke, Priamus's son, founded a new town in the year 307 before the birth of Christ, which from his own name is called Groningen down to the present day. For the duke's name was Grunus, from whom the peoples also, although Franks by origin, were for a time called Gruni.

Antenor, after many deeds bravely performed, died in the thirtieth year of his reign, and in the 382nd year before the Lord's nativity. The Sicambrians, escorting him with great pomp according to pagan custom, counted him among the gods by order of the queen.

*The Third.*

Priamus, the only son of King Antenor by Queen Cambra, reigned after his father over the Sicambrians, who were later called Franks, for twenty-six years. In his time the Sicambrian people gradually began to forget their ancestral speech and to use the language of the Saxons, on whose borders they dwelt. Nevertheless, from the use of the old speech many words remained among them, which seem rather to echo a Greek origin than the property of the Teutonic or German language; anyone who has full knowledge of both languages will easily discern this. Nor was the change of the ancient speech among the people sudden: what began with time at length, through usage, passed into nature.

In the sixth year of King Priamus, Duke Marcomir died. He was the grandson of the first Sunno, of whom it was said above that, with the other dukes, he led the people into Germany.

*6. COMPENDIUM, BOOK I.*
[Margin: Theocalus, pontiff and historiographer of the Sicambri. The sacred rites were performed in the Greek tongue.]

Among his many children he had one son, by name Theocalus, a man most outstanding in all the wisdom of the Greeks, the Scythians, and the Germans, whom the Sicambri [made their] great pontiff.

In the eighth year, therefore, of Priam, king of the Franks—Cambra his mother and queen, and Theocalus the pontiff, commanding [it]—the Sicambri built two cities between the mouths of the Rhine, of which the one they called Neopagus, the other Neomagus, in memory of their acquired name. In these two cities, and especially in Neopagus, was the residence of the king of the Franks for a long time.

They also established in the same city of Neomagus a great and most strong temple to Jupiter, in which Theocalus the pontiff, dwelling with the priests, instructed the sons of princes and nobles in morals and knowledge, spoke prophecies to the people, and wrote in songs the brave deeds of the kings—which the youth, compelled to learn by heart, were wont to sing in the temple on feast days. Yet at certain seasons of the year the priests dwelt not in the cities but in the wilderness, whose food too was sparing, and [whose] exercise of talent [was] the continual learning of the course of the stars, and songs, and the histories of the ancients.

But king Priam, after many incursions had with the Gauls, after battles and victories, at last dies, in the twenty-sixth year of his reign, 356 years before the nativity of Christ from the Virgin Mary, leaving several sons and daughters from four wives, whom he had had at once and together.

HELENUS, the elder-born son of king Priam, succeeding [his] father, reigned among the Sicambri nineteen years, a man severe against [his] enemies—whose infants, as often as he could capture [them], he immolated to Pallas and other demons. But to his own people he was not cruel, but mild, and very humane, grievous or troublesome to no one, and therefore pleasing to all.

In the first year of his reign he had a war with the Transmosan Gauls and the Tungri, in which he laid low more than sixteen thousand of the enemy, and turned the rest to flight. He slew also, with his own hand, the first-born of the king of the Morini, by name Guedo, and subjected to his dominion a great part of the land beyond the Meuse, which he commended to his dukes to be guarded. Frequently thereafter he fought with the Gauls with varying fortune, now victor, now vanquished; of whose battles and deeds we have written more in the first volume of the annals.

At last, after many [things] bravely done with the Gauls and other enemies round about, Helenus, king of the Sicambri, dies, in the nineteenth year of his reign, 337 years before the nativity of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ.

DIOCLES, the elder son of king Helenus, after [his] father reigned twenty-nine years, a man tall of stature in body, harsh in morals, and, by excessive gravity, severe, bold, brave, and most warlike, who waged many battles.

In the twelfth year of his reign, a multitude of the Gothic people went out from the Scanzian islands, which are now called Gothic, and, poured into the borders of the Saxons, began to exercise a most grievous devastation, consuming with iron and fire whatever it could find. Against this most savage people, which was wont to spare no one, five kings advanced to war—namely, the king of the Thuringians, the king of the Teutons, the king of the Rugii, and Diocles himself of the Sicambri, with princes, dukes, and many warriors, whose army was numbered at two hundred and sixty thousand men.

The war is waged; a fierce battle is joined with the enemy, in which there fell of the Gothic army more than one hundred thousand warriors. But on the part of the five kings, twenty-five thousand fell, among whom Heriman also, king of the Thuringians, perished. But the Saxons, having gained the victory, divided the spoils of the enemy among [their] allies with an equal balance, and, the enemy having been put to flight afar, the kings returned to their own [lands].

Meanwhile, when the Gauls dwelling beyond the Meuse had understood that king Diocles had stripped [his] country of the army, [Blank page in the source scan.]

led against the enemy, they divided into three parts: two of these they arranged each as a battle-line, but the third they placed in hiding-places for ambush. As the Gauls approached and brought forward one battle-line, when they saw the Sicambri coming against them with two, they were thrown into confusion; but there was no time to order their forces otherwise, since their adversaries were hastening to close battle.

For as soon as the Gauls came within sight of the Sicambri, the Sicambri, impatient of delay, directed one battle-line against the enemy wedge. When the battle had already begun, wheeling the second line around at Neomagus against the enemy from the flank, they threw their order into confusion. And when the fighting was fierce on both sides, and the army of the Gauls was already inclining toward flight, suddenly the Sicambri burst forth from ambush and, making an attack, held the Gauls enclosed among themselves, so that no place for flight lay open to those ready to flee. Thus the wretched Gauls, enclosed in the midst of the Sicambri, were butchered to death like cattle, and they suffered so great a slaughter that, out of eighty-eight thousand of them who had assembled for the war, scarcely ten thousand escaped, saved by the benefit of night, in flight. Of the Sicambri, Duke Marcomir, Duke Helenus, and Duke Antenor fell, with about four thousand men. Nevertheless the victory, with the spoils of the enemy, fell to the Sicambri.

Diocles the king, throughout all the days of his reign, stood bravely in contest with the Gauls, and scarcely in the meantime was there a year in which he did not trouble them by some incursion or battle. At last he died in the thirty-ninth year of his reign, 298 before the birth of the Lord. By the queen he had four sons, Henus, Priamus, Nicanor, and Basanus; by other wives he had several sons.

*The Sixth.*

Helenus, the eldest son of the aforementioned king Diocles, succeeding his father, reigned fourteen years: a sluggish, wanton man, and memorable for no activity of virtue. In his time the Gauls, making incursions several times, stirred up no few disturbances for the Sicambri. Against them his brothers, with the nobles of the kingdom, often led out the army, and, fighting with varying fortune, were sometimes defeated, sometimes victorious. But the king sat at home, idle among the gatherings of concubines, dissolving in lust, useful neither to the kingdom nor pleasing to the people, stupid for peace and unfit for war.

Therefore, before the fourteenth year of his reign had yet been completed, the nobles of the kingdom, gathering at Neopagus, together with the whole soldiery of the army, by the common decree of all deposed him from the kingdom as useless and harmful to the people, in the year 284 before the birth of the Lord.

*The Seventh.*

Basanus, the younger son of the above-mentioned king Diocles, after the deposition of his brother Helenus from the kingdom, was raised to the kingdom of the Sicambri by the common election of the dukes, nobles, and soldiers, and reigned thirty-six years: a man in his generation most prudent, brave, bold, and exceedingly warlike.

When Theocalus died, the Sicambri appointed him chief priest of Jove; because of the greatness of his prudence and the magnificent deeds accomplished by him, they called him Basanus the Great. The Sicambri held him in such reverence that they paid him honors not only royal but almost divine. No one was ever allowed to contradict his commands with impunity, whether in a small matter or in a great one, under the undoubted penalty of bitter death. For he was most eager for the estimation of divinity; on that account he both did and said great things. Hence, wherever he went, he ordered a rope and a sword to be carried before him, as a manifest sign of justice; and he was accustomed to preserve it so tenaciously that he would spare neither his own son nor any of the princes who, knowingly, had offended even a little against the law of equity which he had established.

He had a son named Sedanus. Accused of adultery, he was soon judged by his father to death, according to the law which he had established for the Sicambri. When the nobles pleaded for the youth, the father answered: “Do not, O noble men, fight against justice and the laws which I decreed with you as mature witnesses; for it is easier to bind by hand the wind blowing in the air than to turn the mind of King Basanus away from the execution of equity.” When this had been heard, the princes fell silent; but the father himself said to his son: “I do not kill you, son, but the law of the fatherland, which you knowingly transgressed”; and, seizing him, he cut off his head with his own hand.

At that time the Sicambri began to fear their king Basanus to such a degree that no one among them, great or small, presumed to say or do anything evil against the law. Hence the priests of the gods, by a Greek word [unclear], that is, called the king Just Basanus. But the common people called him Theobasanus, which in the German tongue is Basangoth [unclear].

signifies, because all revered him as a friend of the gods who was afterward to be deified.

From this a proverb arose among the Sicambri: whenever one man saw or heard from another anything contrary to the law, he would say, “Hort opp lieffman, kent gyn nit dy grote kunig Basan.” As if he had said, “Cease, good men, from such things; do you not know how just the great King Basanus is? If he perceived you saying or doing such things, he would without doubt kill you as transgressors.”

In the fifth year of King Basanus, the king of the Orchades, having many island petty kings as auxiliaries, declared war on the Sicambri because of the rejection of his daughter, whom King Basanus, having had her as wife, had repudiated and sent back to her father. The reason for her repudiation we described in the first volume of the annals. But King Basanus, having learned of the approach of his adversaries, advanced against them with a great multitude of fighters to the seashore, not far from the place where the Franks later built Mesoburg. Seeing from their ships so great an army of the Sicambri, the Orchades did not dare to advance onto land.

When the Gauls and Morini again broke eastward, where the Sicambri had placed settlements in the region of the Tungri, King Basanus met them with the strong hand of his men and laid them low with such slaughter that scarcely a few escaped out of many. Having won the victory, he built many castles and very strong fortifications on both sides of the river Meuse, in which he stationed garrisons of the Sicambri.

In the upper part of the river, moreover, he built a very strong castle, which from his own name he called Basanburg; in it the kings of the Sicambri and Franks after him resided for a long time, because of the pleasantness and strength of the place.

In the twenty-sixth year of his reign, King Basanus, after many battles bravely fought with various nations round about, wishing to present himself as pontiff of the gods, renewed their rites with much superstition. He appointed many priests most skilled in the worship of the divine powers, attentive to the course of the stars, trained after the manner of the ancients in prophecies, in foreknowledge, in the interpretation of dreams, in ethical and physical doctrines, and also very well practiced in composing and singing, in both languages, the songs and histories of the ancient kings and heroes only of their own people. Among these Heligastus, once the son of the pontiff Theocalus, surpassed the others in talent and practice of writing; he was in charge of educating the sons of the dukes and nobles, and described the deeds of heroes in verse.

Concerning this man Hunibaldus, historian of the Franks, writes many marvelous things; unless they are granted to have been done by the artifice of some demons, they should be thought rather to have been fabricated by some writer than performed by a man devoted to idols. He foretold to the Sicambri many future things; he presented Jupiter visibly to the priests; he brought men’s secret counsels into public view; and he disclosed to King Basanus the hidden plans of the enemy in difficult causes and affairs. It seemed that nothing escaped him of all the things that the enemies, even in most secret counsel, had discussed against the Sicambri. This matter inspired confidence in friends, but despair in enemies.

For King Basan, with all the princes of the kingdom, depended wholly on the counsel of Heligastus; what he ordered, all did; whatever he forbade, no one dared attempt. At his command the Sicambri met the enemy; and if he commanded the contrary, they remained peacefully at home. As often as he foretold victory to the Sicambri, they conquered; as often as he foretold otherwise, they were conquered. While he lived, the Sicambri prospered in all things; whenever their name was heard, it terrified enemies and made them dreadful to all throughout [unclear].

After he had spent thirty-two years in his office, on a certain solemn day of Jove, standing in the midst of the priests, hurling thunderbolts in the temple and troubling the air with his voice, resounding with frenzies in the manner of soothsayers, he suddenly disappeared, and, vanishing completely, no one was ever found who could know where he had gone. The Sicambri, thinking that he had become a god, proclaimed that he had been taken up into marriage with Diana, and they decreed sacred rites for him each year.

In the thirty-third year of his reign, Basanus moved a mighty army to the upper parts of the river Rhine, to the region called Tegaraña, which lay toward the south between the Saxons and the Cisrhenane Mainz people, under the protection of the Treviri, having its own petty king named Thaborinus. King Basanus killed him along with many others and subjugated his whole region to his own dominion. These things were done in the year 251 before the birth of Christ. The place in which the aforesaid King Thaborinus of the Tegaranes fell was called Mount Thabor from his name; it is about four miles distant from Confluentes. There Basanus, king of the Franks, founded a very strong castle, which, as a perpetual memorial of the victory, he named Mount Thaborinus; but, the word having been corrupted, it is today called Monthahur by the inhabitants.

In the year [Blank page in the source scan.]

*Annals of Trithemius*

In the thirty-sixth year of his reign, Basanus, king of the Sicambri, at the solemnity of his birthday at Nijmegen, summoned his sons, brothers, dukes, nobles, and distinguished members of his household to a very great banquet. With them, feasting lavishly for seven days, he performed sacrifices to the gods of his country, and showed Jupiter visible in the air above the temple [unclear]. On the eighth day, with the consent of all the nobles, he designated his son Clodomirus king over the Sicambri; in his native song he foretold many future things to the people, commended his sons and the kingdom to the princes, enjoined justice, and, entering the chapel of the temple, appeared nowhere again.

I do not know what I should assign to these little tales, indignation or laughter. Whether he was removed by deceit or by art remains uncertain; but this one thing I judge to have been the cause: the desire of a man, undoubtedly withdrawn either by his own ingenuity or by the voluntary will of a demon, to attain the reputation of divinity. For, as Amerodacus, philosopher of the Sicambri, writes, King Basan was most eager for divinity; he cultivated justice, loved his people, overthrew the enemy, was most dutiful to the good, and always cruel and severe to the unjust.

He vanished, however, or, to speak more correctly, withdrew himself, as Amerodacus is the authority, from the public assembly of the nobles, as we have said, in the thirty-sixth year of his reign; but before the birth of the Lord, in the year 248. The Sicambri, judging that he had been translated into the company of the gods, worshipped him under the name Basangot.

*The Eighth*

Clodomirus, the elder son of Basanus, succeeding in the kingdom, as his father had ordained with the consent of the princes, reigned eighteen years. In his first year, as soon as the Gauls learned that Basanus had vanished, whom they did not doubt to be dead, they sent messengers to Clodomirus and demanded back from him all the land between the Meuse and the Rhine, and around the [unclear] in circuit, which the Sicambri, from their first entry into the Cisthenan borders, had violently usurped for themselves contrary to justice. If he disdained to return it, they threatened that they would be ready to recover it by the sword, whether he sent back a negative answer through the appointed messengers or made no answer at all.

King Clodomirus, however, prudently and deliberately detained the messengers of the Gauls with him for a long time, as though he were going to take counsel with his princes concerning the urgent matter; and, taking the greatest care that the secret of his counsel and mind should not come to their knowledge, he ordered his servants to feed them abundantly and arrange that they should have cheerful days.

Meanwhile King Clodomirus sent messengers to the kings of the Saxons and Thuringians, urgently asking that they very secretly and quickly send forces to aid the Sicambri, their friends, against the Gauls, their common adversaries. The Saxons came with the Thuringians to assist their friends, as they were asked, bringing forward an army of one hundred thousand fighters. When matters had been arranged most secretly at his command, King Clodomirus allowed the messengers of the Gauls, furnished with gifts, to depart; and, lest anything of the foregoing could come to their knowledge on the road, he assigned escorts for a safe journey to those setting out, who would accompany them and observe them more carefully, with letters of this sort:

“Clodomirus, great king, to the Gallican satraps. We marvel at your rashness, that you demand back from us the land which our forefathers long ago, by right of war, most justly vindicated by the sword from yours, as from wrongful [unclear], their manifest enemies. Consider that our strength is far superior to yours. Cease from this rashness of unjust folly. Remember the defeats which you long ago deservedly received from our begetter, translated among the gods, and from his parents. Rest in your caves, hiding with foxes. It is ours to command you; yours, however, humbly to obey our precepts. But if you presume to come against us, we have decreed to meet you powerfully and to defend by the sword what our ancestors handed down to us.”

When the Gauls received these letters from the messengers, they were stirred to anger and resolved to avenge themselves upon the Sicambri as quickly as possible. Having skillfully built a bridge over the Meuse, they led across a huge army of fighters. King Clodomirus met them most powerfully with two hundred sixty-four thousand men; and, having divided the army into parts, he stationed one part in ambush; another he sent from the region at a distance so that, after killing the guards of the Gauls, it might seize the bridge first; the third part, which was greater in number of soldiers, he led against the adversaries.

The Sicambri and the Gauls engage in a place not far from the river Meuse, which is called Delon; for some time they are driven back in an uncertain battle. At last the Sicambri, pretending flight, began to withdraw little by little, until at length they drew the Gauls farther from the river Meuse to the place of ambush. There the Sicambri then stood immovable, and those who had previously feigned flight fought back most bravely like giants. Meanwhile the soldiers, circling around, came to [unclear].
