...the crossing of the river, and, after the enemy guards had been killed or driven far away, they seized the bridge in advance. The rest at once burst out from the ambushes and, attacking the enemy bravely, cut them down from the rear, slaughter them, and kill them without pity. At last those who could, seeking safety in flight, since they did not know that the bridge had been occupied in advance by the Sicambri, were shut in on every side and were cut down by the enemy; nor was there any place to escape the death pressing upon them before their eyes. A few, with night coming on, escaped safe out of many, those who were able to flee into the dark groves and forests.

Thereafter the kingdom of the Sicambri rested from the turmoil of wars for a few years; but afterwards, when peace was broken, the people more often took up arms on a great scale. The other deeds and wars of King Clodomirus, which he had with foreign nations, following Hunibald we have written down in the first volume of our annals.

King Clodomirus died in the eighteenth year of his reign, 230 years before the birth of the Lord, leaving three sons by Queen Ermendrude, who had been the daughter of the king of the Teutons: Nicanor, Helianus, and Helenus.

*Ninth.*

Nicanor, the elder son of King Clodomirus, succeeding his father, reigned for thirty-four years. He was a stern man, just in his generation, warlike, and most impatient of any injuries from enemies, especially from the Gauls; for this reason, with varying fortune, he very often fought against them very fiercely.

For from that time when this people, sprung from the stock of the Trojans, first came from the borders of the Scythians into Germany, to the mouths of the Rhine, it never ceased from the harassment of the Gauls, until at last, not without much bloodshed among its own people, it powerfully brought all Gaul under its yoke. No one was ever able fully to overcome the Franks or Sicambri; no one imposed the bridle of subjection upon these most fierce men, but they did not lay aside the desire of ruling, which they had once drunk in, before they had brought all Gaul, and Italy as well, into their power, after the Roman empire had been annihilated and many kings destroyed.

For, as was said above, it is clear from the calculation of the times that, from the beginning of the Franks’ entry, as they are now called, into the lands of Germany on this side [of the Rhine], down to Clovis the great king, who, first as victor over the Alemanni, believed in Christ, 930 years elapsed. During these years the Sicambri fought with the Gauls, never ceasing to make war upon them, although more often defeated in part, until finally they overcame them all.

It should be known, however, that they were not always called either Franks or Sicambri, but frequently changed their names along with their settlements. For indeed, as Hunibald bears witness, when after the destruction of Troy they wandered among various nations for many years and did not long have fixed settlements in one place, among the Scythians they were called Scythians; among the Armenians, they were called Armenians. When they dwelt at the mouths of the Danube, they were called neither Franks nor Sicambri; but because they were neighbors to the Scythians, they received the name of the Scythians’ languages. Afterwards, driven out through the Goths by the envy of the Romans, as Amerodacus is the authority, they descended into the territories of Germany, and, settled in their seats, as has often been said, at the mouths of the Rhine, they learned the speech of the German Saxons. At first they were called Neomagi, afterwards also Germans; then, named Sicambri from Cambra, they changed even that name with time, stirred by love of King Francus, from whom the name of the Franks, as will be said later in its proper order, took its beginning. Hence it has happened that the writers of other peoples, whenever in the descriptions of their histories they introduce mention of the deeds of this people, often call them Germans rather than Sicambri, or Franks. This has usually brought no small harm of error to those who do not know the true origin of the Franks, while they believe that the Franks were either natives or began from a conspiracy of a few men.

King Nicanor, joined with the Saxons and Thuringians, in the fourteenth year of his reign advanced to war with a great multitude against the Goths, who were again breaking into the lands of the Teutons and Saxons. In the first encounter they were superior to the Goths and crushed the Germans with great slaughter. But soon, when the army had been restored, they were defeated by the Goths; many thousands of them perished, both by the edge of the sword and submerged in the waters; the rest sought safety in flight.

In the twenty-first year of his reign he waged a naval war against King Orhadus, in favor of the king of Britain, whose sister, named Constantia, he had as wife. But he did not wage the war successfully enough, because many of his men, on account of their inexperience in naval combat, in [unclear] perished at sea. He was also always in conflict with the Gauls, and fought many battles with them, and, very often fighting most bravely with his men, he triumphed gloriously.

At length he died in the thirty-fourth year of his reign, in the one hundred ninety-sixth year before the birth of Christ, leaving five sons: Marcomirus, who succeeded to the kingdom; Antenor, who ruled the maritime region; Priamus, who died at his uncle’s in Britain; Helenus, who held the Cisthenan duchy, between Saxony and the Rhine, over the Tegarani; Clodius, duke of the Mosani.

*Tenth.*

Marcomirus, son of King Nicanor, the elder by birth, succeeding his father, reigned twenty-eight years, a prince singular in modesty and prudence in his generation: pious, mild, and beneficent toward his subjects, but severe toward enemies at all times. Instructed from youth by the priests of the gods sufficiently in all the wisdom of this world, he became a most learned astrologer, augur, seer, interpreter of dreams and events. As often as he could, in leisure, he ordered the brave deeds of his ancestors to be sung before him, both in the palace and in the temples, so that by their example his spirit might be stirred to the defense of his people and always to the increase of the kingdom. This was the custom among our ancestors, the Franks and Germans: that the deeds or sayings of heroes worthy of remembrance should be entrusted by the priests of the temples to songs in the fatherland’s tongue, in the learning, remembering, and singing of which the talents of the young were exercised. This custom lasted for many years, until at last it failed.

But King Marcomirus, in the twenty-eighth year of his reign, which was the one hundred sixty-eighth year before the incarnation of our savior Jesus Christ,

*Eleventh.*

Clodius, first-born of Marcomirus king of the Sicambri, reigned after his father for eleven years. In his time the sword of the Romans, directed into Gaul, brought no small harm upon the Sicambri. For in these times the Romans increased the strength of the Gauls, who, making an incursion beyond the Meuse, very grievously and often afflicted the foreign people. The Sicambri, fierce in spirit, meeting them, repelled force with force.

After many battles joined with the Gauls, King Clodius, in the last year of his reign, having gathered a huge army both of his own men and of Saxons, again fought with the same not far from the fortress of Basanburg. In this battle, while he was reconnoitering too incautiously, he was slain in the line by the adversary. But the Sicambri, encouraged by the exhortation of their leaders, notwithstanding the death of the king, continued the war, and fighting bravely at length defeated the Gauls; after killing many of them, they put the others to flight. King Clodius died, slain in the war of the Gauls, as has been said, in the eleventh year of his reign, and in the one hundred fifty-seventh year before the birth of Christ.

*Twelfth.*

Antenor, son of King Clodius, the elder by birth, reigned after his father for sixteen years. He made truces, which our people call *Treugae* from the pledge of faith interposed, with the Gauls for ten years. This one thing was also [pleasing?] to the Romans: because, being more humane than the rest, he forbade human beings to be sacrificed to the gods. This displeased many nobles of the Sicambri, who thought that the fear of them among foreign nations was diminished. But because this pious measure had been decreed with the counsel of the priests, the constitution itself remained inviolable. For priestly authority among them was always greater and more excellent than that of all leaders and princes. King Antenor died in the sixteenth year of his reign, and in the one hundred forty-first year before the birth of the Lord.

*Thirteenth.*

Clodomirus, son of Antenor, reigned after his father for twenty years. In his first year the Romans, overthrowing the Numantines through Scipio, reduced them into their power. In his sixth year, the truces which they had made with his father now ended, the Gauls, having gathered a great army of their men, resolved to move against the Sicambri; and, crossing the river Meuse, first [unclear]

*The ancient [unclear] always pursued the Gauls in war. Marcomirus reigned twenty-eight years. A praiseworthy custom in a prince; [unclear] instructed in memorable matters. Marcomirus brought down the kingdom of the Sicambri. Clodius reigned eleven years. Clotharius reigned sixteen years. Truces were made between the Sicambri and the Gauls. Antenor reigned ten years. Truces were made between the Sicambri and the Gauls. The priests of the Sicambri had great power. Clodomirus reigned twenty-eight years. The ancient [unclear] always pursued the Gauls in war.* *12. Compendium, Book I.*

*The war of the Sicambri with the Gauls; the Gauls are overcome by the Sicambri.*

They declare [war] upon their enemies. Clodomir, supported by the aid of the Germans, confidently met the Gauls without delay. A very fierce battle was fought for people and kingdom; many fell on both sides. At last the Gauls turned their backs, and the Sicambri pursued them as far as the river, and laid low the greater part of the army by the edge of the sword. If they had either destroyed the bridge or seized it beforehand, as Clodomir the king, son of great Basanus, had once done, not even one of the Gauls could have escaped. After the Gauls had suffered this disaster, as long as Clodomir survived they no longer crossed the Meuse with an army, though they often committed raids in their usual fashion. King Clodomir, after many battles fought with the Romans, the Gauls, and the peoples farther up around the Rhine and the Moselle, died in the twentieth year of his reign, which was the one hundred twenty-first year before the birth of Christ.

*The Fourteenth.*

Merodacus, son of Clodomir, succeeding his father, reigned twenty-eight years. He was a high-minded, vigorous, and very bold prince; how warlike he was the Romans and the Gauls could perceive, for he often fought bravely with them, even with his own hand. For with the Saxons, Doringi, and Germans bringing auxiliaries, he led into Italy against the Romans an army of two hundred and twenty thousand fighting men; and, devastating everything round about, he came with his forces as far as Ravenna, and returned victorious, enriched with many spoils. On his return he also severely afflicted many colonies of the Romans, subjected them to very grave hardships, and made his name formidable to all.

Greatly stirred by these events, the Romans, having joined many nations to themselves, declared war on the Sicambri; the necessary preparations having been made, they assembled for battle. And lest the Saxons or Doringi bring aid to the Sicambri, the Romans had first induced the Goths and Slavs, by promised gifts, that at one and the same time these should attack the Saxons and they themselves the Sicambri. King Merodacus, therefore, being necessarily abandoned by the Saxons and Doringi, called upon the king of the northern island, whom today we call Danes; he came with one hundred thousand men as auxiliaries and increased the number of the Sicambri.

And so, in the twenty-second year of his reign, he learned that a great army of the Romans was coming against him. For Marius, prince of the Romans, sent the Roman legions with the Gauls, under Duke Theodomenus, beyond the Meuse. They boldly engaged the Sicambri, whom they themselves called Germans, and fought fiercely together; many thousands of men fell on both sides, and the Sicambri fled, having lost more than twenty thousand fighting men. After this, Merodacus, his army restored, became more powerful than the Gauls and Romans and afflicted them with much slaughter, as, following Hunibald, we have said more fully in the first volume of our histories or annals. But afterwards, when he had fought many battles with the Gauls and Romans and had enlarged the borders of his people by no small amount, King Merodacus died in the twenty-eighth year of his reign, but in the ninety-third year before the birth of Christ.

*The Fifteenth.*

Cassander, the elder son of King Merodacus, succeeding his father, reigned twenty-one years. He was a very warlike man, in whose time the Gauls, with the aid of the Romans, more often crossed the river Meuse and invaded the borders of the Sicambri. Cassander, the aforesaid king of the Sicambri, gathered the armies into one and advanced to battle against them; when the clash had taken place, the fighting was fierce for a long time, and many fell on both sides. For all the days in which he ruled the Sicambri he was in conflict with the Gauls and Romans.

In these times Borbista, king of the Goths, with an innumerable multitude of fighting men, entered the borders of Saxony, devastating the region with fire and sword. Against him three very powerful kings, namely Arthari king of the Saxons, Hamer king of the Doringi, and Cassander, the aforesaid king of the Sicambri, gathered their armies into one and advanced to battle. When the clash had taken place, the fighting was fierce for a long time, and many fell on both sides. At last King Borbista turned his back, and the Germans obtained the victory. On another occasion after this, King Borbista again entered Saxony with a very great multitude of Goths, and cruelly devastated the region with fire and sword as far as the river Vistula; and, having seized many spoils of the Germans, he withdrew, nor did he presume to advance farther that day. For he knew the forces of the Germans to be unconquerable, although at the Romans’ urging he had often tested them. King Cassander, after many battles bravely waged with the Gauls and Romans, died in the ye*The Sixteenth.*

[unclear] in the twenty-first year of his reign, but in the seventy-second year before the birth of the Lord; he was buried at Neopagus with many treasures.

Antharius, son of King Cassander, reigned after his father for thirty-five years. Hunibald writes of him that he crushed the people of Mainz, Roman colonists, in a wretched disaster, burned and overthrew the city, which afterward is seen transferred and built in that place where now [unclear] and the valley are, on the slope of the mountain by the bank of the Rhine. This pitiable devastation of the Mainzers took place in the sixteenth year of King Antharius, which was the fifty-sixth year before the birth of Christ, as is shown from the sequence of times.

King Antharius entered Gaul with the help of the Germans, burned villages, very often carried off boundless plunder and spoils, caused great devastation throughout Gaul, burned cities, destroyed villages, overthrew castles, broke the strength of the people, and reduced a region long fruitful to solitude.

But when King Antharius had grown old, in the last year of his reign, which was the thirty-seventh before the birth of Christ, the Gauls again burst into the region of the Sicambri and crossed the Meuse. He met them with the army of his own men to fight; there, while he fought too incautiously, he was surrounded by the enemy and [unclear] with twenty thousand Sicambri. This Frankish king was accustomed to fight, not to flee; he was very gentle and beloved by his own people, but always exceedingly to be feared by all enemies.

*Francus, from whom they are called Franks, reigned 28 years.*

In the first year of his reign he contracted a perpetual treaty with the Germans, Saxons, and Thuringians, with the consent of all the dukes and nobles of the Sicambri, confirming the friendship on silver tablets, according to the ancient custom of the people: namely, establishing the terms of the agreements so that the Sicambri, Germans, Saxons, and Thuringians, under distinct kings and princes, should thereafter be regarded as one people, like full brothers, should remain so forever, and that any war which threatened the kingdom of one of these, from whatever people, should concern them all and be repelled with united arms and common expenses. This confederation of kingdoms terrified, more than can be said, the senate and people of Rome; in various ways, by different devices, and with manifold contrivance, they labored, though in vain, to dissolve the treaty contracted by the Germans. From that time the courage and power of the Franks were always suspect to the Romans, who feared, as later happened, that the Germans would gain possession of the monarchy of all Europe. And this was the reason why Octavian Caesar of the Romans afterward, under the birth of Christ, caused the whole world obedient to the Romans to be registered by heads, thinking that by the multitude of the nations the Franks were to be destroyed; at that time the writers of histories still called them peoples of Germany.

But in the third year of Francus’s reign, when the Romans saw that they could by no device dissolve the treaty of the German kings, they again sent the Goths into the borders of the Saxons. Settling for almost ten years in the borders of Germany, they gradually and successively planned to spread themselves into the interior of the aforesaid nation. Meanwhile King Francus often fought with the Gauls, avenged upon them with harsh retaliation the death of his father, and killed many thousands of them during that time. But when the Goths broke more and more each day into the interior of Germany, the Saxons with the Teutons, at last compelled by necessity, resolved to make war on them. Having summoned as allies, according to the agreements, the Sicambri and Thuringians, they led out to battle an army of two hundred and thirty thousand men. But the Scanzians, who are Goths, having themselves summoned allies, set against the approaching Germans an almost innumerable multitude. A most savage battle was joined between the parties in that place which was called Colmasus; with many falling on both sides, they fought from morning until night with doubtful fortune. On the next day the Germans divided the army into three parts and set individual commanders over each; but the Sicambri, fighting very boldly under their king Francus, more frequently shouted the name of their leader Francus as if it were some divine power, crying: “Here Frank! Here Frank!” At last the Goths were defeated, more than eighty thousand of them were slain, and the rest slipped away in flight with [unclear].

*Antharius reigned 35 years.*

*Mainz destroyed.*

*The Sicambri burned [unclear] Gaul.*

*The Seventeenth.*

Francus, the elder son of King Antharius, from whom the Sicambri were thereafter called Franks, as Hunibald is the authority, reigned after his father for twenty-eight years. He was a fierce, bold, warlike man, a most vigorous defender of his people, who avenged the death of his father harshly enough upon the Gauls, waged many wars with foreign nations, always a victorious and glorious triumphator; the people of the Franks not undeservedly boast that he was the first author of their name and honor. This king Francus was accustomed to fight, not to flee; he was very gentle and beloved by his own people, but always exceedingly to be feared by all enemies.

In the first year of his reign he contracted a perpetual treaty with the Saxons and Thuringians of Germany, with the consent of all the dukes and nobles of the Sicambri, confirming the friendship on silver tablets, according to the ancient custom of the people: namely, establishing the terms of the agreements so that the Sicambri, Germans, Saxons, and Thuringians, under distinct kings and princes, like full brothers, should thereafter be regarded as one people, should remain forever, and that the war which threatened the kingdom of one of these, from whatever people, should concern them all and be repelled with united arms and common expenses. This confederation of kingdoms terrified, more than can be said, the senate and people of Rome; in various ways, by different devices, and with manifold contrivance, they labored, though in vain, to dissolve the treaty contracted by the Germans. From that time the courage and power of the Franks were always [unclear] to the Romans, who feared, as [unclear].

*Compendium, Book I*

...and wives, returned to their former hiding-places; thus the Saxons, with the aid of the Franks and Thuringians, joyfully recovered their own territories, devastated and occupied by foreigners for ten years.

From that time the Sicambri, laying aside their ancient name, began, out of love for their king, to call themselves Franks. Indeed, as Hunibald bears witness, not only the nobles, but also all the soldiers, the whole people of the entire nation, were so delighted by the very novelty of the name that they induced the king by entreaties to decree by public edict that thereafter they were forever to be called not Sicambri but Franks. This the king established all the more gladly, the more eagerly he loved the immortality of his own name. Therefore they were called Franks, who previously by some were called Sicambri, and by others, by reason of their alliance, Germans. And it is indeed remarkable how they gloried in the novelty of this word, since for many times thereafter, whenever they met one another, they greeted one another thus: “A good day, free Frank.” Nevertheless, not suddenly, but at last after much time, this name came into unity, so that the people itself were called Franks even among other nations; for to the Romans and especially the Gauls the name of the Franks was hateful. Hence among their writers they were more often called Germans than either Sicambri or Franks. Hunibald did not pass over in silence whence, or from whom, the name of the Sicambri had its origin.

*Whence the Franks are called free, “Die fryer Francken”; by what names they were known.*

That the Franks were previously called Sicambri is attested not only by Hunibald, but also by the blessed archbishop Remigius, who, as Gregory, bishop of Tours, records, when he was to baptize Clodoveus, king of the Franks, the first of the kings of the Franks converted to Christ, as we shall say in its proper place, said before the assembly of nobles, while he was putting off his royal ornaments and humbling himself for the sacred washing, with all hearing: “Gently bow your neck, Sicamber; worship what you burned; burn what you worshipped.” Of the history of this matter I have already spoken more fully, after Hunibald, in the first volume of the Annals.

*The Franks were previously said to have been Sicambri.*

*The saying of St. Remigius to Clodoveus.*

*The Frankish name was always distasteful to the Romans and Gauls.*

And so in the twenty-fourth year before the birth of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, which was the fourteenth year of King Francus, the Sicambri changed their ancient name to a new one, although both before and afterward they were more often called Germans, or Sicambri, among writers. For although they themselves wrote and always retained the name Frank, taken up under the aforementioned king, nevertheless it could not immediately come into use among foreign nations, [unclear]

*King Francus, after the Goths had been overcome, returns.*

*He attacks the Gauls, joining battle.*

*Three hundred thousand Franks and Germans against the Gauls.*

...a people hostile to us, or to die fighting.

Gladdened by these words, the king at once sent messengers to the Saxons, the Germans, and also the Thuringians, asking aid by right of alliance against the assault of the Gauls. All these, with great eagerness, sent the requested supports of soldiers: the Saxons, namely, eighty-four thousand fighting men; the German Theutones, sixty thousand; and the Thuringians, forty-six thousand. Joined with these, the Franks with great forces very hastily brought out an army of three hundred thousand men against their adversaries. But King Francus, seeing the desolation of the region which the Gauls had made, moved with great indignation of spirit, said: “See, my bravest fellow-soldiers, you who rightly grieve for the shed blood of your fathers, what these most treacherous Gauls have done. I swear by the head of my little son Antharius, whom these most wicked men killed, that I shall give no rest to my head until I have avenged myself on them in a notable way.” And they all praised his swift resolve.

Therefore, after a bridge had been constructed with boats and many timbers, in two days he led the army across, leaving forty thousand men to guard the crossing; with the remaining multitude he advanced into Gaul, and he made such a slaughter as no one of the Sicambri before him was able to make, or is believed to have conceived in his mind. For, having advanced as far as the river Tabul, [and] the western sea...

*Francus, after constructing a bridge over the Meuse, devastates Gaul.* *Annals of Trithemius.*

[the southern] than the northern, the Tungri, the Tarubani, and the people of Liege, and whatever lies between or adjacent to these, he savagely laid waste with fire and sword.

When the Gauls joined battle with him, he overcame, routed, and destroyed them with such ease that he was thought to be not a man, but some divine power sent from heaven. Hence all the nations round about, excessively terrified, feared thereafter to engage the Franks, as though they were the fiercest monsters. In that encounter and devastation, more than two hundred thousand of the Gauls themselves fell by the sword of the Franks, together with children, infants, and women. For just as the Gauls had previously done when they devastated the Sicambri, sparing no parents, so they received from the same.

Then the Senate and People of Rome, moved with indignation, [unclear] an expedition of legions of soldiers against the Germans, under the command of Marcus Lollius. For they did not think it would be safe to engage the Franks, whom they themselves called Germans, before they had subdued the Saxons and the Doringi. The Romans therefore entered Saxony; at first they indeed conquered, killing eighteen thousand Germans.

The Sicambri, sparing none, so received from the same.

But Francus, hearing this, weighed down by labors and old age, sent a legion of soldiers against the Saxons into Germany, under the command of Marcus Lollius. For he did not think it would be safe if they engaged the Franks, whom he himself called Germans, before they had subdued the Saxons and the Doringi. The Romans therefore entered Saxony; at first they indeed conquered, killing eighteen thousand Germans.

*The Romans are overcome by the Franks in war.*

Then in the twenty-fourth year of King Francus. Finally King Francus, weighed down by labors and old age, after many battles most victoriously fought with the Romans, Goths, Gauls, and other nations, and after the kingdom of the Franks had been increased not a little and its territories enlarged, died in the twenty-eighth year of his reign, in the ninth year before the birth of the Lord. His wars, character, institutions, laws, and victories were written by Clodomirus, high priest of the Franks, in German verse, and by Hunibald in prose, in the Latin language; under their guidance we have treated them thus in the first volume of the annals of German and Frankish affairs which we wrote.

*Clogius the Eighth.*

Clogio, the eldest son of Francus the king, succeeding his father, reigned over the Franks for thirty years: a most cunning man, versatile in talent, an augur, a magician, and a most inquisitive astrologer. Concerning him the aforementioned high priest, counselor, and seer of the Franks, Clodomirus, arranged many astonishing and wonderful things in verse, of which we made mention in the first volume.

His mother, named Lothildis, daughter of the king of the Doringi, was the chief officiant, or priestess, of the temple of Pallas, devoted to magical arts, by the practice of which she did many marvelous things. For, as the authors already named wrote, by her songs and incantations she destroyed whichever enemies of her son she wished, made them unfortunate, and slew them through the ministry of demons, however far away they were; by sorcery she procured victory for the Franks and fear, terror, and flight for their enemies; rains, thunder, lightning, and horrible storms in the air were brought on by her spells whenever, wherever, and against whomever she wished. In the fourth year of his reign, the Romans again launched an expedition into Germany; the allied kings, meeting them energetically, did not cease bravely to drive back force with arms, until they compelled the enemies to retreat and flee. [unclear] the Franks, but called Germans, fought with Tiberius the Roman and most bravely for his people; finally, after many had fallen on both sides, the Romans departed without victory.

In the tenth year of the reign of the aforementioned Clogio, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of January, the Lord, savior of the whole universe, Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, was born in Bethlehem of Judah from the ever-virgin Mary. In that year, as Hunibald bears witness, by the edict of Caesar Augustus, the world subject to Roman rule was registered by heads. This, apart from the meaning of the mystery, accomplished by divine providence, was not without literal significance, since the Franks supplied the cause. [unclear] and from the name of its leader Phirisia it is called Phirisia, as Hunibald holds, down to the present day.

Again after ten years, with the consent of the aforementioned King Clogio and all the princes, all the kings of Phirisia, like the other leaders, were to remain forever subject to the king of the Franks, and each year were to pay a tribute of two hundred sixty oxen; and, in the manner of the Franks’ other friends, they were to fight against any enemies whatsoever.

King Clogio of the Franks died after many brave deeds, in the thirtieth year of his reign, which was the twentieth year of the Lord’s nativity. Concerning his character, prophecies, oracles, and wars, Hunibald writes many things.

*Compendium, Book I.*

*Nineteenth.*

Herimer, the elder son of King Clogio, succeeding his father, reigned for twelve years, a warlike man and excessively bold. In the third year of his reign, the Gauls, making an incursion, came as far as the Meuse, devastating with hostile rashness everything that belonged to the jurisdiction of the Franks, except fortifications and castles, and after this they quickly withdrew to their own lands with plunder and spoils.

But afterwards, when this incursion of the Gauls became known to King Herimer, he was moved to anger; and, having summoned to himself the dukes beyond the Meuse, through whose negligence the Gauls had broken in, [unclear] according to the laws of the Franks: whoever is established in ducal authority shall diligently protect the province entrusted to him. But if through his negligence enemies enter the region, if they injure our people, or if they despoil the inhabitants of the land of their property, let him pay half of his goods into the king's purse, and let him no longer be duke, but live deprived of honor. If he willingly permitted entry to the enemies, let him be buried alive or be punished capitally; and let his wives, with his children and all his property, pass to the king's service.

Then, having called to his aid allies, Germans, Theutonici, and Thuringians, King Herimer entered against the Gauls with a heavy multitude and subdued them with so great a slaughter that for many years they could not recover their former strength. Finally, however, in the last year of his reign, when he had again led an army across into Gaul, being excessively bold, not to say rash or presumptuous, and fighting rather incautiously, he was killed by them in battle, in the thirty-second year of the Lord.

*Twentieth.*

Marcomir, brother of the aforementioned King Herimer, who had been slain by the Gauls, succeeding his brother in the kingdom of the Franks, reigned for eighteen years: a man tall in stature, harsh in manners, yet favorable to friends, but feared and terrible to enemies. He engaged in many battles with the Roman Gauls, and often severely afflicted the people of Mainz, Trier, and the Agrippinians together.

In the second year of his reign, the only-begotten Son of God, the Lord Jesus Christ, Savior of the world, born man from Mary, ever a most pure virgin, without mixture with a man, according to that same humanity was crucified at Jerusalem, the city of the Jews, under Pontius Pilate, governor of the Romans; he suffered, died for our salvation, and was buried. He descended to the lower world, snatched the righteous from there, rose from the dead on the third day, and, ascending into heaven, sits at the right hand of the Father, to judge the living and the dead; he lives forever.

In the tenth year of King Marcomir, Claudius Caesar of the Romans led an army into Britain, which we now call England by the customary term, and by force of arms made it, together with the islands of the Orkneys, tributary to the Romans. On the journey there and back, he severely afflicted the Franks dwelling between the Meuse and the Rhine, though not without bloodshed among his own men.

At that time Guiderius, son of the late King Kymbelinus, was reigning in Britain. When he had been slain in battle by the army of Claudius, his brother Arviracus at once rose up in his place; putting the royal diadem on himself and killing many of the Romans, he pursued Claudius as far as the ships. Caesar, seeing that he could not overcome Arviracus, offered peace and gave him his daughter as wife. He recovered the tribute denied to the Romans, and with the help of his son-in-law also led his army across to the islands of the Orkneys.

But Marcomer, the aforementioned king of the Franks, died in the eighteenth year of his reign, in the fiftieth year of the Lord's nativity, in the eighth indiction of the Romans.

*Twenty-First.*

Clodomer, son of the aforementioned King Marcomir, succeeding his father, reigned over the Franks for twelve years, a restless and very warlike man. Hunibald reports of him that he was most hostile to the Roman Gauls; he desired nothing more than to erase the memory of them. There was scarcely a year in which he did not move an expedition into Gaul at least once.

In the first year of his reign, three suns appeared at the same time, which gradually returned into one. There followed throughout all Europe a great and immense famine, and a mortality not only of men but also of draft animals.

Mainz, destroyed by the Romans, is repaired.

In the ninth year, however, King Clodomer, with a great army of his men, crossed the Rhine and the Meuse and expelled the Gauls, recovering everything previously lost. With the help of the Germans he fought with the Romans at Mainz, but he could not prevent them from repairing the city. He died in the twelfth year of his reign, and in the sixty-second year of the Lord's nativity, in the fifth indiction of the Romans.

*Twe-* *Annals of Trithemius. The Twenty-Second.*

Antenor, son of King Clodomer, reigned after his father for six years. During the whole time in which he reigned he waged war with the Gauls and the Romans; and at length, on account of this, he miserably perished with many nobles of the kingdom, when, as we shall say, the bridge broke and he was drowned in the river Meuse.

In the last year of his reign, then, after a bridge had been built of wood over boats in the ancient fashion, he led his army across the river into Gaul. Having laid waste the region, he hastened his return into Francia with much booty and many spoils. And when the greater part of the army had already crossed the river, while the king himself with the nobles and the last of the rest was still waiting on the bank, suddenly the bridge, weighed down by the number of horsemen, collapsed; and the boats, released from one another when the ropes broke, gave all a miserable spectacle, with very many falling into the river. The king, stunned and surely troubled in mind, began to take counsel with those who were present about repairing the bridge, when behold, at once the Gauls were announced to be coming behind them in a great multitude of fighters, ready for battle. On hearing this, all who were with the king were thrown into consternation; time and place denied them flight, while the smaller army forbade battle. Therefore, since no way of escape lay open except that of swimming through the river, they threw into the water their arms and whatever could weigh them down, and tried for safety by swimming. The king also, having thrown off his cuirass and being girded over his tunic only with belt and sword, committed himself with his horse to the waves. Compelled by necessity, all the rest committed themselves to like danger. They all began to swim at once, some on horses, others with hands and feet sustaining the force of the waters. Many of them reached the bank by swimming; many also who had no skill in swimming, choked by the waters, perished amid the waves. Among them King Antenor too was drowned, with nine princes, whose names are these: Duke Priam, Duke Clodius, Duke Richimer, Duke Antenor, Duke Marcomer, Duke Walther, Duke Clogio, Duke Herimer, and Duke Rutwicus, with sixty-three other nobles of the Franks. Thus King Antenor of the Franks perished in the sixth year of his reign, in the sixty-eighth year of the Lord’s Nativity, in the eleventh indiction of the Romans.

*The Twenty-Third.*

Ratherus, or, as he is written by others, Rhatherius, the eldest son of the aforementioned King Antenor, after the death of his father reigned over the Franks for twenty-one years. He was a great-souled, bold, and brave man, who always most vigorously defended the people of the Franks by his sword from every incursion of the Gauls, fearing no one, dreading no one, but himself to be feared by all. In his second year, Nero, the wicked emperor of the Romans, stirred up the first persecution against the Christians, killed Peter and Paul, princes of the apostles, at Rome, and throughout the whole empire cruelly destroyed many thousands of believers.

Ratherus, moreover, king of the Franks, crushed the Gauls repeatedly; he avenged his father’s death with arms, fire, and sword; he restored the borders taken from his people; he built castles, cities, and fortifications; he renewed the treaty with the kings of the Germans, Saxons, and Thuringians, which King Francus had once struck a hundred years before, as we said above; and he enlarged the boundaries of the kingdom of the Franks.

After these things he finally died in the twenty-first year of his reign, in the eighty-ninth year of the Lord’s Nativity, in the second indiction of the Romans, and was buried in the city of Ratherdama, which he himself had newly built from the foundations and dedicated to his own name. His magnificent deeds [unclear] Arebaldus, pontiff of the Franks, [unclear] Saxons and Thuringian kings, which King Francus had once [unclear] Arebaldus, chief priest established as pontiff by the people of the Franks, which he willingly accepted.

In his twelfth year the Goths again poured into the borders of the Saxons, [unclear] the region in their custom [unclear] in all things magnificent, bold, warlike, excessively superstitious in the worship of the idols of his people, indeed one who wished not only to equal the Romans in the number of gods, but even to conquer and surpass them. Wherefore, when divinities had been multiplied by him, after [unclear] was dead, Richimer himself, king of the Franks, together with the German brothers and the Teutons, in accordance with the ancient treaty renewed a few years before, as we said, quickly led out a great army; and when a gathering had been made, they killed more than twenty thousand Goths, and turned the rest, wounded and stripped, to flight.

*Antenor the king reigned 6 years.*

*The Franks, [unclear] the Gauls, acted unhappily.*

*The bridge [unclear] the crossing [unclear] with drawn swords he fights.*

*The Gauls force the Franks, hostilely [unclear], to cross.*

*King Antenor with nine dukes and sixty-three nobles perished in the river.*

*Nero, most ruined man of the ruined.*

*Between the Franks and Saxons the treaty is renewed.*

*Ratherdama.*

*Arebaldus the pontiff, a historian [unclear].*

*Richimer reigned for 24 years.*

*Arebaldus, pontiff of the Franks, died.*

*The Goths again invaded the borders of the Saxons.* *Compendium, Book I.*

After the Goths had again been driven out of Saxony, the Franks held a conference with the Germans and the Teutons, debating among themselves how they might thereafter bar the Goths and the Scanzian peoples from returning into the territories of the Saxons or Germans. At last it pleased all the kings and nobles that from the people of the Franks, Saxons, Thuringians, Germans, and Teutons, who around the sea were nearer neighbors to the Dacians and Goths, they should gather one nation, with children, wives, and beasts of burden, to inhabit the land beyond furthest Saxony, nearest to the Scanzians, and to prevent the incursions of enemies.

When this agreement had been concluded, Richimer, king of the Franks, sent eighteen thousand men, with children and wives, into that region; over them he appointed as leader and prince Sunno, his second-born son. To him, according to the agreement, many then came together from the Germans, Saxons, and Thuringians; from diverse peoples they became one, and within a short time they grew into a great nation, and thereafter did not permit the Scanzians to devastate Saxony. Yet they were rather often harassed by the Romans.

This duke Sunno established the seat of his nation with power in the borders of Saxony, having to the east the Sarmatians; to the south the Slavs of Bohemia; to the west Saxony and the Teutons; and to the north the Cimbri, the sea, the Dacians, the Scanians, the Goths, and island-dwelling men inhabiting marshy places.

Sunno duke,
Clodomer,
Sunno duke of the Franks.

Sunno increased not a little the possession he had received. After him Sunnon received [unclear] his principate, who in the year of the Lord’s nativity one hundred forty-six, indiction [unclear], received the nation, who in the year of the Lord’s nativity one hundred forty-six, on the banks of the river Oder, built a new city, which, out of love for his forefathers, he called Frankfurt. After this he also founded another city at the mouth of the aforesaid river, not far from the sea, which from his own name he called Sunda, or, as Hunibald testifies, Domicianus.

The name of the Franks remained for some time in these lands, until at last, when the dukes had multiplied, the region was divided into several parts, and each division received its name from individual princes or events. From Marcomer and his son Brando, who founded the city [unclear] Brandenburg, some were named [unclear]; from Brando his son, who founded the city [unclear] Brandenburg, others were named Braburgi; and others took other names from others.

Previously, in the fifth year of King Richimer, Domitian Caesar had worn down the Sarmatians and Dacians who dwelt on the borders of Germany toward the east, and afflicted them greatly. And, adding sin to crime, after the most impious Nero he stirred up the second persecution against the Christians; he was the first of all the Caesars to command that he be called God and Lord by all.

In the eleventh year of his reign Richimer, king of the Franks, had a war with the Romans and Gauls, not far from the city of Basana, aided by the common votes of the Germans, in which many fell on both sides. Meanwhile, when the Roman legions had returned to Cologne Agrippina, word was brought that Nerva Caesar was dead; in his place the soldiers raised Trajan, a man of Spanish nation, to be Caesar. He ruled nineteen years, six months, fifteen days.

But Richimer, king of the Franks, after many brave deeds, finally died in the twenty-third year of his reign, and in the year of the Lord’s nativity 113, the eleventh Roman indiction. Ruthvicus the Frank wrote in verse of his life, character, deeds, and worship of the gods.

ODEMARS, the elder son by birth of the aforesaid Richimer, king of the Franks, reigned after his father for fourteen years, a prince of the Franks very beloved by the people, who refrained from wars as far as could be done without damage to the commonwealth. For he made truces, which the Franks, because of the pledge interposed, call, as it were, “confidences,” with the Gauls and the Romans, to whom thereafter he showed himself so much a friend that he compelled all to lament his death.

Thus as long as he lived among men he kept the promised peace, and devoted all his zeal to the honor and adornment of his nation; he [built/adorned?] very many castles, cities, and fortifications throughout the kingdom. For the Franks, Saxons, and Germans at that time were still subject to the vanity of idols and far removed from knowledge of the Christian faith. They worshiped Mars as a fierce god of war, from whose divine power they sought victory at all times. To each of their gods also they [made] not only individual altars *Annals of Trithemius*

[groves?] and temples, but also individual cities and villages; nor was there any number of senseless gods.

In these times the chief priest of the Franks, pontiff, elder, and prophet was named Vechtanus, born from the ancient stock of kings, eloquent in the Greek and Latin tongue; most skilled in astronomy, music, medicine, and the philosophy of the Greeks, since he had spent much time both at Rome and at Athens in the study of the writings of secular men, together with certain other fellow students of his. At length, having returned to his homeland, he taught the sons of kings and nobles, according to the ancient custom of the Franks, under an oak.

He wrote many things, in Greek poems, on the sacred rites of the gods; and he composed histories of the ancient kings, ten in number, in German, with which he exercised the talents of the young and greatly strengthened their memory. In the fifth year of King Odemar this man perished in a small river, to which, having been drowned in it, he gave his name, so that it is called in German, from Vechtanus, the Vecht down to the present day. Over his tomb King Odemar founded a new city, which he named Odemarsheim from his own name; it remains to the present in the territory of the diocese of the church of Utrecht.

But where Odemar, king of the Franks, among the Nitrians was [unclear] by the duke, called Marcoburg: Clogio, who perished in Britain; Francus, who was duke on this side of the Rhine among the Hogii, from Confluence as far as the mouth of the river Main toward the east, between the Mainz people and the Saxon Germans, who, restoring an ancient city, named it Frankfurt. And Meroda, struck by a [unclear] in hunting, died; Nicanor, who was an island duke at the mouths of the Rhine; and Odemar, whom his father, after the death of Vechtanus, [made?] pontiff [unclear] of the Romans the tenth, whose body is buried at Odemarsheim beneath a pyramid, as he had ordained while alive.

*The Twenty-Sixth*

Marcomer, son of King Odemar, succeeding his father, reigned twenty-one years. He had a wife named Athildis, daughter of Marus king of Britain; by her he begot seven sons, whose names were these: Clodomer, the firstborn, who succeeded his father in the kingdom; Marcomer, who held the duchy among the Nitrians, where he founded a city of his own name, called Marcoburg; Clogio, who perished in Britain; Francus, who was duke on this side of the Rhine among the Hogii, from Confluence as far as the mouth of the river Main toward the east, between the Mainz people and the Saxon Germans, who, restoring an ancient city, named it Frankfurt. And Meroda, struck by a [unclear] in hunting, died; Nicanor, who was an island duke at the mouths of the Rhine; and Odemar, whom his father, after the death of Vechtanus, [made?] pontiff [unclear] of the Romans the tenth, whose body was buried at Odemarsheim beneath a pyramid, as he had ordained while alive.

Doracus, prophet and writer of the Franks, flourished at that time, a former hearer and disciple of Vechtanus, born from the noble lineage of kings. Afterwards, when Odemar had died, he succeeded in the highest pontificate by the election of the governors. He obtained such authority among the Franks, and was held in such esteem, that he was worshipped by all almost as some divine power, and commanded not only the common people as he wished, but also the kings of the Franks and all the nobles. Writing in verse, he continued the histories of the nation.

The Franks had peace throughout all the days in which Marcomer reigned, and under his direction they greatly increased in riches, power, and honor. Doracus writes in the annals, as Hunibald testifies, that the Romans always held the Franks suspect both in peace and in war, as future overthrowers of the empire, having long since been forewarned by the oracle of Phaedrus, and that for this reason they often conspired with all their forces for their destruction, though in vain. For afterwards under King Faramund and his successors they both obtained all Gaul by their own forces and overcame the Roman empire.

Marcomer, king of the Franks, died in the twenty-first year of his reign, and in the year of the Lord’s nativity 148, in the first indiction.

*The Twenty-Seventh*

Clodomer, eldest son of the aforesaid Marcomer, king of the Franks, reigned after his father for seventeen years, a man of singular prudence, modest and most humane toward his own people. He had a wife named Hasildis, daughter of the duke of the Rugii; by her he begot three sons, Faraertus, Nicanor, and Roricus. The first of these, as we shall say, succeeded his father in the kingdom; the second was king of Frisia; the third, drowned in the water not far from Neuss, died and left his name to the river, which is called the Rur down to the present day. The place of Roricus’s drowning was between the Neocum castle [eischenanū?] and the old city which the inhabitants called Moradunum. In those times both Francia and all Germany were estranged from knowledge of the Christian faith.

Clodomer, king of the Franks, died in peace in the seventeenth year of his reign, in the year of the Lord’s nativity 165, in the third indiction of the Romans. In his time the Gauls were preparing an inroad [Source page illegible in the scan; the page image is the authoritative witness.]

*Compendium, Book I.*

[unclear] against the Franks. But King Clodomer himself, wisely anticipating their movement, restrained them from doing it.

*The Twenty-Eighth.*

*Farabertus reigned 20 years.*

Farabertus, the elder son of King Clodomer, succeeded his father and reigned twenty years, beginning in the aforementioned one hundred sixty-fifth year of the Lord’s nativity, in the third Roman indiction. He renewed and again ratified with the Germans, Saxons, Thuringians, Theutons, Marcomanni, and Cimbri the treaty and friendship formerly contracted by King Francus, as we said above, and then confirmed by other kings, renewed, and often strengthened and continued by a new ordinance. This greatly displeased the Romans and stirred them to arms.

*The legions of the Romans into Germany [unclear].*

For in the sixth year of this King Farabertus, which was the one hundred seventy-first year of the Lord’s nativity, in the times of Lucius Aurelius Commodus Caesar, the Romans, not bearing calmly so great a concord of the Franks with the Theutons and Germans, tried with every effort to overthrow it. And so, having sent legions through Sarmatia into Germany against the Dacians, Marcomanni, Theutons, Saxons, and Franks, they brought forth a great army of their men. Against their incursion the kings of the aforesaid peoples sent out such great forces of fighters that the said Romans were compelled to withdraw without victory, with loss and confusion.

*Another expedition of the Romans into Germany, in the time of Antoninus Pius.*

In the eleventh year of King Farabertus, under the emperor Antoninus Pius, the Romans again led an army back into Germany by way of the Sarmatians, and fierce fighting went on for a long time, and many on both sides fell wounded by the sword. Concerning the circumstances, outcome, and miracles of rains in this war, which were then reported on behalf of the army of the Romans, following Hunibald we have set out a sufficient narrative in the first volume of the Annals; we judge it superfluous to repeat it here.

Farabertus, king of the Franks, after many brave deeds, died in the twentieth year of his reign, in the 185th year of the Lord’s nativity, in the eighth indiction.

*The Britons, who are now called English, receive the faith of Christ.*

*Faganus and Diuanus, bishops of the Britons.*

In the times of this reign of Farabertus, namely in the one hundred eighty-second year of the Lord’s nativity, Eleutherius, pope of Rome, at the request of Lucius king of Britain, son of Coillus, sent into that Britain itself, which is now named England, the bishops Faganus and Diuanus, so that they might announce the word of salvation to the said king, and also to the nobles and the whole people of the British kingdom of his island, and baptize them, converted to the faith of Christ, in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. When they came to the appointed place, in a short time they converted not only King Lucius but also the people of the whole island to the faith of Christ.

*Priests of idols in Britain: pontiffs, 28; archflamens, 3.*

[unclear], the aforesaid apostolic preachers consecrated their temples of idols to the honor of the one God, the almighty Father, appointing as many bishops in place of the flamens, and archbishops in place of the archflamens. Gildas wrote of these matters more fully in the book which he entitled On the Victory of Aurelius Ambrosius, king of the Britons; and after him Geoffrey of Monmouth, a Briton, who, for Duke Rupertus of Claudiocestria, completed in ten books the history of the Britons and the successions of all their kings, from the first entry of the people, with Brutus from the Trojans, into that island itself, down to the six hundred eighty-ninth year of the Lord’s nativity. His contemporary Caradocus of Llancarfan also described the successions, years, times, and deeds of the kings of the Franks in lucid speech.

*Sunno reigned 28 years.*

Sunno, the elder son of Farabertus king of the Franks, succeeded his father and reigned twenty-eight years. He was a strong, vigorous, and bold prince, who fought many battles against the Romans and also the Gauls. In his time, when Lucius king of Britain, whom we said had first most humbly received the Christian faith, died without children, the Romans sent the senator Severus into Britain with two legions. He fought many battles with Fulgenius, by whom at last, in the siege of the city of Eboracum, he was killed along with many Romans; his son, named Bassianus, they accepted as king.

*Severus the Roman is killed in Britain.*

He laid waste [unclear] the Gauls, and, after devastating the region round about, returned victorious, enriched with spoils. The rest, however, which Hildegast, philosopher of the Franks and distinguished seer, described in a German song, and afterward Hunibald in prose in the Latin language, we too have spoken of in the first book of the Annals.

Sunno, king of the Franks, died in the twenty-eighth year of his reign, but in the year 213 of the Lord’s Nativity, in the sixth Roman indiction.

*The Thirtieth.*

Hilderic, the elder son of King Sunno, reigned after his father for forty years: a high-souled, prudent, bold, warlike man, who at all times stoutly defended his people no less by prudence than by arms, and powerfully extended the boundaries of the kingdom far and wide. For he was of such virtue and power that he was to be feared in no small degree not only by the Gauls but also by the Romans; to them the Frankish name was so hateful and odious that they were never accustomed to write or name that people otherwise than German.

The Franks gloried in their name; the Romans, laboring under hatred of them, begrudged them the word. Nor did the written histories of neighboring peoples, especially of the Romans and Gauls, by common consent grant the Frankish name to the people of Sicambria before the Franks, by arms and virtues, had subjected almost all Europe to their dominion. For previously, as we have said, the Romans, the Gauls, and the other hostile nations, as Hunibald testifies, moved by envy, named the Franks by no other word than Germans. For the author already mentioned says thus: Our ancestors had no less care, by common decree, for the name of their people, which they once received from their King Francus, than for the kingdom; for they thought it would be glorious for them no longer to exchange the Frankish name for another, once it had been assumed by their forefathers with the highest honor.

In these times there flourished under King Hilderic [unclear], also [unclear], [unclear] Hildegast, seer and philosopher, [unclear], most learned of all, who in his own time said, did, and wrote marvelous things. And he was of such esteem and authority among his own people that all always obeyed his command.

On the birthday of Hilderic, king of the Franks, standing in the temple of Jove at Neopagus, before a multitude of the Frankish people, Hildegast, philosopher, counselor, seer, father of kings, elder, most learned of all, because in his own time he said and did marvelous things, after prayers poured out before the image of that very god for the obtaining of a prophecy, suddenly began to rave, as is the custom of the frenzied, with a song of [unclear], and, with head tossed and hands bent back, he prophesied thus, not using verses composed according to the law of meters, but rhythms without measure, uttered very confusedly in prophetic frenzy; Hunibald made their interpretation thus:

Victory will come to the Franks from the western God,
whom the old Dardanian ancestors worshiped.
Whatever the Gaul possesses, whatever all Germany possesses,
all will yield to your right, warlike Sicamber.
When he gives you first a king from the name,
whom the leaders, then without a king, shall appoint,
then, with him victorious, the Frank shall reign without end.

He also added thus concerning the empire of the Romans:

Behold, the great God will give the brothel-camps to the Frank,
and the lion will break the eagle, crushed together with the serpent.

Hunibald explains this meaning concerning the standards of the Franks, which they used in battles, which we call the insignia of princes.

The kings of the Franks, he says, from that time when they began to have war with the Romans, on the advice of the pontiffs of their people, took these new arms or insignia: after throwing away the three frogs which they had once brought from Scythia on a white fleece, they depicted a lion with the forepart of its body on a fleece of blue color, its feet stretched out for seizing, its mouth open in the manner of one roaring, whose lower part of the body ended in the tail of a serpent; with this it seemed strongly to bind, press, and choke the neck of an eagle depicted beneath on a golden fleece with wings spread.

The Romans had the eagle as their sign when fighting. Desiring to suppress and annihilate their proud and arrogant power by strength and at the same time prudence, the Franks took the lion for one part and the serpent for the other. For by the lion the Franks mystically designated their strength, but by the serpent their wisdom and prudence.

These insignia, or arms, although they are improperly so called, all the kings of the Franks thereafter used down to Clovis the Christian, who is read to have adopted, in place of the lion, three lilies sent down from heaven, as will be said in its proper place.

At length, when the kingdom of the Franks was divided into two by the sons of Louis the First, the emblem of the lilies remained with the Gallic, or western, Franks; but the eastern or German kingdom of the Franks retained its own arms of the lion and the serpent’s tail. Since that kingdom has the Roman Empire annexed to itself, the earlier insignia having been brought into oblivion, it has been accustomed to use only the eagle, the mark of the empire, from that time of division down to the present day.

*Hildegast, teacher of the noble Franks in every science.*

The aforesaid Hildegast also, the wise man of the Franks, taught the sons of the nobles to sing in their mother tongue, with citharas and various other musical instruments, the deeds of their ancestors in songs; he advised the people to live by civil customs, to build houses, and to go about more cultivated in dress; and he ordered them to lay aside ferocity. For indeed the Franks until then cared little for cultivation or adornment, both in buildings and in clothing. Hildegast made all these things more cultivated, and most wisely instructed them to crush and subdue the pride of the Romans not only with arms, but also with possessions and manners. From that time the Franks began to build larger and more beautiful houses, divided into various chambers. For whatever they had built in earlier times was contemptible in its excessive simplicity and rustic, since, because of their frequent changes of settlement, they had been more accustomed to live in fields than in cities. Hence the Germans, taking up a proverb, whenever they saw something made or painted with ancient simplicity, were accustomed, praising antiquity in this way, to say: “That is a good old Frankish work.”

*The Franks had become more cultivated in manners and buildings.*

Hunibald records the remaining marvelous sayings, writings, or deeds of Hildegast. In the twenty-fourth year of Hilderic, king of the Franks, Alexander, son of Mammaea, Caesar Augustus of the Romans, is killed at Mainz, a city of Germany, in a military disturbance, in the thirteenth year of his reign.

But Hilderic, king of the Franks, the first of that name, after many brave and magnificent deeds, at length dies in the fortieth year of his reign, and in the two hundred fifty-third year of the Lord’s nativity, in the first Roman indiction.

*The Thirty-First.*

*Bartherus reigned 48 years.*

Bartherus, son of King Hilderic, succeeding his father, reigned eighteen years. In his time the Romans waged war with the Goths, who, crossing the river Ister, were devastating their cities and towns. The Romans killed thirty thousand of them under the command of Decius Caesar and his son. Many of the Romans also fell, among whom the very son of Decius Caesar [unclear]. But Decius Caesar, a most wicked persecutor of Christians, while fleeing, was drowned in the whirlpool of a certain marsh; his corpse could never be found by his men.

In the tenth year of King Bartherus, when the Romans under the wanton rule of Gallienus were sluggish in idleness, the Franks, thinking that a suitable time was at hand to avenge the insults committed against them, with the assistance of the Germans, Saxons, Bavarians, and Thuringians, gathered a great army of warriors; and, entering the borders of their enemies and devastating everything with fire and sword, they reached Ravenna in a hostile incursion, and, enriched with booty, returned to their own lands.

In the following year, which was the eleventh of King Bartherus, the Alemanni, having assembled their forces, led a strong army into Gaul; and, after laying waste the region with sword and fire, they returned to their own lands with much spoil and booty. In the same year they set an expedition in motion against the Romans in Italy, and inflicted many losses on them, avenging the manifold injuries which they had received from the same.

In the thirteenth year of King Bartherus, which was the two hundred sixty-sixth year of the Lord’s nativity, in the fourteenth Roman indiction, the Franks, with the aid of the Germans and Saxons, assembled an immense army; and, after crossing the Rhine and the Meuse, under the leaders Antharius and Luther they entered Gaul, laying waste everything in hostile fashion. Antharius the leader was the son of Bartherus, the aforesaid king of the Franks; and Luther was the son of Marbod, king in Saxony. Beginning from the region nearest to the Tungrians, and from there proceeding hostilely through the Bellovaci beyond the Seine, they reached as far as Spain; and, surrounding the noble city of Tarragona with a siege, they destroyed it utterly.

But Bartherus, king of the Franks, at length dies in the eighteenth year of his reign, in the year 50 *Annals of Trithemius.*

Clodius, the elder son of King Barther, succeeding his father, reigned over the Franks for twenty-seven years. Against their incursion the Alemanni advanced armed, having in their army thirty thousand fighters. A very hard battle was joined not far from Lake Benacus, in which almost fifteen thousand of the Alemanni were killed.

*Compendium, Book I.*

*The thirty-fifth.*

*Chlogio reigned for only two years.*

Chlogio, son of King Dagobert, succeeding his father, reigned for only two years. For in the second year of his reign, the Romans and the Gauls fiercely invaded the kingdom of the Franks in the Cismosanian regions and began to lay everything waste with fire and sword. But King Chlogio, having gathered what forces he could, went to meet the enemy with the help of the Germans; and, when he fought too incautiously, he was killed. Yet the Franks did not on that account shrink from the battle, but fought bravely. For Clodomir, brother of the slain king, drew his body back from the battle-line and clothed himself in his arms, so that all might think that he himself was the king, lest either his friends, once the king’s death was known, should lose heart, or the enemies, exulting, should conceive certain hope of victory. And so Duke Clodomir, clothed in the king’s arms and returned to the battle-line, since he was thought by everyone to be the king himself, inspired steadfastness in his own men and fear in the enemy. By fighting very bravely he restored the battle, turned the Gauls together with the Romans at last to flight, obtained the victory, gathered the spoils of the enemy, and freed the kingdom from destruction.

Accordingly Chlogio, king of the Franks, fell in the second year of his reign, and in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 309, in the seventh indiction of the Romans. He left two sons, of whom the elder by birth, Helenus, was then in his twentieth year, while the younger, Richimer, was in his eighteenth. But by law the Franks were forbidden to advance anyone as king before he had completed the twenty-fourth year of his age. Hence it came about that neither of the sons of Chlogio came to the kingdom, but their uncle Clodomir was chosen as king.

*The thirty-sixth.*

Clodomir, brother of the slain King Chlogio, chosen as king by the common decree of the Franks, thereafter reigned eighteen years, a distinguished, prudent, and strong prince, who kept his people in peace and enlarged the kingdom of the Franks.

For in these times, when the Suevi were being grievously afflicted by the Romans, they resolved to call the Franks, Saxons, and Thuringians to their aid; and they trusted that they would find them willing all the more easily because they knew that they had always hated the Romans. But the Franks, otherwise ancient enemies of the Romans, after holding counsel among themselves, readily gave consent to the petition of the Suevi, judging it more wholesome to fight with their enemies in lands far from their own borders than in their own territories.

Therefore Clodomir, king of the Franks, appointed his brother Genebald as commander of the army that was to go, and entrusted to him eighty thousand fighters. The other kings called by the Suevi to their aid did likewise; the soldiers assembled into one and arranged made up a sufficiently great army. Then, having joined battle with the Romans, they fought most fiercely, killing many thousands of them, while the rest sought safety in flight; and so the Romans were driven from the territories of the Suevi.

When the Germans had gained this victory and were dividing the spoils in the camp according to custom, a dangerous quarrel arose between two soldiers, of whom one was named Adelbert, while the other was a Sueve named Doringus. The cause of the disturbance was this: that the Sueve soldier had accused Doringus of having secretly taken something or other from the common booty. When he denied it, a serious sedition arose, the Thuringians defending Doringus and the Suevi the Sueve. For each had many adherents from his own people, whose minds were stirred up. But when Doringus steadfastly denied the theft, the Sueve offered to prove the truth by duel. When the princes had permitted this, single combat was arranged between them on the appointed day; and in it Doringus, at the second encounter, was killed by the Sueve. When, on account of this matter, he had been stripped of his clothing and arms, the theft too, concerning which he had been accused, was found hidden upon him. After receiving this disgrace, the Thuringians were exceedingly angry; but, concealing their anger, they afterward held secret counsel among themselves as to how they might avenge Gunther’s fall upon Adelbert. When the plan had been settled, namely that they should kill the Sueve that same night, one hundred twenty of them conspired together concerning the matter to be kept secret. Therefore on the following night they silently rushed upon the tent in which they suspected Adelbert to be, demanding that the murderer be handed over to them to be killed. Roused by these voices, the Suevi ran to arms, firmly resolving either to defend their innocent soldier from death or to die with him. When the deed was presently reported in the camp of the Thuringians, they were greatly moved and, as if turned to fury, immediately seized arms; and, having formed a column, they rushed upon the Suevi, who suspected no such thing, raising shouts on high like men raging. But the Suevi were not idle: when they could not call the Thuringians back from the tumult with fair words, they themselves put on arms and strove to resist bravely. A fierce battle was joined between friends, in which more than two thousand of the party [unclear]

This conflict had remained hidden from the Franks and the Saxons until the contest came to an end; they had pitched their camps not in the same place, but in different stations. But afterwards, when the Franks, together with the Saxons, had learned the cause, they labored with many negotiations for peace and concord between those at variance. Yet since each party complained that it had been gravely injured by wrong, they could not restore full concord between them. They did, however, establish truces, or armistices, of three years between them, in which they ordered the parties to abstain from war until anger should cool with time and the disturbance be quieted.

From that time the Suebi always held the Thuringians suspect of treachery, as Hunibald says, and they were troubled by a hidden and manifest hatred against them, although many do not know the cause of this mutual hostility.

[unclear] to the present day, as we learned long ago from the report of Hunibald, our dearest brother, what the cause of dissension was between you, friends, Thuringians, and the Suebi, and what is the occasion of those disturbances which today stand at the doors. The [Thuringians] sent to [Clodomir], king of the Franks, and to the nobles of the realm, begging with great urgency that, in view of the former alliance, they should bring them the owed and friendly aid against the Suebi. At that time there were great movements of peoples in Britain and in all the adjacent islands neighboring the kingdom of the Franks; in consideration of these, King Clodomir was distressed, fearing the treachery of the Romans, lest, while the army of fighters was absent, they should contrive some new incursion into the kingdom.

After counsel had been held with the nobles of the realm, King Clodomir gave the envoys of the Thuringians this answer in a public assembly of the magnates. From the report of Duke Henebald, our dearest brother, we learned long ago what the cause of dissension was between you, friends, the Thuringians, and the Suebi, and what is the occasion of those disturbances which today stand at the doors. We confess to you that for a long time [unclear].

They sent to the king of the Franks and to the nobles of the realm, begging with great urgency that, in view of the former alliance, they should bring them the owed and friendly aid against the Suebi. At that time there were great movements of peoples in Britain and in all the adjacent islands neighboring the kingdom of the Franks; in consideration of these, King Clodomir was distressed, fearing the treachery of the Romans, lest, while the army of fighters was absent, they should contrive some new incursion into the kingdom.

Therefore it in no way seemed prudent to the counsel of the Franks, especially in these dangerous times, to divide the people and, neglecting their own affairs, to undertake the defense of others, since perhaps with God’s favor we might suffice for one of the two; for even to protect this our kingdom from the incursion of enemies in these days is not in our power. Moreover, the very great distance of places greatly hinders us from being able to bring you aid so often against the Suebi, since they hold the source and beginning of the river Rhine, while we hold its farthest mouths and its western end. Nevertheless, lest we seem to have been altogether lacking to you in the friendship of the Franks, it has pleased our counsel that we direct our messengers and envoys to the Suebi, through whom we may again obtain for you three-year truces and armistices. Meanwhile let the Thuringians take counsel, so that they may either obtain a lasting peace with the Suebi, or by some other means interpose the necessary wall of defense, that is, either from their own people or from friendly foreign peoples.

When these things had been set forth by the king of the Franks, the envoys answered: Excellent, O king and you Frankish princes, is your counsel, if indeed you will be able to obtain three-year truces from the Suebi. But as for your counsel that we place between ourselves and the Suebi a wall of defense, either from ourselves or from any foreign people, this is the judgment of our king and of all the nobles of the Thuringian people. Hear our consultation concerning this matter, we beg, and at the same time, as faithful friends, provide aid. We have a land broad in extent toward the south, fertile in abundance of fruits, whose furthest boundaries separate the Suebi and the Thuringians. If you wish to place inhabitants from among your people in it, with a duke, this will certainly be a perpetual honor and advantage to you and to the kingdom of the Franks, but to the Thuringians a wall of defense, and to the Suebi a cause of fear. No difficulty concerning the grant will be able to intervene, by which it should not, through the voluntary offering of the princes of the Thuringian people, come into your power.

After consultation had been held on these matters, the Franks gladly agreed, as men who had nothing more at heart than to extend the Frankish name and kingdom at the same time. Therefore, first sending letters and envoys to the Suebi, they obtained peace for the Thuringians for three years, keeping secret their plan concerning the new possession to be undertaken. Then they sent their own men with the aforesaid envoys of their friends into Thuringia, so that they might confirm, according to the judgment of the king and nobles, the proposed business concerning the grant of the promised region. When all these things had been duly completed, the events which we shall write followed.
