Theodoric was deposed from the kingdom of the Franks in the first year of his reign, which was 667 from the Lord’s Nativity, in the tenth indiction of the Romans; and his brother Hilderic, who was reigning in Austrasia, was chosen by common consent.

*The Fifty-Fifth*

Hilderic, brother of the two preceding kings, who was reigning in Austrasia, after the deposition of Theodoric was, by the common election of the nobles, taken up as king and monarch of the whole kingdom of the Franks. He reigned twelve years. His mayor of the palace was Wolfrad, a noble man, powerful in deed and speech.

In the ninth year of his reign, King Hilderic, by the levity of his own conduct, kindled against himself the hatred of many nobles. Saint Leodegar, from a monk of our order made bishop of Autun, was driven from his see and thrust into Luxeuil.

In the twelfth year of his reign, moreover, and the 679th year from the Lord’s Nativity, in the seventh indiction, a certain Frank named Bodilo, whom King Hilderic himself had ordered to be bound to a post and flogged, killed him while he was hunting, together with his pregnant wife Blithild, by a cruel blow.

After the killing of King Hilderic, his brother Theodoric was called out from the monastery of the holy martyr Dionysius and restored to the kingdom of the Franks; and thereafter he reigned a second time for fourteen years. His mayor of the palace was Leudesius, son of Erchenwald, appointed for one year by the counsel of Saint Leodegar the bishop, then recalled from the monastery of Luxeuil, and of the other princes.

For in the following year Ebroin came out from the aforementioned monastery, recovered his strength, and harried his ambushers with hostile pursuit. He rushed upon King Theodoric, plundered his treasures and those of the church, killed Leudesius, the mayor of the palace, in battle, put the king himself to flight, and, pretending that a certain Clovis was the king’s son, made him king for himself. By threats and blandishments he induced to obedience to him whomever he could, and with many disturbances he troubled the kingdom of the Franks.

In the third year of Theodoric’s reign, the holy bishop Leodegar was captured by Ebroin and was gravely afflicted together with his brother Gerinus. Gerinus, however, not long afterward, by order of that tyrant, was buried under stones and killed.

In the sixth year of his reign, Theodoric received Ebroin back into favor, and at his persuasion summoned a synod of bishops. In it, at Ebroin’s sentence, he deprived many of them of their episcopal office, while others he condemned to perpetual exile. Among them Saint Lambert, son of Count Aper, removed from his own bishopric of Maastricht, entered at the monastery of Stavelot into the harbor of monastic quiet, and remained in it for seven years.

In the same year Saint Leodegar, bishop of Autun, long tortured by Ebroin, after hunger and bodily filth, after the tearing out of his eyes, after the cutting of the soles of his feet, after the cutting out of his tongue and lips, completed his martyrdom, at the tyrant’s command, by the cutting off of his head. Many miracles proved his innocence and merit.

In the eighth year of Theodoric, after the death of Wolfrad, mayor of the palace of the Franks, Pippin, son of Ansegis, together with Duke Martin, held the chief power in Austrasia. Ebroin, engaging with them, killed Martin.

In the same year Conon was ordained pope at Rome; he [unclear] Saint Kilian, a Scot by nation, in the place called Vultaburg, which is now named Ultraiectum, compounded from the name of the people of the Vulturi and from traiectum, as if “the town of the Vultari,” because, as Sigebert holds, in the Gallic tongue traiectum means “town.” But in our days it is called Lower Traiectum, to distinguish it from the Upper one, which, situated on the bank of the river Meuse, is commonly called Maastricht, where the holy fathers Servatius, Amandus, Remaclus, and Lambert the martyr once had the episcopal see which is now among the people of Liège.

In the year of the Lord’s nativity 698, the eleventh indiction of the Romans, Saint Lambert, bishop of Upper Traiectum, having dared to rebuke Prince Pippin because he had taken a concubine named Alpaida in addition to his lawful wife Plectrude, was killed at Liège by Dodo, the brother of that Alpaida, and was martyred; in the church of Saint Servatius at Upper Traiectum [unclear].

*[Choret?] and [Offa?], kings of England, became monks at Rome and spent the time of their life under the rule of Saint Benedict.*

In the tenth year of Hildebert, king of the Franks, in the year of the Lord’s nativity 707, the fifth indiction of the Romans, [Choret?] and [Offa?], kings of England, despising the kingdom of the world for love of almighty God, came to Rome, became monks, and the remainder of this

*The episcopate of Upper Traiectum is transferred to Liège.*

Alpaida, was killed at Liège and martyred; in the church of Saint Servatius at Upper Traiectum he was buried, shining with many miracles. After him Saint Hubert of Upper Traiectum [unclear].

*[Charet?] and [Offa?], kings of England, became monks at Rome and spent the time of their life under the rule of Saint Benedict.*

In the thirteenth year of Hildebert, king of the Franks, Saint Hubert the bishop, warned by divine revelation, brought back the body of Saint Lambert the martyr from Upper Traiectum to Liège with great glory of miracles, in the twelfth year after he had undergone martyrdom for the truth. The same Hubert also transferred the episcopal see from Traiectum to Liège.

In the sixteenth year of Hildebert, king of the Franks, Grunwald, mayor of the palace of the Franks, now weighed down by greater old age, had appointed [unclear] as substitute; while praying at Liège before the altar of Saint Lambert, he was killed by Ranegarius, a retainer of Radbod, duke of the Frisians.

After his miserable death, Theobald, son of [Progo?], was appointed prince of the court by his grandfather Pippin, mayor of the palace of the Franks. In this principate he could scarcely rule for two years, but was cast down by the Franks.

In the following year, which was the year of the Lord’s nativity 713, Pippin, son of Ansegis, mayor of the palace of the kingdom of the Franks, died. He designated as heir of his principate his son named Charles, surnamed Tutides or Martel, born from the concubine Alpaida.

But Plectrude, the lawful wife left by Pippin, seized that Charles, her stepson, and in Cologne Agrippina assigned him to very close custody; with her grandson Theobald she invaded the principate.

Meanwhile Hildebert, king of the Franks, died in the eighteenth year of his reign, which was the year of the Lord’s nativity 715, the thirteenth indiction.

*The Fifty-Eighth.*

Clodoveus, son of King Hildebert, succeeded his father in the kingdom of the Franks and reigned four years, or, as others will have it, five. Many writers of histories affirm that this man was not named Clodoveus, but Dagobert; whether this difference occurred through the fault of copyists or from some other occasion, we do not know. The greater part, however, call him Dagobert, but the fewer, agreeing with Sigebert, the monk of Gembloux and a most diligent writer, have named him Clodoveus. Whether he had two names I do not know.

The Franks, laboring under hatred of Theobald, conspired together; after forces had been gathered from here and there, they waged against him a quite dangerous war, in which, after many had been killed on both sides, Theobald was finally defeated, put to flight, and cast down from the principate. After him the Franks appointed Regenfred mayor of the palace.

Meanwhile Charles, son of Pippin, freed by divine will from the custody of his stepmother, soon strove to wrest the ancestral principate from the hand of Regenfred; and first, having attacked Radbod, duke of Frisia, who was helping the enemy, he suffered loss of his army.

In the third year of Clodoveus or Dagobert of the Franks, Charles, in the district of Cambrai at Vinciacum on Palm Sunday, which was the third day before the Kalends of April, engaged Hilperic and Regenfred and turned them both to flight; he pursued them as far as Paris. Now Hilperic was by rank a priest, named Daniel, whom the Franks had made king for themselves in Neustria.

After this Dagobert, or Clodoveus, king of the Franks, died in the fourth year of his reign, and in the year of the Lord’s nativity 719, the second indiction.

Here I choose to insert the false opinion of certain persons concerning the foundation of the monastery of Saint Peter the Apostle at Erfurt, who grant to King Dagobert the Great the honor of this foundation, something which neither the time nor reason permits. I would willingly have passed over this idle repetition of the unlearned,

*Regenfred becomes mayor of the palace of Neustria. Charles, freed from custody, having resumed his paternal principate. War between Charles and Daniel Hilperic. Daniel the priest is made king of the Neustrians. Concerning the foundation of the monastery of Saint Peter in Erfurt, against [unclear].* a monk by profession, he ordained as bishop, sending him with two monks, Colonatus the priest and Totnanus the deacon, into Germany to preach to the peoples the faith of Christ and the true salvation of souls in him. Coming into eastern Francia, to Würzburg, a city of the Franks, he devoted himself for some time to the office of holy preaching, and by word and example brought many back to knowledge of the truth. At last, with his aforesaid disciples, he suffered martyrdom through the secret instigation of Gailana, wife of Gosbert, duke of the East Franks, because she feared being separated from her husband, since Saint Kilian reproved him for having as wife her whom his brother had previously had as wife.

In the ninth year of King Theodoric, Ebroin, mayor of the palace in Neustria, since he did not cease cruelly to oppress the Franks by his tyranny, was killed by a certain Ermenfrid, a noble man; this Ermenfrid soon fled to Pippin, who held the principate of the mayoralty of the palace in Austrasia. After the most impious Ebroin had been slain, a certain Waratho was appointed mayor of the palace.

In the following year a battle was fought near Namur between Pippin and Gislemar, son of Waratho. And not long after, Gislemar having been punished by divine agency, and Waratho also having died, his son-in-law Berthar was mayor of the palace. But the Franks, suffering under Berthar’s hostility, sought Pippin’s friendship through hostages, promising aid and loyalty if by war he should wrest the principate from him.

In the twelfth year of his reign King Theodoric and Berthar, his mayor of the palace, declared war on Pippin, who had acted as mayor of the palace in Neustria against their will. But Pippin won in that battle, and having captured King Theodoric, bound him, as he wished, by his own conditions. Berthar, however, was killed by his own men in favor of Pippin. And so Pippin subjected Neustria together with Austrasia to himself; under Theodoric he alone ruled and governed the whole kingdom of the Franks for twenty-three years. He restored Saint Lambert, brought out from the monastery of Stavelot, to the pontificate of the church of Maastricht upon the Meuse, and accomplished many useful things in the kingdom of the Franks.

At that time Saint Willibrord, a monk, came from England into Gallican Francia with twelve companions of the same profession, and lived most holily.

In these times also Saint Wandregisel, who was Wando, grandson through Walgis, his brother, of Ansegis, formerly mayor of the palace of the kingdom of the Franks, built two monasteries of monks under the rule of divine Benedict in Gallican Francia, namely Fécamp and Fontenelle, which is now in the borders of Normandy; in these, many most holy and most learned men afterward became illustrious in the course of time.

Theodoric, king of the Franks, died in the fourteenth year of his reign, but in the year of the Lord’s birth 693, in the sixth Roman indiction, leaving two sons, Clovis and Hildebert, who succeeded one another.

*The Fifty-Sixth.*

Clovis, the elder son of the aforementioned King Theodoric, succeeding his father, reigned over the Franks for four years, with Pippin existing as mayor of the palace. In that year the Ewalds, the White and the Black, monks and priests, coming from England into Saxony for love of Christ, were martyred, and were buried at Cologne by order of Prince Pippin.

In the first year of King Clovis, Pippin, mayor of the palace of the Franks, in whose hands all power of the whole kingdom had been placed, made war on the Frisians and defeated their duke Radbod. He also appointed Saint Willibrord, English by nation, of whom we have spoken, as teacher and apostle of the Frisian people.

In these days there flourished in Gallican Francia, from the disciples of the blessed bishop Kilian, previously martyred at Würzburg, Arnuald and Adelan, abbots; Adelmus and Wilfrid, bishops from among the monks, who gave the souls of many to salvation.

Clovis, king of the Franks, died in the fourth year of his reign, which was the year of the Lord’s birth 697, in the tenth Roman indiction.

*The Fifty-Seventh.*

Hildebert, brother of the aforementioned King Clovis and son of the late King Theodoric, reigned alone after his brother for eighteen years. His mayor of the palace was Pippin, son of the younger Ansegis: count in Namur, duke in Brabant, a most noble and energetic man, sprung from the ancient lineage of the kings of the Franks.

In the same year Saint Willibrord the monk was sent by Pippin, mayor of the palace, to Rome with letters; on the feast of Saint Clement he was ordained bishop of the Frisians by Pope Sergius. From the gift of the aforementioned Prince Pippin he established an episcopal seat [unclear]. [The bishopric?] was sent to eastern Francia.

*Saint Kilian the martyr [unclear] course is set below. Ebroin, mayor of the palace of Neustria, is killed. Waratho, mayor of the palace. Battle between Pippin and Gislemar. Berthar becomes mayor of the palace of Neustria. The war of King Theodoric with Pippin, mayor of the palace. Pippin, mayor of the palace, 28 years. Saint Lambert restored to the church. Saint Willibrord, abbot. Saint Wandregisel illustrious; he usefully carried out [unclear] monastery. Clovis reigned four years. The two Ewald monks suffered in Saxony. Pippin defeated the Frisians in war. Saint Willibrord preaches in Frisia. Arnuald, Adelan, Wilfrid, of Saint Kilian the martyr. Clovis, king of the Franks, dies. Hildebert reigned 13 years. Pippin, son of the other Ansegis.* of learned men, unless the defense of my writings compelled me to bring trifles into the open. For some time ago, at the urging of the abbots Blasius and Johannes, we wrote two volumes, not small in size, of chronicles or annals of the famous monastery of Hirsau of our order, which is situated in the diocese of Worms, or Speyer; in the first of these, by many arguments, we sufficiently proved that the aforesaid monastery of Saint Peter in Erfurt was first founded not by Dagobert, king of the Franks, but by Saint William, the twelfth abbot of Hirsau. And because we have now come to know that this assertion of ours is all the more true, from the very foolishly fabricated letters which we saw in the aforesaid Erfurt monastery, supported by no seal of anyone, and which we read under the name of Dagobert and copied, lest anyone accuse us of falsehood, we thought it worth the effort to join a copy of those letters, with other arguments, to our assertion.

*In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity.* I, Dagobert, king of the Franks, make known both to clergy and to people, both to Christians and to pagans, that our city named Merovegesburg, which had come to us by hereditary right from our own grandfather Meroneus, namely the founder of the same city in Thuringia: we, by royal power, have given to Saint Peter and to his monks serving God there, to possess after our death, with all its servitudes; from him the mountain itself, after the foundation of the monastery which I built in honor of the aforesaid apostle, took its name, having previously been called by its pagan name [unclear], but by its new name Petrimons. How this was done by the ordinance of God we shall relate.

There was in the aforesaid city, next to the church of Saint [Ulastus?] the martyr, a man of God named Adeodatus, enclosed at my request by Rigibert, bishop of Mainz. This recluse, because of danger to his soul, not wishing [unclear] by the excommunication of clerics, and [unclear] to savor the word of true faith, asked that I summon for him from some cloister of mine a monk from whom he might hear the divine office and the word of true faith, and receive the communion of the sacred mystery. Assenting to his petition because of our mutual familiarity, I sent to the monastery of monks which I had built in like manner in Selsenburg, and, summoning from there a venerable senior monk named Truckindus, I directed him as teacher and rector to the aforesaid recluse Adeodatus. When he had come there, gradually, by the teaching and persuasion of the recluse, the number of believers began to be multiplied, both through the conversion of pagans to baptism and through that of clerics and laymen to the monastic habit. Seeing this, and understanding divine favor in this matter, I handed over my often-mentioned city, with all things belonging to it, to Saint Peter and his monks, so that monastic religion might be maintained there and an abbey established with my aid.

Moreover, I gave to Saint Peter and his monks, for various uses, the forest which, because of the great number of stags, is called Hirsbrulis, from the southern side of the city toward the east, as far as the borders of the region of Orlant, which region I handed over as a benefice to Pippin, count palatine. I nevertheless gave to the above-mentioned monastery villages made by the Slavs in the same forest: [S.] Tuneckdorf, Tubrachtet and Tuttellet, Hochdorf, and several others; and the water of the Gera, [unclear], to the monks on the southern side of the city as far as the boundary of the manor of my ministerial Gisbotus. I also gave from my court, for the uses of the brothers, fifty measures of wheat, one hundred of barley, and as many of oats, and all my other possessions in Thuringia. To maintain this place beloved to me, I gave my ministerials, with all their offspring and possessions, whose names are these: Gisbotus, Gilbertus, Eckhardus, Volffoldus, Hysen, Egenhen, Volffgeirius, Omarus, Sigeberius, Theodoricus, Aidelborus, Adelgerus, Gelferatus, Hingfridus, Huntzelin, Guntherinus, and all the rest of my male and female servants in Thuringia.

So that this handing-over to my lord Jesus Christ may remain firm forever, we have caused it to be confirmed by our letters, and we have asked it to be confirmed by the [unclear] of Rigibert, bishop of Mainz; we have fastened it with our ring, and with our seal affixed we have completed the charter. At Mainz, on the Kalends of March, in the presence of Bishop Rugebert. The sign of the most [unclear] lord Dagobert, king of the Franks. Witnesses of all these matters are these: Pippin, mayor of the palace, and his son Charles; Rikebert, bishop of Mainz; Gunther, a pagan count; Count Eckebi; the whole church in Thuringia around the Rhine in Mainz. These things were enacted in the seven hundred sixtieth year of the Lord’s incarnation, in the ninth indiction.

Far be it from me, Trithemius, to fight against the truth of this asserted foundation, so ancient, if it stands; but I do not quite see how truth can subsist in it. Therefore I shall here also briefly note the reasons which occur to me for doubting, after those, that is, which I wrote on behalf of Hirsau.

The first consideration, which prevents me from granting that Dagobert was the founder of the often-mentioned Erfurt monastery, is that the calculation of the years does not agree; for if this very foundation is ascribed to Dagobert the Great, it conflicts with the written instrument no less than with the truth of the computed time. For he died, as we said above, in the six hundred forty-fifth year of the Lord’s nativity, in the third Roman indiction, not less than sixty years before the donation on this page. But if it is assigned to that last Dagobert, who is Clovis, the disagreement of the years follows nonetheless, because he began to reign in the year of the Lord 715 and died in the year 719. How, then, could he have handed over letters of a foundation of this kind in the year of the Lord 706?

*Edited [Rasol?], fol. 82. It is shown to be false by the brothers of Hirsau.*

*Copy* *Annals of Trithemius, 61*

...as was said above, he once built; he often visited it in person; for some time he lived there among the brothers in the diocese of Trier. He formed the morals of the brothers according to the intent of the Rule of Saint Benedict, and adorned the place.

*Schuttern.* The monastery of Schuttern also, which stands three miles above Strasbourg, a city of Alsace, was founded by the same Saint Pirminius, as is found clearly written in the original volume of his Life, which we have in our possession. Nor is it an objection that the brothers of that same monastery, showing no documents of truth, say that Offo, king of England, when he was making for Rome out of devotion, in the times of Saint Gregory the First, pope, was moved by the pleasantness of the place and founded a monastery there; since King Offo and his brother, as we said above under King Hildebert, made for Rome and became monks in the year of the Lord 707, in the fifth Roman indiction. But Saint Pope Gregory, under whom they say that Offo, king of England, came to Rome, had died earlier, in the year of the Lord 605, in the eighth Roman indiction. Sigebert bears witness for our assertion in the Chronicles. *A false opinion is seriously refuted.*

The monastery of Schwarzach, situated in the diocese of Strasbourg, the same saint likewise founded, as the writer of his Life testifies in the original.

The monastery of Gengenbach in the diocese of Strasbourg, which is one mile distant from Schuttern, the same writer of the Life of Saint Pirminius testifies was founded by him.

The monastery which the Latins call Mauri monasterium, but in the vernacular Morsmunster, in the diocese of Strasbourg, the same saint founded.

The monastery of Neuwiller also, in the same diocese of Strasbourg, the same saint built; its monks, with their abbot, in our times withdrew from the order.

*There are two monasteries in Bavaria, Altach Upper and [unclear].* There are two monasteries of our order of one name in Bavaria, of which one is called Altach Upper, but [the other] Lower. In the Deeds of the Dukes of Bavaria we read that Duke Odilo, father of Duke Tassilo, founded Lower Altach. But in the deeds of Saint Pirminius [unclear] is expressed, nor Lower; therefore it is clear that Pirminius built Upper there. The monastery of the same Benedictine order, which is called Murbach, [he also built], as is contained in his Life.

The monastery also in the town of Amorbach, in the diocese of Wurzburg, of our aforementioned order, in which the saint appointed his disciple Amor as abbot, he built anew from the foundations. And many other things which we do not know.

In the fifth year of Theodoric, king of the Franks, Bede the Venerable died, priest and monk in England, a learned and holy man, who wrote many volumes for the benefit of readers, to the honor of the supreme and undivided Godhead. Theodoric, king of the Franks, died in the fifteenth year of his reign, but in the year of the Lord's nativity 741, in the ninth Roman indiction.

*The Sixty-First.*

Hilderic, son of King Theodoric, succeeding his father, reigned in name only for nine years. For all the power and wealth of the kingdom were held by the mayor of the palace, Charles, surnamed Martel, that is, the Hammer, to whom the sum of affairs belonged. Nor was anything else at all permitted to the king except that, content with the royal name, with flowing hair, [unclear], he should hear those coming [unclear] and give to them as they departed the answers which he had been taught or ordered, as if from his own power; he possessed nothing else except what the mayor of the palace furnished at his own discretion.

In the same year Charles Martel died, mayor of the palace of the Franks, duke of Brabant and count of Namur; since he was very warlike and fortunate in all things, he greatly enlarged the borders of the kingdom. He conquered in war and overcame with the sword the Saxons, Bavarians, Burgundians, Sorbs, the Bulgarians dwelling beyond the Danube, also the Gascons, Vandals, Goths and Saracens in Spain, the Frisians, and many other nations round about. Concerning his deeds, whether good or bad, and how he [unclear] ecclesiastical [things] to his soldiers...

60 *Compendium, Book I.*

In the year of the Lord 711 the Roman indiction was the fourth, not the ninth.

The letters of foundation which they have were never sealed.

It is manifest that the Hirsaugians founded the place.

The second consideration, which made me doubtful, is this: that in the aforesaid written instrument of the letters the ninth Roman indiction is given, although it was the fourth, and by no means the ninth, as a skilled ecclesiastical computist will clearly find.

The third consideration gives rise in me to a strong suspicion of fabrication, because the aforementioned letters of foundation, which the brothers at Saint Peter’s in Erfurt show as originals, are protected by no seal, although a hole appears in the parchment, as if the seal had fallen off because of excessive antiquity.

The fourth consideration is in no way inferior to those set out above, because it would be found plainly written in the life and deeds of the blessed William, abbot of Hirsau, that he built seven new monasteries of our order, among which the often-mentioned monastery of Saint Peter in Erfurt is counted fourth in order. I deliberately pass over many other considerations, lest prolixity create tedium for the reader.

Therefore, just as I wrote and long ago showed by many arguments in the very first volume of my Chronicles of Hirsau, so it has been necessary for me to think, and to set before the fabrication which I believe I have discovered, the truth.

*The Fifty-Ninth.*

Lotharius, brother of the aforesaid King Clodoveus, or Dagobert, after his brother’s death, in the year of the Lord, as we have said, 719, in the second indiction, by the advancement of Charles Martel, mayor of the palace of the Franks, was raised to be king and reigned seven years. Against him the priest Daniel, whom the Franks in Neustria had appointed king for themselves, together with his mayor of the palace Regenfrid, contended in dissension. Daniel, however, had changed his name, calling himself Helperic.

In the year of the Lord 720, Hilperic the anti-king, Regenfrid the mayor of the palace, having Eudo, duke of Aquitaine, as their ally, gathered forces and advanced to war against King Lotharius and his mayor of the palace Charles. But, defeated by Charles’s troops, they fled with great difficulty. Eudo, returning in confusion to Aquitaine, took Helperic, who was Daniel, away with him.

In the third year of King Lotharius, Charles Martel, mayor of the palace, pursuing Regenfrid, besieged him at Angers; and, when the city had been taken, he accepted him in surrender. After peace had been established between them, he granted him the city to live in; thereafter he himself powerfully held everywhere the principate of the whole kingdom of the Franks.

In the fifth year of the aforementioned Lotharius, king of the Franks, which was the seven hundred and fourth year of the Lord’s Nativity, in the seventh Roman indiction, the Bavarians, refusing to pay tribute to the Franks, prepared themselves for open rebellion. When this matter had become known to Charles, mayor of the palace, he assembled a great army of the Franks, set out into Bavaria, and attacked the disobedient in war; he powerfully brought them back to complete subjection.

In the following year, Charles, mayor of the palace of the Franks, moved an expedition into Alemannia; joining battle with the rebellious Alemanni, he emerged victorious. He overcame Lanfrid, their duke, and forced their land into subjection.

Lotharius, king of the Franks, reigning in name alone, died in the seventh year of his reign, in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 726, in the seventh indiction.

*The Sixtieth.*

Theodoric, Lotharius’s nephew through his brother, namely the son of the aforesaid King Clodoveus, whom others called Dagobert, after his uncle had died and Helperic Daniel the priest had likewise departed this life, who while Lotharius was alive and after his death had acted as king for eight years, was raised to be king of the Franks by the mayor of the palace, Charles Martel, and reigned fifteen years.

In these times there flourished in Gallic Francia Saint Pirminius, formerly a monk of the monastery of Saint Maurus the abbot, bishop of Meaux in the province of Sens, a man admirable for learning and holiness. For love of Christ, to preach the right faith to peoples, he came into the regions of Germany, where by word and example he converted many to the worship of truth and founded several monasteries.

Among these, the following, known to us, are counted as principal: the monastery of Saint Maurice the martyr in Dolegia, in the diocese of Trier, which the great King Dagobert, as above 

*Compendium, Book I, of the Annals of Trithemius.*

[unclear] dignities, and plundered churches, and because of those crimes was seen after death buried in hell, we have related more fully in the first volume of our Annals, of which this is the compendium.

He left three sons: Pippin, Carloman, and Grifo. Of these, Pippin and Carloman divided their father’s principate between themselves, excluding Grifo, and in this way ruled over the Franks for four years. After four years, however, Carloman, moved by the divine spirit, resigned the whole principate to his brother Pippin, went to Rome, and became a monk on Monte Cassino. Pippin then ruled the principate alone for six years, and, after King Hilderic had been deposed, was made king by common vote.

*Grifo is captured and consigned to custody. Carloman became a monk. Pippin holds the principate in the [unclear] year.*

Grifo, grieving that he had been scorned by his brothers, on the advice of his mother seized the city of Laon in advance and declared war on his brothers. His mother was the stepmother of Pippin and Carloman. They quickly gathered their army, surrounded Laon with a siege, took the city, and held their brother captive for four years.

*Saint Winfrid, who is Boniface, archbishop of Mainz. The monasteries of Hersfeld and Fulda are founded. Convents of nuns at Kitzingen and Bischofsheim.*

In these times there flourished in the kingdom of the Franks Saint Boniface, English by nation, a monk by profession, archbishop of the church of Mainz by rank, an apostolic man, who by preaching converted the Thuringians and many others to Christ, for whom he afterward suffered martyrdom while preaching in Frisia. He [founded?] two [monasteries?] in the forest of Buchonia, [unclear] diocese: one of them is called Hersfeld, in the diocese of Mainz; the other, from the river Fulda flowing past it, in which he was buried, is in the diocese of Würzburg.

He also built several convents of nuns; among them there still stands out the monastery in the town of Kitzingen beside the Main, in the diocese of Würzburg. Over it he appointed a holy virgin named Hadeloga; [the reading concerning] Thecla, whom he named, born from England, [is unclear]. Another was near the town of Bischofsheim, beside the Tauber, in the diocese of Mainz; over it he appointed Saint Lioba, a virgin beloved by God, likewise English by homeland. Of that convent nothing survives today.

*Odilo, duke of Bavaria, [took Pippin’s sister as wife?]. Adelung the priest, blind, receives sight. The bishopric of Würzburg is established.*

In the year of the Lord’s nativity 746, which was the fifth year of King Hilderic, in the fourteenth Roman indiction, Adelung, a priest at Würzburg, blind and warned in a dream to seek the bodies of Saint Kilian the bishop and his companion martyrs, recovered his sight when the [unclear] bones had been found. When Saint Boniface, archbishop of Mainz, learned of this miracle, with the help of Pippin, prince of the court of the Franks, he obtained from Pope Zacharias that he should establish a new episcopal seat at Würzburg, to the honor of almighty God and of Saint Kilian the bishop and his companion martyrs.

Therefore, in the seventh year of Hilderic, king of the Franks, and in the year of the Lord’s nativity 748, in the first indiction, Saint Burghard, English by nation and a monk by profession, was ordained by Saint Boniface, archbishop of Mainz, as the first bishop of the church of Würzburg, and presided for forty years. And in the same year little crosses, marked as if with oil, appeared on people’s linen garments.

In the year of the Lord’s nativity 759, in the second indiction, Hilderic, king of the Franks, [unclear] in the [unclear] of the kingdom. Pippin [unclear]. *The compendium of the annals of Johannes Trithemius, abbot, follows [unclear]. It comprises in all 1189 years. Born in the year 1462, on the first of February, at [unclear].*

*The end of the compendium or abridgment of the chronicles, or annals, of Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Saint James at Würzburg, formerly of Sponheim, concerning the origin and kings of the Franks.* Completed on the twentieth day of the month of November, in the year of the Lord 1514, in the fifty-second year of his age.

And *To the Reader.*

And this, indeed, is all that remains to us from those most splendid and most carefully composed Trithemian annals of German affairs, preserved through the efforts of Christian Wechel, a printer most deserving of letters, from whose press it was published at Paris sixty years ago. Since, however, we hope, and certainly desire, that those works survive somewhere complete, or at least a good part of them, though hidden, we earnestly ask their possessors or custodians, and adjure them in the public name, that they would be willing to communicate them to the commonwealth and to posterity with the same generosity with which they see us act; meanwhile we offer our own labor, as far as it lies in us, for publishing them correctly and elegantly.

*A Compendium of Johannes Trithemius, Abbot, on the Origin of the People of the Franks, from the Last Twelve Books of Hunibald, of which Wasthaldus wrote the first six, from the entrance of the Sicambri into the regions of the Rhine in Germany. In which there is also an enumeration of the Bishops of Würzburg.*

[unclear]

In the year before the birth of the Lord 439, in the times of Cyrus, king of the Persians, and also of Ezra and Nehemiah, leaders of the Hebrews, in the 751st year after the destruction of the Trojans, the people of the Goths, having gone out from the island of Scandia, which is now called northern Gothia, attacked in war the Sicambri, who were remnants of the Trojans and were settled near the mouths of the Danube; they killed their king Anthenor, together with many Sicambri, and withdrew after taking spoils. Anthenor left two sons, Marcomirus and Suimon. Now it was the custom among the Sicambri that, from all the sons of the king at the time, if he had several, they should choose only one, whom they believed would be more useful and profitable for the kingdom. But if he had no son, they chose from his kinsmen one who was more suitable.

Marcomirus, therefore, the elder son of Anthenor, succeeded his father in the year before the birth of the Lord 411, and reigned over the Sicambri for twenty-eight years.

In the fourth year of his reign, when the Sicambri were being excessively harassed by the incursion of the Goths and of other neighboring peoples, they resolved to change their settlements. Accordingly, an embassy was sent to the Saxons in Germany, who themselves had come from the Trojans, and they begged them as brothers to permit them to dwell in some corner of their land, without harm to their people. The Saxons consented, promising that they would give them the best settlements, as they did. And in the seventh year of King Marcomirus the Sicambri came into Germany, in the month of April: 175,658 men most ready for war, bringing with them their wives, children, and whatever substance they had.

In the twentieth year of his reign, Marcomirus crossed the Rhine and made war with the Cisalpine Gauls; he killed many, occupied the land, and entrusted it to his brother to be guarded, as to a duke, or under a petty king. From that time, for 910 years, the Sicambri, who were afterward called Franks, never ceased from the harassment of Gaul, until at last they obtained it all with much blood of their own. And finally they subjected to their rule not only Gaul, but Alamannia, Swabia, Bavaria, Alsace, the Helvetians, Thuringia, Saxony, Burgundy, and that land which, situated between the Thuringians and the Swabians, is today called ancient or eastern Francia, and alone retains the old name of the Franks; Austria, the whole Rhine from its source to the sea, the Menapii, Batavians, Mosellani, Treveri, Metz, indeed all Germany together with the whole threefold Gaul and Spain.

It is certain that the Sicambri received their first settlements where the people of Guelders, Westphalians, Münster, and Cleves now are. Then, after crossing the Rhine, they subjected to themselves the land of the Tungri, Liège, Maastricht, Holland, and the rest. For a long time the name of Sicambri remained among them.

*64 Johannes Trithemius.*

until at length under a Frankish king, whom his enemies called fierce, the name gradually began to be changed. But King Marcomirus, after many deeds bravely done, died in the year 410 before the Nativity. He left three sons: Antenor, Priam, and Nicanor.

*The chronicle of Wasthald ends here.*

Down to this year Wasthald brought and completed his twelve books, on the origin of the Sicambri from the destruction of Troy, continuing them year by year for 768 years. From here Hunibald, in six books, continues the history of the kings and deeds of the Sicambri for 930 years, down to the death of Clovis the great king.

Antenor, succeeding his father in the kingdom, reigned for thirty years. He was held in great honor among his Sicambri, and obtained the very strong friendship of the Saxons; with their auxiliary help he undertook many wars against the Gauls and Romans. For his brothers Priam and Nicanor faithfully assisted him, and they bravely carried out several incursions against the Gauls after crossing the Rhine. But Suimo, his uncle, was always his most faithful helper on his side.

In the eighth year of his reign, when the Sicambri complained of the narrowness of their settlements, especially because pastures were lacking for their cattle, he ordered them to wait a little until the time was suitable for the matter. When a very cold winter set in and all the rivers were frozen, he assembled 80,000 armed Sicambri and invaded the land of a neighboring people, which lay between the northern sea and their territory. All the males, even infants, were slaughtered; only the women he spared. He distributed the region to his people; it abounded in excellent pastures. This land was later called Frisia from a certain Sicambrian prince who was called Friso.

*Suino, duke, brother of Marcomar.*

*Antenor reigns over the Sicambri for thirty years.*

In the twelfth year of Antenor, Suimo his uncle died. He left two sons, Marcomirus and Hector; the first of these perished in the Rhine, and the second administered the county beyond the river Rhine in his father’s place under King Antenor. Priam was appointed by his brother King Antenor as prince of the northern land which they had newly acquired, that is, around the Germanic Sea. From these many princes were born in the course of time, of whom Hunibald records several, some dukes, some counts, but all remained under the command of one king. King Antenor died when the twenty-seventh year of his reign was completed, which was 380 before the Nativity of the Lord, leaving one son named Priam.

Priam, son of Antenor, succeeding his father in the kingdom, reigned for twenty-four years. In his time the Sicambri, already having a great familiarity with the Saxons, began to forget their old language and fatherland, and gradually to use Germanic, until at length they all knew no other language except Theutonic alone. Many words remained among them which seem to have a Greek rather than a Germanic origin, as one who understands both Greek and Theutonic well knows; so it remains now.

*Theocalus, pontiff of the Sicambri, priest of Jove.*

In the sixth year of Priam, Marcomirus died, the duke of King Priam, a kinsman from Suimo. He left a son named Theocalus, whom the Sicambri appointed high priest of Jove; he was for them a prelate, seer, and father of kings. Up to that time the Sicambri had no temples of the gods, but stood and took counsel under oaks. In the eighth year of Priam, among many buildings the Sicambri constructed one very strong city, which they named Neopagus, near the Rhine, where the kings sat for a long time. They made a temple to Jove, whom they worshiped above the others. Theocalus was the priest of this shrine. Priam, after excellently executed invasions against those beyond the Rhine and the Gauls, died in the twenty-fourth year of his reign, 356 before the Nativity of Christ.

*Helenus reigned nineteen years.*

Helenus, son of Priam, succeeding his father, reigned for nineteen years. He venerated Pallas, for whom he built a sanctuary; he sacrificed the boys of captives. He had a bloody war with the Gauls in the region of the Tungri, in which he killed more than 16,000 of them and turned the rest to flight. Having occupied the region, he placed Sicambri there to inhabit it; he appointed princes with many fighters throughout the circuit, so that they might defend the people. King Helenus died in the nineteenth year of his reign, 337 before the Nativity of the Lord.

*King Diocles, reigning thirty-nine years.*

*King Diocles.*

*Saxons. Thuringians against the incursions of the Goths.*

In the tenth year of his reign, a multitude of peoples came out from the Scandinavian islands, which are now called Gothic. Pouring into the borders of Saxony, it carried off everything and devastated the region with sword and iron. Against this people the king of the Saxons, the king of Thuringia, and Diocles himself, king of the Sicambri, marched out to war, having in their army 210,000 brave men. A fierce battle was joined, in which more than 100,000 fighters fell on the side of the Goths. On the side of the Saxons, among the foremost fell Heriman, king of Thuringia, with 20,600 men, and the Saxons [unclear] all the plunder.

66 *Johannes Trithemius.*

... great or small, would presume to say or do anything evil against them. Hence the priests who were educating the sons of the nobles in the temples named the king Dickeobasan, that is, the just Basan. From this arose a proverb among the Sicambri: whenever one saw or heard another doing or saying evil, “Kennent gy die groten Basan nitt.” That is: “Do you not know great Basan?” As if he were saying, “Do you not know how just King Basanus is, who, if he has perceived you doing or saying such things, will without doubt cut off your head?”

In the fifth year of his reign, the king of the Orcades, having as helper the king of the Britons, came with many ships and armed men against the Sicambri and declared war on them. But King Basanus met them near the seashore, around the island where afterward a city was built by the Franks, whose name is Mesoburgus. But when the Orcadians and Britons saw from the ships so great an army of the Sicambri, they did not dare to disembark from the ships, but went back without accomplishing anything. The cause was the repudiation of Basanus’s wife, whom he had sent back, as I have said, to her father, the king of the Orcades.

When the Gauls again broke in toward the Rhine, where the colonies of the Sicambri were, Basanus came against them in the great strength of his men; there the Gauls were again routed and driven beyond the river Meuse. Having obtained the victory, the aforementioned King Basan built many castles and very strong fortifications on that side of the river Meuse toward the Rhine, where it turns to the east, in which he placed very strong military garrisons against the incursions of the Gauls. In the upper region between Agrippina and the Meuse he built a fortified castle bearing his own name, which he called Basan. In it many kings of the Sicambri and Franks afterward, for many years, held the palace and seat of the kingdom.

In the twenty-sixth year of his reign, Basanus, after many wars and very fierce battles which he waged with various peoples and nations, appointed priests in the temple of Jove, men most learned in Greek and German, in prophecy, in dreams, in the judgment of the stars, in ethics, in physics, and in metaphysics, who, with the gods conveying it, could give sound and right counsel to all who questioned them in any necessity whatsoever. When the king, who was the chief pontiff, was absent, the highest power of decrees rested with the priests, except for the person of the king, on whom they did not pass judgment.

At the temple of Pallas and of Venus the Tritonian goddess he appointed only virgins as priestesses. At certain times all men everywhere were permitted to enter to them, provided they were not joined to wives, and to do in the temple of Venus what her very name signifies. Whatever priestess conceived by such intercourse offered the offspring to Pallas, not to be killed, but to serve forever. Whoever from among these Tritonian priestesses obtained such a one as a wife was, after the birth of a child, praised as holy and very close to the gods. After the first birth each one was compelled to leave the temple, because the priestess who was now a mother had offered her chastity to Venus, and she could marry whomever she wished. Hunibald says more about these matters, which I pass over no less for the sake of modesty than of brevity.

Finally King Basanus led an army from the north toward the south, against the people called the Tegarañ, and it lies between Mainz and Saxony as far as the river Main. King Basan possessed all this land from the northern sea as far as the Main, between the Saxons and the Rhine, that is, from the mouths of the Rhine as far as Mainz; and, having built very strong cities and many garrisons, he fortified it so that it could not easily be overcome. The Saxons and Thuringians, enemies of the Romans, rejoiced together.

After this victory, the great King Basanus, on his birthday at Neopagus among the marshes of the Rhine and the sea, summoned his brothers and sons with many nobles of the kingdom to the solemnity. For seven days he performed sacred rites to the ancestral gods; he showed Jove, visible to all, clouded above the temple. On the eighth day, with the consent of all the nobles, he designated his firstborn son Clodomirus as king over the Sicambri. Afterward, in a marvelous song in the language of his people, he foretold future things to the nation, commended his sons, enjoined justice, and suddenly appeared nowhere. I do not know what divinity I should infer. As Amerodacus says, he was most eager for it; he cultivated justice, loved his subjects, was most dutiful to the good, most cruel to the wicked. To this day it is not known where he went. But the Sicambri, together with the Franks, having enrolled him among the gods, celebrated him for many years with sacred songs. He vanished in the public council.

*Clodomer reigns for 18 years.* The author is Ameradatus. In the thirty-sixth year of his reign, in the year 240 before the birth of Christ, he whom his own people named Basangot [unclear]. Clodomer, the firstborn son of Balangot the great king, succeeding in the kingdom just as his father had ordained with the consent of the princes, reigned eighteen years. In his first year, as soon as the Gauls heard that Basan had vanished, they did not doubt that he was dead; and therefore, sending envoys to Clodomer his son, they demanded back from him all the land between the Meuse and the Rhine which their ancestors, contrary to justice, had made violently subject to the Sicambri. But if he refused to do this, they threatened that they would recover everything by the sword. King Clodomer, however, as if he were going to hold counsel with his nobles concerning the pressing business, [unclear] the envoys of the Gauls...

*On the Origin of the Franks.*

Recovering the booty for their own men who had been despoiled, they returned. But the spoils of the enemy, which were many, they divided among their allied friends.

Meanwhile, when the Gauls who were living beyond the Rhine as far as the British Sea, the Morini, Ambiani, Tungri, and their friends who were in those regions, had heard that Diocles had left the kingdom with a great army of his people, they gathered in a great multitude and resolved utterly to destroy the Sicambri, who were on that side between the Meuse and the Rhine. When the leaders of the Sicambri learned this through scouts, they divided the army into three parts, arranging two in separate battle-lines against the enemy, while they placed the third in ambush. As the Gauls approached with only one line, when they saw that the Sicambri had two lines, they were thrown into confusion; but there was no time to arrange the lines otherwise, since the Sicambri at once directed their first line straight against the Gauls. The second line, breaking in from the side, shattered the order of the Gauls. And when the battle was fiercely fought, and the strength of the Gauls was giving way into flight, the Sicambri came upon them from ambush. Enclosed by the Sicambri, the Gauls were slaughtered like cattle, so that out of 88,000 scarcely 10,000 remained. For many were drowned in the river as they fled.

Exulting in this victory, the Sicambri sacrificed to their gods Jupiter and Venus not only animals, but also children and as many of the Gallic enemy as they had led away captive, offering the males to Jupiter and the females to Venus. From that time the Sicambri, enriched by the spoils of their enemies and by the deeds they had accomplished among the neighboring peoples, became feared throughout the surrounding region. Diocles, through all the days of his reign, had war with the Gauls, and there was scarcely a year in which he did not at least once move his army against them.

He died in the thirty-ninth year of his reign, 297 years before the birth of Christ. He left four sons, whose names were these: Helenus, Priamus, Nicanor, and Basanus, who themselves also left many sons after them.

Helenus, the eldest son of Diocles, reigned after his father for fourteen years, a wanton and idle man, in whose time the Gauls, often making raids, inflicted many losses on the Sicambri. Against them his brothers, with the princes of the kingdom, frequently led the army and fought with varying fortune, sometimes defeated and sometimes also victorious. But the king remained at home, idle and given over to lust.

In the thirteenth year of his reign, the Sicambri, assembled at Neopagus, by the common judgment of all deposed Helenus, an idle and useless king, from the kingdom and compelled him to return to private life, in the year 283 before the birth of Christ our Savior. In his place they elected his younger brother.

Basanus, the younger son of the late Diocles, after his brother Helenus had been deprived of rule, was appointed king by the common will and election of the Sicambri, and reigned for [unclear] years: a man wise in his generation, high-minded, warlike, and not inferior to his father in fortune. The Sicambri made him both king and pontiff of the sacred rites. Because of his wisdom and his wonderfully performed deeds they commonly called him great Basan, in the vernacular die groten Basan. For the Sicambri held him in such reverence and honor that they venerated him no differently than a true god. Under penalty of certain death, no one was permitted to contradict his command, even in the least matter. Wherever he went, he ordered a rope or cord to be carried before him, and a sword as a sign of justice, which he observed so firmly that he spared neither son nor brother, neither princes nor dukes, indeed no one, who had committed even a small offense against the law. By law he marked robbery, theft, adultery, deceit, fraud, and every injury or insult among the Sicambri as subject to the penalty of death, and he punished without any mercy all who offended even a little in these matters against the legal sanctions.

He had a young son named Sedanus. This man, led astray by youthful desire, had committed with the wife of a certain man of humble condition what he knew to be forbidden by law, and [unclear]. His father the king, learning of this matter, ordered him to be arrested and beheaded with a sword. Because of this, the mother of the young man and the king’s wife, who was the daughter of the king of the Orcades, was moved by very bitter sorrow, and, driven by womanly lack of restraint, cried out against the king: “O cruel tyrant, not king, you who practice cruelty under the title of law, how will you spare others, when you have slain your own son?” To her the king said before all the people: “Woman, it is yours to obey your husband, not to reproach the king. I swear to you by my god, Saturnian Jupiter, that if I were not moved by anger, I would kill you this very hour, you who have always been most dear to me.”

After eight days the king, by the judgment of the princes and nobles of the kingdom, repudiated the woman, although she was very beautiful and uniquely beloved by him above all the rest, and sent her back to her father, the king of the Orcades. From that time the Sicambri began to fear Basanus their king so greatly that no one among [unclear].

*The Gauls, in the absence of their king, attempt to lay waste the Sicambri.*

*The Sicambri sacrificed to Jupiter and Venus.*

*Helenus reigned after his father for 14 years.*

*King Helenus is deposed.*

*Basanus, a great king and pontiff, reigns for 36 years.*

*The king, out of love for the law, beheads his own adulterous son.*

*King Basan repudiates his wife, who is angry over the killing of her son.* *On the Origin of the Franks.*

... in the matter, having drawn them out with fair words, he kept them with him for a rather long time; and, prudently taking care that no rumor of the things he had conceived in his mind should come to their knowledge, he ordered his men to provide for them abundantly in all things and to spend pleasant days with them. Meanwhile Clodomer, secretly sending messengers to the kings of Thuringia and Saxony, called them to his aid; with his own men, once a great army of fighters had been assembled, he conceived war in his mind against the Gauls. When matters had been arranged, he honorably dismissed the messengers; and lest anything concerning the armies already sent ahead could come to their knowledge on the road, he added companions from among his own men, as if for the conduct of a safe journey as far as Gaul, with letters.

The tenor of the letters contained this: “Clodomer the Great King. We marvel at you, Gauls, that you seek to receive from us the land which our forefathers once obtained from yours by the law of war, as from their enemies, from whom they had received many wrongs, by just vicissitude. Consider that your strength is unequal to ours; cease from this rashness of yours. Since I know that you wish to come against us, we have resolved to meet you with spirits unbroken, and to defend with the sword what our ancestors acquired with the sword.” When the Gauls learned these things, they assembled a great army and, after a bridge had been built over the river Meuse, led the army across against the Sicambri, leaving a guard around the bridge lest it be occupied by their adversaries.

King Clodomer dissembled all these things as though he did not know them; and, having drawn up his soldiers, he divided the army into four parts, having in each one more than thirty-six thousand fighters. He arranged two parts into as many battle-lines. The third he placed in ambush. The fourth he sent around from the flank so that, after killing the guards, they might seize the bridge first. Therefore the Gauls came, themselves having two battle-lines; they engaged with the Sicambri not far from the river Meuse, near the fortress of Delon. But the Sicambri, like men in flight, gradually withdrew, until they had drawn the Gauls farther from the river, as far as the place of the ambush. There indeed a fierce battle was joined. For the Sicambri stood firm, fighting bravely with the Gauls. Meanwhile Clodomer’s fourth army, wheeling around, occupied the bridge. When the signal of this event had been received, those who were lying hidden burst out from the ambush and attack the Gauls, fighting fiercely. At last the Gauls took flight; since they did not know that the bridge had been occupied beforehand by the Sicambri, they hastened to retreat. And behold, suddenly they saw that they were shut in among the enemy, and almost all were miserably cut down and slaughtered, a few escaping to the woods by the speed of their horses. Hunibald wrote at sufficient length the rest of the brave deeds done by King Clodomer. King Clodomer died in the eighteenth year of his reign, in the year 224 before the birth of Christ, leaving three sons: Nicanor, Helianus, and Helenus.

Nicanor, the firstborn of King Clodomer, succeeding his father, reigned twenty-six years. In his time the Goths and Slavs again invaded the borders of the Saxons; against them, when asked by the king of Saxony, he went forth to war and returned victorious, enriched with many spoils. He waged battle with the king of the Arcadians in favor of the king of Britain, his father-in-law, whose daughter, named Constantia, he had as wife. By her he had five sons: Marcomer, Anthenor, Priam, Helenus, and Clodius. The firstborn succeeded his father in the kingdom. The second ruled the maritime regions. The third died in England. The fourth held the duchy in Germany on this side of the Rhine, between Saxony, the Rhine, and Mainz. The fifth was duke between the rivers Meuse and Rhine. King Nicanor died in the twenty-sixth year of his reign, in the year 196 before the birth of Christ.

Marcomer, the elder son of Nicanor, succeeding his father, reigned eighteen years: a prince of singular prudence and moderation, dutiful toward his subjects, severe toward enemies. For he, excellently taught by the priests of the sacrifices of Jove in all the wisdom of the ancients, in prophecies, predictions, dreams, and auguries, had no equal among the Germans. He frequently had the brave deeds of his ancestors recited before him in the temple in the palace and sung in his native songs. He waged many battles, victorious against the Romans, Gauls, Goths, and various peoples; Hunibald, the historiographer of the Franks, diligently wrote their sequence. He died in the twenty-third year of his reign, in the year 158 before the birth of Christ.

Clodius, the firstborn son of King Marcomer, succeeding his father, reigned eleven years. In his time the Gauls, with the aid of the Romans, making an incursion beyond the Meuse, greatly crushed the Sicambri. In the last year of his reign, after assembling a very great army both of his own men and of Saxons, he again fought with the Gauls, by whom, since he did not keep himself sufficiently cautiously in the column, he was killed. The Sicambri, however, notwithstanding the king’s death, pursued the war and defeated the Gauls. King Clodius was killed in the year 156 before the birth of Christ, and in the eleventh year of his reign.

Anthenor, the elder son of Clodius, reigned after his father for sixteen years. He made a truce with the Gauls for ten years; it pleased the Romans. King Anthenor was more a lover of peace than of war. He would gladly have avenged his father’s murder, but at that time he could not. This king forbade the sons of enemies to be sacrificed to the gods. He died in the year 121 before the birth of Christ, and in the sixteenth year of his reign.

*The Gauls demand Monapia back from the Sicambri.*

*Clodomer replied to the Gauls’ demands in this manner.*

*The Sicambri overcome, defeat, and kill the Gauls, [unclear].*

*Nicanor, son, king, reigns twenty-six years.*

*Marcomer reigned after his father twenty-eight years.*

*Clodius the Sicambrian reigned eleven years.*

*Anthenor the Sicambrian reigned sixteen years.*

*Amber the Sicambrian reigned [unclear].* *Johannes Trithemius*

*King Clodomer reigned 20 years.* Clodomer, son of Anthenor, reigned after his father for twenty years. In his first year the Romans overthrew the Numantines through Scipio and brought them under their power. In his sixth year the Gauls, after the truce which they had made with his father, King Anthenor, ten years before had ended, gathered a great army and crossed the Meuse. Clodomer met them, and a very severe battle was joined, and many fell on both sides. But the Gauls who remained withdrew, and as long as King Clodomer lived they crossed the Meuse no more. King Clodomer died in the 121st year before the birth of the Lord, and in the twentieth year after receiving the kingdom of the Sicambri.

*King Merodactus reigned twenty-eight years.* Merodach, the first-born son of Clodomer, reigned after his father for twenty-eight years, a vigorous, very bold, and exceedingly warlike prince, who waged many wars against the Romans, the Gauls, the Mainz people, the Trier people, and the Cologne people. For, with Saxons and Germans as auxiliaries, he led an army of 220,000 fighters against the Romans into Italy; and, devastating the region, he reached as far as Ravenna with his forces, and, enriched with much spoil, returned victorious to his own lands. Yet on his return he grievously afflicted many colonies of the Romans and inflicted great losses upon them. Hence, after many victories as well as battles, the Romans at last, joining the Gauls to themselves, advanced to war against him in the borders of the Sicambri, between the Meuse and the Rhine. And lest the Saxons, according to their custom, should come to the aid of the Sicambri, the Romans first drew away the Slavs and Goths, who were to make incursions into the borders of eastern Saxony. King Merodach therefore had as his helper the northern king of the Cimbri with one hundred thousand fighters and islanders. Of his own men, however, he had two hundred thousand.

And so in the twenty-second year of his reign Marius, prince of the Romans, sent the Roman legions together with the Gauls, under the leadership of Theodomenus, beyond the Meuse against the Sicambri, and at the same time they fought fiercely; and many thousands on both sides fell dead, and the Sicambri fled. For on their side twenty thousand were killed and more were captured.

After this Merodach, renewing his army, again both invaded and overcame the Gauls. He died in the ninety-third year before the birth of Christ, in the twenty-eighth year of his reign.

Cassander, succeeding his father in the kingdom, reigned for twenty-one years. In his time the Gauls, with auxiliary Roman soldiery, crossed the river Meuse and often harried the borders of the Sicambri. Borbista, king of the Goths, fought bravely against them, and came with a very great number of fighters together with the king of the Saxons; a fierce battle was joined. Borbista, king of the Goths, fled, having lost many of his own. Afterwards [Pugnatus?] again devastated the region, plundered the Saxons as far as the river Vistula, and fled back. He often fought against the Gauls, often victorious, and no less at times scorned by fortune. He died in the seventy-second year before the birth of Christ, in the twenty-first year of his reign.

Antharius, the first-born son of King Cassander, reigned thirty-five years. Of him Hunibald writes that he crushed the Mainz people, Roman colonists, with a pitiable slaughter. With an innumerable army he entered Gaul, burned villages, and carried back endless booty and spoils. But when he had grown old, in the last year of his reign, the Gauls again burst into Batavia; he met them with an army and was killed with twenty thousand of his men. The Gauls made a great slaughter against the Sicambri. He was killed in the thirty-eighth year before the birth of Christ, in the thirty-fifth year of his reign.

Francus, the elder son of King Antharius, succeeding his father, reigned twenty-six years. From him the Sicambri thereafter obtained the name of Franks, which they retain down to the present day. For he was a fierce man, warlike, and the most keen defender of his people; he waged many wars with foreign nations, always victorious, and a glorious triumphator. In his third year the Goths again, together with the Scandinavian peoples, laid waste the borders of Saxony and settled there for ten years. But when, successively, they were always bursting into Saxony more and more, the Saxons, compelled by fear of them, called Francus, king of the Sicambri, together with the Thuringians, to their aid; and with a multitude of 230,000 fighters they advanced to war against the Goths. The Sicambri, however, fighting more boldly than the rest and frequently invoking the name of their king in battle as if it were some divine power, cried out, shouting: “Here, Frank! Here, Frank!” From that time that people changed its name, and little by little not only among themselves but also by other nations they were called Franks rather than Sicambri, until at last that name prevailed everywhere, so that they were called Franks and no longer, or only rarely, Sicambri, as Salagastald testifies. For the people itself took such delight in the novelty of the name that they asked the king and princes to sanction by perpetual edict that they should no longer be called Sicambri, but Franks. This request pleased the king, as one who desired the immortality of his name-*On the Origin of the Franks*

…to attain immortality, and for the nation to be distinguished by his own name. He decreed that henceforth they should no longer be called Sicambri, but Franks, that is, noble, free, or warlike, and to be feared by the other nations. Yet the name Sicambrian was brought into oblivion not suddenly, but over much time and by degrees, as is found among the writers of those times, who sometimes called them Sicambri, sometimes Franks.

Remigius also, bishop of Rheims, when he was about to baptize Clovis, king of the Franks, who was the first of the Frankish kings to become Christian, after the Alemanni had been overcome, in the presence of a multitude of nobles, said to him as he laid aside the royal ornaments and humbled himself at the font, with all of us hearing, in another intelligible voice: “Meekly bow your neck, Sicamber; adore what you burned; burn what you adored,” that is, adore Christ, whose churches you burned as a pagan; burn the idols which you then adored.

This King Francus, after the Goths had been driven from the borders of the Saxons, on his return with his army met a messenger saying that the Gauls had crossed the Meuse, had laid waste the region, and had withdrawn with a great booty of spoils. Immediately King Francus, having accepted eighty thousand Saxons as auxiliaries, joined with his own an army of [unclear] thousand fighters, crossed the Rhine, and came as far as the Meuse. Seeing the desolation of the region which the Gauls had made, he was moved in spirit and swore, saying: “See, my fellow-soldiers, what these treaty-breaking Gauls have done. I swear by the head of my father Antharius that I will give no rest to my head until I have avenged myself on them.” And all praised his purpose.

Thus, when the Meuse had been crossed, he stationed forty thousand to guard the bridge; with the rest of the army he advanced into Gaul and made such slaughter as none of the Sicambri before him either could or dared to imagine. For, advancing as far as the river Tabul toward the sea, from the north he consumed the Tarubani, the Tongri, the Legii, and whatever lies between or beside them, with fire and sword so cruelly that he spared neither infants nor women. He routed the Gauls who engaged him with such fierceness that he seemed to be some divine power, not a man. Hence all the nations round about, greatly terrified, called them Franks, that is, fierce men. More than two hundred thousand Gauls fell by the sword of the Franks, with men, women, boys, and infants.

Moved by this, the Senate and People of Rome sent legions of soldiers against the Germans, with Marcus Lollius as commander; for they could not safely attack the Franks unless they had first overcome the Saxons. At first the Romans were victorious and killed eighteen thousand Germans. But when King Francus heard of the slaughter the Romans had made, he sent his son Chlogio as commander, with a great army of fighters, against the Romans; after many of them had been killed, they compelled the rest to flee, in the twenty-fourth year of King Francus.

Francus, king of the Franks, after many deeds bravely done, died in the twenty-eighth year of his reign, but in the ninth year before the birth of Christ. His wars, customs, institutions, and laws were written by Clodomer, the supreme pontiff, in verse, and by Hunibald in prose.

Chlogio, the elder son of King Francus, succeeded his father and reigned thirty years: a most cunning man, an augur, seer, and wondrous magician. His mother Lothildis, daughter of the king of the Thuringians, was high priestess of the temple of Pallas; by her arts she drove mad all the enemies whom she wished against her son and the Franks. Clodomer, counsellor of the Franks, writes great things about these matters in Hunibald, things which exceed belief.

In the tenth year of his reign, King Chlogio, at the insistence of his mother, appointed his second-born son, named Phrisus, prince and duke of that region which afterward from his name has been called Phrisia down to the present day, against the incursions of the Cimbri and the Orchades. After ten years, with King Chlogio and all the Franks permitting, Phrisus was raised to kingship, yet on this condition, that he should pay tribute to the Franks each year: three hundred sixty oxen, twenty talents of pure butter, and three thousand royal cheeses. And thus Phrisia became a most powerful kingdom.

In the tenth year of the aforesaid Chlogio, king of the Franks, our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, the Son of God, was born in Bethlehem, a city of the tribe of Judah among the Jews in the province of Palestine. Before this, in the fourth year of Chlogio, the Romans laid waste Germany in hostile fashion, sometimes defeated and sometimes also victorious. Concerning the other deeds of Chlogio, his wars, prophecies, oracles, truces, and actions done with the Romans, see Hunibald. He died in the year of the Lord 20, but in the thirtieth year of his reign, after many deeds magnificently performed.

Herimer, the second-born son of King Chlogio, reigned after his father for twelve years, a man exceedingly warlike and bold. In the third year of his reign the Gauls, leading an army as far as the Meuse, in an unexpected hostile incursion [unclear] everything which seemed to belong to the Franks, or to consent to them [unclear].

*Johannes Trithemius*

They laid waste [unclear], and, after gathering booty, withdrew. When this became known to Herimer, he summoned to himself the leaders beyond the Meuse, deposed them, and, after fining [unclear] with the goods of the Franks, reduced them to private life. For he had prescribed this: a man placed in authority under the king of the Franks [unclear]. For he had prescribed this: a man established in authority under the king of the Franks [unclear] is reduced to private life. For this was the chief provision: if through [his?] negligence enemies invade and injure the land of our people, he shall pay half of his honors into the common purse of the king, and shall no longer be prince. If he willingly permitted this, he shall be punished with death, and his wives, with his children and goods, shall belong to the king.

After this he himself crossed the Meuse, fought many wars with the Gauls, and withdrew and fled, sometimes victorious and sometimes also defeated. At last, however, when the Romans were bringing aid to the Gauls in the war, he was killed in the twelfth year of his reign, and in the thirty-second year of the Lord’s nativity, while Christ himself was preaching salvation to the human race in Judea.

*Marcomerus reigned eighteen years.*

Marcomerus, brother of Herimer, succeeding to the kingdom of the Franks, reigned eighteen years. In his second year Jesus, the Son of God, suffered and died in Judea according to the flesh, and, rising from death on the third day, lives forever. In his fourteenth year Claudius Caesar of the Romans made Britain and the Orkney islands tributary to the Romans. By crossing between the Meuse and the Rhine he grievously afflicted the Franks, and with the aid of the Gauls forced them to retreat as far as the islands of the Rhine. King Marcomerus died in the fiftieth year of the Lord, and the eighteenth of his reign.

*Clodomarus reigned twelve years.*

Clodomerus, son of Marcomerus, succeeding his father in the kingdom, reigned twelve years. Crossing the Rhine with the army of his own people and of the Saxons, he compelled the Gauls to retreat beyond the Meuse, and recovered everything that had been lost. With the aid of the Germans he waged war against the Romans not far from Mainz and laid waste the fields of the Treveri. He died in the twelfth year of his reign, and in the sixty-second year of Christ.

*Anthenor reigned six years.*

Anthenor, son of Clodomarus, succeeding his father, reigned six years. Throughout all the time he reigned he waged war with the Gauls, and for this cause he died miserably. For in the last year of his reign he led an army over the river Meuse after a bridge had been built, and, laden with much plunder, returned without waiting for the Gauls. When part of the army of the Franks had crossed the river and the king with others was remaining last on the bank, suddenly the bridge, overloaded by the multitude of horsemen, broke and fell, and many were killed. The king, stunned and dismayed in spirit, was taking counsel with those who had remained with him about recovering the bridge, when it was announced to him that the Gauls were present with a great army and ready to fight. But since they were few, it did not seem safe to him to await the presence of the Gauls; and yet he could not flee otherwise than through the river. Therefore, throwing away his arms and whatever could weigh him down, keeping his belt over his tunic and his sword, he mounted his horse and tried to cross the river. The other foot-soldiers did likewise, having nowhere to flee, and entrusted themselves to the waters. Some of these reached the bank by swimming; the rest were submerged by the force of the waves, among them King Anthenor. With him perished nine most noble dukes of the Franks, all born of royal stock, namely: Duke Priamus, Duke Clodius, Duke Richimer, Duke Anthenor, Duke Marcomet, Duke Walther, Duke Clogio, Duke Herimer, and Duke [Luthvicie?], with sixty-three other nobles. And so Anthenor perished in the sixth year of his reign, the sixty-eighth year of the Lord’s nativity.

Ratherius, after the death of his father, reigned twenty-one years. In his second year Nero Caesar of the Romans began the first persecution against the Christians, in the fourteenth year of his rule, and committed other dreadful crimes. King Ratherius, however, was in conflict with the Gauls and Romans on all the days of his reign, and fought several battles with them. He died in the twenty-first year of his reign, in the eighty-ninth year of the Lord’s nativity.

Richimer, succeeding his father, reigned thirty-three years. He waged war with the Goths and came out victorious. For in the eleventh year of his reign the Goths were again laying waste the territories of the Saxons and Germans by a hostile incursion. Therefore Windekind, king of the Saxons, Richimerus, king of the Franks, and Hermanfrid, king of the Thuringians, engaging the Goths with a very great army of their peoples, killed twenty thousand of them and put the rest to flight. There is a town beside the river Oder named Franckenfurt, which the Franks are said to have founded at that time, after obtaining victory over the Goths. There King Richimerus appointed his second-born son duke, and left with him a great part of the army. The king [unclear] the wives, children, and all their household goods back into [Cisthenan?] Francia to them.

The name of the duke, the king’s son, was Suimo. His son Clodomer succeeded him in the dukedom, and the successor and son of that man was Suimo the Second, who in the year of the Lord 146 founded a city at the outlet of the river Spre-[Sui?], not far from the Germanic Sea, and from his own name called it Suimonia. They remained in that land for a long time, retaining the name of Franks, until at last they were called Marcomeri from a certain duke Marcomerus, whose son Brand built the city of Brandenburg.

*On the Origin of the Franks*

In the fifth year of King Richimer, Domitian Caesar of the Romans, the younger brother of Titus, after Nero stirred up the second persecution against the Christians; he also, first of all the Caesars, in his sixth year, ordered himself to be called Lord and God.

King Richimer, in the eleventh year of his reign, waged war with the Roman Gauls not far from the city of Basana, which is now called Aachen. At the same time the legions of Roman soldiers at Cologne, after a war with the Franks had been engaged not very successfully, on receiving news of the death of Caesar Cocceius Nerva, made Ulpius Trajanus Crinitus, a Spaniard by nation, emperor. He stirred up the third persecution against the Christians. Later, having been instructed, he ordered that Christians should not be sought out, but that only those who presented themselves voluntarily ought to be killed. Afterwards, however, changed again, he raised a fourth persecution against them. Richimer, king of the Franks, died in the year of the Lord 113, in the twenty-fourth year of his reign.

Odemar, the first-born son of Richimer, king of the Franks, reigned after his father for thirteen years, a prince very beloved by the people of the Franks. He abstained from wars as far as could be done. He made truces, that is, truces or assurances, with the Gauls and Romans, and showed himself so much a friend of both that all lamented his death. Therefore, having peace with everyone, he devoted all his zeal to the dignity and adornment of the nation, renewing laws and establishing new cities and fortifications.
