Sitting one day among his courtiers he said: “Woe to me, who have remained alone like a stranger among foreigners; no one of my kin lives who could help me in necessity.” He did not say this with the intention that he was either sorry for the cruelty he had committed against his kinsmen, or grieved for those killed, but in deceit, so that if perhaps anyone of his stock were still hidden, he might be betrayed by some incautious disclosure of one of those listening.

Clovis waged many wars, which we have not written here for the sake of brevity, since they are contained more fully in Hunibald, book eighteen. He also subjected many peoples to the kingdom of the Franks, and by injury to very many greatly enlarged the kingdom. He was fifteen years of age when he began to reign; he reigned thirty years. He did many good things, and likewise evil things. His mother’s name was Basina, the legitimate wife of Basin, king of the Thuringians; he himself was born in adultery.

For Hilderic, king of the Franks, fleeing into Thuringia, was received for eight years as a guest by King Basin, his kinsman, and had secret intercourse with his wife Basina. She conceived by him and bore the aforesaid son Clovis, in the second year of his flight, which was the year 369 of the Lord’s nativity, in the seventh indiction of the Romans. But afterward, in the eighth year of his flight, he returned into Gaul; Basina followed him with the son and came into exile, in the year of the Lord 376, with the boy now seven years old. King Hilderic survived eight years and died.

Clovis succeeded his father when he was fifteen years old. He reigned [unclear] years. He died in the forty-fifth year of his age, or the thirtieth of his reign, but in the year 524 of the Lord’s nativity, in the seventh indiction of the Romans, and was buried at Paris in the church of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, which he himself had newly built with his wife Clotilde.

He left four sons: Lothar, Theodoric, Clodomer, and Hildebert, who *On the Origin of the Franks.*

who divided their paternal kingdom among themselves in a friendly apportionment. And because afterward many kings proceeded from these, lest we confuse the order of the principal lineage once begun, our chief intention will be to remain in the direct line, continuing the sequence of the family down to Hilderic the last, [unclear].

Up to this point Hunibaldus continued the history of the Franks, for seventeen hundred years from the destruction of the Trojans. What follows concerning the deeds of the Franks has been taken from Hoduardus, Richer, Hermanfredus, and other authors.

Lotharius, son of Clodoveus, through whom the direct line is continued, reigned after his father at Soissons for fifty-one years. His brothers each reigned in their own places. For Theoderic, son of Clodoveus by a concubine, reigned among the people of Metz for thirty-two years; after him his son Theodebert reigned, that is, at Metz, which contains part of Upper Champagne, and also through Alsace and the Alemanni bordering the Rhine, for fourteen years. His son Theodebald succeeded him and reigned for nine years; when he died without children in the year of the Lord 560, Lotharius received the kingdom of Austrasia.

Clodomir, the third son of Clodoveus, reigned at Orleans. He was killed in war by Gundovald, king of Burgundy, leaving three sons, Theobald, Gunther, and Clodoald, whom, after their father’s death, their grandmother Crothildis kept with her to be raised.

Not long afterward Hildebert and Lotharius killed two of the boys with their own hands; the third, Cloald, slipped away in flight with the help of the nobles and escaped. He became a cleric and lived well.

Hildebert, already mentioned, the fourth son of Clodoveus, reigned for forty-five years. He died in the year of the Lord 559, and was buried at Paris in the church of St. Vincent; Lotharius his brother received his kingdom together with all his treasures. At the same time Theodobald, his nephew, also died, who had held the kingdom of Austrasia of his grandfather Theoderic; this passed to Lotharius. And thus Lotharius alone obtained the whole kingdom of the Franks.

In the tenth year of Lotharius, king of the Franks, Ermenfrid, king of the Thuringians, at the urging of his wife Amalberga, deceitfully killed Bertharius and Baldeticus, his brothers, as if they were aiming at his kingdom. They were, like him, of the noble blood of the kings of the Franks. When this became known to King Theoderic, he was greatly moved, and resolved in his mind to avenge the death of his kinsmen. For Theoderic was staying among the Austrasians in the city of Metz, where he had placed the seat of the kingdom; he ruled over the Austrasians, that is, the people of Metz, Liege, Cologne, Trier, the Westrasii, the Alsatians, and the Alemanni on this side of the Rhine.

Fortunatus assigns another cause of the war, which we shall state briefly. Amelberga, wife of Ermenfrid, king of Thuringia, was the daughter of Clodoveus and Crothildis. She took it very badly that her husband was placed under tribute to King Theoderic, whom she considered unworthy of the kingdom, because he was the son of a concubine of his father Clodoveus, not of the queen. Hence she complained that the kingdom of Austrasia was owed by right rather to her, who was the legitimate daughter of the king and queen, than to Theoderic, who had been born illegitimately. With these and many other words the woman continually harassed Ermenfrid, and finally drove him by her excessive importunity so that, sending letters and messengers to Theoderic, he demanded from him the kingdom of Austrasia, as owed to himself together with his wife, with insulting and abusive reproaches. Moved by this, King Theoderic, when Ermenfrid threatened that he would come into Austrasia with an army of fighters, resolved to forestall him. Therefore, calling to his aid his son Theodebert and his brother Lotharius, kings, he entered Thuringia with a great army of Franks, captured King Ermenfrid with his wife and sons, killed him, and subjected the whole region of the Thuringians to himself. From that time the Thuringian kings ceased down to the present.

When the kings were dividing the booty among themselves, Radegundis, a very beautiful virgin who had been the daughter of King Bertharius, killed by his brother Ermenfrid, fell by lot to King Lotharius. He took her with him into Gaul as a captive and received her as his wife. She shone with great sanctity, and after the death of King Lotharius became a nun.

Lotharius, king of the Franks, undertook many battles. He fought twice with the Saxons: the first time he was victor, the second time he was defeated, with many Franks killed. He himself slipped away in flight and returned with a few men to Soissons. The cause of the war was the matter of tribute.

He had seven sons, one of whom, named Granus, from whom the baths at Aachen are said to be named, [unclear], rebelled against his father. After he was finally captured, Lotharius ordered him to be burned with his wife and two children, with many Franks having been killed.

*Here Hunibaldus ended the history.*

*Lotharius reigned for fifty-one years.*

*Theoderic reigned in Austrasia.*

*Clodomir reigned at Orleans.*

*Ermenfrid, king of Thuringia.*

*Another cause of the war between Theoderic and Ermenfrid, and [unclear].*

*The Thuringian Franks are subjected by order to King Ermenfrid [unclear].*

*Radegundis, a captive virgin, is led away.*

*Granus, son of Lotharius, is killed by his father.*

*Whence Aachen.* *Johannes Trithemius*

At last Lotharius died, in the fifty-first year of his reign, and in the year of the Lord's nativity 564, in the twelfth Roman indiction, leaving four sons: Heribertus, who, being the elder by birth, reigned at Paris after his father's death for a few years, leaving nothing else recorded, I do not say worthy, except that, given over to lust, he was the slave of shamefulness, and soon died without children.

*Guntramus reigns at Orleans and in Alsace and Helvetia.*

The second-born of Lotharius was Guntramus, who reigned at Orleans and in Burgundy for 33 years, and died in the year of the Lord 597, leaving two sons, Theodobertus and Theodoricus. His wife was called by the name Austrigildis, a most wicked woman, who, when she was sick unto death and saw that she could not recover, ordered two innocent physicians to be killed.

Theobertus, the elder by birth, begot Sigebertus; Sigebertus begot Odobertus, Gunthramus, and Adelbertus, brothers. Theodertus, the younger, begot Lutfridus and Udalricus, counts, one of whom resided in Habsburg, the other in Hohenburg, the kingdom already having been divided into the four counties of the Helvetii, Alsatians, and Alemanni on this side of the Rhine. From this Lutfridus the genealogy of the counts of Habsburg is continued down to Rudolph, king of the Germans, and further to Maximilian, from Gunthranus of the Franks through 917 years, down to the twenty-eighth year of Maximilian's reign. But in the present place I have not been able to continue the straight line of his genealogy.

Sigebertus, the third-born of Lotharius, reigned in Austrasia, that is, at Metz, Trier, Liege, Cologne, Mainz, over the Thuringians and Saxons, for fourteen years, whom Hilpericus [unclear]

Odobertus begot Theodobertus, who after his father's death reigned 21 years and died in the year of the Lord 599. After him his son Theodoricus reigned 16 years; at the instigation of Brunihildis, his grandmother, he expelled Saint Columbanus from the kingdom in the year of Christ 614, and died shortly afterward, leaving three illegitimate sons, Sigebertus, Corbus, and Meroveus. Sigebertus, routed in battle by Lotharius, son of the following Hilpericus, appeared nowhere. Corbus was killed by the same Lotharius. Meroveus, whom he had lifted from the sacred font, he preserved alive; but Brunihildis, the murderess of ten kings, he killed.

*Sigebertus reigns at Soissons after his father for 24 years.*

Hilpericus the younger, son of Lotharius, from whom the line of the kings of the Franks descending in the right order is continued, succeeded his dead father and reigned among the Soissons for 24 years. He began to reign in the year of the Lord 561, two years before his father died. He had a wife named Andovera, whom, after she had by the deceit of Fredegundis been made his godmother, he cast off, and he took the deceiver Fredegundis herself in addition to the queen. By Andovera, his first wife, he had two sons, Clodoveus and Meroneus, both of whom perished through the deceit of their stepmother. Fredegundis, however, bore Lotharius, who succeeded his father in the kingdom.

In the sixteenth year of his reign, which was the year of the Lord's nativity 578, King Hilpericus, after many persecutions, at last killed his brother Sigebertus; Meroneus, son of Hilpericus, took Sigebertus's wife Brunihildis as an ill-fated wife. Then, after Sigebertus had been wickedly slain, Theodebertus his son succeeded for 21 years.

Lotharius, son of King Hilpericus by Fredegundis, reigned after his father for 44 years. He had several wives, and begot Dagobertus by Berchtrudis, who succeeded him in the kingdom, and Heribertus, who reigned at Toulouse in Aquitaine.

A little before these times, while King Sigebertus, brother of Hilpericus, was still alive, namely in the year of the Lord 576, when the Saxons, at the request of the Winuli, who are now the Lombards, departing from the borders of Scandia, had entered Italy with them and, after some years had been spent there, saw that they were despised by the Lombards, they returned with their children and wives through Gaul to Saxony under the escort of King Sigebertus. But the Alemanni were inhabiting Saxony, which, when its inhabitants departed, they had immediately occupied. When the Saxons came, the Alemanni had been prepared to give them a third part of the region. But when they refused to accept it, in the fifth [year] of King Lotharius Gunthramus, king at Orleans and of part of Burgundy, died, leaving two sons, Theodobertus and Theodoricus, against whom Lotharius, at the instigation of Fredegundis his wife, made war. But *On the Origin of the Franks*

But the holy abbot Columbanus warned Lotharius not to pollute himself with the murder of his nephews, for in the end it would come to pass that he would become their heir and monarch of the whole kingdom.

But Brunhild, the grandmother, was inciting those same grandsons without interruption into mutual war. The grandmother pursued Theodobert with particular hatred, and for that reason diligently provoked his brother against him. Hence at last Theodoric moved an army against his brother Theodobert, and a fierce battle was joined, in which many thousands of the Franks fell on both sides. At length Theodobert, having been defeated, fled and withdrew within the walls of the city of Cologne Agrippina. His brother pursued him and surrounded Cologne with a siege. The citizens asked Theodoric for peace; he answered them: “You will have no peace from me unless you throw down to me from the wall the head of my brother Theodobert.” The citizens therefore cut off the head of Theodobert, their lord, and threw it through the wall to Theodoric his brother, as he had ordered. Thus, made victor in his brother’s blood, he entered Cologne peacefully, an impious warrior, and subjected to himself all Austrasia, which his brother had possessed.

Theodobert had three sons, Sigebert, Gunthram, and Lotharius, and one very beautiful daughter. Sigebert, the eldest, escaped by flight and lay hidden very secretly until the death of Theodoric with his uncle Genebald, duke of the eastern Franks; after the death of Theodoric, through the intervention of the nobles, he received the kingdom of the Helvetians, as will be said below hereafter, yet he was not permitted to put on the diadem or to possess royal dignity. From this Sigebert was born Odobert, through whom the counts in Habsburg, as we said a little earlier, together with many others, arose in Upper Alemannia of Helvetia.

Theodoric the king, their uncle, led away the two brothers and the sister of the aforesaid Sigebert, who were still little children, to Metz. Brunhild, meeting him, as soon as she saw the little grandchildren, rushed upon them like a raging lioness and cruelly killed them with her own hand. Thus Theodoric obtained Austrasia.

Not much time elapsed after this, namely in the year of the Lord 618, which was the thirty-second of King Lotharius, and King Theodoric perished by Brunhild’s poison, in the twenty-first year of his reign. After his death, Lotharius, according to the prophecy of the holy abbot Columbanus, was made monarch of the whole kingdom and thereafter reigned alone over the Franks and Gauls for thirteen years. He insisted that Brunhild, the murderess of ten kings, captured at Worms, undergo cruel [unclear] by judgment of the nobles.

Lotharius, therefore, now entrusted the provinces of the kingdom to four counts. He appointed Garnerius, a noble man of the ancient stock of the kings of the Franks, prefect of his palace; from this his descendants were called counts palatine of his house, succeeding afterward in the same office. Burgundy he entrusted to a certain Harpo, who was himself a count sprung from the most ancient line of the kings of the Franks, and who performed many brave deeds. To Rado, a most noble count of the Franks, he entrusted Austrasia, that is, Metz, Liège, Cologne, Trier, and whatever lies between them. Mainz, Worms, Speyer, and all Westria, together with the adjoining regions, he entrusted to Clodomir, who was duke of the eastern Franks at Würzburg, a high-spirited man descended from the lineage of kings. Lower Francia, or northern Gaul, he entrusted to Pippin; in it are these more important cities: Thérouanne, the Morini, Tournai, Arras, Cambrai, Maastricht, and whatever lies between them. Alsace and Alemannia on this side of the Rhine, that is, Constance, Basel, Strasbourg, whatever right the Franks had between the Burgundians, the Rhine, and the Lombards, and the Helvetians themselves, he committed to Sigebert, son of the late Theodobert, king of the Austrasians, whom his brother Theodoric killed, as has been said. This Sigebert, as long as his uncle survived after the killing of his father, brothers, and sister, together with Brunhild, lay hidden among the dukes of eastern Francia.

By Lotharius, however, through the intervention of the nobles, he was made count in the aforesaid regions, and he begot Odobert, Gunthram, and Theodobert by Engeltrude, daughter of Heribert, duke of the eastern Franks. He presided over the province committed to him for thirty-eight years. Odobert, after his father died, received four counties in the land of the Suebi, Habsburg, Kyburg, and two others whose names are not now [unclear] to me.

Gunthram was count in Homburg and begot Udalric, father of Saint Othilia, virgin of Christ and nun. Theodobert was count of the Rauraci. From these many counts descend.

At the time when Lotharius began to reign at Soissons in Gaul, Garibald reigned in Bavaria. His daughter, named Theodolinda, Antharius king of the Lombards had as wife; this woman was most devoted to Christ, to whom the blessed Pope Gregory [wrote] four *Johannes Trithemius.*

He sent books of dialogues, in the year of the Lord’s nativity [unclear]. At that time there were kings of Bavaria, under the power of the kings of the Franks, and they paid them tribute every year.

In the year of the Lord 602, in the fifth Roman indiction, which was the sixteenth year of Lothar, Garibald, the aforesaid king of Bavaria, died; in his place the aforesaid king of the Franks, Lothar, appointed Tassilo king.

Bertrudis, wife of Lothar king of the Franks, bore Dagobert; after her death he married Sigehild, who bore Heribert. These will be discussed in their proper place. The father had entrusted Dagobert to Saint Arnulf, bishop of Metz, to be raised and instructed; at this time Arnulf was held in great esteem. This Arnulf, of the race of the Franks, was count of Namur; from count he was made bishop of Metz, and from bishop a monk and hermit, in the opinion of all most holy. The matter prompts me to trace his genealogy further back, because he came both from the blood of kings and because several of his descendants were raised to the kingship.

For in the year of the Lord 343, Clogio, king of the Franks, begot Marcomer the king and Dagobert the duke. Dagobert begot Genebald. Genebald begot Marcomer and Sunno. Sunno begot Diocles. Diocles begot Meroneus. Meroneus begot Leontius. Leontius begot Heribert. Heribert begot Priam. Priam begot Sigebert. Sigebert begot Nicanor. Nicanor begot Ansegis. Ansegis begot Arnulf, count of Namur in Austrasia, afterwards bishop of Metz and hermit, of whom we are speaking.

Arnulf begot Ansegis, count of Namur and mayor of the palace of the Franks, or count palatine. Ansegis begot Pippin, mayor of the palace and duke of Brabant, father of Saint Gertrude, whose wife Ida built the monastery of Nivelles in Brabant at the urging of Saint Amandus, or, as usage has it, in Brabant. This Pippin died in the year of the Lord 657, under Dagobert king of the Franks. Pippin begot Grimoald and Charles, surnamed the Strong, mayors of the palace. Charles begot Pippin, Carloman, and Grifo. Pippin, from count palatine or mayor of the palace of the Franks, was made king after the deposition of Hilderic, and begot Charles the Great; these will be discussed later.

In the year of the Lord 611, Dagobert, whom his father Lothar had already previously made king of Austrasia, declared war on Berthold, duke of the Saxons, because he refused to pay tribute to the Franks. Having gathered his forces and crossed the Rhine, he fought with him, and at first was defeated and seriously wounded. When his father Lothar, who was then in the Ardennes forest of the diocese of Cologne, heard this from a swift messenger reporting it, he hastened to his son’s aid. After he had crossed the Rhine at Novellus, battle was again joined. Berthold, or, as others hold, Berthulf, duke of the Saxons, was killed. The Saxons fled after their duke was slain. King Dagobert pursued them and killed all males who exceeded the length of his sword, and compelled the people to pay a tribute of 500 oxen.

After these things, in the year of the Lord 631, in the fourth Roman indiction, Lothar the king, son of Helperic and father of Dagobert, died in the forty-fourth year of his reign.

Dagobert, surnamed the Great, son of Lothar, reigned after his father’s death for thirty-three years. His mother’s name was Bertrudis. He had two sons, Sigebert and Clodoveus, or, as others write, Lodovegus, whom we today would rather call Ludovicus in German.

When Sigebert himself, a little infant of forty days, was baptized by the bishop, and during the prayer Amen was to be answered by those standing around, and all were silent because their thoughts were distracted, the infant himself answered Amen in a clear voice.

Heribert, Dagobert’s brother, who was reigning at Toulouse in Aquitaine, lifted him from the sacred font; this Heribert, that is, after his brother was now reigning, later died together with his son Hilperic, and the monarchy returned to Dagobert.

The Saxons, sending envoys, asked Dagobert to deign to remit their tribute to them, namely the enormous oxen which they were compelled to give every year to the kings of the Franks. The king consented for a time, on this condition: that the Saxons themselves should wage war against [unclear], which they did.

King Dagobert made his son, the said Sigebert, king of Austrasia, that is, of the people of Metz, Cologne, and Liege, placing the diadem upon him and commending him to Saint Cunibert, archbishop of Cologne, and to Adelgis, count palatine of Namur, so that he might be governed by their prudence.

Clodo*On the Origin of the Franks.*

Clodoveus, however, king of Neustria and Burgundy, son of King Dagobert and Nanthildis, was declared king by his father; while he was still a very small child, his father entrusted him to Pippin, duke of Brabant, and to Count [Againus?], to be brought up and instructed in morals.

*Pippin, count of Namur, duke of Brabant.*

This Clodoveus, son of Dagobert, had a wife named Bathildis, an illustrious woman of the Saxon nation, who bore him Lotharius, Hilderic, and Theodoric; concerning these, in their proper places, something must briefly be said in order.

Dagobert, great king of the Franks, died in the thirty-fourth year of his reign, but in the year of the Lord’s nativity 665, in the eighth Roman indiction.

Clodoveus, son of the great Dagobert, succeeded his father and reigned sixteen years. His mother’s name was Nantchildis. Under him the mayor of the household, or count of the palace, was Ansegisus, son of Saint Arnulf, bishop of Metz, a vigorous and magnificent man, who was count of Namur; his son Pippin was duke of Brabant.

Clodoveus reigned, as has been said, in Neustria and Burgundy, that is, at Paris, Beauvais, Amiens, Blois, Reims, Lyon, Toulouse, and in the whole Gallican kingdom as far as the sea and the Spains through Alemannia. In eastern Francia, Bavaria, Alsace, Thuringia, and other provinces subject to the kingdom of the Franks, dukes and counts of the noble blood of the ancient kings of France had been appointed, who administered them under the kings.

Sigebert, however, the brother of Clodoveus, as we have said, reigned in Austrasia, which is joined to lower Champagne, among the people of Metz, Cologne, Liège, Trier, the Mosellans, Toul, Mainz, [Neometenses], and Worms.

King Clodoveus died in the sixteenth year of his reign, but in the year of the Lord’s nativity 681, in the ninth Roman indiction, leaving three sons, as has been said, by his wife Bathildis: Lotharius, Hilderic, and Theodoric.

Lotharius, the elder son of Clodoveus, succeeded his father and reigned only four years. His mayor of the household was Ebervinus, an impious man, who tore out the eyes of Saint Leodegarius the bishop and made him a martyr of Christ. King Lotharius died in the year of the Lord 675, in the fourteenth indiction.

Theodoric, brother of Lotharius and son of Clodoveus, succeeded his dead brother and reigned almost seven years. For he was made king twice. First, succeeding his brother and given over to leisure and sloth, he began to arrange all the affairs of the kingdom through the count of the palace, whom they called the mayor of the household, showing himself once a year, on the Kalends of May, for the people to see and greet; all the rest of the time he spent in idleness. Hence the commonwealth of the Franks suffered no small loss. For everything was carried out at the discretion of the mayors of the household. His mayor of the household was Ebervinus, whom others wrongly write as Ebroinus, because it is a Germanic name, a wicked and impious man who did many evils; moved by these, the nobles of the Franks cast Theodoric down from the kingdom and confined both him and Ebervinus, separated from one another, in two monasteries.

Hilderic, the middle brother of the two preceding kings and son of Clodoveus, after his younger brother Theodoric had been cast down from the kingdom of the Franks, was called from Austrasia to the kingdom by election of the nobles and reigned a few years. Since he was harsh in character and hateful to many nobles of the Franks, he was killed while hunting.

Theodoric, after his brother had been killed while hunting, together with his pregnant wife Ulida, was restored to the kingdom by the Franks, and thereafter reigned three years. He died in the year of the Lord’s nativity 692, leaving by Queen Clothildis two sons, Clodoveus and Hildebert, who reigned after him.

Clodoveus, the elder son of Theodoric, succeeding his father in the kingdom of the Franks in the above-noted year of the Lord 692, reigned three years with his brother Hildebert. The mayor of the household of the kingdom of the Franks at that time was Pippin, son of Ansegisus, count and renowned duke of Brabant. In the last year of this King Clodoveus, Saint Willibrord, who was also called Clement by Pope Sergius at Rome, was ordained bishop on the day of Saint Clement and sent into Belgic Gaul, Austrasia, and also Frisia, to preach.

This King Clodoveus of the Franks died in the year of the Lord’s nativity 696, in the ninth Roman indiction; his brother succeeded him.

Hildebert, succeeding his dead brother Clodoveus, afterwards reigned fourteen years. In his fifth year Saint Lambert, bishop of Liège, was killed.

King Hildebert died in the year of the Lord’s nativity 610, in the eighth Roman indiction, leaving his son Dagobert.

Dagobert the younger, succeeding his father in the kingdom of the Franks, reigned five years, par*Dagobert reigns [unclear] years.*

[Two?] kings of the Franks of slight authority and importance existed in these times, but everything was done through the mayors of the palace, among whom various disturbances and seditions also frequently arose. For after Ebroin, under Theodoric, had died, the Franks made Garaco count of the palace; not long afterward Gillemarus, his son, removed him from office. After wars against Pippin, duke of Brabant, whom the Franks had driven out of the mayoralty of the palace, this man died suddenly, and Garaco his father recovered the dignity. When he too had died shortly afterward, Bertharius, a useless man, was appointed mayor of the palace.

*Pippin wages war against Bertharius.*

Pippin, duke of Brabant, perceiving the dissension of the Franks, gathered troops and led an army against Theodoric and Bertharius. The battle was fiercely fought; Theodoric, his army routed, took flight. Bertharius was killed. At last, when peace had been confirmed with King Theodoric, Pippin recovered the office, and died in the year of the Lord 715, in the thirteenth Roman indiction, leaving a son named Charles Martel, surnamed the Strong. Plectrude, his stepmother, Pippin’s last wife, placed him in custody at Cologne, and [made?] Theobald mayor of the palace.

*Pippin recovers the mayoralty of the palace.*

Not long afterward the Franks removed Theobald from office; war was undertaken; the party of King Dagobert was weakened. For after Theobald had been driven from office, the Frankish nobles made Raganfrid mayor of the palace. Meanwhile Charles Martel, Pippin’s son, escaped from the custody of his stepmother.

But Dagobert, the younger king of the Franks, at last died in the year of the Lord 715, in the thirteenth indiction, leaving a son named Theodoric.

After the death of King Dagobert, the Franks appointed a certain priest named Daniel mayor of the palace; afterward, raising him to be king, they gave him the name Chilperic. He often fought against Charles Martel. But Charles, having miraculously slipped away from the custody of his stepmother, labored with the greatest zeal to be able to recover his father’s principate. Therefore, since he was powerful, he set up a certain Lotharius, of royal stock, as king of the Franks against Daniel, by whom he himself was also made mayor of the palace. Charles fought many battles with Daniel, sometimes defeated, yet more often victorious.

Ragenfrid, duke of the Frisians, and Eudo, prince of the Wascons, had conspired with Daniel against Lotharius and Charles; but all were defeated, and Lotharius, with Charles’s aid, powerfully held the kingdom for eight years.

This Lotharius, the interrex, died in the year of the Lord’s nativity 723, in the eighth year of his reign, in the sixth Roman indiction. When he had died, Daniel, who was also Chilperic the priest, was restored to the kingdom. He did not survive long, but died in the following year, that is, 724.

*Theodoric reigns.*

Theodoric, son of King Dagobert the last, brought up, as they say, for fear of enemies in a certain convent of nuns, after the death of the two interreges Lotharius and Daniel, was taken up as king by the Franks with the counsel of the mayor of the palace Charles Martel, who was now very powerful; and he reigned fourteen years. But all power in the whole kingdom was in the hands of the mayor of the palace, and the king was compelled to be content with the name alone.

This Charles, mayor of the palace of the Franks, count of Namur and duke of Brabant, restored the kingdom of the Franks, almost desolated, to wholeness, enlarged it, and made it glorious. He fought many battles with the peoples, and always came out victorious. First he led a great army beyond the Rhine and the Danube through the subdued Suevi and Bavarians to the Bulgars, the Rhaetians, and those peoples whom today we call Austrians beyond the Danube; powerfully subjecting them to the kingdom of the Franks, he returned to Gaul with much spoil.

When the Suevi defected from their pledged subjection to the Franks, Charles declared war and, having gathered forces of soldiers, fought with them. The battle was fiercely fought, and many fell on both sides, yet more of the Suevi than of the Franks. Hence in the end the victory fell to Charles, and, after Leutfred, duke of the Suevi, had been killed, he subjected that people, together with its region, to the Franks.

In the ninth year of Theodoric king of the Franks, which was the year of the Lord’s nativity 733, Charles, mayor of the palace, waged war with the Frisians, who were trying to vindicate themselves into freedom from subjection to the Franks. A savage battle was joined, and the Frisians, after Radbod, their leader, had been slain, were overcome.

In the following year Charles moved his army into Wascony. For Eudo, prince of the Wascons, with Abdiramus, king of Spain, as his ally, when he had an infinite multitude of fighters, broke into the territories of the Franks and, having set up camp at Bordeaux, took the city by storm, after all the churches had been plundered and burned. Advancing from there with similar destruction, *On the Origin of the Franks.*

He afflicted the Poitevins and burned the church of Saint Hilary. Then he moved his army against the city of Tours, which he attacked by a like stratagem and wished to storm.

But Charles, meeting the enemy with his men, stood in the way, so that he should not obtain what he wished. Battle was joined and the fighting was extremely fierce; but God granted victory to Charles. On that day he laid low 385,000 of the enemy, although only five hundred from the army of the Franks had fallen in that battle. Not long afterward, when Edulo, also called Eudo, had died, Charles moved into Wasconia, subjected it to his rule, and checked the Burgundians as they were attempting new disturbances.

*Charles subjected Wasconia to his rule.*

In the eleventh year of King Theodoric, the Vandals, from their remaining settlements, after they had greatly troubled the peoples neighboring them, at last burst into Francia with a cruel multitude and came as far as Sens. But when an attack was made upon them, Eppo, bishop of the city, the siege having been lifted, put them to flight.

*The Vandals who entered Francia are put to flight.*

The Goths, bursting from the borders of the Spains into Francia, Charles received bravely in battle, laid them low, and compelled them to flee with the greatest disgrace. Finally, he also completely subdued the peoples on this side of the Rhine, the Mosellans too, the Cynonoti, the Westrasii, the Mainz people, the Vangiones, and the Neometes, ancient enemies of the Gauls.

*Charles Martel overcame the Goths.*

Theodoric, king of the Franks, died in the thirteenth year of his reign, which was the year of the Lord’s Nativity 737, in the fifth indiction.

Hilderic, son of King Theodoric, succeeding him after his death, reigned in name alone for fourteen years. *Hilderic reigned fourteen years.* For the wealth and power of the kingdom were in the hands of [unclear].

*Johannes Trithemius*

and the dukes of Brabant, after their father’s death, as has been said, having obtained the chief office of mayor of the household or palace, applied their minds most zealously to appointing the king and to recovering the provinces which after their father’s death had fallen away from subjection to the Franks.

First, therefore, stirred with common resolve to recover Aquitaine, they led an army against Himold, duke of that province, and declared war on the prince. But he, seeing that he was able [not?] to resist, sought favor and submitted himself to their will.

At the same time, while Pippin and Carloman were still in Aquitaine, in the castle called Lucasi, before they departed from there, they resolved to divide between themselves the principate of the whole kingdom of the Franks, the administration of which they held under the wretched king. They therefore divided, as they wished, all the provinces of the kingdom, without the advice or consent of the nobles in the province of King Childeric being sought for this. For Childeric was, as we have said, not a king but rather the shadow of a king, bearing the empty name of one of his servants, without substance. The nobles of the kingdom approved the intention of the princes, as the time required.

And so by common decree Pippin and Carloman divided between themselves all the provinces of the whole kingdom of the Franks in that place which is called Old Poitou. In this division Carloman obtained by lot Austrasia, Alemannia, and Thuringia; the names of the districts and cities of these provinces are these: Trier with the Mosellans; Metz with the Austrasians; Liege with the people of Namur, the Brabanders and Hollanders between the sea and the Rhine; Cologne with the Tungri, Batavi, Menapii, Frisians, and Hogii, who are now the Westphalians; Mainz with the [Cristheneni?], Vangiones, Nemetes, Westrasii, and [Cynonoti?]; Strasbourg with the Alsatians; Constance with the Alemanni, Helvetii, Raurici, and the people of Chur, who today are called [Valesii?]; Wurzburg with the Suevi and the eastern Franks, among whom are towns and cities: Nuremberg, Bamberg, Forchheim, Windsheim, Hall, and many counties, Schweinfurt, Rothenburg, Frankenburg, the castle of [Sebalsein?], [Wicharshein?], Wertheim, and many others; Bavaria with its cities, Regensburg, [Viuarium?], [Driopolis?], and others. Thuringia and Saxony, with almost all Germany, fell to Carloman; in almost each of these provinces dukes or counts administered the commonwealth under the power of the Franks, removable at the will of the princes.

Pippin, however, in that division obtained Burgundy, Westria, Provence, Aquitaine, Champagne, Gascony, and whatever lies between them. The names of the cities through the territories of these provinces are these: in Burgundy, indeed, Lyon, Vienne, Avignon, Besancon, [Loanna?], Valence, Marseille, and whatever today is contained in Savoy and the Dauphinate. In Westria: Paris, Chalon, Toul, Tours, [Cathalonia?], Toulouse, [Cotonagus?], whatever there is throughout all Gaul, Reims, Orleans, Soissons, Beauvais, Blois, Amiens, from the Spains as far as the river Scheldt.

After this division had been made between them, Pippin and Carloman returned home. At the same time, as soon as the Alemanni heard of the death of Charles Martel, they withdrew from subjection to the Franks and unanimously conspired in rebellion. As soon as this rebellion of the Suevi became known to Carloman, he gathered troops and moved his army into Alemannia, which he devastated with sword and fire. But the Alemanni, seeing that they were unequal to the Franks in strength, submitted themselves to them again and paid the annual tribute, as they had been accustomed to do before.

In the seventh year of King Childeric, which was the year of the Lord’s nativity 744, Carloman and Pippin, having joined their forces, advanced to war against Odilo, duke of Bavaria, who had himself fallen away from subjection to the Franks. For he had placed the royal diadem upon himself and by his own authority had ordered himself to be called king, which had been forbidden by decree of the Franks, because they had reduced all kingdoms subject to their dominion into provinces, establishing from them all one monarchy, over which the one king of the Franks alone presided. Duke Odilo, however, met the Franks coming against him in war, but was overcome by them, and Bavaria was again reduced into submission to the Franks.

At the same time part of the Saxons also, after the death of Charles Martel, fell away from loyalty to the Franks. Therefore Carloman, returning with his men from the slaughter of the Bavarians, moved an expedition into Saxony, and, after capturing the castle which the inhabitants call Osnabruck, today an episcopal city, received into surrender Theodicic, the chief count of that district, who did not keep faith.

For this reason Carloman and Pippin, with their armies joined, in the following year, which was of the Lord— *On the Origin of the Franks.*

In the year of the Lord’s Nativity 745 they entered Saxony again, and they caused the captured Theodoric, so often a transgressor of faith, to be beheaded. And again the Saxons, compelled to submit to the Franks, began to pay tribute.

*Again the Saxons are overcome by the Franks.*

In the ninth year of Childeric, named the idle king of the Franks, but in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 747, Carloman, the most noble prince of the Franks, mayor of the palace, count of Namur, duke of Brabant by birth, and vice-king of Germany, also principal prefect, sole and only lord, powerful and to be feared, of Trier, Metz, Liege, Cologne, Mainz, Speyer, Strasbourg, Basel, Constance, the Alemanni, Suevi, Bavarians, Helvetians, Bohemians, Austrians, eastern Franks, Thuringians, Frisians, and Saxons, [unclear] the principate, which once at one time sufficed for twelve kings; and, having despised the riches of the world and all honors, he set out for Rome and offered himself to Zacharias, the supreme pontiff. By him he was soon made a cleric; and, his dress changed, he had himself clothed in monastic garments, and, made a monk on Mount Soracte, built the church of Saint Silvester, in which he served the Lord. But after some years, when many nobles from Francia came to Rome on pilgrimage out of devotion, [unclear] he withdrew to [unclear], remaining as a monk among monks and serving God until death.

*Carloman surrendered the principate of the Franks to his brother.*

Pippin alone thereafter administered the whole kingdom of the Franks for five years still; when these had elapsed he was raised to kingship and reigned sixteen years. And the whole time of his principate after his father was twenty-six years.

*Pippin obtained the monarchy of that kingdom.*

*Saint Burghard, first bishop of Wurzburg.*

In the thirteenth year of Childeric, king of the Franks, but in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 751, in the fourth Roman indiction, Saint Burghard, English by nation, a monk by profession, was made the first bishop of the church of Wurzburg; he presided in great sanctity for forty years.

*The nobles of the Franks choose Duke Pippin for the kingdom.*

In the same year the nobles of the whole kingdom, assembling together, began to take counsel concerning the removal of the useless king Childeric. It pleased all in common that they should depose King Childeric, who had neither skill nor power for ruling, and should raise to kingship Pippin, in whose hands the supreme authority of the whole kingdom remained. But Pippin would not consent to this matter unless the counsel of the Roman pontiff Zacharias were first sought, alleging the reasons that moved him. Therefore, after counsel had been shared, Saint Burghard, bishop of Wurzburg, and Abbot Fulrad were sent to Rome to Pope Zacharias, to consult him concerning the aforesaid business of the kings: namely, what seemed to him better, more just, and more right; whether the royal name with the diadem ought to remain with him who was always idle and did nothing worthy of the royal name, or rather should be conferred on another, that is, on Pippin, who disposed all the affairs of the kingdom and alone performed the labor. The pope answered the envoys that it seemed just to him that he who bore the labors of the kingdom and disposed all affairs should bear the royal name and diadem, rather than Childeric, who, always idle, did nothing for the advantage of the kingdom. He therefore wrote to the bishops and nobles of the Franks and advised them that, after Childeric had been removed and thrust into a monastery, they should make Pippin king. He also commanded Saint Boniface, archbishop of Mainz, by apostolic letters, to anoint the same Pippin as king of the Franks.

Pippin, by order of Pope Zacharias, was anointed and crowned king of the Franks in the city of Soissons by the hands of Saint Boniface, archbishop of Mainz, in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 751, in the fifth Roman indiction; he reigned sixteen years. Pippin was the son of Ansegisus, who was the son of Arnulf, who was the son of Ansegisus, who was the son of Nicanor, who was the son of Sigebert, who was the son of Priam, who was the son of Heribert, who was the son of Leontius, who was the son of Merovech, who was the son of Diocles, who was the son of Simon, who was the son of Genebald, who was the son of Dagobert, who was the son of Marcomer, who was the son of Clodio, king of the Franks reigning in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 301. Moreover King Childeric, deposed according to the pope’s judgment, was made a monk, and in him the line of the kings of the Franks descending from Pharamond came to an end.

In the same year in which Pippin was crowned king, there was the discovery and translation of the bodies of Saints Kilian the bishop, Colman the priest, and Totnan the deacon, martyrs, at [unclear].

*Translation of the bodies of Saints Kilian and Totnan.*

*Carloman, Roman prefect, [unclear].* *Johannes Trithemius*

At Würzburg [it] was done in the sixty-third year from their passion, in the Roman indiction, as we said above, the fifth, with the rejoicing of the people.

*The city of Würzburg is given to Burghard, its first bishop.*

In this same year also, King Pippin, considering, at the appeal of Saint Boniface, archbishop of Mainz, the faith and holiness of the holy pontiff Burghard of Würzburg, through whose mediation he had obtained from the pope of the city of Rome the kingdom of the Franks, and because his bishopric, still new, had not been sufficiently provided for in temporal possessions, with the consent of his sons Charles, later surnamed the Great, and Carloman, and likewise of all the nobles of the whole kingdom of the Franks who were present that day at Soissons when he had been anointed and crowned king, gave by royal munificence the city of Würzburg, with all its revenues and advantages, to the cathedral church, that is, to the aforementioned Saint Burghard, bishop of Würzburg, and to his successors as their perpetual property. The new king Pippin also conferred upon the aforesaid church the castle of Karlsburg with the town called Karlstadt, and many other things. The same King Pippin also gave as a perpetual gift to the Church of Würzburg, to Saint Burghard its bishop and to his successors forever, the title, dignity, and emolument of the duchy of the eastern Franks; to them he gave the power of arranging judgment and judging according to the law and custom of the Franks, in all cases throughout the whole duchy.

In the second year of his reign King Pippin entered Saxony with a great army of the Franks; the Saxons resisted him with the utmost obstinacy. At last, however, they were defeated, and again pledged themselves to the king’s words, although they did not long keep faith. In this expedition Hildegarius, bishop of the Franks, who was also the brother of King Pippin, was killed by someone in the same year.

In the year of the Lord 755, in the eighth Roman indiction, which was the third year of King Pippin, Saint Boniface, formerly a monk and then archbishop of Mainz, suffered martyrdom in Frisia near Dokkum for the faith of Christ; his body was brought back to the monastery of Fulda and honorably buried there in the crypt.

In the sixth year of his reign Pippin, having again gathered a strong army of the Franks, moved into Saxony; battle was joined, and he killed many thousands of them, received the rest in surrender, and compelled them to promise that they would do everything whatsoever he commanded, and that each year they would give him 300 horses as tribute or as a gift of honor, in sign of most faithful subjection. When these matters had thus been arranged and confirmed according to the Saxon custom, King Pippin returned to his own lands.

In the year of the Lord 758, in the sixth Roman indiction, King Pippin of the Franks died on the eighth day before the Kalends of October, in the twenty-sixth year of his principate and the sixteenth of his kingship; his body was buried at Saint-Denis. He left a wife named Bertrada and two sons, Charles and Carloman.

Charles the Great, king of the Franks, reigned for 46 years. When he began to reign he was in the twenty-sixth year of his age. He undertook many wars and greatly enlarged the kingdom of the Franks. First he led an army against Hunold, who had invaded Aquitaine; Hunold at once fled from his face to Lupus, duke of Gascony. But Charles, sending an embassy to Lupus in Gascony, received the fugitive from him together with his wife; and Lupus himself, with all Gascony obeying him, returned.

In the year 770 King Charles held a general assembly of the princes of the kingdom in the city of Worms. Bertrada, the mother of the kings, staying with Carloman her younger son at Seltz, set out for Italy for the sake of peace; and, when the business for which she had gone had been completed, and the vow of prayer to the holy Apostles duly fulfilled, she returned to her own people. In the same year the body of Saint Othmar, once abbot of the monastery of Saint Gall, was found incorrupt and, having been taken up, was buried in the basilica of Saint Gall. Although he was abbot of that same monastery, of good and most religious conduct, he was driven out by the envy of certain perverse brothers and relegated to the aforesaid island of Stein, where he died in the year of the Lord 760, in the forty-third indiction. In the year of the Lord 761 King Carloman died; his wife fled with her children into Italy to Desiderius, king of the Lombards, from the face of King Charles, because she was conscious to herself of evil plots against him, together with others of her party who, on Carloman’s side, were always sowing discord. From then on Charles the Great alone held the kingdom of the Franks for 43 years.

In the year *On the Origin of the Franks.*

In the following year King Charles, having again assembled at Worms a general council of the princes, with the common consent of all declared war on the Saxons. Having gathered a considerable army of Franks, he entered Saxony and laid everything waste with sword and fire. When he had taken a certain fortress, Eresburg, he destroyed the idol called in the Saxon language Ermensul. Departing thence he advanced to the river Weser, where the Saxons, coming together, sought the king’s favor and promised fidelity. But the king, after receiving twelve hostages, granted peace.

*The first expedition of King Charles the Great against the Saxons.*

In the year of the Lord 773, when Pope Adrian could no longer endure the insolence of Desiderius, king of the Lombards, and the oppression of the Church, he sent an embassy to Charles and implored his aid. Charles, having gathered an army, entered Lombardy and besieged Desiderius in the city of Ticinum, which is now Pavia. At length, after a long siege, he compelled the city to surrender; the remaining cities followed it and subjected themselves to King Charles’s power. Therefore the king, after Italy had been subdued and set in order as time permitted, returned to Francia, bringing King Desiderius with him as a captive. Adelgisus, however, Desiderius’s son, fled to Greece, to the emperor Constantine, and there ended his life.

*King Charles, in favor of the Roman Church, defeats the Lombards.*

Meanwhile, because King Charles was engaged in war in Lombardy, the Saxons, taking opportunity from his absence, began to devastate the neighboring territories of the Hessians. And coming to the place called Fritzlar, they attempted to burn the church which the holy archbishop Boniface had once consecrated. For the Saxons at that time were still worshippers of idols. And when they were trying with great force to burn it, there appeared to certain persons, both pagans and Christians, two young men in white garments preventing the whole fire; terrified by their presence, the Saxons all turned to flight, though no one pursued them.

In the year of the Lord 774, Charles, having returned home from Lombardy, before the Saxons perceived that he had come, sent a three-part army into their land; devastating everything with plundering and fires, and killing very many of those who attempted to resist, they returned with immense booty. And this was the second expedition of King Charles into Saxony.

In the year of the Lord 775, King Charles the Great resolved to enter Saxony and to remain in it so long until either they should receive the faith of Christ or all be exterminated. Therefore, making for Saxony with the whole force of the Franks, in the first assault he took Sigiburg, a very strongly fortified castle opposite the Rhine, two miles from Bonn, in which there was a Saxon garrison; restoring Eresburg, which had been destroyed by the Saxons, he fortified it and placed a Frankish garrison in it. After causing great slaughter, and after receiving hostages from them and from the Westphalians, he granted peace to those capable of giving it and withdrew.

*The third expedition of King Charles made against the Saxons.*

In the year of the Lord 777, King Charles the Great, after holding council with the princes of the kingdom of the Franks at the place Paderborn, on the borders of Saxony, where there is now an episcopal city, now for the fourth time led an army into Saxony and found all of them deceitfully devoted to him. For all came to him except Widukind, one of the foremost men of the Westphalians, who, conscious of many crimes, feared the king and fled with a few men to Sigefrid, king of the Danes. The rest, however, who had assembled submitted themselves so far to the king’s power that they then merited pardon on this condition: that if they should hereafter violate his statutes, they would be deprived of homeland and liberty. Many were baptized at the king’s insistence, yet few of them proved true Christians.

*The fourth expedition of King Charles against the Saxons.*

In the year of the Lord 778, King Charles moved into Spain, and the cities which he brought under his authority, and received hostages from the Saracens. Meanwhile the Saxons, discovering that the king was far away, took up arms and advanced as far as the Rhine. But since they could not cross the river, whatever there was of hamlets and estates from the village of Deutz, which is opposite Cologne, as far as Koblenz, where the Moselle flows into the Rhine, they laid waste with fire and sword, making no distinction of sex or age, but killed infants together with their mothers.

*Saxons devastate parts of the Franks.*

When the king, stationed at [Altfiodoro], heard this, he immediately sent the eastern Franks and the Alemanni to drive them back. Hearing of their arrival, the Saxons at once withdrew. But those men, following them on their trail, found them in the regions of the Hessians beside the river Eder, and immediately attacked them in the very ford of the river and laid them low with such slaughter that very few remained.

*The Saxons devastate parts of the Franks.*

In the following year, which was the 779th from the Lord’s nativity, Charles now for the fifth time moved an expedition into Saxony, leading the army across at that place where the Lippe flows into the Rhine, not far from the village called Wesel. When the Saxons met him armed,

*Charles the Great moves for the fifth time into Saxony.* 98 *Johannes Trithemius*

*Bucholtz.*

at Bucholtz they were defeated and many of them slain; the rest sought safety in flight. But King Charles entered the region of the Westphalians and received them all in surrender. Moving from there to Wesfaram he pitched camp. There the Angrarians and Eastphalians gave hostages and swore oaths; when these things had been done, the king returned to Worms.

In the year of the Lord 780, King Charles now for the sixth time moved into Saxony. As he came, all the Saxons of the eastern parts met him, and many of the people were baptized. Coming from there to the place where the Ohre and the Elbe flow together, the king set in order both the Saxons and the Slavs; and, having returned into Francia and held counsel, he set out for Rome for the sake of prayer with his wife Hildegard and his children, and celebrated the Nativity of the year at Pavia. 800.

In this year of the Lord’s Nativity, in the ninth indiction, Charles, king of the Franks, son of King Pippin, after he had reigned thirty-three years, in the fifty-ninth year of his age, was made emperor of the Romans and ruled as emperor for thirteen years. For when he was at Rome because of the charge made too wrongfully against Pope Leo III, and was celebrating the Lord’s Nativity there, on that most sacred day itself, coming to the solemnities of the Mass, while before the confession of the blessed Apostle Peter, after prayer, he was thinking of, not to say hoping for, nothing less than the empire, Leo, adorned with the papal insignia, placed a crown upon his head and proclaimed him emperor of the Romans.

At once it was shouted by the whole Roman people: “To Charles Augustus, crowned by God, great and peace-bringing emperor of the Romans, life and victory.” After these acclamations, he was anointed by the apostolic hand and, in the manner of the ancient princes, adored by the pope; and, the title of patrician, with which he had previously been distinguished, having been removed, he was called Emperor and Augustus by the favor of many nations.

In the year of the Lord 804, Emperor Charles wintered at Aachen. But in summer, having led an army into Saxony, he transferred into Francia all the Saxons who lived beyond the river Elbe, and granted the districts beyond the Elbe to be inhabited and cultivated by the Obodrite peoples under an annual tribute.

In the year of the Lord 805, the emperor sent his son Charles with an army into Bohemia; after laying everything waste, he killed the duke of that land, named Lecho, and made his duchy subject to the kingdom of the Franks.

In the year of the Lord 811, the elder son of Emperor Charles, himself also called by his father’s name Charles, died on the day before the Nones of December.

In the year of the Lord 813, Emperor Charles, after holding a general assembly of the princes at Aachen, called to himself his son Louis, king of Aquitaine, and, placing the crown upon him, made him his partner in the imperial name. But Bernard, his grandson, the son of his son Pippin, he appointed king of Italy.

In the same year the bridge over the Rhine at Mainz, which the emperor had constructed of wood over ten years with immense labor and marvelous workmanship, so that it seemed able to last forever, in the month of May was so consumed in three hours by an accidental fire that, apart from what was covered by the water, not even one little splinter of it remained. Many councils of bishops were held in the same year by order of the emperor.

In the year of the Lord’s Nativity 814, in the eighth indiction of the Romans, on the twenty-eighth day of the month of January, Charles, surnamed the Great, king of the Franks and ever-august emperor of the Romans, died at Aachen, and there in the church of blessed Mary ever virgin, which he himself had built, was honorably buried, in the seventy-second year of his age, the forty-sixth of his reign over the Franks, and the thirteenth of his empire; he added no fewer provinces to the kingdom of the Franks than it had had before.

*Louis king and emperor, son of Charles, 26 years.*

Louis, according to the custom of the Sicambrians, who change L into V, a count in East Francia, with the consent of Saint Burchard, bishop of Würzburg, built the monastery of Schwarzach, not far from the Main, with the help of his wife Imma; he caused its church to be consecrated in honor of our Lord Jesus Christ, and also in memory of the holy Mother of God and of the holy martyrs Sebastian and Felicity, and established monks of the order of the divine father Benedict there.

In the year of the Lord 817, Emperor Louis held an assembly of the princes at Aachen, in which he [unclear] Lothar, his firstborn, as his partner in the name and empire *On the Origin of the Franks.*

there he appointed, the others being called kings; he set one over Aquitaine, another over Bavaria, [unclear], retaining for himself the kingdom of the Franks together with the empire.

In the year of the Lord 840, in the third indiction of the Romans, Louis, king of the Franks and emperor of the Romans, died and was buried in the church at Metz. After his death Lothar, under the name of emperor, held Italy; Pippin obtained Aquitaine; Charles, Gaul; and Louis, Germany.

*The division of the kingdom of the Franks into two kingdoms, the German and the Gallican.*

In the year of the Lord's nativity 861, from the entry of the Sicambri, or Franks, into the kingdom in Germany and the seats accepted at the mouths of the Rhine, the year 1280, in the fourth indiction of the Romans; in the 2030th year from the destruction of Troy, the three sons of King and Emperor Louis divided among themselves the very broad kingdom of the Franks, together with the empire of the Romans. In this division Lothar, as has been said, obtained Italy with the title of the Empire; Louis obtained Germany; Charles, Gaul; and Pippin their nephew, Aquitaine.

From that time the division of the kingdom of the Franks, begun as a twofold division, has remained, now for 673 years down to the present day, and will remain henceforth perpetual. This division, confirmed by the writings and law of the ancestors, made from one kingdom of the Franks two kingdoms, of which one is that of Germany, the other only of Celtica and Aquitaine. For the greater part of Belgic Gaul, in the later division, was adjudged to the kingdom of Germany; in that kingdom are these provinces, with their cities.

All Alemannia, or Swabia, with its cities: Constance, Basel, [Biriensibus?], the Helvetians, Lausanne, the people of Sion, who are also the Valaisians; also the Burgundy of Besancon; Lotharingia, Metz, Liege, Cambrai, Arras, Flanders, Holland, Zeeland, Brabant, Utrecht, Cologne, Trier, with the Mosellans, Mainz, Worms, and Speyer, with the [Cynonoti?] and [Westrasi?] and the Vosges people, Strasbourg with Alsace, and all the rest adjacent to these, belong to the kingdom of Germany, and are called cities of the German kingdom, not of the Roman Empire.

Next, all Germany is subject to this kingdom, in which are: the Frisians, Saxons, Hessians, Westphalians, [Hogij?], who are also the Wetterau people, Thuringians, Meisseners, the margraves of Brandenburg, Pomeranians, Rugi, people of Stettin, Holsteiners, Danes, Swedes, Norwegians, Prussians, Poles, Silesians, Sorbs, who also are the Bohemians of old and are called Slavs, Austrians, Carinthians, [Siturij?], Tyroleans, Bavarians, Rhaetians, and whatever lies among these. But it is also clear that all Italy, apart from the goods of the Church, by ancient right belonged to the kingdom of the Franks of Germany, under the rule of Charles the Great.

Therefore the king of Germany, whoever he may be for the time, has two things: the kingdom and the empire. To the kingdom he is elected by the princes and needs confirmation by no one; but to the empire, which is joined to the kingdom by right, he must be confirmed and anointed by the Roman pontiff. The kingdom is to be called by the name of the Germans, but the empire by the name of the Romans. Those who call Maximilian king of the Romans speak confusedly, since they ought rather to have said king of the Germans. Likewise those who say that Cologne, Trier, Liege, Metz, or other cities of Germany are imperial cities do not speak correctly, since they are royal cities. For if it should ever happen that the empire were taken away from the Germans, the kingdom of Germany would nevertheless remain, free as it now is, having subject to itself all the provinces and cities throughout all the places written above, as it has them subject today.

Louis, therefore, brother of the emperor, son of the elder Louis and grandson of Charles the Great, having obtained the kingdom of Germany in the division, reigned thirty years. After him his son, named Charles the Younger, was king of Germany and emperor of the Romans for eleven years; under him the kingdom was divided among his brothers. For he himself, with Germany, had the empire; Louis had East Francia; Charles, Alemannia; and Carloman, Bavaria, with his son Arnulf afterward obtaining the monarchy of the whole German kingdom and also of the empire. From this point the name of the Franks remained with Gaul to the kings of Gaul, and gradually began to depart from the Germans. We are German Franks; they, however, are Gauls.

1514.

*End of the Compendium of Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Saint James at Wurzburg, on the origin of the people of the Franks, and also on their kingdom, name, and kings.* *Chronicle of the Succession of the Dukes of Bavaria and of the Counts Palatine, by Johannes Trithemius, Abbot: to Philip, Count Palatine, Prince-Elector.*

Bavaria, as certain writers say, took its name and origin from a certain Duke Boiarus, whom they report to have come from Armenia into this region before the Trojan War with a great people. After the inhabitants had been driven out, being very rude and living like beasts on acorns, he committed the excellent land to cultivation by oxen.

Boiarus, the first duke of Bavaria, from whom the people and the region received their name, reigned in Bavaria for many years, and after him his sons down to the destruction of Troy; their names and deeds, because of their excessive antiquity, we do not know.

Norix, king of Bavaria, son of the most valiant Hercules, from whom Bavaria was afterward called Norica, built a notable city upon the Danube, which today is called Regensburg, and which Tiberius Caesar, a long time afterward, called Tiberina. Many dukes succeeded this Duke Norix in Bavaria at intervals of time down to Tiberius Caesar; their names and deeds antiquity has brought into oblivion.

Boamundus, duke of Bavaria, a noble prince, driven from Armenia by Tiberius Caesar, came into Bavaria with Ingramus, a man equally noble, and there reigned over the Bavarians for many years.

Adelgerus, duke of Bavaria, a brave and vigorous man, after Boamundus and Ingramus ruled the Bavarians for many years.

Theodo, king of Bavaria, after the aforesaid Duke Adelgerus, reigned over the Bavarians; his deeds are found scattered here and there.

Gerobaldus, king of Bavaria, in the time of the Emperor Maurice, was a most Christian man. Among other children he had a most devout daughter named Theodelinda, whom he gave as wife to Otharius, king of the Lombards; through her many good things were done in the Church of God. To this holy queen blessed Gregory wrote the four books of the Dialogues and many letters, in the year of the Lord 600.

Gondoaldus, king of Bavaria, son of the aforesaid Gerobaldus and brother of Queen Theodelinda, reigned after his father in Bavaria in the time of Childebert, king of the Franks, having under him Bavaria and Austria and the province of Noricum.

When Otharius, king of the Lombards, had died, Agilulf was elected king after him; he married his widow Theodelinda. Blessed Gregory asked her by letter to induce her husband to accept peace with the Romans, and she did so.

Childebert, king of the Franks, being at war with the Lombards, expelled Gondoaldus, the queen’s brother, from Bavaria, because he was bringing aid to the Lombards, and gave his duchy to Tassilo, son of Othilo, king of Bavaria. For Bavaria, being extensive, was at times subject to several princes.

Othilo, king of Bavaria, and afterward duke, was the father of Tassilo. He had as wife Hiltrud, sister of King Pippin, that is, the father of Charlemagne; by her he begot this same Tassilo.

Tassilo, duke of Bavaria, son of King Othilo, after his kinsman Gondoaldus had been expelled by Childebert, received his duchy from this same Childebert, king of the Franks. He had as wife Luitburg, daughter of Desiderius, the last king of the Lombards, who bore him a son Theodo, whom Saint Rupert, bishop of Worms, baptized at Regensburg in the year of the Lord 561. This man begot a son Theobert.

Duke Tassilo defeated the Slavs, built the monastery of Lorsch, and many other things. Othilo, his father, among other things also founded the monastery of Altaha, of the Order of Saint Benedict in Bavaria, which still exists today.

When Desiderius, king of the Lombards...

*Chronicle of the Dukes of Bavaria*

he finally brought it to the point that, with the Huns allied to him, in vengeance for his father he attacked Charlemagne, his kinsman, in war.

Pope Adrian, having sent legates to Tassilo, duke of Bavaria, warned him to submit himself to Charles. Persuaded by the entreaties of the legates, he came to Worms to the emperor, with the legates accompanying him, and there swore fealty to Charles; but he did not remain in fealty. Therefore he was excommunicated by Pope Adrian, together with all who adhered to him.

Charles, having returned from Rome to Worms after his coronation, summoned Tassilo, on the counsel of the princes, to an appointed day, and demanded obedience and fidelity from him; but Tassilo neither came to the assembly of the princes nor wished to obey the emperor.

The emperor, moved to anger, attacked Bavaria and Tassilo in war and surrounded them with three armies. He himself, with one army, set up camp near Augsburg, and between Bavaria and Alemannia, in the place called the Lech. Pepin his son arrived with the Italians in the valley of Trent, and the Saxons, coming with the Franks to the Danube, surrounded Bavaria with a threefold battle-line. At last Duke Tassilo, seeing that he was unequal to such great armies, sought pardon, and obtained it, giving his son Theodo, with twelve others, as hostages into the hands of the emperor.

Charles celebrated Easter at Ingelheim; there he ordered Duke Tassilo to be present. When he had come, he was gravely accused by the Bavarians and others of infidelity shown to the king. Therefore, although by the judgment of the princes he ought to have undergone a capital sentence, by the indulgence of the king, whose kinsman he was, he was thrust into the monastery of Lorsch for penance together with Theodo his son, and afterwards lived in great holiness.

This Tassilo founded very many monasteries in Bavaria, namely Wessobrunn, Kremsmünster, Lorsch, Weltenburg, and Pfaffenmünster. He renewed the walls of the city of Passau, and at that time transferred the episcopal see from Lauriacum.

There are those who say that he was blinded in prison by Charles the great emperor, by the continuous application of two heated plates. However that may be, it is agreed that in his own monastery of Lorsch, which he had previously built in [Straramontensi], not far from Worms, at great expense, he ended his life under the rule of Saint Benedict; and they say that he was buried there not without a reputation for holiness.

After Tassilo had been deposed from the duchy and had entered the monastery, the emperor entrusted the duchy of Bavaria to Count Gerold, who was killed by the Huns, who are the Hungarians, in the year of the Lord 1299, as is clear in the Cologne Chronicle.

At the time when Saint Boniface governed the church of Mainz, Occarius and Albertus, brothers and most illustrious dukes of Noricum, strong, noble, and most devout men, went out of love to see Rome. Pope Zacharias told them of the calamity that he was suffering from the unbelievers; wherefore the most Christian dukes, moved by zeal for the faith, armed themselves together with the Romans, bravely attacked the enemies, seized the spoils, and compelled them to leave the boundaries of the Church. But they left the spoils to the Romans, since they declared that they had come and fought not for bodily goods, but for the honor of God. Among the many relics which he gave them, the pope also granted them the body of Saint Quirinus. These two most holy dukes founded many churches in the province of Noricum.

Naynus, duke of Bavaria, in the time of the emperor Charles the Great, did many brave deeds against the unbelievers, by whom at last he was killed, a man altogether most excellent in zeal for the Christian faith. See the rest of what he did in the twenty-fifth book of Vincentius, chapter twenty-one, of the *Speculum*.

At almost the same time Lanfridus, Wairamus, and Hellandus, most Christian princes of Bavaria, bestowed many benefits on the church of God, fighting the wars of the Lord with a great fervor of piety. Among other things they built four monasteries, namely Burtochlarum, Schlechdorf, and Scheyern.

It should be known that the father of the two brothers named above, the dukes of Noricum Albertus and Occarius, was Burgundian, whose wife, their mother, was Bavarian. Of these, Occarius remained in Burgundy, in his paternal principality; but Albertus, younger by twelve years, held counties in Bavaria. These two, in the time of King Pepin, father of Charles Martel, [Gernoldum] and [Diogenem]. Further, Charles Martel begot King Pepin, father of Charles [unclear].

*Karoli Magistri Inveniens Per Mortem Origine*.

*Johannes Trithemius* of Charlemagne, Carloman and Grifo, duke of Bavaria, by his wife Swanahild, who was the daughter of the duke of Bavaria.

*Grifo.* This Grifo, entering Bavaria, wishing to claim the duchy for himself by hereditary right, drove out Duke Tassilo. But King Pippin, his brother, restored the duchy to Tassilo and led Grifo into Francia, giving him twelve cities in the manner of counts. He, by no means content, stirred up many wars against his brothers; hence, with little fortune, he was killed in the fifth year thereafter.

Therefore, after Grifo had been expelled from Bavaria by his brother Pippin, Tassilo obtained the duchy; him at last Charlemagne, son of Pippin, as has been said, deposed, and entrusted the province to counts or prefects.

Pippin, therefore, the brother of Grifo, begot Charlemagne. After the surrender of Duke Tassilo, he caused Bavaria for some time to be governed not by dukes but by counts. Charlemagne begot Louis, surnamed the Pious, who succeeded him in the empire; his second wife was Judith, daughter of Welf, count of Bavaria; hence also he established him as duke or king of Bavaria after the counts had been driven out. He also begot Charles, whom he established as king of Germany, and Pippin, whom he made king of Aquitaine and Spain. When the emperor Charlemagne had died and been buried at Aachen, Louis, duke of Bavaria, his son, succeeded him.

*Louis,* surnamed the Pious, son of Charlemagne and afterward Roman emperor, had a wife named Margaret, by whom he received three sons: Lothar, Pippin, and Louis. The first of these, Lothar, he placed over Bavaria, and he also was emperor after him. When his wife Margaret had died, he married another, named Judith, daughter of Welf, count of Bavaria. [unclear] king of Bavaria, after the counts had been driven out. He begot also Charles, whom he established as king of Germany, and Pippin, whom in some way he made king of Aquitaine and Spain. When the emperor Charlemagne had died, and is found in the tomb at Aachen, Louis duke of Bavaria, his son, succeeded him.

*Louis Prust,* surnamed the Pious, emperor, after many distinguished deeds, died and was buried at Metz; Lothar his son, king of Bavaria, succeeded him. Against him his brothers waged a very grave war near Auxerre, in which antiquity testifies that many thousands of men fell.

*Lothar.* This emperor had as wife Egilla, daughter of the king of England; she bore him two sons, Lothar and Louis, who succeeded him in the empire. They say that from this Lothar Lotharingia was so named.

*Louis,* son of the emperor Louis the Pious: when his brother Lothar had been raised to the empire, he himself obtained the kingdom of Bavaria and Germany. He had three sons: Charles, afterward the third emperor of this name; Louis, king of the Franks; and Carloman, the last king of Bavaria.

When Carloman, king of Bavaria, had died and been buried at Ötting, his brother Louis, king of the eastern Franks, subjected Bavaria to himself and gave to Arnulf, his brother's son, the duchy of Carinthia and Moosburg. And thus kings ceased in Bavaria.

*Louis,* brother of Carloman, king of the eastern Franks, after a war had been fought with the Northmen, died at Frankfurt on the Main and was buried in the monastery of Lorsch; and Arnulf returned to the duchy of Bavaria.

In the year of the Lord 855, Lothar the emperor abandoned the empire, when he had already ruled for fifteen years, and, having assumed the garb of a pilgrim, became a monk in the monastery of Prum, of the order of Saint Benedict. Louis's son succeeded him in the empire for twenty-one years.

*Louis,* the second of this name, son of the emperor Lothar, succeeding his father in the empire, ruled for forty-one years. His father Lothar, before the empire, was king of Bavaria. Theutberga, daughter of Charles the Bald, his father's brother, bore him one son, named Charles, and one daughter, named Gilla, whom he gave to a certain nobleman Boso, and made him duke of Burgundy. Afterward he gave up the empire to his son Charles the Bald, and, entering monasteries, died.

*Charles the Bald,* son of the emperor Louis the Pious and of Judith, daughter of Welf, count of Bavaria, after Louis his nephew, ruled for almost four years. He had as wife Adeltrude, sister of Boso, duke of Burgundy; she bore him one son named Louis and two daughters, Theoberga, whom he gave as wife to King Louis, his nephew, and Judith, wife of Baldwin, count of Flanders. This Charles built many monasteries.

When the emperor Charles the Bald had died, Charles, the third of this name, brother of Ca[unclear], [unclear] twelve, had as wife Adelburga, daughter of the king of Granaria. He at last, terrified by a horrible vision of hell, ordered many of his relatives, because of their bad administration of the people and the kingdom, to be tormented with very severe punishments; and, having given up the empire, he is said to have set out abroad. He left no heir, and his surname was Charles the Fat.

*Charlo-* *Chronicle of the Dukes of Bavaria.*

... Rudolf, duke of Bavaria, having been reduced to a count, he himself took up the duchy of Bavaria. And thus the duchy of Bavaria remained with the Saxons until Henry the Third, emperor; under him, when the stock of this Henry failed, the duchy reverted to the nephews of the aforesaid count Rudolf, as we shall say in its place. This duke Henry had as wife Lucardis, daughter of Arnold, duke of Bavaria, sister of the aforesaid count Rudolf; she bore him two sons, Bruno, margrave of Saxony, and Henry, later duke of Bavaria, and one daughter named Gerburg, abbess in Gandersheim.

And since we have said that all the modern dukes of Bavaria descended from the stock of Charlemagne, we must continue the line of descent from Count Rudolf, though the dukes of the Saxons were interposed for some years, until the duchy of Bavaria returned to the nephews of that Rudolf, so that the truth of what has been said may shine more clearly for all.

Rudolf, from duke become count of Bavaria, together with his brothers, pursued Duke Henry, the husband of his sister, as an invader of his paternal inheritance; he besieged and took Regensburg, and drove out Henry’s wife with her sons. Note that, when Arnold, duke of Bavaria, had died, Emperor Otto I had entrusted it to Berthold, his brother; and when he too had died, he appointed his own brother Henry duke, as has been said.

Welf, count of Bavaria, son of the aforesaid count Rudolf, had as wife Adelaide, daughter of the count of lower Baden; she bore him a son named Conrad, whose son Welf again obtained the duchy of Bavaria, as we shall say later.

*Henry.* Henry, duke of Bavaria, son of the aforesaid Duke Henry the Saxon, brother of Otto I, succeeding his father in the duchy of Bavaria, had as wife Bertha, daughter of the duke of Lotharingia; she bore him three sons and two daughters: two Henrys, of whom the elder was later emperor; Bruno, bishop of Augsburg; Gisela, wife of Saint Stephen, king of Hungary, who was converted to the faith of Christ; and Hedwig, whom Lothar, burgrave of Magdeburg, took as wife.

*Conrad.* Conrad, count of Bavaria, son of the aforesaid count Welf, had as wife a woman named Atza, daughter of the margrave of Mount Calym; she bore him three sons: Welf, who [unclear] the duchy.
