Saint Henry, emperor and duke of Bavaria, son of the aforesaid Henry, duke of Bavaria, after Otto III had died without children, was made emperor of the Romans by election of the princes: a vigorous, devout, and most holy man, who did many good things in the commonwealth. He had as wife Cunegund, daughter of Sigfrid, count palatine of the Rhine, most holy in conduct and life; both remained in holiness until death through love of Christ, and both were also enrolled in the catalogue of the saints.

Note: the counties of Bavaria at this time were several, namely Trubensis, Valaisiensis, [unclear], Burchard, bishop of Halberstadt, Simon, archbishop of Bremen.

Henry, emperor and duke of Bavaria, son of the aforesaid Henry, duke of Bavaria, after Otto III had died without children, was made emperor of the Romans by election of the princes: a vigorous, devout, and most holy man, who did many good things in the commonwealth. He had as wife Cunegund, daughter of Sigfrid, count palatine of the Rhine, most holy in conduct and life; and both remained in holiness until death through love of Christ, and both were also enrolled in the catalogue of the saints.

Note: the counties of Bavaria at this time were several, namely Trubensis, Valaisiensis, Burchard, bishop of Hall, Simon, archbishop of Bremen.

*Trube. Valey.* When at length all the counts of Trube-Valey had died, their county [unclear]. Dachau, Andechs, Wittelsbach, Bogen, Kastl, Amertal, Scheyern. In the course of succession there were many counts in these places; to recount them all by name would be too lengthy and difficult.

When the count of Dachau had died, those three counties devolved upon the counts of Scheyern. The counts palatine of Wittelsbach were few; and when they too at length failed, the county in Wittelsbach also devolved upon Scheyern.

Henry, emperor from duke of Bavaria, among the many good things that he did, established the bishopric of Hamburg, and constructed the monastery of Monks’ Mountain of the Order of Saint Benedict [unclear]; Saint Cunegund, his most chaste wife, with help from her own patrimony, [unclear] with an army returns to her father.

In the year of the Lord 1005, Henry, the Bavarian emperor, entered Italy; in the siege of a certain castle he was captured, but, with the Lord’s help, was freed, lowering himself down through the wall.

Since the region of Bavaria is very broad, it was subject, at intervals of time, to different dukes at different times: sometimes to one, sometimes to two, and at times even to several.

*Ernest.* Ernest, duke of Bavaria, coming from the Maeotic Marshes into Bavaria, in the times of O[unclear].

*Chronicle of the Dukes of Bavaria*

After Charles III had been deposed from the empire, Arnulph, duke of Bavaria, son of Carloman, the last king of Bavaria, was made emperor by the consent of all. He ruled for twelve years, a powerful, wealthy, and fortunate man, who accomplished many outstanding things in the commonwealth. He had as wife Agnes, daughter of the emperor of the Greeks, by whom he had two sons, Arnold and Bernher. Arnold married Agnes, daughter of the king of Hungary; and his brother Bernher married her sister, likewise a daughter of the king of Hungary, named Beatrice. These two sisters, daughters of the king of Hungary, were baptized in the castle which the emperor Arnolph built in Bavaria, a very strong one, named Scheyern. Arnold obtained the duchy of the Noricans, and his brother Bernher received the county of Scheyern and the county of the Palatine of the Rhine. Arnold himself gave his daughter, named Adelheid, as wife to Otto, duke of Saxony; she bore a son named Henry, whom Arnold made duke of Bavaria, against the will of Bernhert, his count of Scheyern. And thus the duchy of Bavaria came for some time to the Saxons; but afterward it was again restored to the Bavarians.

When the empress Agnes, mother of the aforesaid Arnold and Bernher, had died, Arnolph took another wife, Lucard, daughter of Vulp, duke of Bavaria, by whom he had two sons: Louis, who succeeded him in the empire, and Conrad, father of Conrad, the first emperor, who was made duke of Lotharingia; and one daughter, named Lucard, whom the duke of the Saxons took as wife. He also had a son by a concubine, named Rindebald, whom his father afterward made king of Lotharingia, in the year of the Lord 896.

And so Arnold, son of the emperor Arnolph, duke of the Noricans, begot his daughter Adelheid for Otto, duke of the Saxons; she bore Henry, the above-named duke, and a daughter Adelheid, who later became abbess in Quedlinburg, a virgin of holy conduct.

Bernhard, his brother, count in Scheyern, begot by his wife Beatrice, daughter of the king of Hungary, Otto of Wittelsbach, count Palatine of the Rhine, and Echard, later count of Scheyern in Bavaria. Echard begot Arnold, Otto, and Conrad. Further, Arnold begot Conrad, called the Monk of Scheyern; and this Arnold was lord in Dachau, his brother Otto in Scheyern, and Conrad in Valley. From these three brothers, sons of Count Echard, many counts and princes of Scheyern took their beginning, so that at one time in a certain court of Vulp, duke of Bavaria, at a tournament, there were thirty-four counts, all descended from Scheyern, although not all of them dwelt there; for each one was established in his own lordship. And thus the castle of Scheyern, deprived of inhabitants and at length ruinous from age, was changed into a monastery in the year of the Lord 1304, as we shall say later. But all those thirty-four died within three years afterward, except two, Arnold of Dachau and Otto of Scheyern. This Arnold, lord of Dachau, begot Conrad; Conrad begot Arnold and Conrad; Arnold begot Conrad, duke of the Ruthenians, who was killed near Milan and buried in Scheyern.

The emperor Arnulph, powerful and an outstanding defender of the Christian faith, overcame the Normans in a fierce war, killed innumerable numbers of them, and drove them from the territories of the Christians after they had afflicted Germany for forty years. In the same war he killed Sigifrid, king of the Normans, and Gotfrid, king of the Danes. Returning from Gaul to Bavaria after the slaughter of the Normans, the emperor brought with him the body of blessed Dionysius the Areopagite, which he placed at Regensburg in the monastery of Saint Hemeranus the martyr, where it is still honorably preserved today.

Conrad, by Lucard, the second wife of the emperor Arnulph, duke of Lotharingia, begot two sons, Eberhard, who was killed, and Conrad, afterward emperor of the Romans; Arnold, the aforesaid brother of his father, opposed him, as we shall say more fully later in its time.

After the capture of Rome, the defeat of the Northmen, and many other glorious deeds, the emperor Arnulph died. There are those who write that he was consumed by lice, which, growing from the excessively frequent eating of garlic, no one could ward off by any skill.

Louis, son of Arnulph, was a Bavarian emperor. After the emperor Arnulph had died,

*Louis III, emperor:*

Louis his son, the third of this name in the empire, succeeded him, born of Lucard, daughter of Vulp, duke of Bavaria; and thus by both parents he was Bavarian. He was the brother of Arnold, duke of the Noricans, and Bernher, count of Scheyern. He had as wife Lucard, daughter of Ludolph, duke of Saxony, sister of Otto, and died without children.

The Bavarians fight with the Hungarians and are defeated; to them Bavaria and Franconia *Johannes Trithemius*

...while they were attacking fiercely, the Bavarians again make ready for battle, and, when the army of the emperor Louis comes up, they kill many of the Hungarians and turn the rest to flight. Conrad, duke of Lotharingia, brother of this Louis and son of Arnolph, a Bavarian by birth, was killed by the treachery of Adalbert, margrave of Bamberg.

Louis III, emperor of the Romans, son of the Bavarian emperor Arnolph, dies without children in the year of the Lord 813; after him Conrad, the son of his brother, is elected.

Conrad the emperor, born of a Bavarian father, the duke: when the emperor Louis, son of Arnolph, had died, Conrad, son of his brother Conrad, duke of Lotharingia, whom Adalbert, margrave of Bamberg, had killed, from the line of Charlemagne, was made the last emperor in the empire. He did not have a wife. Eberhard, of whom we shall speak later, [unclear].

Arnolph, duke of Bavaria, brother of Conrad, father of this Conrad, duke of the Romans, that is, son of the emperor Arnolph, opposed this emperor Conrad; defeated at length by him, he fled with his wife and children into Hungary, until the death of the aforesaid Conrad.

King Conrad, after Duke Arnolph had been driven out of Bavaria, planned in like manner to attack Henry, duke of the Saxons, and so he besieged Merseburg. There on the king’s side fell Eberhard his brother and Hatto, archbishop of Mainz, and he himself scarcely escaped. Thereafter Henry, duke of the Saxons, devastated all the king’s land. When King Conrad was about to die, he sent the crown of the kingdom to the above-mentioned Henry, duke of the Saxons, who reigned after him; and he died in Eastern Francia, buried at Würzburg.

Arnolph, duke of Bavaria, having heard of the death of King Conrad, returns from Hungary to Bavaria and is received by all with great honor, all asking that he deign to take up the kingdom of the Romans. Since Henry, duke of the Saxons, was succeeding in the kingdom, and all the princes except the aforesaid Arnolph, duke of Bavaria, obeyed him, Henry gathered his army and advanced against him in war, and besieged Regensburg. And Duke Arnolph, seeing that he could not resist so great a multitude, opened the gates, sought favor, and obtained it. Accordingly a very firm peace is made between them under these conditions: that the king confer upon Duke Arnolph the full fief or lordship over all the bishoprics in Bavaria, leave him to possess his duchy peacefully, and hold him chief among his friends; and so it was done. And so Henry remained in the kingdom. When he died, Otto I, his son, succeeded; after him Otto II, son of the first; then Otto III, son of the second, who died without children. And Henry, duke of Bavaria, succeeded the aforesaid in the empire by election, as we shall say later in its place.

Under Otto I the emperor there was a very grave war between the Christians and the Hungarians. At that time they were still unbelievers at Augsburg, where the emperor himself triumphed with the Christians. There fell Conrad, duke of Bavaria, and Count Theobald, brother of Saint Ulrich, bishop of Augsburg.

The cause of the war [unclear] just: Count Bernher was claiming the duchy of Bavaria as the legitimate heir; the sons of his brother, one of whom was emperor, opposed him. Moved by this, he summoned the Hungarians, asking for aid. After Count Bernher of Scheyern was killed by the Hungarians, Eberhard and Bernher, his sons, succeeding in the place of their father, were claiming the duchy of Bavaria, which Eberhard at last [unclear], as we shall say.

Arnolph, duke of the Noricans, dies, leaving, among other children, Duke Rudolph after him, and a daughter named Lucarda, whom Henry, duke of Saxony and later also of Bavaria, son of Henry I the emperor and brother of Otto I, took as wife, as we shall say later.

Rudolph, duke of Bavaria after the death of the aforesaid Henry I, rebels against Emperor Otto, his son; hence from duke of Bavaria he was made count in Scheyern.

Henry the Saxon, duke of Bavaria, son of Henry I the emperor, and brother of Otto I, and *Johannes Trithemius*

... of Emperor Otto I, obtained the duchy of the Norici. The same Emperor Otto gave him a part of the forest in the province of the Norici, namely in that place where the Castellense monastery of the order of Saint Benedict now stands; after rooting out the woods, he made the land fit for ploughs. From this duke Ernest many notable lords of Bavaria descended in the Norican province, especially the counts of Castello-Sultzbach.

This Ernest, duke of the Norici, had as wife Adelheid, daughter of the duke of Burgundy, who bore him a son named Ernest, of whom marvelous things are told. When Duke Ernest the elder died, Emperor Otto I joined his wife Adelheid, mother of the younger Ernest, to himself in marriage; she bore him Otto II, emperor, and a daughter Mechthild, who was abbess in Quedlinburg.

Ernest the younger, duke of the Norici, son of the aforesaid Duke Ernest, after his father’s death, gave himself to the service of masters, so that he might learn Latin, Greek, and Italian speech; afterwards he did marvelous things.

Henry, count palatine of the Rhine, a friend of Emperor Otto, hating this duke Ernest, was accustomed to accuse him gravely before the emperor his stepfather, though unjustly, as if he were plotting against the life of the empire itself; this was by no means hidden from Ernest. Hence, when the emperor one day in the city of Speyer was secretly engaged with the son of Count Henry, with the doors closed, Ernest, with Count Wetzel his uncle accompanying him, burst in, broke down the doors, killed Henry the palatine as he was sitting at the emperor’s side, and then, having taken up the cross, went with Wetzel his uncle and many others to the Holy Land. But after a delay at sea in a storm, all except himself [unclear]; he accomplished many outstanding deeds, on land and sea, in many distant regions, which are preserved in writings. Then, returning with Count Wetzel to his homeland, he brought back several men of diverse nations and forms. The emperor, when he had learned of his innocence, received his son back into his favor, appointing him ruling prince of the whole imperial court.

In the year of the Lord 1008, Saint Henry the emperor, duke of Bavaria, defeated Baldwin, count of Flanders, who was rebelling against him, and subjected him to himself; he took Ghent, and, after an engagement, overcame Boleslaus, duke of Poland, who was repeatedly plundering the Saxons, and converted him with his people to the faith of Christ, having in his army Saint Stephen, king of Hungary, his sister’s husband.

Saint Henry the emperor died in the year of the Lord 1025, and was buried at Bamberg in the greater church which he himself had built; his deeds are preserved in writings. Conrad, duke of Franconia, succeeded to the empire; after him Henry III, and after him the fourth emperor.

Henry, duke of Bavaria, brother of Conrad, duke of Swabia, after Saint Henry, from duke became emperor and obtained the duchy of Bavaria. He built a monastery in Osterhofen, in the diocese of Passau; Bernard and Eckhard at length obtained the kingdom, as we said above.

Cuno, duke of the Norici, son of the aforesaid Duke Eckhard, took up the duchy of Bavaria, which his father had held, after his death. He entered into a treaty with the Hungarians, whom he called to his aid against Emperor Henry III, in the year of the Lord 1054.

Cuno, duke of the Norici, at length driven out of Bavaria by Emperor Henry, fled to the Hungarians in the year of the Lord 1055. There, as long as he lived, he remained in exile. The emperor gave his duchy to his brother Conrad, who died a little later.

Conrad, duke of Bavaria, brother of Emperor Henry IV, after Cuno had been expelled, received his duchy from the emperor; he died not long afterward, namely in the year of the Lord 1056.

Agnes the empress, mother of Henry IV, after the death of the aforesaid Conrad, received the duchy of Bavaria from her son; after some years she gave it to a certain noble Otto, living among the Saxons, of whom we shall speak later. In the year of the Lord 1061, Agnes the empress, mother of Emperor Henry IV, conferred the duchy of Bavaria on Otto, count of Northeim; she herself went into Italy.

Otto, duke of Bavaria, a Saxon by race, count in Northeim, received the duchy of Bavaria from the empress, as has been said: a noble, vigorous, and just man, powerful and very acceptable in the court of King Henry. The aforesaid Otto, duke of Bavaria, founded in Northeim a monastery of the aforesaid order of Saint Benedict, giving it many estates, gifts from his county. This Otto, duke of Bavaria, since he was distinguished in the court of King Henry and was acquiring public authority for himself, was unjustly accused, through a certain subordinate, by the envy of certain impious men, that *Chronicle of the Dukes of Bavaria.*

because he had conspired for the murder of the king, he was driven first from the court and then also from the duchy, and waged war against the emperor with the princes of Saxony and Thuringia. Welf, or Welff, obtained the duchy of Bavaria.

*Welf, also called Welff, duke of Bavaria*, son of Conrad, count of Bavaria, received from the emperor, as the legitimate heir, the duchy of Bavaria after Otto; his forefathers had possessed it before. For his great-grandfather Rudolph, son of Arnolph, duke of Bavaria, had been duke; rebelling against Otto, the first emperor of that name, and defeated by him, he was made count of Scheyern from duke, as was said above.

Thus, after the duchy of Bavaria had been restored to the line of the emperor Arnolph, let us continue the sequence of generations of the dukes descending from Charlemagne, begun earlier. I am not unaware that some among the writers have dared to maintain that this duke Welf was a Swabian by nation, while others say that he was an Italian, the son of a certain marquis. But it is established that he was the son of Conrad, count of Bavaria, son of Arnolph, duke and emperor of the Romans. Nor does it matter where he was born, provided that the sequence of descent is established to have come down to the lawful dukes of Bavaria.

Therefore this duke Welff betrothed to himself as wife Ethelina, daughter of the aforesaid duke Otto, count of Northeim. But when Otto was driven from the duchy, he sent the daughter back to him, fearing King Henry, from whom he had received the duchy and who was Otto's enemy. Count Hermann afterward took her as his wife, left as a widow by the king of England. She bore him three sons and one daughter: Henry, surnamed the Black, who was duke of Bavaria after him; Welf, who went into Italy; Sigebert; and Adelheid, whom Conrad, burgrave of Magdeburg, took as wife.

*Otto, formerly duke of Bavaria and count in Northeim*, had many battles against the emperor in Saxony; in one of them Ernest, marquis of Bavaria, son of Duke Ernest [unclear], who had often been victorious in Hungary and in various other regions, fell, in the year of the Lord 1075.

The other things that the aforesaid Otto did with the Saxons against the emperor, and suffered from him, and how at last he was received back into his favor, are written very fully by Lampert, the monk of Hersfeld, in the deeds of that Emperor Henry; it would be too tedious to set them out here.

*Welf, duke of Bavaria*, learning that the Saxons were being unjustly oppressed by King Henry, refused to give him aid against them; whence he too was judged an enemy of the commonwealth and was also deprived by him of the duchy. But afterward, received again into the emperor's favor, he deserved not only to recover the duchy but also to have his son confirmed as duke of Bavaria. Then, having taken the cross in the time of Pope Urban II, in the year of the Lord 1106 he set out for the Holy Land, and died in Cyprus; and almost all his men, with many other Christians, were destroyed and captured through the treachery of Alexius, emperor of the Greeks.

This duke Welff, among other things that he did, built monasteries, namely Steingaden, Altdorf, Weingarten, Altenmunster, and Nietenbach. When he died and was buried in the monastery of [Artesheym?], Henry, surnamed the Black, succeeded him in the duchy of Bavaria. Some write that this duke Welff, after the death of his wife Jutta, took as wife Agnes, the mother of Emperor Henry IV.

*Ecchard, duke of Bavaria*, brother of Werner of Scheyern, who for the recovery of his father's duchy brought the Hungarians out for the third time against the emperor, of whom mention was made above, in the time of Pope Urban II, took the cross with Godfrey, duke of Lorraine, and set out for the Holy Land, and Jerusalem was recovered by the Christians. There was also in these times Otto, bishop of Bamberg, and Frederick, count in Ammerthal, who lies buried in the monastery of Kastl. He had a daughter named Sophia, whom Otto, duke of Bavaria in Ammerthal, son, as some think, of Ernest, took as wife; he did many good things for the monastery of Kastl and was buried there.

*Henry, duke of Bavaria, surnamed the Black*, son of the aforesaid duke Welff, had as wife Wulfhild, daughter of Magnus, duke of Luneburg. She bore him two sons and four daughters: Henry, Welf, Sophia, whom he gave to Berthold, duke of Thuringia; after he was killed, she took Leopold II, marquis of Steyr, as husband. The second daughter was called Wulfhild, whom he gave to Rudolph, count of [Praegnicen?]. The third *Of Johannes Trithemius*

... named Mechtild he gave to Margrave Theobald the Younger; after his death, he gave her to the count of Sulzbach. The fourth, named Jutta, Frederick duke of Swabia took as wife; she bore Frederick, the first emperor.

Welf, duke of Bavaria, son of Duke Welf and brother of the aforesaid Henry, a most warlike man, left the duchy of Bavaria to his brother, sought Italy, and took as wife Mechtild, daughter of the duke of Milan; both died without children. This Duke Welf is said to have done many marvelous things, and he devastated Swabia with fire, sword, and slaughter.

Sigebert, count of Bavaria, brother of the aforesaid Henry and Welf, had as wife Oda, daughter of Gebhard, count of Supplinburg and lord in Arnsberg. This count, remaining in the province of Bavaria, yielded the duchy to his brother.

Henry, duke of Bavaria, surnamed the Proud, son of the above-mentioned Duke Henry, a strong and very daring man, had as wife Gertrude, daughter of Lothar the second emperor. She bore him Henry, the most noble duke of the Saxons, who, on account of his strength and the magnificent deeds he accomplished, was called the Lion, and powerfully extended his dominion from the Rhine as far as the river called the Elbe.

To this Henry, duke of Bavaria, Emperor Lothar, together with his daughter, conferred the duchy of Saxony; from him all the dukes of Brunswick and Luneburg thereafter, down to those who exist today, descended by lineal succession, as we shall easily show.

For Henry, duke of Bavaria and Saxony, Lothar's son-in-law, begot by Gertrude his wife Henry surnamed the Lion, concerning whom the common people report marvelous things: that he fought with griffins, carried off a lion, and, from danger at sea, was carried by a griffin sewn into a horse-hide; and many other things, which I neither reject nor affirm. This Henry begot by Mechtild, sister of Richard king of England, a son named William, who succeeded his father in the duchy; also Otto, afterward king of the Romans; Henry, count palatine of the Rhine; and two daughters, Mechtild and Rita. William begot Otto by Helena, daughter of the king of Denmark. Otto begot Albert and John, which two divided between themselves the paternal inheritance, namely the duchy of Brunswick and Luneburg, provision having been made for the brothers elsewhere.

In the year of the Lord 1238, Emperor Frederick II, being at Mainz, transferred the name and duchy of Saxony from the aforesaid Otto to Albert, son of Henry count of Anhalt, whom he made duke of Saxony and electoral prince of the empire. And thus Otto, son of Duke William, remained duke of Brunswick and Luneburg. These same dukes, moreover, are continued in succession from the line of Henry the Bavarian down to those who live today, inclusively; [unclear] of the Rhine, and two daughters, Mechtild and Rixa. William begot Otto by Helena, daughter of the king of Denmark. Otto begot Albert and John, which two divided between themselves the paternal inheritance, namely the duchy of Brunswick and Luneburg, provision having been made for the brothers elsewhere. For it is enough that it be established with the greatest certainty that all the dukes of Brunswick, from the time of Lothar II down to these men, descended from the Bavarians.

*The Transfer of the Duchy of Bavaria to the Margrave of Austria*

After Emperor Lothar died, in the year of the Lord 1138, since Henry duke of Bavaria, surnamed the Proud, his son-in-law, a most powerful man, seemed to be seeking the empire, the princes, fearing his power, assembled at Koblenz and elected Conrad, duke of Swabia, as king of the Romans. When Henry, duke of Bavaria, together with the Saxons, opposed him as one not duly elected, Conrad summoned an assembly of princes for the day of Pentecost at Bamberg, and for that day cited Duke Henry himself. In this matter, when all had assembled together with the empress, Lothar's widow, and had been received into Conrad's favor, he alone did not appear. At last, on the day of the apostles Peter and Paul, at Regensburg, he resigned all these things into the hands of King Conrad; but he did not obtain his favor.

In those days Pope Innocent II was unwilling either to crown King Conrad or to permit him entry into Italy, because of the kingdom of Sicily, which each said belonged to his own authority, and which had already been given in fief by the pope himself to a certain Roger; Conrad was preparing to recover it.

And so the pope hired Henry duke of Bavaria and Welf his brother, for a price, to prevent King Conrad's entry into Italy with a powerful hand. Roger also, the invader...

*Chronicle of the Dukes of Bavaria*

[Roger?] of Sicily; with the pope aiding him, he assembled a very great army against King Conrad from Italy, Gaul, and Sicily. And so King Conrad, intending to go into Italy with Frederick, duke of the Swabians, against the pope and Roger, encountered Welf, duke of Bavaria, opposing him with a great army of Bavarians and others. Duke Henry, however, Welf’s brother, had remained at home because of old age. And so a very severe battle took place between them in the diocese of Augsburg, near a certain monastery of the order of Saint Benedict, which is called Neresheim. There Frederick, duke of the Swabians, on the king’s side, obtained the victory, and many on Welf’s side fell slain, and he himself barely escaped with a few.

Again Duke Welf, having gathered a great army, fought a battle against Duke Frederick near Weinsberg, around the village of Ellenhofen in the diocese of Wuerzburg, in which he too fell back, and the greater part of his army was laid low.

Therefore Henry, duke of Bavaria, surnamed the Proud, excommunicated by the judgment of the princes and deposed from the duchy of Bavaria by King Conrad, came poor and on foot from Bavaria with his wife and children into Saxony, and remained there until death. Leopold, margrave of Austria, received his duchy from King Conrad.

Leopold, margrave, duke of Bavaria: this Leopold, margrave of Austria, received the duchy of the Norici after Duke Henry had been deposed by King Conrad. He was the son of the elder Margrave Leopold, by Agnes, daughter of Emperor Henry IV, who before Leopold had had Frederick, duke of the Swabians. When this Duke Leopold died not long afterward, the king conferred the duchy upon Henry his brother.

Henry, margrave, duke of Bavaria, was the brother of Leopold. After his brother’s death, King Conrad gave to him as wife the widow left by Henry, duke of Bavaria, whom he had deposed, Gertrude, daughter of Emperor Lothar, and established him as duke of Bavaria.

Otto, bishop of Bamberg, son of Count Berthold, a bold man and of most holy conduct, was held renowned in these times.

*Restoration of the Duchy of Bavaria to the Legitimate Heirs*

When Conrad, king of the Romans, had died, Frederick, the first of this name, son of Duke Conrad, succeeded. In the year of the Lord 1156, around the feast of the Nativity of the Blessed Mary ever Virgin, at the request of the princes he restored the duchy to Henry, duke of Saxony, son of the elder Henry the Proud, once duke of Bavaria, removing Henry, brother of Leopold, margrave of Austria. These things were done at Regensburg, in the year as above.

At the same time Emperor Frederick raised the march of Austria into a duchy, appointing as the first duke in Austria the aforesaid Henry, brother of Leopold, whom he had removed from the duchy of Bavaria, releasing him from all jurisdiction of the duke of Bavaria, and giving several counties of Austria to Henry, duke of Bavaria, as recompense and exemption. For previously the margraves of Austria, whenever they had been summoned by the dukes of Bavaria to their court, were accustomed to appear as subjects to them, just as counts and other nobles are still bound to obey. The same Emperor Frederick I raised the duchy of Bohemia into a kingdom.

Henry, duke of Bavaria and Saxony, son of Henry the Proud, restored to the paternal inheritance of both duchies, took the greatest care to rule and govern the people subject to him justly and according to the laws, in all peace and tranquillity. Whoever violated the laws issued by him was punished with death. Therefore, peace having been established for all throughout all Bavaria together with justice, Duke Henry had praise and honor in everyone’s mouth above all the princes of that time.

*Transfer of the Duchy of Bavaria to the Counts of Scheyern*

When Emperor Frederick had prepared an expedition into Italy, he called the already mentioned Henry, duke of Bavaria and Saxony, to his aid. And so Henry, entering Italy with a great army to bring aid, met Frederick himself coming toward him, saying that such a great multitude of armed men was not necessary for him, and he asked the duke to return with his men to his homeland.

But one of the duke’s officers, moved by this, said to him: “Most illustrious prince, you have placed the crown at your feet, so that it cannot ascend to your head.” This word so displeased the emperor that he hated the duke all the days of his life, and from the duchy finally removed him from Bavaria, conferring it upon Otto, count of Scheyern, who was of the race of the Carolingians.

*Otto of Scheyern.*

*It is an error.*

In the *Germania* of Andreas of Regensburg; [unclear] of the Carolingians, that is, or “of the race of the Carolingians,” as it is found in the Latin; [unclear] that the author was deceived here. Scheyern monastery [unclear]. Note well.

*OTTO, duke of Bavaria.* This Otto was count in Scheyern, from the stock of the great duke Cuno, of whom mention was made above, from the line of Charlemagne the emperor. Frederick the emperor conferred the duchy of Bavaria upon him, as the lawful and nearest heir, after Henry had been removed; from him all the dukes of Bavaria and counts palatine of the Rhine who exist today descended, as we shall say in order in what follows.

Thus in the year of the Lord 1180 the aforesaid Otto, count of Scheyern, was made duke of Bavaria, a strong and just man, and most renowned in the Christian religion. He had a very devout wife named Agnes, by whom he begot Louis, his successor in the duchy of Bavaria, and Elizabeth, previously queen of the Jerusalemites.

In the year of the Lord 1124 Otto, count of Scheyern, afterward duke, made the castle of Scheyern a monastery in honor of great blessed Mary ever virgin. There were at that time many counts in Bavaria bearing the title “of Scheyern,” but none of them lived in that castle. Since it had nearly fallen into ruin through extreme age, Otto [unclear] summoned all those having a share in the place, namely Conrad, Count Otto, count of Dachau, Otto count palatine in Wittelsbach, another Otto of Scheyern, Count Arnold, with seven others; all of them unanimously offered to blessed Mary ever virgin, for the building of a monastery, the right which they had in the castle of Scheyern. And they chose that place as the perpetual burial-place of themselves and of their family. Count Arnold, however, offering his part not to God but to the Devil, threw his glove into the air and said: “You, Lord Devil, receive my part into your right.” Demons carried off the glove. The others, however, notwithstanding the treachery of one man, completed the work they had begun with a cheerful spirit.

In the year of the Lord 1181 Gebhard of Burghausen, duke in Bavaria, died, a vigorous and just man, and one who feared God. In the same year Conrad, duke of Bavaria, Dalmatia, and Croatia, died in Scheyern; by his magnificent deeds he won for himself eternal remembrance among posterity.

*HENRY,* son of Duke Henry of Saxony called the Lion, brother of Otto the fourth emperor and of William duke of Brunswick, having been made count palatine of the Rhine, took as wife Agnes, daughter of Conrad count palatine, of whom we shall speak later; Gertrude, whom the duke of Bavaria took as wife; and Adelaide, whom Eric count of Baden took. When Agnes, his first wife, had died, Henry took another Agnes, daughter of the most noble count of Landsberg, by whom he had no children.

In the year of the Lord 1198 Otto, most noble duke of Bavaria, died; he was buried in the monastery of Scheyern next to his brother Bernher, leaving a son named Louis.

*LOUIS, duke of Bavaria:* son of the above-mentioned Otto, he succeeded his father as prince after his death. He had as wife Ludmilla, daughter of the king of Bohemia, who bore him a son named Otto, duke of Bavaria and count palatine, of whom we shall speak later. This Ludmilla before Louis had married Albert, margrave of Bogen, to whom she bore two sons, namely Albert and Berthold, margraves after their father.

*LUDMILLA,* duchess of Bavaria, wife of Louis, built a monastery in Bavaria named Stedental, in which she lies buried.

*LOUIS,* duke of Bavaria, went to the Holy Land with Emperor Frederick the second, Pope Honorius the third, and Leopold duke of Austria. He was later killed through the plots of Emperor Frederick at Kelheim, in the year of the Lord 1231.

*OTTO,* duke of Bavaria, count palatine of the Rhine, son of the above-mentioned Louis duke of Bavaria, succeeding his father, had as wife Gertrude, daughter of Henry count palatine of the Rhine; she bore him two sons, Henry and Louis.

This Otto, son of Duke Louis, obtained the duchy of Bavaria after his father as lawful heir, and with his wife took possession of the Palatine county of the Rhine, Heidelberg, together with what belonged to it. She gave Braubach as a fief to the count of Katzenelnbogen.

Thus Otto, duke of Bavaria and count palatine of the Rhine, at the beginning of his rule was a pious, vigorous, and just prince; but afterward, because of the agreement which he had with Emperor Frederick and his son Conrad, he was excommunicated by Pope Innocent. For this reason, flaring up in hatred of the clergy and adding evil to evil, in the year of the Lord 1245, when *CHRONICLE OF THE DUKES OF BAVARIA.*

…when, on the vigil of Saint Andrew the Apostle, he had been merry with [his] wife and household, he died a sudden death.

Otto, duke of Bavaria, being dead, his sons Ludwig [and] Heinrich divide their father's princedom between themselves. To Ludwig fell the county Palatine of the Rhine, with the others in upper Bavaria; but to Heinrich fortune gave Landshut, with lower Bavaria. In the year of the Lord 1256.

LUDWIG, count Palatine of the Rhine, duke of Bavaria, son of Otto duke of Bavaria, brother of the aforesaid prince Heinrich, first married Maria, daughter of the duke of Brabant, whom in the year of the Lord 1247 he himself killed. Afterward he took Anna, daughter of the king of Poland. He begot three sons: Ludwig; Rudolf the count Palatine; [and] another Ludwig, afterward king of the Romans—of whom we shall speak below in order.

In the year of the Lord 1247, duke Ludwig, for the defense of Bavaria, built the fortress which is called Friedberg, against the bishop of Augsburg, [as] a city. Ludwig, after many [things] excellently accomplished, dies; he is buried in Fürstenfeld, which he himself had built before; after whom his sons rose up, as we shall say in [its] place.

HEINRICH, duke of Bavaria, son of Otto duke of Bavaria, count Palatine of the Rhine, brother of the said Ludwig, had as wife Elizabeth, daughter of Béla king of Hungary, who was brother of Saint Elizabeth the widow; [she] bore him three sons: Otto king of Hungary, Ludwig, [and] Stephen, dukes of Bavaria, of whom we shall make mention in what follows.

In the year of the Lord 1231, Albert, the last count of Bogen, dies, whose county is turned over to the dukes of Bavaria. The aforesaid Heinrich, duke of Bavaria, dies in the year of the Lord 1291; he is buried at Landshut. Others say that he was buried at Burghausen. But he left three sons, of whom we shall speak afterward.

RUDOLF, count Palatine of the Rhine, duke of Bavaria, son of Ludwig, whose brother was [Bogen]. Ludwig [afterward] king of the Romans [had a wife] who bore him three sons—Rudolf, Rupert, [and] Adolf—of whom it will be spoken afterward. From this Rudolf descended all the counts Palatine of the Rhine who live today, as will clearly appear from their genealogy in what follows.

When Ludwig, brother of the aforesaid Rudolf, count Palatine, had been elected king of the Romans, Rudolf, bearing this ill, elected Frederick, duke of Austria, as king of the Romans. Which deed the emperor Ludwig took so ill that he expelled him, despoiled of all paternal possession, from [his] country; [and] he, fleeing into England, died there. His sons, however, were admitted by [their] uncle the emperor to the paternal inheritance, as we shall say.

LUDWIG, count Palatine of the Rhine, duke of Bavaria, emperor of the Romans, son of the aforesaid prince Ludwig, brother of Rudolf of whom we have already made mention, was made emperor of the Romans in the year of the Lord 1315. He had as wife Margaret, granddaughter—through a daughter—of Philip king of France. For the sister of king Philip had married William, count of Hainaut, who bore William duke of Holland [and] Margaret, wife of this emperor Ludwig, who bore him six sons—namely, Ludwig margrave of Brandenburg; Stephen at Landshut; Albert at Straubing; William duke of Holland, Zeeland, [and] Friesland, of Breda; Ludwig who was called the Roman (because he was born at Rome); [and] Otto of Brandenburg. From this Margaret, therefore, wife of the emperor Ludwig, the duchies of Holland, Zeeland, Friesland, [and] Hainaut, with the other lands pertaining to her, came to the dukes of Bavaria by hereditary right, in the year of the Lord 1324.

Hereafter I shall bring in the sons of Heinrich, duke of Bavaria dwelling at Landshut, son of Otto the duke and brother of Ludwig; I shall unfold the order of their generation. They were three: Otto king of Hungary, Ludwig, [and] Stephen, dukes of Bavaria, as is shown above.

OTTO, duke of Bavaria, king of Hungary, son of Heinrich the duke dwelling at Landshut, brother of Ludwig [and] Stephen, dukes of Bavaria, had as wife a daughter of the duke of Poland, who bore [him] a son by name Heinrich, fourteen days before the death of Otto himself, in the year of the Lord 1309. The king of Hungary died without sons; whence the princes of Hungary, an embassy having been sent, elected the aforesaid Otto, duke of Bavaria, as the nearer heir of the kingdom (because he was the son of Béla, king of Hungary), as king of Hungary; whom… also crowned him with the sword, in royal fashion. Therefore, when he had entered Pannonia with a strong force, after some days the Hungarians gathered and promised him complete fidelity; he sent his soldiers back into Bavaria, and after his coronation, when he had penetrated farther into Hungary, he was captured by a certain prince of the region. Since he would not take that prince’s daughter as his wife, with the help of a certain servant he was let down over the wall, changed his clothing, escaped alone, and in rustic guise, after traversing Prussia and many lands, came to Wrocław, where, being recognized and betrayed, he was again captured by the duke of Poland. After taking his daughter in marriage, he was received with great honor in Bavaria; and not long afterward he died.

*Otto.*

OTTO, king of Hungary and duke of Bavaria, when he saw that the time of his death was drawing near, entrusted his son Henry, a boy of fourteen days, who afterward was called prince of [Natternberg?], and the two sons of his brother Stephen, Henry, who was eight years of age, and Otto, who had not yet completed his seventh year, to the citizens in Landshut and in Straubing, not to be handed over under oath to anyone except Louis, duke of Upper Bavaria; and he died in the year of the Lord 1312. After his death, the nobles of the land demanded that the aforesaid three boys, entrusted by Otto himself to the people of Landshut and Straubing, be given to them, wishing to place them under the guardianship of the duke of Austria and to transfer this dominion to him.

And so, in the year of the Lord 1314, on the day of Saint Theodore the martyr, through this occasion a great battle took place between Duke Louis, afterward emperor, and the duke of Austria, near a certain village called Gammelsdorf. And Duke Louis emerged victorious and obtained for himself the lordship over the boys, as their legitimate guardian.

*Stephen.*

STEPHEN, duke of Bavaria, brother of the aforesaid Otto, king of Hungary, namely the son of Duke Henry in Landshut, left two sons: Henry, surnamed the Good, and Otto of Burghausen. Henry had as wife the daughter of John, king of Bohemia, as we shall say later. These two princes, together with his own son Henry of [Natternberg?], Otto, king of Hungary and duke of Bavaria, now on the point of death, entrusted to the citizens in Landshut and Straubing, to be conveyed to Louis, afterward emperor, their legitimate guardian, as was said above.

OTTO, son of Stephen, duke of Bavaria, brother of the aforesaid Henry, who lived at Burghausen, died without children in the year of the Lord 1335.

HENRY, son of Otto, king of Hungary, called the Younger, or of [Natternberg?], duke of Bavaria, whose mother was the daughter of the duke of Poland, died without children when he was twenty years old, in the year of the Lord 1333. The aforesaid three dukes, Henry the Good, his brother Otto of Burghausen, and Henry the Younger, or of [Natternberg?], son of Otto, king of Hungary, divided Lower Bavaria among themselves, as follows.

*Division of Lower Bavaria among the aforesaid dukes.*

In the year of the Lord 1331 there was a great disagreement between Duke Henry, surnamed the Good, on one side, and Otto his brother and Henry the Younger, son of Otto, king of Hungary, on the other side, concerning the duchy of Lower Bavaria. Therefore John, king of Bohemia, father-in-law of the elder Henry, held a meeting with other princes in Regensburg, with a sure hope of bringing the aforesaid dukes to concord. For Louis the emperor had already called the Hungarians to aid Otto and Henry the Younger. At last, after many negotiations, they agreed that the duchy should be divided among them; and this was done around the feast of Saint Bartholomew the Apostle, in the year as above. And so the lot fell: the elder Henry obtained Landshut, Straubing, Schärding, Pfarrkirchen, and the other surrounding castles. Otto his brother received Burghausen, Öttingen, Traunstein, Hall, and the remaining castles as far as the Salzburg Alps. Further, the lot gave to Henry the Younger Dingolfing, Landau, Vilshofen, Deggendorf, Cham, Bogen, Kelheim, and other towns and castles lying round about.

In the year of the Lord 1332, Duke Henry the Elder again began to quarrel with Otto his brother and Henry the Younger over the duchy of Bavaria, and these two invoked the aid of Louis the emperor, who earnestly commanded him that as quickly as [unclear] desist from what had been undertaken. When he was unwilling, the emperor, having gathered an army, besieged Straubing sharply in his own person for eight weeks. Meanwhile John, king of Bohemia, coming again, arranged peace between them.

Henry, the younger duke of Bavaria, son of Otto, the aforementioned king of Hungary, died in the year of the Lord 1333, without children, in the twenty-first year of his age. Otto, duke of Bavaria, son of the often-mentioned Duke Stephen, died in the year of the Lord 1335, without children. Henry the elder, brother of Otto, duke of Bavaria, died in the year of the Lord 1349, leaving a son named John, who, living for a short time, succeeded his father in the duchy.

John, duke of Bavaria, son of the aforesaid Duke Henry the elder, succeeded his dead father in the duchy of Lower Bavaria for a few years. He had as wife the daughter of Duke Louis, and not long after his father he died without children. Therefore, when the aforesaid Duke John had died without children, Louis the emperor and duke of Bavaria received his inheritance; from him descend all the dukes of Lower Bavaria who live today, as we shall say in its place. And thus the stock of Henry, duke of Landshut, fails here.

In the year of the Lord 1325, Louis, duke of Bavaria, was elected king of the Romans, as we have said; against him Frederick, duke of Austria, through Rudolf, Louis’s brother, and certain others, was elected king, whence many evils and wars arose. Therefore on the day which precedes the feast of Saint Michael, each proceeded to war with a multitude of armed men, between Mühldorf and Oettingen, in a meadow beside the road. In this battle, when they fought fiercely, Louis came out victor and captured Frederick, duke of Austria, whom he committed to custody in the castle called Trausnitz, not far from Nabburg; but his brother Rudolf, as we have said sufficiently, he despoiled of all his goods and drove into exile. At length Emperor Louis, through the deceits and false letters of the master of Augsburg, his chancellor, incurred the indignation of the pope; and how it happened I shall explain more fully when there is need. To this Emperor Louis, William of Ockham of the Order of Minors, a most learned man, with certain other brothers of his order, having been embittered by Pope John XXII, fled; he remained defended with him, and wrote against the pope and declared him a heretic. Concerning these matters there is a fuller account elsewhere.

Emperor Louis did and suffered many wondrous things, which I can in no way include in this supplement. If it is necessary, I shall write at an opportune time.

In the year of the Lord 1347, on the day of Saint Gereon the martyr, Emperor Louis, being engaged in hunting, had in his company a certain [unclear] of Austria, whom all called Maultasch because of the foul and hideous condition of her body. How this happened I shall explain more fully when there is need. To this Emperor Louis, William of Ockham of the Order of Minors, a most learned man, [unclear] he committed to custody, his brother or other brothers of his order, having been embittered by Pope John XXI, fled; he remained defended with him, wrote against the pope, and declared him a heretic. Concerning these matters there is a fuller account elsewhere.

Now I shall continue the line of descent from the sons of Rudolf, count palatine of the Rhine and duke of Bavaria, brother of the aforesaid Emperor Louis, from whom all the counts palatine of the Rhine of this time have descended. Afterward I shall add the sons of that Emperor Louis himself, from whom the dukes of Lower Bavaria arose. Since the generation of princes, having multiplied, thereafter passed into various successions, I shall write only of the principal dukes of Bavaria and counts palatine of the Rhine.

Therefore, after Rudolf, the aforesaid count palatine of the Rhine and duke of Bavaria, had been driven into England by his brother, as we remember that we have said, and had died, Emperor Louis, when he saw his sons, said: “The father, and not the sons, sinned against me; hence it is not just that they should undergo punishment for another’s crime.” Accordingly he gave them the power of choosing among Bavaria, Swabia, Austria, and the Rhine whichever of these provinces they wished. Having taken counsel beforehand, they chose their paternal inheritance, namely the county palatine of the Rhine with its properties and the other cities in Bavaria, namely Amberg and Nabburg, with others adhering to them, in the year of the Lord 1439, on the sixth feria before the day of Saint Oswald the martyr. The sons of Rudolf were three: namely Rudolf, Adolf, and Rupert. We shall speak of them in order.

Rudolf, the firstborn of the aforesaid Rudolf, count palatine of the Rhine, is said not to have been very wise or shrewd. He had as wife the sister of Louis, king of Hungary; she bore him a daughter named Margaret, whom Charles, king of Bohemia, took as wife,

*I shall have written of the counts palatine.*

*Rudolf.* *Of Johannes Trithemius*

afterwards emperor of the Romans. But Rupertus died without children and was buried before the choir of the church in Neustadt. Margaretha, daughter of Rudolphus and wife of Carolus, king of Hungary, bore three sons and two daughters: Wenceslaus, king of the Romans after his father; Ioannes, king of Bohemia; Sigismundus, king of Hungary and afterwards emperor; Helena, who married the son of the king of England; and Margaretha, wife of the margrave of the Old March.

*Adolphus.* Adolphus, count palatine of the Rhine and duke of Bavaria, son of Prince Rudolphus and brother of the above-mentioned Rudolphus, had as wife the daughter of the count of [Ortingen?], who bore him a son named the younger Rupertus, who was also very often called Adolphus after his father's name; of him we shall speak later.

Rupertus, son of Rudolphus, prince and brother of the aforesaid princes Rudolphus and Adolphus, count palatine of the Rhine and duke of Bavaria, had two wives. The first was Mechtildis, duchess of Brabant, who died without children; the second was Beatrix, daughter of the duke of [Mons?], by whom he had no children. This Rupertus founded the University of Heidelberg, which Pope Benedict XII confirmed. He also built the collegiate church in Neustadt with fine stone paneling. He died in the year of the Lord 1412, on the tenth day of the month of February, and was buried in the choir of the church of Neustadt. Next I shall record the sons of Ludovicus the Bavarian, emperor, and their successions, through whom Lower Bavaria was possessed.

Ludovicus, margrave of Brandenburg, son of Ludovicus the Bavarian, emperor, a pious, just, and warlike man, had as wife the daughter of the count of Tyrol, who bore him a son named Meynhardus, who afterwards was count in Tyrol. He married the sister of Adolphus, duke of Austria, and died without heirs; his wife made the county of Tyrol subject to her brother Rudolphus, duke of Austria, whence no small dissension arose between the dukes of Bavaria and Austria.

*Stephanus.* Stephanus, duke of Bavaria, son of Ludovicus, emperor and duke of Bavaria, and brother of the aforesaid Ludovicus of Brandenburg, dwelt in Landshut. He had three sons: Stephanus, Ioannes, and Fredericus, who after their father's death divided his duchy among themselves in the year of the Lord 1413. Ioannes received Upper Bavaria, namely Munich, with its appurtenances; Stephanus received Ingolstadt; and Fredericus accepted Landshut as his lot. Of these we shall speak in their proper place.

Albertus, duke of Bavaria of Straubing, son of Ludovicus the emperor and brother of the two aforesaid dukes, Ludovicus and Stephanus, received, as his share of his patrimony, Straubing with the places belonging to it; he was a good, just, and pious prince. He had as wife the daughter of Ludovicus, duke of Poland, who bore him three sons: Wilhelmus, Albertus, and Ioannes. Of these Albertus possessed [part] of Lower Bavaria, namely Straubing with the adjacent places. He had no wife and died without children. Ioannes, however, the elect of Liege, after the death of his brother gave up the bishopric which for many years he had possessed as elect, and married a wife, the holy Council of Constance disputing with him about this, as we say in its proper place.

This aforesaid duke Albertus also had [unclear] he dies, namely the son of Ludovicus the emperor, and lies buried in Holland. His title was this: Albertus, by the grace of God count palatine of the Rhine, duke of Bavaria, count of Hainaut, Zeeland, Holland, and lord of Frisia. After Duke Albertus died, his son Wilhelmus governed after him for a few years the counties and lordship of the lower land of Hainaut, Holland, Zeeland, and Frisia; he died [unclear] in the year of the Lord 1409. His daughter, named Jacoba, wishing to claim and possess her paternal inheritance for herself, styled herself daughter of the aforesaid counties. Against her Ioannes, her father's brother, abandoning the bishopric of Liege, as we have said, brought those lands and counties into his power by force in many wars. In hope of succession he married the daughter of Ioannes, duke of Gorlitz; but nevertheless he died without children, poisoned by the master of his household, in the year of the Lord 1415. After his death Lady Jacoba, [daughter] of the brother *Chronicle of the Dukes of Bavaria.*

...the daughter of his brother William, was again hastening toward those lands by hereditary right; against her the younger duke of Burgundy, rising up, invaded the land and obtained it, possessing it in the succession of his stock down to the present day.

William, duke of Bavaria, count of Holland, son of the emperor Louis, and brother of the aforesaid princes, who was called Holland, was a good and vigorous man. Poisoned by impious and perverse men, he lost the free use of reason and died without children. His dominion Albert, his brother, received.

Louis the Roman, duke of Bavaria, son of the emperor Louis, and brother [unclear]. Since he was established at Rome with his wife, he was born there; he himself died without children.

Otto, called of Brandenburg, duke of Bavaria, son of the emperor Louis, brother of the aforesaid princes, and margrave, also died in the year of the Lord 1379, without children.

In the year of the Lord 1448, lord Conrad von Deck was killed in his own house in the city of Munich by [Suickerus?] von Gundelfingen. Albert, duke of Bavaria, son of the emperor Louis, fortified the castle of Notterberg at Straubing against fear of the emperor Charles, of whom there was a rumor that he wished to attack him in war. But, agreement intervening, the dissension was settled.

Rupert, count palatine of the Rhine, duke of Bavaria, son of Adolf, prince palatine, of whom we made mention above, also called the Younger to distinguish him from the elder Rupert, his father’s brother, had as wife Beatrice, daughter of the king of Sicily. She bore him Rupert the Little, afterward king of the Romans, concerning whom in his own place [unclear] of Bavaria divided, of whom it has been spoken. Done at Regensburg on the day of Saint Oswald.

In the year of the Lord 1348, lord Conrad von Deck in his house [unclear], a vigorous man, very ready in the art of warfare, in the time of the emperor Charles entered Saxony with an armed force, and on one day triumphed twice over the Saxons; but in the third encounter, defeated by them, he was captured.

Now let us pursue the line of generation of the dukes of Bavaria descended from the sons of the emperor Louis, because from the stock of Rudolf, count palatine, apart from the aforesaid Rupert, there was no male seed.

Meinhard, count in Tyrol, son of Louis of Brandenburg, who was son of Louis the Bavarian, emperor: he had as wife [the daughter?] of Adolf, duke of Austria; he died without children. His wife handed over his duchy to her brother Rudolf, duke of Austria, not without prejudice to the dukes of Bavaria. Besides this Meinhard, Louis left no sons.

Stephen, duke of Bavaria, son of Duke Stephen, who had been the son of the emperor Louis, who possessed Ingolstadt together with what adhered to it, begot two sons: Louis, duke of Bavaria in Ingolstadt, and John, bishop of Regensburg; and one daughter named Elizabeth, whom the king of the Franks took as wife.

John, duke of Upper Bavaria, son of Duke Stephen, son of the emperor Louis, and brother of the above-mentioned Stephen, had as wife the daughter of the duke of [Görlitz?]. By her he begot sons, Ernest and William, and one daughter, Sophia, whom he gave as wife to Wenceslaus, king of the Romans. This Duke John, in the division of the paternal inheritance, obtained Munich with the other surrounding castles.

Frederick, duke of Bavaria, son of Stephen, son of the emperor Louis, and brother of the aforesaid princes Stephen and John, in the division of the paternal inheritance obtained Landshut with what belonged to it. He had as wife the sister of the duke of Milan, who bore him one son, Henry in Landshut, and two daughters, namely Margaret and Elizabeth, whom he gave as wife to Frederick, burgrave of Nuremberg, whom the emperor made margrave of Brandenburg. Stephen also, mentioned above, brother of this Frederick, took as wife another sister of the duke of Milan, the sister of this man’s wife.

The division of the paternal inheritance among the aforesaid three princes of Bavaria was made in the year of the Lord 1412.

Now let us speak of the line of generation of the sons of Albert, son of the emperor Louis and brother of the aforesaid Louis and Stephen. They were three: William, Albert, John.

*116. JOHANNES TRITHEMIUS.*

WILLIAM, duke of Bavaria, son of Albert, son of the aforesaid emperor Ludwig, made—for [his] portion of the paternal inheritance—count of Hainaut, Holland, Zeeland, and Friesland, left no male seed, but had one daughter by name Jacoba [Jacqueline], who first married the Dauphin of France, afterward the duke of Brabant, then the brother of the king of England, [and] lastly a certain noble called Francken. This William, his father being dead, possessed by hereditary right the county of Hainaut [and] Holland [and] the lordship of Friesland.

This William, duke of Bavaria, died, no son being left, in the year of the Lord [MCCCCXVII?]; after whom John, bishop-elect of Liège, his brother, the daughter of [his] brother, Jacoba, being repulsed, acquired his lordship with the blood of many.

ALBERT, duke of Bavaria, son of Albert duke at Straubing, son of the emperor Ludwig, brother of the aforesaid William, a brave man, young, fair of face, who after [his] father's death obtained among his brothers Straubing with the adjacent castles, villages, [and] properties. He had no wife; he died without sons; he was buried in the middle of the choir of the Carmelite brothers at Straubing.

JOHN, duke of Bavaria, son of Albert the duke, son of the emperor Ludwig, brother of the aforesaid princes William [and] Albert, was for a long time bishop-elect of the church of Liège. He, after many years—his brother William having died—obtained the county of Hainaut [and] Holland with the rest of his lordships, Jacoba his brother's daughter protesting. Hoping to have himself [as] the legitimate possessor of his inheritance, a dispensation of the Council of Constance having been obtained, he married the daughter of John, duke of Jülich, [kinsman] of the brothers of the emperor Sigismund, from whom he received no legitimate heir. In the year of the Lord 1408.

This John, duke of Bavaria, still bearing himself as bishop-elect of the church of Liège, is besieged by the Liège-men, set in Maastricht, to whose aid run his aforesaid brother William, [and] John duke of Burgundy, son of his sister, with two thousand. The battle being joined, John [and] William were made victors; they laid low more than twenty-five thousand of the Liège-men. But of their own army only ten are reported to have fallen.

In the year of the Lord 1415, the aforesaid John, duke of Bavaria, count in Hainaut, Holland, [and] Zeeland, lord in Friesland, perished by poison, by the treachery of a certain official of his, whom they call Master of the solemn court. But he being dead, John duke of Burgundy, son of his sister—Jacoba, daughter of the aforesaid duke William (who was the legitimate heir), contradicting—powerfully obtained the county of Hainaut, Holland, Zeeland, [and] the lordship in Friesland; thus this princedom was taken away from the dukes of the house of Bavaria.

RUPERT, count Palatine of the Rhine, duke of Bavaria, king of the Romans, son of the most illustrious prince Rupert (of whom it is spoken above), a powerful, just man, merciful to the poor, had as wife Margaret, daughter of the Burgrave of Nuremberg, who bore him six sons [and] three daughters: Rupert called the Pious, Frederick of Amberg, Ludwig the Bearded the prince-elector, John of Neumarkt, Stephen of Zweibrücken, Otto of Mosbach, Agnes, Margaret, [and] Elizabeth. Of these princes we shall speak afterward.

In the year of the Lord 1400, about the feast of the Assumption of Blessed Mary ever-Virgin, the princes meeting together at Frankfurt, Wenceslaus being deposed, the aforesaid Rupert, count Palatine of the Rhine, duke of Bavaria, was elected king of the Romans; he reigned ten years.

This duke Rupert, a magnificent king, led an army into Bohemia against Wenceslaus, and inflicted many evils on the Bohemian people, both by iron and by fire, and brought back to the dukes of Bavaria some castles and lordships of Bavaria possessed by them. He did also many other magnificent things, which we cannot relate in this place. He dies at Oppenheim, in the year of the Lord 1410, the 18th day of the month of May; he is buried at Heidelberg, in the church of the Holy Spirit (which he himself built), with [his] wife.

Consequently I shall first continue the order of the generation of the dukes of Bavaria descending from the emperor Ludwig, and then I shall add the sons of king Rupert, the counts Palatine of the Rhine.

LUDWIG, duke of Bavaria, son of Stephen duke at Ingolstadt, brother of John bishop of Regensburg [and] of Elizabeth queen of France, count at Mortain, had a wife by name Anna, sister of [the king] of Cyprus, who bore him a son Ludwig, who was called Hogel, who as a boy was carried in a basket from Paris into Bavaria. But his mother Anna, dying, was buried at the Preachers in the city of Paris.

This Ludwig, duke of Bavaria, count of Mortain, [brought] those precious images of our Savior Jesus Christ, of holy Mary, [and] of the twelve Apostles, which today are with the duke [of Bavaria]… *Chronicle of the Dukes of Bavaria.*

...brought Duke George, surnamed the Rich, with him from France into Bavaria.

John, duke of Bavaria, bishop of Regensburg, son of Duke Stephen in Ingolstadt, and brother of the above-mentioned Louis and of Elizabeth, queen of the French, presided over the Church of Regensburg for twenty-six years.

Ernest, duke of Bavaria, son of Duke John in Munich, and brother of the following William and of Sophia, the second wife of Wenceslaus, king of Bohemia and of the Romans, dwelling in Munich, begot a son named Albert of Munich, of whom we shall speak afterward in his own place.

Henry, duke of Bavaria, son of Duke Frederick in Landshut, had as wife Elizabeth, daughter of the duke of Austria. She bore him a son named Louis, whom he called the Rich, and two daughters, one of whom he gave to Duke Otto of Mosbach, the other to Count Ulrich of Württemberg. He also had two sisters, as we said above, one of whom, named Elizabeth, was the wife of Frederick, burgrave of Nuremberg; from her were born Albert, John, Frederick, another Frederick, margraves of Brandenburg; and Margaret, whom Louis Hogel, duke of Bavaria, took as wife. This Duke Henry of Landshut was at the beginning frugal and poor, but at the end was found to be very rich. His wife, moreover, was an ingenious woman, and loved all honorable arts and sciences.

*He returns to the Palatines descended from King Rupert.*

Rupert, count palatine of the Rhine, duke of Bavaria, first-born son of Rupert, king of the Romans, who was called Pipan, armed with zeal for the faith, set himself against the Turks, not without great expense. For in the year of the Lord 1396, John, duke of Burgundy, son of the sister of Albert, duke of Straubing, came with a great army into Bavaria to fight against the unbelievers; this Duke Rupert joined himself to him, with many others. And when, having crossed Hungary, they had come to a certain city of the Turks, which they call Nicopolis, but our people call Schiltau, through the discord of the princes they were defeated by the unbelievers. The duke of Burgundy was captured with many others; innumerable men were killed; Rupert himself, scarcely escaping, returned poor into Bavaria. And not long afterward he died without children and was buried in Amberg.

Frederick, count palatine of the Rhine, duke of Bavaria, second-born son of Rupert, king of the Romans and count palatine, died before his father without children.

Louis, palatine of the Rhine, duke of Bavaria, elector, third son of Rupert, king of the Romans, was an upright, just, holy man, who for love of Christ visited his holy sepulcher in Jerusalem. Having become gravely ill at sea, blind and lame, after making the pilgrimage, in the month of May he took as his second wife Mechthild, daughter of the duke of Savoy, a devout and most holy woman. By her he begot three sons, Louis, Frederick, Rupert, and certain daughters, of whom two became nuns; the third the count of Württemberg took as wife, and afterward Albert, duke of Austria, brother of Emperor Frederick III.

Many praises and proclamations of honor ought to have been spoken concerning this prince, which require leisure and another volume. This Duke Louis was elected protector, defender, and advocate of the most universal Council of Constance. John XXIII, pope, handed over to him by the council, he kept in custody for almost three years in his castle of Mannheim.

In the year of the Lord 1438, on the twelfth day of the month of May, Mechthild, wife of this most serene prince, died. At last this most Christian prince Louis, because of blindness and various infirmities, was removed from his administration; not long afterward he died, in the year of the Lord 1449, on the last day of December.

John, count palatine of the Rhine, duke of Bavaria, fourth son of King Rupert, the Neunburger, was a good and just man. He had two wives: Catherine, daughter of the duke of Pomerania, who bore him six sons, Christopher, king of Denmark, Norway, and Sweden, Otto, John, another John, Frederick, and Adolf. The last five all died in childhood. His second wife was the daughter of Ernest, duke of Bavaria in Munich; by her he had no children. This Duke John did much against the schismatic Bohemians, and suffered much from them for the Catholic faith. [He died?] in Neunburg, a man beloved by God.

Stephen, count palatine of the Rhine, duke of Bavaria, fifth son of King Rupert, called Zweibrücker, because he received this place as an inheritance, was a just, upright, devout man. He had as wife Anna, daughter of the last count of Veldenz, who bore him five sons: Frederick of Simmern, who obtained the county of Sponheim; Louis, surnamed the Black, who obtained the county of Veldenz; Rupert, bishop of Strasbourg...

[unclear]; Stephen, a canon in the church of Cologne, and John, bishop of Munster and afterward archbishop of Magdeburg. We shall also speak of these in their proper place. Otto, count palatine of the Rhine, duke of Bavaria, surnamed Mosbach, which, together with its dependencies, he possessed by inheritance among the brothers, the youngest son of Rupert, king of the Romans, had as wife Joanna, daughter of Henry of Landshut, duke of Bavaria; by her he begot Otto of Mosbach, Rupert, bishop of [unclear], and John and Albert, canons. This Otto at length died and was buried at Reichenbach. For the sake of brevity I am compelled to omit many things about these princes, which at another time could be explained more fully. Now we shall set forth in order the line of the dukes of Bavaria descended from the line of the emperor Louis.

Louis, duke of Bavaria, called Hogel, son of Louis, duke of Bavaria, count in [unclear], born of his mother Anna, sister of the king of Cyprus, had as wife Margaret, daughter of Frederick, burgrave of Nuremberg and afterward margrave; by her he had no children. After Louis Hogel had died, she is said secretly to have taken Martin Valenrode in marriage; she possessed Friburg, which afterward she sold to Louis, duke in Landshut, surnamed the Rich.

Albert of Munich, duke of Bavaria, son of Duke Ernest, had as wife the daughter of the duke of Brunswick; by her he begot five sons: John, Sigismund, Albert, Christopher, and Wolfgang. We shall speak of them in their proper place. This Albert in his youth had a certain concubine, the daughter of a certain bathkeeper in Straubing, exceedingly beautiful, whom he loved with a too-blind passion. His father, Duke Ernest, wishing to consult his son’s advantage rather than his pleasure, had her drowned; nevertheless he later grieved over this, since from his son’s violent grief many evils followed.

Adolphus, duke of Bavaria, [son of?] the emperor, died without children.

Louis, duke of Bavaria, surnamed the Rich, son of Henry the Rich, prince in Landshut, took as wife the daughter of the duke of Saxony, who bore him one son named George, who today possesses his father’s duchy, and a daughter, Margaret, a most devout woman, whom Philip, count palatine of the Rhine, prince-elector, took as wife. Mention of them will be made in its proper place.

*The line of the generation of the counts palatine of the Rhine and dukes of Bavaria must consequently be continued in order.*

Rupert, count palatine of the Rhine, duke of Bavaria, firstborn of Duke Louis with the Beard, born of his first wife Blanca, called Engellant, because his mother was English, died without children in the year of the Lord 1426.

Louis, count palatine of the Rhine, duke of Bavaria, prince-elector, second-born of Louis the Bearded, namely born of his second wife Mechtilde, took as wife Margaret, daughter of the duke of Savoy; by her he begot one son named Philip, a distinguished prince of his father’s virtue, who, adorned with noble offspring, today possesses his parent’s rights. This Louis, the father of Philip, was a good, just, pious, and gentle man, very devout toward God in all fervor of spirit, as the account of those who knew him closely bears witness, his life and conduct having in part been described.

When he was about to die, this most Christian prince commended to his brother Frederick his only-begotten son Philip, who was only one year old, his very dear wife, and all his land, on the condition that, when Philip reached his eighteenth year, he should restore to him his paternal principality and dominion, as to the legitimate heir, without opposition. And so Louis, a most merciful prince, died in the year of the Lord 1449, on the day of Saint Hippolytus the martyr, and was buried in the church of the Holy Spirit at Heidelberg.

Frederick, count palatine of the Rhine, duke of Bavaria, the third son of Louis with the Beard, brother of the aforesaid Prince Louis, had no wife and left no legitimate heirs. Yet he begot two sons by a certain Clara [unclear]; the first of them, Frederick, was a canon in the church of Speyer, and the second, Louis, made count in Lowenstein, is still living today. There are those who say that he contracted marriage with the aforesaid woman clandestinely in the face of the Church. And because the wars waged by this Frederick are known to all, I shall pass them over in silence.

Rupert, count palatine of the Rhine, duke of Bavaria, the fourth son of the aforesaid Louis, *Chronicle of the Dukes of Bavaria*

son, and brother of Louis and Frederick: what he suffered, and how, and by whose treachery he was captured, even boys in the streets, so to speak, know; on this occasion there is no need to set it out in writing.

Now let us pursue the sequence of the Counts Palatine of the Rhine and Dukes of Bavaria, descended indeed from Rudolf, but divided into another line, after King Rupert and his son Stephen, with John and Otto of Mosbach.

Christopher, Count Palatine of the Rhine and Duke of Bavaria, son of John, son of Rupert, king of the Romans, after the death of Erik, king of Dacia, Norway, and Sweden, took as wife the daughter of John, Margrave of Brandenburg. When he had had her for three years, [unclear] without children. He was buried at Helmensberg.

Frederick, Count Palatine of the Rhine and Duke of Bavaria, son of Stephen of Zweibruecken, [unclear] son, [took as wife] Margaret, daughter of the Duke of Guelders, who bore him John, heir of the paternal possession; Stephen, dean of the church of Cologne; Frederick, canon and cantor of the church of Mainz; Rupert, bishop of Regensburg; and William, canon of Trier, who died as a young man in Trier. This Frederick, a just and pious prince, died in the year of the Lord 1480, and was buried in the choir of the monastery of the regulars at Ravengiersburg.

Louis, Count Palatine of the Rhine and Duke of Bavaria, son of Stephen of Zweibruecken, son of Rupert, king of the Romans, took as wife Margaret, daughter of the Duke of Guelders, who bore him Caspar, Alexander, and John. The wars that took place between him and Frederick, Count Palatine of the Rhine, prince and guardian of our Philip, and how great were the losses he suffered from them, are known to all round about.

Rupert, Count Palatine of the Rhine and Duke of Bavaria, son of Stephen, son of Rupert, king of the Romans, was bishop in the church of Strasbourg.

Stephen, Count Palatine of the Rhine and Duke of Bavaria, son of Stephen, son of Rupert, king of the Romans, was bishop in the church of Cologne.

John, Count Palatine of the Rhine and Duke of Bavaria, son of Stephen, son of Rupert, king of the Romans, a learned man and most renowned for integrity of morals, was first bishop of Muenster and afterward archbishop of Magdeburg. Many heralds of praise concerning him present themselves to me, which at present are not to be entrusted to the service of the pen. In the year of the Lord 1475 he died, not without suspicion of poison.

Otto, Count Palatine of the Rhine and Duke of Bavaria, son of the elder Otto of Mosbach, [unclear] of Rupert the king, and brother of the above-mentioned younger Otto, is bishop of Strasbourg. See [Wimphelingius?]. [unclear] wrote, and many letters; we have only these few things from Irenicus. We shall append them.

Frederick was succeeded by Philip, whom Rudolf Agricola, Jerome Aleander, and Jakob Wimpheling, men of the greatest weight, testify to have surpassed so many mortals in piety, magnanimity, clemency, and in every measure of virtue. He was most handsome both in the strength of his limbs, in the endowments of marriage, and in the habit of his body; and he would have been most fortunate, had the German wars raged less against him. Eight sons survived him, so great a hope of descendants. Dying, he handed over the Palatinate to the elder Louis; Bavaria to the sons of the deceased Rupert, over whom he placed Frederick, a most accomplished duke. Three others act as prelates; the remaining two are very great provosts. Among the daughters, Elizabeth, the eldest by birth, as Alexander says, was given in marriage to Philip, Margrave of Baden; Amelia to the Duke of Pomerania; Helena to the man of Mecklenburg: three heroines to as many heroes and to the greatest princes in Germany. Catherine, however, most worthy of such a name, imitating the example of the saint who shared her name, despised the enticements of perishable things and sought Christ as her bridegroom. So great was the lineage of the Palatines! So many bishoprics, that one would be wearied merely by recounting the names; so many kings of Bohemia, Denmark, Hungary, and of the Romans came forth from that stock, that if one must rely on the opinion of the ancestors, there is no family in Germany to which the nobility owes more.

This is Irenicus, book 3 of the *Exegesis of Germany*, chapter 50.

*Catalogue* *Catalogue of Illustrious Men Who Adorn Germany in Every Way by Their Talents and Lucubrations, by Lord Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Spanheim, of the Order of Saint Benedict, to Jakob Wimpfeling of Sélestat, Theologian.*

*Letter of Master Matthaeus Herbenus of Maastricht to the Distinguished Man Jodocus Beyselius, Patrician of Aachen.*

[unclear]

When recently I was leaving my paternal soil to set out for the further parts of Germany, and had come to Aachen, and had met you at home, Jodocus, most worthy of regard among friends, for the sake of greeting you, in view of our now almost long-standing association and friendship, I received instructions that on that journey I should visit certain very learned men, Germans indeed, bound to you by favor and goodwill, whom you had in the regions of the Rhine, and greet them in your name.

After therefore I had landed by boat at the place where the Nahe, flowing into the Rhine near Bingen, shows the road through Kreuznach to those going to Spanheim, soon, having left the boat, I make my way to Trithemius, abbot of that monastery. First I greet him, and then hand over your letters. Accordingly he embraces me so that I could not have been received more splendidly or more graciously by a great prelate.

But when an opportunity for walking about was granted, which for most people comes after the gatherings and refreshments of first friends, he leads me around, and immediately introduces me into his admirable library, where I behold very many Hebrew and Greek volumes. For of Latin books in every art, science, and faculty there was an immense abundance. And so I marvel at the exact diligence of one man in acquiring and arranging such varied monuments, and I am vehemently astonished; for I would not have thought that in all Germany there existed so great a number of foreign volumes. For I found there books of five languages, widely differing from one another in speech and character, in very ancient codices, which Trithemius, wakeful and assiduous, had brought together not without much toil.

In this way, therefore, most learned Jodocus, I found the library of Spanheim furnished. Nor that alone, but I also saw the walls of the whole abbatial house, which is spacious, and the vaults of the rooms most fittingly adorned with Greek, Hebrew, and Latin words and characters. Wherefore I too reckon thus with myself: if there is a Hebrew academy in our Germany, it is that monastery of Spanheim, where one can take in more learning from the walls than from the dusty and empty libraries of books belonging to many others. For whatever antiquity and learning Germany can possess in books, the monastery of Spanheim possesses, through the care of Abbot Trithemius.

I stayed with our abbot eleven days, not without exact remembrance of you. There, when one day in conversation we fell upon discussion of his book, which has been published on ecclesiastical writers, I said that I marveled that our Germany had had such distinguished writers, whom I had come to know in that book, and still had them at the present day; and I recalled that I had heard from a certain most learned Italian philosopher that he had never anywhere, in his reading, found any learned German except the one Albertus Magnus.
