Then the abbot, smiling, said: “Therefore all the more is it to be believed that the Italians have deliberately passed over the praises of Germans in their writings, so that by passing over others their own glory might appear greater. I can indeed openly make known to you that there have existed far more very ancient and very celebrated German writers than you recognized in my book on ecclesiastical writers.” And bringing forth from that library of his a huge book, containing nothing except Germany’s most learned writers and men of most holy memory, he showed it to me. When I had looked at it, I began most urgently to beg and entreat him, as I do not doubt that you and any learned man would have done, that he should bring it about that our Germany should not henceforth go deprived of so great a glory of our ancestors, and that he should see to it that it be entrusted at the first possible day to the printer’s workshop. For when printed, through reading and imitation, it would bring it about that we would have more holy men and students of the good arts.

And so I prevailed upon the abbot, who in any case shows himself obliging to friends, and obtained that volume to be printed for the praise of our Germany. These are the things, most pleasant Jodocus, which I learned, saw, and accomplished with the lord abbot of Spanheim, and which, impatient of a longer delay, I resolved to write to you. Farewell. From the monastery of Spanheim, the thirtieth day before the Kalends of September. In the year of the Virgin’s giving birth 1495.

*Of Johannes Trithemius*

*Letter of Lord Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, to Master Jacob Wimpfeling of Sélestat.*

Since there are some, my very dear Jacob Wimpfeling, who, blindly treading upon the histories of the times, despise our Germany as though it were barren and devoid of the liberal arts; who contend that in it outstanding men of intellect and writers on ecclesiastical discipline have flourished only few and rare. For they have become such shameless praisers of their own nation that they believe they can become more famous by disparaging others. They extol the slight deeds of their own people and the small talents in their own men with painted colors of eloquence, and, blinded by envy, utterly conceal the great virtues of the Germans, their brave deeds, their most brilliant talents, their faith, fervor, and devotion. If they find among ancient authors anything of virtue, anything of learning, anything of praise concerning our people, lest it come to the knowledge of many, they either scrape it away at once, or, publishing their own things, omit ours. Thus, indeed, Pliny on the wars of the Germans is said by report to have perished; thus many and various histories, written in antiquity concerning the deeds of our people, are said to have been lost.

But you, most learned man, stirred by this rashness of rivals, have appeared as a true lover and defender of our fatherland, since you do not cease to write various things in praise of the Germans, and to urge others by words and examples to do the same. You have won over to yourself Lupold of Bebenburg on the fervor, zeal, and constancy of the ancient German princes in the Christian religion; and you have brought many volumes of ancient authors on these very matters into your library. Sebastian Murrho of Colmar also, a man most learned from every quarter and not moderately skilled in the three principal languages, you have brought by your exhortations to the point that he has published a very fine epitome on the praises of the Germans, in which he set in order, in lucid speech, the brave deeds of our princes on behalf of the Catholic faith, the commonwealth, and the holy Roman Church; and he reviewed in brief compendium the most brilliant talents, works, and inventions of our nation.

But not even content with these things, you always raise your mind to greater proclamations of our praises; and the more things worthy of our praises you find, the greater things you desire. Hence you also exhort me by frequent letters and entreaties that I ought to write something on the praises of the Germans, and to arrange a catalogue of the illustrious men of this nation who, outstanding in learning and intellect, wrote various works. I confess I put it off for a long time, partly detained by concern for domestic affairs, partly occupied by the sweat of higher study. But now at last I have been overcome by your excessive persistence, and I confess myself defeated.

Receive therefore, my Jacob, the catalogue which you have so greatly requested; correct it with the file of your chastening and learning, and then at last allow it to come to the examination of others. Nor should you think that I have gathered together all who made our Germany illustrious by their talents and little works, but only that I have kept the memory of those whose writings, amid my preoccupations, I could find ready to hand. I have reviewed a few out of many, so that by these the envious detractor may perceive how many are still lacking to us whom this catalogue by no means contains. For neither was leisure given me to seek out the rest, nor expense to gather them through others.

Finally, at the end, after I have woven together the sequence of those who have departed life, I have added certain men still living in the flesh, lest, if they should now be passed over by us, they would by no means reach the knowledge of posterity. For indeed those who are now very well known to us will quickly fall into oblivion if they have not been commended by letters and writings. I have no less concern to bring to the knowledge of posterity learned men who have written something for the benefit of readers than to bring the little works of the ancients into the library of my monastery.

Yet I know that it does not sufficiently please certain people that I wished to commend in writing the talents of the living, who think that this was done not for the benefit of posterity but for the vain praise of the human condition. I think these men must be answered briefly, since I hasten to other matters. And if I ought not to praise a man before death in those things which are meritorious, I am not forbidden to commit to writing talent, which is natural and common to good and bad alike; I observe that Jerome, Prosper, Gennadius, Isidore, Honorius, Sigebert, and many others did this. Indeed, what the most holy fathers laudably did for the benefit of posterity, no wise man should forbid me, who desire to do the same with the same intention. Finally, there are many most learned men in these times whose memory it is pious, and of no less benefit, to commend to posterity. Unless antiquity had done this with equal piety, not all the most famous ancient writers would long since have come down to our memory *Catalogue of Illustrious Men.*

[unclear]. There are also those who think that in this age there are either no illustrious writers in the humanities, or only a few; and I trust that I have done something pleasant and welcome for them, if I have brought even a few out of many to their knowledge. For although I could not mention all men outstanding in talent, nevertheless I have provided an occasion for our studious Germans, so that henceforth they too may be able to add others to these and enlarge our work by their own diligence. Farewell. From Spanheim, on the sixth day before the Ides of February, in the year of the Lord MCCCCXCI.

*Preface of Lord Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Spanheim, to the Book on the Illustrious Men of the German Nation, to Jacobus V. [Sletslatinus?].*

Germany, which, because of its fertility in all good things, could rightly be called Germania, if Caesar did not think the contrary, from the beginning of its conversion to the Christian faith has always shone with famous teachers; through their talent and most holy morals it deserved to be illuminated more abundantly than other nations. Of these, many have been inserted into the catalogue of saints; many preceded this custom of canonizing saints in time.

This is proved by the very ancient books composed by them; miracles prove it. Nevertheless, at the request of friends, I have resolved to gather the works of certain talents into this catalogue, intending to provide an opportunity for posterity, so that, where they know that we have stopped, they themselves may by their own zeal complete the praises of the Germans. For I, situated in a corner of Germany, have not had the opportunity to search out the others who are lacking from our catalogue; but those whom I had at hand I offer to our Germans, asking that each one add to ours the writers who come his way, and thus finally learn, in rivalry with us, that they have been and are learned. Nor should it escape anyone that I have placed among the Germans all illustrious writers whom I found to have been Teutons. For the Mosellans and Treverans, although they inhabit a great part of Belgic Gaul, are nevertheless German in customs and language, and for that reason they have not undeservedly been numbered among our Germans. Concerning the other Teutons round about, too, a similar opinion should be held. But let this much about these matters suffice; now, God granting it, let us take up the beginning of writing according to the proposed subject.

*Book of Lord Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Spanheim, on the Luminaries, or on the Illustrious Men of Germany, who, outstanding in talent, wrote various works.*

Maximus, the seventh bishop of the church of Mainz, a man most holy in life and conduct, nobly learned both in secular letters and in the divine scriptures, was ready in talent, distinguished in speech, and outstanding in action. Since he was an eloquent and celebrated preacher of the divine word, he converted many to the faith of Christ by word and example, not only throughout his own diocese but also through neighboring and more distant regions, sowing the word of faith. He is said to have written many letters to various persons and to have committed many homilies to writing; but antiquity has not allowed any of these to come into our hands. Finally, against the Arians, who in his time did many evils in the Church of God, he composed some excellent works. He flourished at Mainz in the times of the emperors Constantius and Constans, under Pope Liberius, in the year of the Lord CCCLX.

Paulinus, the twenty-eighth archbishop of Trier, by nation indeed an Aquitanian, but in life and conduct for the most part dwelling among the Treverans, disciple of the blessed Maximinus, archbishop of Trier, and his son in baptism, a learned and most holy man, was banished into exile by the Arian heretics for the faith of Christ; in Phrygia he triumphed by a glorious suffering. He wrote many elegant letters in matters of the Catholic faith, in which he appeared no less learned than holy. But he also wrote some other works for the faith against here*Of Johannes Trithemius* [unclear] he published. He died in Phrygia under Constantine, Constantius, and Constans, in the year of the Lord 357, in the fifteenth indiction.

Boniface, also called Winfrid, first archbishop of the church of Mainz, a monk of the Order of Saint Benedict, English by nation but German in his way of life and dignity: a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, subtle in intellect, eloquent in speech, upright and most holy in life and morals. By his learned preaching he converted many to the Christian faith, so that he was deservedly held to be the teacher and apostle of the Germans. He wrote several distinguished little works, of which I have seen the following: To Pope Gregory II, On the Faith of the Holy Trinity, one book; The Life of Saint Lebuin, one book; Letters to Various Persons, one book; On Various Deeds of the Saints, one book; and certain other things. At last, while preaching the word of God in Frisia, he was crowned with martyrdom under Pippin, king of the Franks, in the year of the Lord 755, in the eighth indiction, in the thirty-seventh year of his episcopate, on the Nones of June. He was buried in the monastery of Fulda, which he himself built.

Walafrid, abbot of the monastery of Saint Gall, of the Order of the divine father Benedict, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, and remarkably learned in secular letters, subtle in intellect, eloquent in speech, excelling in verse and prose, a monarch of regular discipline, father of many monks, wrote, among other little works of his talent: The Life of Saint Gall in prose, one book; the same afterwards in verse, one book; On the Divine Offices also, one book; and various letters to various persons, and certain other things. He flourished about the times of the emperor Tiberius, in the year of the Lord 700.

Willibald, priest of Saint Boniface, a monk of the divine father Benedict, brother of Saint Walpurga, virgin abbess of Heidenheim, and afterwards bishop of Eichstatt, a learned and most holy man, ready in intellect and sweet in speech, wrote, at the command of Saint Lullus of Mainz, archbishop after Boniface, The Life of the same most holy martyr Boniface, two books, and, as is reported, certain letters to devout servants of God. He flourished under Pippin, father of the emperor Charlemagne, in the year of the Lord 760.

Ryggandus, bishop of Metz, grandson of King Pippin by his sister, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures and in secular letters as well, venerable no less in life and conduct than in dignity. Among other monuments of his talent he wrote The Rule of the Canons of the Church of Metz, one book, and various letters to various persons. He transferred from Rome the bodies of the holy martyrs Gorgonius, Nabor, and Nazarius; of these, he deposited the body of Saint Nazarius in the monastery of Lorsch, then of our order in Germany, in the diocese of Worms. He flourished in the times of Pippin, his uncle, king of Charlemagne, in the year of the Lord 870.

Haymo, third bishop of the church of Halberstadt in Saxony, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and second to none in his time in secular letters, acute in intellect, eloquent in speech, devout in life and conduct, was of most celebrated industry in delivering homilies to the people; from him he became most learned in every discipline of the good arts. Then, as his merits advanced, he was appointed third abbot of the monastery of Hersfeld. Finally, likewise, he was chosen third bishop of Halberstadt. He wrote many, almost innumerable volumes, of which the following are extant: On the Five Books of Moses, five books; On Joshua, one book; On Tobit, one book; On Ezra and Nehemiah, three books; On the Book of Judith, one book; On Esther also, one book; On Job, one book; On the Song of Songs, one book; On the Proverbs of Solomon, one book; On Ecclesiastes, one book; On Isaiah the Prophet, four books; On Jeremiah the Prophet, one book; On Ezekiel also, four books; On Daniel, one book; On the Twelve Minor Prophets, twelve books; On the Psalms, one book; On the Gospels, homilies through the cycle of the year, two large volumes, two books; On All the Epistles of Paul, fourteen books; On the Canonical Epistles, seven books; On the Apocalypse of John, one book; On the Holy Trinity, one book; On the Memory of Christian Things, ten books; On the Variety of Books, four books; On the Acts of the Apostles, one book. He composed sermons, homilies, letters, and various other treatises, but they have not yet come into our hands. He died under Louis, the first emperor, in the year of the Lord 934, in the twelfth indiction, in the thirteenth year of his episcopate, and was buried in the church of Saint Stephen at Halberstadt.

Charles the Great, emperor, son of Pippin the second duke and king, German by nation, from the imperial castle of Ingelheim, where to this day the chamber of his birth, consecrated as a chapel, is shown, a man most Christian in life and conduct, *Catalogue of Illustrious Men.*

[of men?] not undeservedly included, most devoted to the divine Scriptures and excellently learned in secular letters, subtle in intellect, clear and eloquent in speech, distinguished by knowledge of many languages, skilled in Greek, Latin, and Hebrew, by no means to be rejected from the catalogue of the illustrious men of Germany. Indeed, he most zealously cultivated the liberal arts, and, greatly venerating their teachers, honored them with great distinctions. In learning grammar he heard Peter of Pisa, an aged deacon; in the other disciplines he had as teacher Albinus, surnamed Alcuin, a monk of the order of Saint Benedict and formerly a deacon, a disciple from Britain, a man of Saxon stock, most learned in every respect. With him he spent very much time and labor in learning rhetoric and dialectic, but especially astronomy. He learned the art of computation, and with keen attention most carefully investigated the course of the stars. The Christian religion, with which he had been imbued from infancy, he cultivated most devoutly and with the greatest piety, and he made many arrangements for its honor. He attended church zealously and with great devotion in the morning and evening, likewise in the night hours and at the time of the sacrifice, so far as his health allowed him. In his palace at Aachen he assembled a most precious library, filled with a very great abundance of books; when he died, he had it sold and distributed as alms to the poor. Among the other works of his intellect he published many and various additions of the laws and rights of all the nations that lived under his kingdom and empire, in many volumes. Likewise he composed the laws of the Saxons; likewise the laws of the Alemanni; likewise the laws of the Franks; likewise he published many and various songs concerning the deeds of the ancients. He also began a grammar of his native tongue, namely Teutonic or Alemannic, which, occupied with other matters, he could not finish. I have seen fragments of this grammar, and also certain volumes composed according to its rules; mention of these will be made below, when we come to Otfried, monk of the monastery of Weissenburg. Many volumes also were published by various men at his command; these we leave to their own authors. Happy is the commonwealth whose prince was so glorious a philosopher. At length, after many most holy exercises, he died in the basilica of the blessed Mother of God, which he himself had built at very great expense, and was buried at Aachen, in the year of the Lord 814, in the seventh indiction, on the fifth day before the Kalends of February, in the seventy-second year of his age and the forty-seventh of his reign.

Einhard, once chancellor of the aforesaid Emperor Charles the Great, and afterward a monk of the order of the divine father Benedict, and first abbot of the monastery of Seligenstadt in the diocese of Mainz above the Main, a man most learned in secular letters and not ignorant of the divine Scriptures, acute in intellect, eloquent in speech, outstanding in life and conduct, skilled especially in Greek and Latin, and excellent both in meter and in prose: among the other little works of his intellect, he abbreviated the Gallican Psalter, extracting from it all the verses containing words of prayer. He also wrote, both in his own person and in that of the emperor, many elegant and useful letters to various persons on various affairs and cases. Also *The Deeds of Emperor Charles*, one book. Moreover, a notable history of the times concerning the deeds of the Germans and Franks, two books. And certain other things which have by no means come down to us. He flourished under Emperor Charles the Great and his son Louis, in the year of the Lord 820.

Freculph, bishop of Lisieux, once a monk of Fulda, of the order of the divine father Benedict, a disciple of Albinus, to whom Rabanus, abbot of Fulda, exercised his talent in many volumes, a man most devoted to the divine Scriptures and very learned, and sufficiently fit for teaching the people; no less distinguished in conduct than in knowledge: he is said to have written certain excellent little works. Of these there are extant seven volumes addressed to Helisachar, containing a history of events from the beginning of the world down to the birth of the Savior, both of the gentiles and of the Jews. In this work he also subtly untangled many difficult questions of the divine Scriptures. He wrote, moreover, elegant and varied letters to various persons; I remember having read some of these to Rabanus. But he also published several other things which are unknown to us. He flourished under the rule of Louis the First, son of Charles the Great, in the year of the Lord 840.

Hamularius Fortunatus, the sixty-third archbishop of Trier from Saint Eucharius, and, as they say, cardinal of the most holy Roman Church, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and excellently taught in secular letters, skilled in Greek and Latin, wrote little works of reading not to be despised. Of these the following are reported: *On the Divine Offices*, one book. To Emperor Louis on the same matter, seven books. *On the Sacred Mysteries*, one book. Various letters also to various persons. Sent by Emperor Charles to Constantinople, to Michael, emperor of the Greeks, he, by his wondrous 126 *Of Johannes Trithemius* by [unclear] wisdom and diligence he established and confirmed true and perpetual peace and friendship between them. He flourished under the emperors Charlemagne and Louis his son, in the year of the Lord 810.

*Rabanus Maurus, archbishop of Mainz.*

Rabanus Maurus of Mainz, after Saint Boniface the sixth archbishop of Mainz, a Thuringian by nationality, sprung from the city of Fulda, a disciple of Alcuin, was first made a monk of the monastery of Fulda when he was still a boy of ten years. Thereafter he turned all his study to the knowledge of the Scriptures. In all learning, both of secular and of divine writings, he became by far most learned: a distinguished philosopher, an eminent poet, an eloquent rhetorician, a most celebrated astronomer and computist, skilled in Greek, Latin, and Hebrew; in his time the Church had no one like him. Then, as his merits increased, in the thirty-fifth year of his age he was elected abbot of the same monastery by the vote of all the brethren. Presiding over its government for twenty-four years, he composed many, almost countless, volumes. At last, after the death of Otgar, archbishop of Mainz, he was consecrated bishop of the same church; sitting for nine years in the episcopate, he did many good things for the Church. Of his little works the following are reported: To Bishop Freculph, On Genesis, four books; On Numbers, four books; On Leviticus, four books; On Deuteronomy, four books; On Joshua, two books; On Judges, two books; On the Book of Ruth, one book; On Kings, to Hildewin, abbot of Saint-Denis, four books; also On Paralipomenon, four books; On Ezra and Nehemiah, three books; On Tobit, one book; On the Book of Judith, seven books; On [unclear], one book; On the Psalms, one book; On the Proverbs of Solomon, one book; On Ecclesiastes, one book; On the Song of Songs, one book; On the Book of Wisdom, three books; On Ecclesiasticus, ten books; On Isaiah the Prophet, eight books; On Jeremiah the Prophet, twenty books; also On Ezekiel the Prophet, twenty books; On Daniel the Prophet, three books; On the Twelve Minor Prophets, twelve books; On the Books of Maccabees, three books; On the Gospel of Matthew, eight books; On the Gospel of Luke, three books; On the Gospel of Mark, four books; On the Gospel of John, two books; On all the Epistles of Paul, twenty-one books; On the Catholic Epistles, seven books; On the Acts of the Apostles, one book; On the Apocalypse of John, one book; On the Faith of the Most Holy Trinity, one book; also On the Praise of the Holy Cross, a work of wondrous genius, two books; To Bishop Haymo, On the Universe, or Etymologies, twenty-one books; also On Universal Nature, one book; to Bishop Haistulf, On the Instruction of Clerics, three books; On the Divine Offices, one book; On the Ecclesiastical Computus, two books; To Emperor Louis, one book; On Questions of the Canons, one book; To Bishop Regenbald, one book; On the Blessings of the Patriarchs, one book; a Homiliary of the ceremonies of the whole year, two books; also Letters to various persons, one book. But he composed various epigrams and many treatises in humane letters which have not yet come into our hands. He died under Emperor Lothar, in the year of the Lord 855, in the third indiction, in the sixty-eighth year of his age, when the ninth year of his episcopate had been completed. He was buried in the monastery of the holy martyr Alban near Mainz, then of the order of Saint Benedict.

Strabus, a monk of Fulda, once the disciple and notary of the aforesaid Abbot Rabanus, was certainly himself a most learned man, fully instructed both in divine Scripture and in secular letters, a theologian, philosopher, and most celebrated poet, quick in talent and clear in speech. He wrote several little works in sacred volumes, by which he commended his memory to posterity. But few of them have come to my knowledge. Chiefly there are reported commentaries On Genesis, one book; also On Exodus, one book; On Leviticus, one book; and many others. This Strabus, a most studious man, was the first to compile over the whole Bible the gloss which they call the master gloss or ordinary gloss, from the sayings of the holy fathers; others afterwards enlarged it by adding certain things. He flourished under the emperors Louis and Lothar, in the year of the Lord 860.

Lupus Servatus, priest, to whom Saint Rabanus, abbot of Fulda, is read to have written eight books on Paul’s Epistle to the Romans, was a man studious and learned in divine Scripture, and learned also in secular letters. Among the other little works of his talent he wrote a book On Three Questions, that is, on free will, on predestination, and on the blood of Christ, concerning a certain superfluous assessment or redemption extending to the salvation of the impious. For over this matter there arose a certain disturbance of faith in the Church in the year of the Lord 848. Besides these he published several other works, but they have not come to my knowledge. He flourished with Rabanus under Emperor Lothar, in the year of the Lord 850. Notge*Catalogue of Illustrious Men.*

NOTGER, bishop of Liège, formerly abbot of the monastery of Saint Gall, once very close to Rabanus, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and easily the most learned of all men of his time in the disciplines of secular letters, a philosopher, poet, musician, astronomer, and very celebrated theologian, venerable no less for his way of life than for his knowledge, wrote many excellent and necessary little works, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of many. Of these, a few have come to the notice of my reading. I have seen the original work of proses or sequences for the cycle of the year concerning the feasts, which he wrote to Lutward, bishop of Vercelli, archchaplain of the great emperor, book I; to Salomon, afterward bishop of the church of Constance, On the Principal Expositors of Sacred Scripture, book I; On Music, the Modes of Harmonies, book I; Letters to Various Persons, book I. He composed sermons and various homilies. And he elegantly expounded certain books of Sacred Scripture; he wrote many other things. While this Notger was still a monk at Saint Gall, Pope Nicholas I confirmed the sequences and allowed them to be sung in the Mass. He wrote many various hymns, chants, antiphons, and responsories, which down to the present day are used frequently in the Church of God in praises. He flourished in the episcopate under Emperor Lothar, in the year of the Lord 850.

SALOMON, bishop of Constance, formerly a monk of the monastery of Saint Gall, of the order of the divine father Benedict, once hearer and disciple of the above-named Notger, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, and exceptionally taught in secular letters; practiced in verse and prose, subtle in talent, eloquent in speech, and venerable no less for his way of life than for his knowledge. He wrote one book On the Seven Arts which they call liberal. Also one book, a Vocabulary, not to be despised. One book of Letters to Various Persons. He is also said to have composed many sermons and various treatises, which have not come into my hands. He flourished under Emperor Lothar in the year of the Lord 860.

WANDELBERT, deacon and monk of the monastery of Prüm, of the order of Saint Benedict, in the diocese of Trier, a man most learned both in the divine Scriptures and in secular letters, sharp in talent, eloquent in speech, a philosopher, rhetorician, and most learned poet, wrote, among other little works of his talent, to Abbot Marquard, the Life of Saint Goar the priest, one book; On the Miracles of the same most holy man, one book. He composed a very beautiful Martyrology in verse. He also published several other works, which have not come into my hands. He flourished in the times of the emperors Lothar and Louis, in the year of the Lord 849.

CHRISTIAN, who is Druthmar, monk and priest of the monastery of Corbie, Aquitanian indeed by nation but German by way of life, certainly a man most learned in every respect, skilled in Greek and Latin, wrote, among other monuments of his talent, [unclear] which he is said to have made, although none of these has come to the notice of my reading; On Matthew, book I; also many sermons and various homilies, one book, and many other things which I have not seen. In the prologue to the exposition of Matthew he promises that he would also write on the other evangelists, because [unclear] requested sermons, [unclear] he wrote many excellent volumes; by which [unclear] he wrote many excellent volumes in verse and prose; by which [unclear]

*Ofrid, monk of the monastery of Wissenburg.*

OTFRID, monk of the monastery of Weissenburg, of the order of Saint Benedict, in the diocese of Speyer, once hearer and disciple of Rabanus Maurus, abbot of Fulda, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, exceptionally taught in secular letters, a philosopher, rhetorician, astronomer, poet, theologian, second to none in his time, excellent in talent and eloquent in speech, wrote many excellent volumes in verse and prose, by which he transmitted his name and talent to posterity. From that volume in which Emperor Charles, once the Great, [unclear] the barbarism of our German mother tongue according to the same grammatical rules, many wonderful things [unclear] that language and speech regulated [unclear] differs more from ours, and then anyone skilled in our speech; indeed since that speech, regulated, differs more from ours [unclear] he composed in meter or verse, which no one in our age can easily read and understand, although [unclear] from Latin. Yet whatever this man composed is wonderful and worthy of reading, since in German speech he set rules, as if in verses he preserved feet and numbers. Of his little works there are extant [unclear]. To Luitbert, eighth archbishop of the church of Mainz, On the Four Gospels according to the aforesaid metrical rules *Johannes Trithemius*

a great and admirable work, which he entitled, in German, *Grace*, in five books; to King Louis, one book; to Solomon, bishop of Constance, one book; to the monks of Saint Gall, one book; on the Psalter, three great volumes in the same kind of speech. Likewise, On the Last Judgment, one book; also On the Joys of the Heavenly Kingdom, one book. He published sermons and homilies, both for the season and for the saints, in two books; letters to various persons, one book; many epigrams in both languages, in various kinds of meter, two books. He also published many other things which, lost through the negligence of earlier men and scraped away and torn by the ignorance and sloth of monks and abbots, have not come into our hands. He flourished in the times of the emperors Louis and Lothair, in the year of the Lord 870.

Franco, bishop of Liege, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and excellently instructed in the study of secular letters, a philosopher, rhetorician, poet, and excellent musician, keen in intellect, eloquent in speech, devout and most holy in life and conduct, presided for many years over the public school and trained many very learned pupils in every branch of knowledge. Among other little works of his talent he wrote many very useful sermons for the edification of the faithful, one book; also to Hermann, archbishop of Cologne, On the Squaring of the Circle, one book; On the Ecclesiastical Computus, one book; also letters to various persons, one book. Finally, he composed many chants, antiphons, legends, and responsories in honor of the saints, in sweet and regular melody. He is also said to have written some other things, which have not come to the knowledge of our reading.

Werenbert, a monk at Saint Gall of the order of the holy father Benedict, formerly a hearer and pupil of Hrabanus Maurus of Fulda, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and excellently instructed in secular letters, a distinguished philosopher, an outstanding poet, not ignorant of the Greek language, wrote for the edification of readers many splendid volumes, by which he brought back with great profit the talent entrusted to him by the Lord. He composed many elegant sermons, one book; also letters to various persons, one book; epigrams in different kinds of meter, one book; also on the Gospels, four books. He also composed various hymns and chants in honor of our Lord Jesus Christ and of the saints. The rest which he is said to have written, although they are many, have by no means come to my knowledge. He flourished under the emperor Louis II, in the year of the Lord 870.

Hartmud, a monk of the same monastery of Saint Gall, of the order of our blessed father Benedict, formerly a hearer and pupil of Hrabanus Maurus, to whom Otfrid, the monk of Weissenburg, exercised his talent in many letters, a man learned on every side, subtle in intellect, eloquent in speech, devout in life and conduct, skilled in Greek, Latin, and Hebrew, and furthermore not ignorant of Arabic, wrote many splendid little works both in meter and in prose; but I do not remember that any of them has come to the knowledge of our reading. There are said to exist commentaries of his, not to be rejected, on certain books of the Bible; likewise letters to various persons, one book; also sermons, chants, hymns, and various treatises on the sacred Scriptures, which every studious person should seek out. He flourished in the times of the emperors Lothair and Louis his son, in the year of the Lord 870.

Stephen, bishop of Liege after Franco, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and magnificently skilled in the disciplines of secular letters, prompt in intellect, orderly in speech, devout in life and conduct. I have found certain things of no contemptible reading that he wrote: The Life of Saint Lambert, bishop and martyr, one book; also to the bishop of Metz, one book. He also composed many elegant sermons, and several letters to various persons. The office concerning the Holy Trinity, which we sing every year on the octave of Pentecost, this Stephen composed from the volume of Albinus and set to sweet melody. But he also arranged, with beautiful grace, works on the Holy Cross, on Saint Lambert the martyr, and on many others.

Ratbod, the fourteenth bishop of the church of Utrecht, a man very learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, subtle in intellect, distinguished in eloquence, most holy in life and conduct, shone forth with many miracles both while alive and after death. Nanno, a very learned philosopher, instructed him in good letters; from him he advanced in every branch of knowledge, and finally, ordained bishop of the aforesaid city, he presided for seventeen years under the grave persecution of the Danes. He wrote certain splendid little works in praise of the saints, of which I have found only the following: Praises of Saint Martin, bishop of Tours, one book; Praises of Saint Boniface, archbishop of Mainz and martyr, one book; Praises of Saint Amalberga the Virgin, one book; sermons and tomes *Of Johannes Trithemius* 130

of the [unclear] diocese, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, and a philosopher, rhetorician, poet, and distinguished theologian most learned in all the letters of secular studies, skilled in Greek and Latin, subtle in talent, profound in knowledge, sweet, ornate, and eloquent in speech, most excellent in expounding the divine Scriptures. Among the other works of his talent he wrote: On Leviticus, a very celebrated and highly useful work, 20 books; On the Epistles of the Apostle Paul, 14 books; also a History of the Kings and Princes of the Franks, 1 book; also a Chronicle of His Own Times, 1 book; Letters to Various Persons, 1 book; Various Sermons, 1 book; and many poems of diverse kinds. He is read to have made very elegant commentaries on many books of the Bible, and also to have written several other treatises, which have by no means come down to us.

Aribo, the nineteenth archbishop of the church of Mainz, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, renowned in talent and pleasing in speech, wrote, among other monuments of his talent, a very beautiful work on the fifteen Gradual Psalms, 1 book, and various letters to different persons. Having celebrated a synod in the monastery of Seligenstadt with his bishops and abbots, in the year of the Lord 1032, indiction 6, he established many good and useful measures, which are contained in authentic writings. Burckhard, bishop of Worms, a most learned man, of whom mention will be made immediately, was personally present at this synod. To this Archbishop Aribo, because he was a lover of letters, many famous men, exercising their talents, wrote various little works. He died under Emperor Conrad, in the year of the Lord 1031, indiction 14, in the twelfth year of his episcopate.

Burckhard, formerly a monk of the order of Saint Benedict, bishop of Worms, or of the Vangiones, once the hearer and disciple of Albert, abbot of Gembloux, a most learned man (whom Gratian mentions in the Decrees, distinction 73, “In the name of the Lord”), a man certainly most learned both in the divine Scriptures and in secular letters, subtle in talent and renowned in speech. He wrote for the edification of the church several distinguished volumes, by which he commended his name both to the present and to posterity. Of these I have seen that large volume and notable work of decrees, divided into twenty books, which the diligence of jurists used before the compilation of the monk Gratian. He also wrote many elegant letters to various persons. The rest that he composed have not come down to me. He flourished in the times of Henry I, in the year of the Lord 1020.

Berno, abbot of the monastery of Reichenau, of the order of Saint Benedict, in the diocese of Constance, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, and excellently instructed in secular letters, a philosopher, rhetorician, and musician of very celebrated reputation, no less distinguished in life than in learning. He wrote several little works of reading not to be despised, concerning which the following are reported: to Pilgrim, archbishop of Cologne, an excellent volume On Music, of which the original is with us, 1 book; also On Musical Instruments, 1 book; to the aforesaid Aribo, archbishop of Mainz, On the Advent of the Lord, 1 book; On the Office of the Mass, 1 book; On the Fast of the Four Times, 1 book; On the Fast of Saturday, 1 book; On the Measure of the Monochord, 1 book; Letters to Various Persons, 1 book; also Sermons to the Brothers. And many other things. He flourished in the times of Saint Henry, emperor first, but king second, in the year of the Lord 1020.

Adelbold, bishop of Utrecht, formerly a monk of the order of the divine father Benedict (under whose name Heriger, abbot of Lobbes, composed a dialogue On the Advent of the Lord), a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures and excellently instructed in secular letters, subtle in talent, eloquent in speech, outstanding in life and conduct, and on account of those virtues held in great esteem in the court of Saint Henry the Emperor. He wrote some little works of reading by no means to be despised, by which he made his name known to posterity. Among these there is extant the Life and Deeds of that same Saint Emperor Henry, 1 book; On the Praises of the Holy Cross, 1 book; also On the Praises of Saint Mary, 1 book. He also published various sermons in praise of the saints. And many other things, both in verse and prose, which have not come to my knowledge. He died under Conrad II, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1027, indiction 10, in the eighteenth year of his episcopate, on the fifth day before the Kalends of December.

Bruno, bishop of Würzburg. [Würzburg] devoted to and learned, and not ignorant of secular letters, [unclear] in talent and deceased, shone with miracles. He wrote and compiled from the sayings of the ancient fathers a work not to be despised on the whole Psalter, and with wondrous knowledge corrected the text, previously corrupt in many places. If he wrote anything further, it has not come down to me. He died under Emperor Henry II, in the year of the Lord 1045, indiction 13, on the sixth day before the Kalends of June, and was numbered among the saints.

Adel *Catalogue of Illustrious Men*

129

various very elegant volumes, 1 book. He also wrote exhortatory letters to various persons. He also composed, in sweet melody, an Office on the translation of Saint Martin, various chants in honor of the saints, and certain other works that are unknown to us. He died under Emperor Conrad in the year of the Lord 817, in the fifth indiction, on the third day before the Kalends of December, in the eighteenth year of his episcopate. He was buried at Deventer.

REGINO, abbot of the monastery of Prum, of the order of the holy father Benedict, in the diocese of Trier, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, exceptionally instructed in secular letters, subtle in intellect, distinguished in speech, devout in life and conduct, easily held the first place among the teachers of his time. He wrote for Adelbero, bishop of Metz, a history of the deeds of the Frankish Germans from the birth of Christ down to his own times, 10 books. At the command of Ratbod, archbishop of Trier, he compiled from the decrees and decisions of the fathers and of general councils a distinguished canonical work, which he entitled *On Ecclesiastical Discipline and the Christian Religion*, in two volumes, 2 books. He also composed many elegant sermons, 1 book; also letters to various persons, 1 book; and many other things which have not yet come at all to the knowledge of our reading. He flourished in the times of Emperor Arnulf, in the year of the Lord 910.

WIDUKIND, a monk of Corvey in Saxony, of the order of Saint Benedict, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, most learned in secular letters, ready in intellect, distinguished in speech, excellent in verse and prose, wrote in both styles many excellent volumes, by which he consecrated his name to posterity. Of these I have found only the following: to Mechtild, daughter of Otto I, *On the Deeds of the Saxons*, 3 books; to the same, *The Deeds of Otto I*, 1 book; sermons to the brothers, 1 book; letters to various persons, 1 book; the life of Saint Paul the First Hermit, in prose and verse, 2 books; also the passion of the virgin Thecla, likewise in verse, 1 book; epigrams, 1 book. He is said besides to have written many other works, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished in the times of Emperor Otto I, in the year of the Lord 950.

ROSWITHA, a consecrated virgin of the monastery of Gandersheim in Saxony, noble, of the order of the holy father Benedict, devotedly learned in the divine Scriptures, and well imbued with the disciplines of secular letters, outstanding in intellect, distinguished in speech, and no less notable for conduct than for learning, wrote, both in verse and in prose, many excellent little works, by which, surpassing her sex in talent, she transmitted her name to posterity with great glory. Of these I have read the following: to the abbess Gerberga, in heroic verse, on the life and conduct of the unstained Mother of God, the Virgin Mary, 1 book; on the Passion of the Lord, in the same verse, 1 book; likewise on Saint Gangolf, 1 book; on the passion of Saint Pelagius, martyr, who suffered in these times at Cordoba, 1 book; on the fall of Theophilus the vicedominus and his repentance, 1 book; on the fall of a certain young man, converted through Saint Basil, 1 book; on the passion of Saint Dionysius, bishop and martyr, 1 book; on the passion of Saint Agnes, virgin, 1 book. She composed all the aforesaid in very elegant verse. She wrote besides six comedies, imitating Terence in style, of which the first is entitled *The Conversion of the Prince Gallicanus*, including the passion of the martyrs John and Paul. The second is on the passion of Agape, Chionia, and Irene, virgins. The third is on the resurrection of Calimachus and Drusiana through Saint John. The fourth is on the fall and conversion of Mary, niece of Abraham the Hermit. The fifth is entitled *The Conversion of Thais the Prostitute*. The sixth recounts the passion of the holy virgins Faith, Hope, and [Charity?]. She also wrote in verse the deeds of Emperor Otto I, 1 book; epigrams of various kinds, 1 book; and certain letters not without elegance. The rest that she composed have not come to the knowledge of our reading. She flourished in the times of Otto I and II, most illustrious emperors, in the year of the Lord 970.

SMARAGDUS, abbot of the monastery of Saint Michael in Saxony, of the order of the holy father Benedict, a man very learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular letters, acute in intellect, composed in speech, devout in life and conduct, a very celebrated guide of regular discipline, made his name known far and wide in expounding the holy Scriptures and obtained a great reputation for learning. For he wrote many excellent volumes, of which the following are extant: on the Rule of our most holy father Benedict, 1 book; on the whole Psalter, 1 book; on the Epistles and Gospels through the cycle of the year, 2 books; sermons to the brothers and others, 1 book; also a distinguished work on the virtues, which he entitled *The Diadem of Monks*, 1 book. He made a commentary on the greater Donatus that is not to be rejected. He is said also to have written many other volumes, both on divine and on secular writings, which have not come into our hands.

RADULPHUS, a monk of the monastery of Fulda, of the order of the holy father Benedict, *Catalogue of Illustrious Men*

Adelmann the grammarian, formerly a cleric of the church of Liege, bishop of Brixen, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, not moderately learned in secular letters, a philosopher, poet, and dialectician famous in his time, excellent in verse and prose. He wrote, in a twofold style, certain little works not to be despised, by which he commended his memory to posterity. Of these there survives a not unpleasant little book on the body and blood of the Lord, addressed to Berengar of Tours, at one time his fellow pupil under Fulbert of Chartres, who was already then beginning to teach errors on this matter; in it he strives against him with many testimonies of the Scriptures. On the same matter he issued a letter to Paulinus, primicerius of Metz. He wrote many letters to various persons, and certain other things. He flourished under Henry III, in the year of the Lord 1040.

Ratbertus Paschasius, abbot of Corbie of the Order of Saint Benedict, a man very learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular letters, subtle in intellect, eloquent in speech, a distinguished translator of Greek and Latin discourse, venerable no less for his life than for his knowledge. He wrote to a certain Placidus, an abbot of our order, a notable work on the sacrament of the altar, one book; also the life of Saint Adalhard the bishop, one book; on the Lamentations of Jeremiah the prophet, one book; and several other works unknown to me. He translated some things from Greek into the Latin tongue. He flourished in the time of the ruler Charles the Fat, in the year of the Lord 880.

Theoderic, monk of the monastery of Saint Matthias the Apostle near Trier, of the Order of the divine father Benedict, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures and exceptionally learned in secular letters, subtle in intellect, distinguished in eloquence. Among other monuments of his study he wrote on the discovery of Saint Celsus, one book; on the miracles of the same saint, one book; many sermons in honor of the saints, one book. He also published some other works which have by no means come to the knowledge of our reading. He flourished under the emperor Otto III, in the year of the Lord 1000.

Theoderic, archbishop of Trier, the seventy-second after Saint Eucharius, formerly provost of the greater church of Mainz, a zealous and learned man, of outstanding industry in conducting ecclesiastical business. He wrote On the Praises of the Most Blessed Virgin Mary, Mother of God, one book; also the life of Saint Liuttrudis, one book; and certain other things. Under the pontificate of this Theoderic, the canons of the greater church of Trier ceased to be regulars. He flourished in the times of the emperors Otto II and III, in the year of the Lord 967. He was buried at Mainz in the church of Saint Gangolf, which he himself had built and endowed for twelve brethren.

Remigius, monk and abbot of the monastery of Saint Luthwin at Mettlach, of the Order of the divine father Benedict, in the diocese of Trier, a man most zealous and very learned in the divine Scriptures, and nobly instructed in secular letters, subtle in intellect, eloquent in speech, devout in life and conduct, a philosopher, poet, and musician by far the most distinguished of all in his time. He was of such knowledge and learning that from all Germany and Gaul he had most distinguished pupils placed under his instruction to be taught; of these many are read to have been taken up into ecclesiastical rule in diverse regions of the world, some consecrated as abbots, others as bishops. He wrote many excellent little works, by which his name is made known to posterity: on the five books of Moses; not careless commentaries on the Gospel; also Rules on the Apostle; On the Vision of Habakkuk, one book; also an Excerpt from Priscian, one book; a commentary on Donatus, one book. At the command of Eckebert, archbishop of Trier, [unclear] by all of which he shows himself a most learned man. But he published many other things which [unclear].

Goldscherus, monk of the monastery of Saint Matthias near Trier.

also of Saint Valerius, one book; On the Praises of Saint Maternus the Bishop, one book; many sermons on the praises of the saints, one book; also The Deeds of the Treveri, one book. Finally he composed certain other works which have not come to the knowledge of my reading.

*Hermannus*, who was called Contractus, a monk of the monastery of Saint Gall, of the order of our holy father Benedict, son of the Count of Veringen among the Swabians, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and, in secular letters, the most learned of all the doctors of his time; a most celebrated philosopher, rhetorician, astronomer, poet, musician, and theologian; most skilled in three languages, Greek, Latin, and Arabic, and not ignorant of Hebrew; excelling in verse and prose, and also most devout in life and conduct. He wrote many splendid volumes, by which he commended his memory to posterity. Among these the following are given: On Music, one book; On the Monochord, one book; On the Six Ages of the World, one book; On Astronomy, two books; On the Construction of the Astrolabe, three books; On the Eclipses of the Sun and Moon, one book; On Computation, one book; On the Squaring of the Circle, one book; On the Contest of Rithmomachy, one book; also On Physiognomy, one book. He composed lives of several holy fathers in a most elegant style. He also published many letters to various persons, one book, and almost countless poems of different kinds. He also composed many hymns and chants in honor of the saints with very sweet melody. Among them is that antiphon concerning the blessed Mother of God, “Salve Regina,” and that one, “Alma Redemptoris,” with many others. He also translated some volumes of Greeks and Arabs into Latin, as he himself acknowledges in a certain preface to Aristotle. Of what merit this Hermannus was before God, and how great a grace the most blessed Virgin Mary bestowed on him, I remember that I have already described in part, though in few and brief words, in the second book of the illustrious men of our order. He flourished in the times of the emperor Henry III, in the year of the Lord 1040.

*Helperius*, a monk of the same monastery of Saint Gall, of the order of the holy father Benedict, himself also a man much learned in the divine Scriptures and most learned in secular letters; a most celebrated philosopher, astronomer, and poet, subtle in intellect and eloquent in speech, no less notable for his life than for his learning. He wrote many splendid little works, both in verse and in prose, but few of them have come into our hands. For I have only seen and read the very famous book which he published On Ecclesiastical Computation, and another entitled On Music, as well as certain poems. The rest which he composed have not come into our hands. He flourished at the same time as Hermannus Contractus, in the year of the Lord 1040.

*Rogerus*, a monk in Saxony of the monastery of Corvey, of the order of Saint Benedict, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, and not ignorant of secular letters, distinguished in intellect and speech. He wrote the Life and Deeds of Bruno, archbishop of Cologne, brother of the emperor Otto I, one book. He also published certain other works, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished in the times of Otto III, in the year of the Lord 1000.

*Algerus*, from scholasticus a monk of the monastery of Corvey, of the order of our holy father Benedict, a man exercised by constant study in the holy Scriptures, rich also in the reading of the ancients, and magnificently learned in secular letters; prudent in intellect, eloquent in speech, strong in verse and prose. Among other little works of his intellect, he wrote a notable volume On the Sacrament of the Altar, one book; On the Same Matter against Berengarius, one book; also On the Grace of God and the Free Will of Man, one book. He is said to have written certain other works besides, but they have by no means come to the knowledge of my reading.

*Eckebertus*, a cleric of the church of Liege, studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, and exceptionally learned in the disciplines of secular letters; subtle in intellect, distinguished in speech, excelling in verse no less than in prose. He wrote, in both styles, little works not to be despised, by which he commended his memory to posterity. Among these there is extant a volume composed in elegant verse, which he entitled On Rustic Riddles, one book. And afterwards he wrote a somewhat larger work on the same subject. The rest which he composed have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1060.

*Leo*, the ninth pope, previously called Bruno, bishop of the city of the Leuci, which is called Toul, under the archbishop of Trier, by country an Alsatian, from the counts of Egesheim, sat in the chair of Peter after Damasus for seven years. He was a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and exceptionally learned in the disciplines of secular letters, venerable no less in conduct than in knowledge. He wrote to Constantine [Monomachus?], emperor of the Greeks, On Extirpating Heresies, one book; to the bishops of Africa and Egypt, one book; also letters to various persons, one book; and certain other works unknown to us. He died under Henry III, in the year of the Lord 1054, in the seventh indiction, and is reported to have been distinguished by many miracles. *Hum* *Catalogue of Illustrious Men*

Humbert, a monk of Toul, of the Order of Saint Benedict, fellow-countryman of Pope Leo IX, a man most learned in every respect, whom the aforesaid pontiff Leo brought from Lotharingia, namely from the monastery of Toul, to Rome, and ordained bishop to preach the word of God to the Sicilians. Afterwards the holy Roman Church appointed him a cardinal prelate for itself, a most religious and most holy man. Among the other monuments of his talent he wrote many treatises against the errors of Berengar. Sent by Pope Leo to Constantinople for the extirpation of heresies, by his wonderful learning and eloquence he so far refuted and defeated in disputation Nicetas Pectoratus, a monk and heresiarch, in the presence of Constantine Monomachus the emperor and Michael the patriarch, that Nicetas at once anathematized the book which he had published against the Roman Church, and with his own hand threw it into the flames to be burned. He therefore wrote that same disputation of his in the form of a dialogue, under the names of a Roman and a Constantinopolitan speaking with one another, one book; and various letters to various persons, and certain other things which have not come to our knowledge. Lanfranc mentions this Humbert, a most learned man, in his book against Berengar. He flourished in the time of Pope Leo IX, in the year of the Lord 1050.

Bernold, priest of the church of Constance in Swabia, a devout man, studious and learned, ready in talent and distinguished in eloquence, is said to have put forth certain little works of reading not to be despised, by which he commended his name and memory to posterity; but I do not recall that any of them has come into our hands. He wrote and corrected the Roman Order for the use of the church. He flourished under Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1060.

Lambert, monk of the monastery of Saint Laurence at Liege, of the Order of the divine father Benedict, formerly hearer and disciple of Adelmann the Grammarian, bishop of Brescia, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and remarkably instructed in secular letters, a philosopher, rhetorician, and most celebrated poet, distinguished in talent and eloquent in speech, whom the aforesaid excellent pontiff Adelmann commends in notable verses, wrote many splendid volumes both in verse and in prose, by which he commended his name to posterity. But of these I have been worthy to see only a few: the Life of Saint Heribert, archbishop of Cologne, one book; On the Miracles of the Same, one book; also Hymns in varied kinds of verse, one book; Epigrams, one book; letters to various persons, one book. He also composed an office for Saint Heribert and for many other saints, and arranged it with sweet melody. The rest that he wrote have by no means come into our hands. He flourished in the times of Emperor Henry III and Hermann, archbishop of Cologne, in the year of the Lord 1060.

Lambert of Liege, monk of the monastery of Eucharius and Matthias the Apostle outside the walls of Trier, of the Order of the divine father Benedict, a man most learned in every respect, a philosopher, rhetorician, musician, and very distinguished poet, subtle in talent and elegant in speech. He wrote certain splendid little works both in verse and in prose; of these I have found only the following: On the Miracles of Saint Matthias the Apostle, a great work composed in verse, [unclear] books; also on Saint Agricius, one book; to Lambert his abbot he published the Life of Saint Matthias the Apostle, one book; also various sermons in honor of the saints, one book; very many letters to various persons; very elegant poems of different kinds, many and varied; and several other things unknown to us. He flourished under Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1080.

Marianus Scotus, monk of Fulda, of the Order of our divine father Benedict, a man [unclear]. Here, from love of his most celebrated homeland, leaving his native soil, he came as a pilgrim into Germany, and first indeed became a monk in the monastery of Saint Martin at Cologne, and [unclear] for two [unclear]; summoned to Mainz by the archbishop because of his holiness and learning, he lived enclosed at Saint Martin for seventeen years and persevered for others until death. He was, moreover, a very great computist and a most diligent assessor of past time, as the very distinguished monuments which he published prove. Of these the following are extant: a notable volume of Chronicles from the beginning of the world down to his own times, [unclear] books; On the Harmony of the Evangelists, one book; also On Computation, one book; various sermons; and several letters to various persons. He died under Henry, the third emperor but the fourth king, in the year of the Lord 1086, in the ninth indiction, in the fifty-eighth year of his age, and was buried in the church of Saint Martin at Mainz, not without a great reputation for sanctity.

*134 Of Johannes Trithemius*

*Of Theodoric, of the monastery of St Alban at Mainz.*

THEODORIC, a monk of the monastery of Saint Alban the Martyr at Mainz, of the order of the divine father Benedict, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, outstandingly instructed in secular letters, a philosopher and most distinguished poet, subtle in talent and renowned in eloquence, is said to have written certain excellent little works, by which he commended his memory to posterity. Of these the following are extant: To Richard, abbot of Fulda, On the Life and Miracles of Our Most Holy Father Benedict, one book; also On His Translation into Gaul, to the same man, one book; Letters to Various Persons, one book. He also published many varied poems. But there are several others which have not yet come into our hands. He flourished under Emperor Henry II, but the third king of this name, in the year of the Lord 1040.

WENERIC, formerly a cleric of the church of Trier, bishop of Vercelli, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, ready in talent and renowned in eloquence, wrote some little works of exercise, by which he proved his learning. In that discord which existed between Hildebrand, Pope Gregory VII, and Emperor Henry IV, he wrote, in the person of Theodoric, bishop of Verdun, while he himself was still a cleric at Trier, to the same Pope Gregory, a volume furnished with divine Scriptures: for he did not rebuke him, but, as an elder, entreated him as a father, with friendly affection, as though grieving, suggesting to him all the things which talkative rumor had spread abroad that he had done or said against right, divine law, and equity. It is entitled On the Discord of Priesthood and Empire, one book. He also composed many other things, but they have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1080.

ERHARD, a monk of Corvey in Saxony, of the Benedictine order, a man most zealous in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular letters, subtle in talent and ready in eloquence, of very celebrated reputation in delivering homilies to the people, wrote, among the other little works of his talent, a notable work On the Pentateuch, five books; also Homilies, one book. He is also said to have written many other things, and to have expounded the sacred Scriptures in many volumes; these have not come to my knowledge.

WILLERAM, abbot of the monastery of Mersburg, of the order of the divine father Benedict, a man learned in the divine writings and not ignorant of secular literature, skilled in verse and prose, shone forth no less renowned in life than in learning. After he had for some time devoted his labor to the letters of philosophy in the school of Paris, he returned to his homeland, that is, eastern Francia, which is called Franconia. Made scholasticus of the church of Bamberg because of the eminence of his learning, he did not abandon the sweet fellowship of letters. At length, considering that the vain glory of the world passes away with time, scorning the age and despising worldly things for the love of God, he put on the monastic habit in the monastery of Fulda. As his merits increased, he was finally elected abbot at Mersburg. He wrote a work mixed of meter and prose on the Song of Songs, which he entitled On the Nuptials of Christ and the Church, two books; also various sermons to the brothers; and, as they say, several letters to various persons. He also composed many other things, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1080[?].

BERNARD, a monk of the monastery of Saint Vitus of Corvey in Saxony, of the order of Saint Benedict, a man zealous and learned in the divine writings and sufficiently instructed in secular letters, subtle in talent, renowned in eloquence, skilled in verse and prose, wrote some little works of his talent, by which he made his name known to posterity. To Hartwig, archbishop of Magdeburg, he published a volume, indeed in lucid but bitter speech, against Henry IV, king but the third emperor, in which it is clearly evident how grievous and hateful the same Henry was to the Saxons. He wrote besides many varied letters, and several other things unknown to us. He flourished in the times of the same Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1080[?]. He composed various things.

WILLIAM, abbot of the monastery of Hirsau, of the order of Saint Benedict, in the diocese of Speyer, a man most learned in every respect, a philosopher, musician, computist, and most celebrated theologian, devout and most holy in life and conduct, who was renowned for many miracles in life and death, magnificently restored by word and example the monastic discipline among the Germans, which had almost collapsed. He wrote, in lucid speech, little works not to be despised, of which the following are extant: Constitutions of His New Reform, one book; also On Music, one book; also On the Clock, one book; he made a correction of the Psalter, one book; he published various letters to various persons, among which many are said to have been to Anselm II, archbishop of Canterbury, with whom he was most familiar. Some letters of this Anselm to this William are also extant. He also published some other things, which have not come to me. He died under Emperor Henry III, but King Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1091, in the fourteenth indiction, on the fourth Nones of July. He was buried in the middle of his church.

WOLFE*Catalogue of Illustrious Men.*

Wolfhelm, abbot of the monastery of Brauweiler, which is nearly two miles distant from Cologne, born in the district of Ribuarien in the same diocese of Cologne, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, excellently instructed in secular letters, devout and most holy in life and conduct, renowned for the performance of many miracles, subtle in intellect, polished in speech, excellent in verse and prose. He wrote some distinguished volumes, but few of them have come to my knowledge. Against Berengar of Tours, On the Sacrament of the Altar, he published a small but necessary work addressed to Abbot Meginhard, one book; also many sermons to the brothers, various letters to different persons; likewise many elegant poems, composed in various kinds of meter; he arranged epigrams over all the volumes of his library. He is also said to have written several other works, which have by no means come to the notice of our reading. He was first a monk in the monastery of Saint Maximin at Trier, then at Saint Pantaleon in Cologne; afterward he was made abbot at Gladbach; finally he was transferred as abbot to the aforesaid monastery of Brauweiler, where he presided as the third in order. He died under Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1091, in the fourteenth indiction, on the tenth day before the Kalends of May.

Theoderic, abbot of the monastery of Saint Trudo of the order of the divine father Benedict, a man devoted to and learned in the holy Scriptures, and sufficiently instructed in secular letters, subtle in intellect, composed in speech, also practiced in verse and prose. He wrote many distinguished little works in both kinds, by which he brought his name to the knowledge of many. Among these the following are reported: Life of Saint Trudo, one book; Life of Saint Bavo, one book; Life of Saint Remold, one book; various sermons to the brothers, one book; also several letters to different persons, one book; certain other works as yet unknown to us. He is said to have flourished in the time of Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1100.

Conrad, monk of the monastery of Brauweiler, of the order of the divine father Benedict, in the diocese of Cologne, once a hearer and disciple of the most holy abbot Wolfhelm, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular letters. For the edification of the faithful he wrote volumes not to be despised, with which he usefully occupied his talent; of these the following are extant. The Life of the same Saint Wolfhelm, abbot, addressed to Eberhard of Brauweiler and Herman, abbots of Saint Pantaleon, one book; On the Miracles of the same blessed Wolfhelm, one book; sermons in honor of the saints; several other works unknown to us. He flourished under Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1100.

Stephen, also called Herrand, the fourteenth bishop of Halberstadt, formerly abbot of the monastery of Ilsenburg in Saxony, of the order of our most holy father Benedict, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, venerable no less for holiness than for knowledge, wrote, in the person of Count Louis, faithful to the Church, a most elegant letter in the form of a little book, in defense of obedience to the Roman Church, against Henry IV, rebel against the Roman Church, to Waltram, bishop of Naumburg, who stubbornly defended the party of Henry IV against obedience to the supreme pontiff. He also composed other letters in the same cause concerning various ecclesiastical affairs, and various treatises, but they have by no means come into our hands. He died under Henry V, in the year of the Lord 1107, in the fifteenth indiction.

Rupert, abbot of Deutz near Cologne, formerly a monk of the monastery of Saint Lawrence at Liege, of the order of the divine father Benedict, a man in the divine Scriptures, with the Holy Spirit enlightening him, the most learned of all the learned men of his time, not ignorant of secular literature, subtle in intellect, sweet and composed in speech, shone forth renowned no less for holiness than for knowledge. While he was placed in the aforesaid monastery at Liege, when he was still a young man, he applied the greatest zeal to divine letters; but since, because of the slightness of his ability, he made little progress, he turned himself with tears from infancy to prayer, and, the most blessed Mother of God manifestly appearing to him and promising grace, he obtained such knowledge in all Scripture that he had no equal in his time. And lest you think it a fable, he himself confesses these things about himself in many places of his works. Thereafter he had such love for sacred readings that not even while sleeping did he seem to rest from divine conversations, while his tongue and lips were moved as if he were reading something. He wrote almost infinite volumes, of which I have found the following. To Cuno, abbot of Siegburg, afterward bishop of Regensburg, On the Victory of the Word of God, a most beautiful work, thirteen books; On Genesis, nine books; On the Song of Songs, a work to be commended with every praise, seven books; On the Book of Genesis, Job, ten books; On the Books of Kings, On Saint David, fifteen books; On the Old Testament, the great work of Saint Job, twelve books; On the Divine Offices, twelve books; On the Twelve Minor Prophets, thirty books; On the Gospels, twelve books; On the Divine Offices, twelve books; On the Twelve Minor Prophets, thirty books; On the Gospels 136 *Of Johannes Trithemius* ... on the Gospel of Matthew, 8 books; on the Gospel of John, 1 book; Meditations, 3 books, taking as the material to be followed the miraculous fire of the monastery of Tuitium; also on the Rule of Saint Benedict, 1 book; an Apology for the same work, 1 book; on the four most difficult questions, 1 book; also many and various sermons, 1 book; letters to various persons, 1 book. He is also said to have written many other things, but they have not yet come to the notice of our reading. He flourished, shining with much sanctity and learning and with miracles, under Henry V, in the year of the Lord 1120. And he died under Lothar III.

Rupert, abbot of the monastery of Lympurg, of the order of the holy father Benedict, in the diocese of Speyer, a man excellently learned both in the divine Scriptures and in secular letters, distinguished in talent, scholastic in speech, devout in life and conduct. He applied himself to philosophy for not a few years in the gymnasium of Paris, while he was still a secular man, and became learned in every scholastic science. At length, having returned to his homeland, namely to the city of the Vangiones, whence he had drawn the origin of his life, he despised philosophy, useless to the soul, together with the things of the world, for the love of God, and put on the habit of holy conversion in the aforesaid monastery; and finally, as his merits increased, by the consent of all the brethren he was elected abbot. There he established, by word and example, the greatest observance of regular discipline, and he deserved often to be refreshed by divine revelations. At the command, seen in a vision, of the most holy Mother of God, he wrote a very beautiful work in praise of the same Virgin: on the Song of Songs, 1 book; on the contempt and vanity of this world, 2 books; on Saint John the Baptist, 1 book; also of his own revelations, 1 book. He also composed many sermons in honor of the saints whose relics or patronages are held in his monastery, and letters to various persons, and various treatises on the holy Scriptures. He flourished under Henry V, in the year of the Lord [1120?].

Rudolf, abbot of the monastery of Saint Trudo, of the order of the holy father Benedict, in the diocese of Liege, a man devoted to the divine Scriptures and skilled through long practice, and sufficiently learned in the knowledge of secular letters, distinguished in talent and life, excellent also in verse and prose. He wrote little works not to be despised in reading, by which he commended his memory to posterity. Among these there is an excellent work against the Simoniacs, 7 books; also a chronicle of deeds of past time, 1 book. He also published many poems of different kinds. He also composed chants in praise of the saints with sweet and regular modulation. He flourished under Henry V, in the year of the Lord 1125.

Franco, second abbot of the monastery of Hasligem, of the order of Saint Benedict, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and well instructed in the knowledge of secular literature, strong in talent and distinguished in speech. He wrote certain commendable little works, both in meter and in prose, by which he transmitted his name with glory to posterity. While he was still a monk, at the command of Fulgentius his abbot, he began an excellent work on the grace of God, which afterwards, when made abbot, he completed. He also wrote metrically on the state of future glory, 1 book; also letters to various persons and various sermons; and certain other things. He flourished under Henry V, in the year of the Lord 1110.

Eckhard, first abbot of the monastery of Saint Lawrence the Martyr, which is called Vraugia, near the Hercynian forest in the diocese of Wurzburg, of the order of the holy father Benedict, a man devoted to and very learned in the divine Scriptures, and not moderately learned in secular letters, subtle in talent and eloquent in speech, practiced in verse and prose. He wrote little works not to be despised in reading, in which he magnificently exercised his talent; among them the following are reported. In imitation of Boethius he wrote, in both kinds, that is, in an alternating style, an excellent volume which he entitled The Lantern of Monks, 1 book; also various and many sermons to the brethren; also many poems and epigrams of different kinds; and certain other things. He flourished under the Emperor Lothar, in the year of the Lord 1130.

Engelbert, abbot of the monastery of Admont, of the order of Saint Benedict, a man distinguished for learning in the Scriptures and venerable no less for integrity of morals than for knowledge, made his name known by writing and expounding various things, and both by word and example did the lowest things for the edification of his brethren. Among the other works of his talent he wrote: on vices and virtues, 1 book; also many useful sermons to the brethren, 1 book; also several letters. But he also published many other things which have not come into our hands.

Conrad, also called the Pilgrim, monk of the monastery of Hirsau, of the order of the holy father Benedict, in the diocese of Speyer, formerly a hearer and disciple of Abbot William, a man in divine *Johannes Trithemius*

under Emperor Frederick I, in the year of the Lord 1165, indiction 14, in the thirty-sixth year of her age, the twenty-third of her conversion, and the thirteenth of the visitation of the heavenly light, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of July. She was buried in the church of the monks of Saint Florinus the martyr, in the middle of the choir, not without the very greatest reputation for sanctity.

Hildegard, a nun, abbess of the monastery of Saint Rupert the Confessor opposite the town of Bingen, on the other side of the river Nahe, in the diocese of Mainz, of the order of our lord father Benedict, born in the county of Sponheim, once a disciple of the blessed virgin Jutta, sister of Megenhard, count of Sponheim, our founder, a virgin of most holy way of life and from her childhood enlightened by divine revelations, was renowned in her life for many miracles, and spread the odor of sanctity into distant regions, so that Eugenius III, Anastasius IV, Adrian IV, and Alexander III, Roman pontiffs, often visiting her by their writings, commended both themselves and the Roman Church to her prayers. Eugenius III also, in a council held at Trier, with Saint Bernard and many cardinals, bishops, abbots, and clerics present, approved the books of this virgin, read publicly before all, as divinely inspired and consonant with the Catholic faith, and admonished her by apostolic letters to persevere in the undertaking she had begun.

She wrote many little works from angelic revelation, of which the following are extant: a brief explanation on the Rule of Saint Benedict, one book; to Wibert the monk, on thirty questions proposed to her by him, one book; the life of Saint Rupert, duke and confessor, one book; also the life of Saint Disibod, an Irish bishop, who, coming as a pilgrim for Christ into Germany, rests in the county of Sponheim, famous for many miracles, one book.
