He lives near Stuttgart, bound by the bond of marriage, yet no less applying himself to letters and writing various things, under Emperor Maximilian, in the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1495, indiction 13.

*Wilhelmus de Velde*

Wilhelmus de Velde, by homeland a Gueldrian, canon of the order of the regulars of Saint Augustine in Frankenthal in the diocese of Worms, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular literature, a philosopher and astronomer, and a cosmographer of celebrated reputation, deep in intellect, acute, and very subtle; composed in speech, devout in life and conduct. He wrote and is writing certain very beautiful and wondrous volumes, in which he clearly shows to readers the sharpness of his intellect. Of these he recently showed me the following: Statutes of the sisters of his order, one book; a most subtle work on the whole universe, that is, on the beginning, middle, and end of the world, which he entitled The Greater Empyrean, 24 books; likewise a compendium of this work, which he entitled [unclear]; also many tables on various subjects, no less useful than subtle; many sermons to the people; epigrams and various poems; also some things not to be rejected in mathematics; also many letters to me and to others. Finally he composed some other things, which will come to light in their own time. He is still living, fifty years old, in Darmstein, a village of the territory of Worms, serving as parish priest, under Emperor Maximilian, in the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1495, indiction 8.

*Petrus Bo-Landan Lautenburger; Petrus Bolandanus of Ladenburg; Petrus*

Petrus Bolandus of Ladenburg, parish priest in the town of Schriesheim in the diocese of Worms, a man most learned in every respect, a distinguished philosopher, mathematician, theologian, and very celebrated poet, ready in intellect, eloquent in expression, excellent in verse, and also an outstanding declaimer of sermons in prose. He wrote some splendid volumes, by which he commended his memory to posterity. Yet few of these have come to my knowledge: a Sapphic poem for Emperor Frederick III; a Sapphic poem on the death of Rudolf Agricola; innumerable epigrams from the sayings of Seneca and Plato; a long Sapphic poem on the divine Mary; a heroic poem on the work On the Threefold Whiteness; a heroic poem on our work On the Misery of Prelates; elegiac poems, Sapphic poems, and letters to Johann Camerarius Dalburg, his bishop of Worms. He wrote a poem to the students of Heidelberg on account of the plague; of epigrams and elegies almost innumerable, one book; besides these many sermons and elegant orations, and very ornate letters to various persons. He is also said to be writing many other things, but in secret. He is still living in Schriesheim, not far from Heidelberg, being 50 years of age, under Emperor Maximilian, in the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1495, indiction 13.

*Johannes Bertram of Neuenburg; Johannes*

Johannes Bertram Nuenburghen wrote to Berthold, archbishop of Mainz, a long letter in the form of a little book, On the Value of Masses, one book. He also explained various questions disputed in the schools. He is now writing and lecturing ordinarily on the epistles of Paul. Almost ten years before he had lectured on Genesis, a great and pleasing work. He is still living in the academy of Mainz, having passed his forty-fifth year of age, under King Maximilian, in the year of the Lord in which we write these things, 1495, indiction 14.

*Rudolphus de Euschringen*

Rudolphus de Eufstringen, of Baden, [unclear] of the archbishop of Trier, a man most learned in every respect and a most [unclear] cultivator and investigator of all antiquity, a supreme philosopher, a most sagacious interpreter of law, and a most eloquent lover and [unclear] of the divine Scriptures, subtle and ready in intellect, in speech *170  [Works] of Johannes Trithemius*

…the same on the Psalter according to the exposition, one book. From parts of Saint Thomas he [unclear], one book. He began a lecture on the Apocalypse of John, which he will continue in the school at Mainz. He also wrote notably on Aristotle’s books of Economics. He likewise disputed and wrote notable questions on the Ethics. He also composed many other things which have not come to my knowledge. He is still living, almost sixty years old, in the city of Frankfurt, under King Maximilian, in the year of the Lord in which we write these things, 1495.

Johannes Gotfridi of Odernheim, pastor of the church of Saint Catherine in Oppenheim, not far from Mainz, bachelor of sacred theology, a man excellently learned both in the divine Scriptures and in secular letters, subtle in intellect and distinguished in eloquence, of very celebrated reputation in delivering sermons to the people. He wrote many and various treatises, which he has not yet allowed to come to light. He also composed many elegant sermons for the cycle of the year and on various subjects. He wrote letters both to me and to others, composed with grace of eloquence. Finally, he translated many treatises of the ancient authors from Latin speech into the vernacular tongue, with no less eloquence than [unclear], if indeed charm and ornament are allowed to exist in the German language. Among these I have seen Cicero’s *On the Nature of the Gods*, which he translated at the urging of the valiant knight Frederick, chamberlain of Dalberg, no less elegantly than learnedly. He also began to translate Augustine’s *City of God* for the same Frederick, and has now completed almost twelve books. He also wrote and translated many other things, which will come to light in their own time. He is still living in good old age at Oppenheim, writing various things, under King Maximilian, in the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1495.

Werner Rolevinck of Laer, a Westphalian by country, sprung from the diocese of Münster, a monk of the Carthusian order, of the house of Saint Barbara in Cologne, a man most devoted to the divine Scriptures and very learned, subtle in intellect, devout in life and conduct. He wrote many distinguished volumes, among which the following are extant: On all the Epistles of Paul, three great volumes, which work he entitled *The Teaching of Paul*, fourteen books. *Life of Paul*, seven books. *Paradise of Conscience*, one book. On the sacrament of the altar and the value of Masses, one book. To John, bishop of Münster, *Form for God-fearing Bishops*, one book. *Form of Living for Canons and Secular Priests*, one book. On the dignity and power of priests, one book. On true nobility and its origin, one book. To Everwin, count of Bentheim, on the best manner of governing the commonwealth, one book. On the government of rustics, one book. On hospitallers and those occupied with works of mercy, one book. On fraternal correction and monastic visitation, and on those who hinder its good progress, one book. Twelve questions on those to whom it belongs to treat sacred Scripture, and on the degrees conferred in the schools, one book. Ten questions on the advancement of religious, one book. Eight questions, one book. *Fasciculus temporum*, with circles from the beginning of the world down to the times of Pope Sixtus IV, one book. On the praise of Westphalia and its conversion to the faith, one book. On the origin of the Frisians, one book. On contracts, whether they are lawful, one book. On the calendar and martyrology, one book. Twenty rules useful for prelates, one book. A long sermon on Saint Benedict, printed some time ago, which begins thus: “I in my innocence have entered.” A question whether Christ on the cross prayed for all, one book. On the excellence of Albert the Great, one book. To a certain abbot of our order who was compelled to accept the episcopate, one book. On the common brotherhood of those feasting together, one book. On the instruction of novices, one book. On the difference of passions and what a passion is, one book. On the security of the license of prelates, one book. On holy desires and the manner of conducting oneself in them, one book. On the contemplation of simple persons, one book. On devoutly paying the canonical hours, one book. Many synodal, chapter, and popular sermons, the number of which is uncertain. He also wrote almost countless letters both to me and to others. These are the things which he recently confessed to me that he had written, in the seventieth year of his age and the forty-eighth of his conversion, when I was in his cell, under Emperor Maximilian and Pope Alexander VI, in the year of the Lord 1495, indiction 13, on the sixth day before the Ides of May. Many other unfinished works are moreover still in his hands, to be completed in their own time.

Johannes of Keysersberg, priest and distinguished preacher of the church of Strasbourg, a man devoted to and learned in the divine writings, and excellently learned in secular letters, subtle in intellect, eloquent in speech, outstanding in life and conduct, an unafraid herald of truth, a lover of virtue, an enemy of vices, who has often pursued the crimes of the wicked with free voice even to the point of envy. He wrote several distinguished little works, of which, however, he has as yet allowed few to come to light. There are extant his most beautiful sermons to the people, two books. On communicating those who are punished with the final penalty, one book. On remov *Johannes Trithemius*

... made himself useful to those present and memorable to posterity. Of these there is extant a notable Summa on contracts, insofar as it pertains to the forum of conscience and to theological decision, divided into more than one hundred questions, seven books. There is also a not inelegant oration on the reform of monks. The other things that he wrote he always strove so much to keep hidden that not even the bond of friendship could ever induce him to reveal them to me. He sent letters to me and to several others. He is still living, directing the theological school in the college of Tuebingen, a town of Swabia belonging to Duke Eberhard of Wuerttemberg, and he is writing various works, under King Maximilian, in the year of the Lord 1495.

Conrad Celtis Proticius, an East Frank, born at Schweinfurt, a man most learned in every respect, a famous philosopher, an eloquent orator, a distinguished astronomer and cosmographer, and a poet laureate, not ignorant also of the divine Scriptures, skilled in Greek and Latin, excellent in intellect and fluent in speech. He wrote many splendid volumes in meter and prose, by which he commended his memory to posterity. Of these he once read the following to me: To King Maximilian, on both Rhetorics of Cicero, an epitome, that is, a compendium or breviary, one book; a poem on the praises of eloquence, one book; On the Art of Versifying, one book; On Composing Letters, one book; On the Site of the City of Noricus Mons, which work he entitled Nuremberg, one book; his Sarmatian Journey, one book; Poems or Epigrams, four books; Loves, which according to the four sides of Germany are inscribed [Istulae], [four?] books; a Panegyric to the Duke of Bavaria, one book; a Sapphic poem on the life of Saint Sebald, patron of the people of Nuremberg, one book; Germania, one book; many and various orations, one book. He has issued very many most elegant letters, both to me and to others, in meter and prose, and in cosmography, of which he is most learned, he has written various things which hereafter, in their own time, will come to light. He is still living in the college of Ingolstadt in Bavaria, lecturing ordinarily on poetry and oratory, being twenty-five years of age, under Emperor Maximilian, in the year of the Lord in which we write these things, 1495, in the fourteenth indiction.

Johannes of Veteri Aqua, otherwise of Gouda, a Hollander by homeland, a Brabanter by upbringing, of the order of the Brothers of the Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, of the convent of Mechelen, at this time subprior of Kassel in Hesse, a man zealous in the divine Scriptures and skilled by long practice, of excellent talent in delivering sermons to the people, and a fervent lover of his order and a devout cultivator of it. For the instruction and edification of many brothers he wrote a commendable work on the beginning and progress of his order, which he entitled The Three-Part Fascicle of Times of the Order of Carmelites, four books. In the first of these he proves that Elijah and the prophets were founders of the Carmelite order; in the second he enumerates the saints and canonized persons from the same order; in the third he places in chronological order the successions of the priors general of his whole order. He also wrote On the Most Pure Conception Ever of the Blessed Virgin Mary, one book; also countless sermons to the people, two books; letters both to me and to others, almost infinite in number. He wrote besides many letters against a certain Wigand, of the Order of Preachers, lecturer of the Frankfurt convent, who rashly attacked the most pure conception of the Mother of God. For he, attacking with mad loquacity the seventh chapter of our treatise on Saint Anne, wrote against me a long and impudent letter, in which he signed himself “the one weighing,” and fraudulently suppressed his own proper name. To his rashness answer has been made quite sufficiently, both by this Johannes the Carmelite and by other learned men. For I, writing back only one letter, did not wish to contend any longer in words with a Barthologus. The other things which this Johannes composed have not come into our hands. He is still living in the convent at Kassel, holding the office of subprior, and is writing various works. He is more than sixty years of age, under Emperor Maximilian, in the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1495, in the fourteenth indiction.

Rutger Sicamber of Venray, by homeland a Gelderlander, of the order of the Canons Regular of Saint Augustine, of the monastery of the holy Apostle Peter of Dumetum, commonly called Heyen, not far from Worms, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, and outstandingly learned in secular letters, sharp in intellect, eloquent in speech, devout in life and conduct, excellent in meter and prose. He wrote, both in verse and in prose, many commendable little works, the reading of which is no less useful than pleasant. Of these I have read the following: A Dialogue on the Education of Boys, one book; A Dialogue on the Inquiry into the Blessed Life, two books; Hymns on Saint Mary in various kinds of meter, two books, which contain almost twelve thousand verses; A Dialogue on the Various Use of Letters, three books; A Dialogue on [unclear]...

*Catalogue of Illustrious Men.*

[unclear] various addresses to the clergy, one book. He also wrote many very elegant letters both to me and to others. His other works have not come to my knowledge. With great expense and long labor he collected the works of Johannes de Gerson, formerly Chancellor of Paris, of which at last he brought many to us from France, dividing them into three parts in a very fine order and making a quite useful table of all the books; he gave that whole work to the press. Therefore he deservedly ought to be loved in a special way by all learned and devout men, since by his labors and expenses he brought to light so many volumes of that most learned and most devout doctor. He is still living, fifty years old, in the city of Strasbourg, under the Emperor Maximilian, in the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1495, in the thirteenth indiction.

Johannes Wyric of the town of Neuss, a native of the diocese of Cologne, of the order of the brothers of blessed Mary ever virgin of Mount Carmel, of the convent of Cologne, provincial prior of Lower Germany, doctor of divine Scripture, a learned interpreter, a very acute expounder of Aristotelian philosophy, ready in intellect, orderly in speech, devout in life and conduct, a sharp disputant, an excellent preacher of the divine word. He wrote certain commendable little works, by which he made himself useful to those now living and memorable to those to come. Among them there is an outstanding volume on the Sentences, four books; also many sermons to the people, and various questions disputed in the schools; but certain other things are to be brought to light in their own time. He is still living in mature age, residing at Cologne, under the Emperor Maximilian, in the year of the Lord 1495, in the thirteenth indiction.

Johannes Camerarius Dalburgius, Bishop of Worms, a most celebrated jurisconsult, most learned both in divine Scripture and in secular letters, skilled in the three principal languages, Hebrew, Greek, and Latin, a very distinguished rhetor and poet, subtle in intellect, eloquent in speech, notable for experience of many matters, who magnificently adorns the nobility of his family by his character and learning. He wrote and writes, both in verse and in prose, certain works of excellent talent, and he has not yet allowed them to come to light, because, being too much occupied with the affairs of the commonwealth, he cannot complete them to the degree that is his purpose. Yet some of them have become known to us: a Sapphic poem on the death of Rudolf Agricola, his teacher in Greek; [unclear]; On the Origin and Theory of Coinage, one book; very many elegant orations; also many poems and epigrams; and several very elegant letters to various persons; and certain other things. He is still living, [unclear] forty, [unclear] he will write various things in Latin, under the Emperor Maximilian, in the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1495, in the thirteenth indiction.

Johannes de Arundine, of the order of the brothers of blessed Mary ever virgin [unclear], [unclear] of Camerarius, Bishop of Mechlin, Bishop of [unclear], a man studious and learned in divine Scripture, and also excellently instructed in secular philosophy, which they call Aristotelian; subtle in intellect, clear in eloquence, notable as a declaimer of popular sermons. He wrote many excellent volumes, of which the following are reported: a notable lecture on the Book of Wisdom, one book; on the Epistle of Paul to the Romans, one book; sermons on the psalm “Blessed are the undefiled,” one book; also sermons for the season and on the saints, two books. He is said to have written many other things too, which have not come to my knowledge. He is still living in the city of Lower Utrecht, being vicar of the bishop of that place in pontifical matters, under the Emperor Maximilian, in the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1495, in the fourteenth indiction.

Johannes Capnion, otherwise Reuchlin, a native of the town of Pforzheim in Swabia, my teacher in Greek, an outstanding doctor of imperial law, and counsellor of the illustrious duke Eberhard of Württemberg, at once most eloquent and most upright in law and faith, a most diligent investigator of all the most ancient philosophy and literature, a most skilled interpreter of the three principal languages, Hebrew together with Chaldaic, likewise Greek and Latin. He is also especially distinguished in French and in the more polished form of our vernacular, most learned in every respect both in divine writings and in secular letters, since he has for many years penetrated with the greatest effort the secret mysteries of the Greeks and Hebrews. Truly he is worthy to devote himself to letters alone, not also to be burdened in the noisy popular court. For not only Italy, but not even our age, could set against us anyone equal to so great a man. He wrote many excellent volumes, by which he commended the memory of himself to posterity. Among these there is a volume furnished no less with eloquence than with learning, which he wrote to lord Johannes Camerarius Dalburgius, bishop of the Vangiones, on all the secret and hidden mysteries of the philosophy of the Greeks, Hebrews, and Christians, which he entitled, from the name of his family, with the Greek title Capnion, or On the Wonder-working Word, one book; On the Preliminary Exercises of Rhetoric, ten books; On the Diversity of the Four Idioms of the Greek Language, one book; epigrams and elegies, one book; a funeral oration on the death of Rudolf Agricola; letters both to me and to others; orations *Catalogue of Illustrious Men.*

[In speech?] elegantly composed, worthy of the presbyterate in life and conduct. He wrote most ornate orations delivered by him before various princes, and also many very elegant letters both to me and to various others, and certain other things still wholly unknown to me. If only he could have leisure for letters as much as he is compelled to give himself to affairs of the commonwealth, our Mosellan land would have no one equal to him in learning and in the publication of books. He is still living with his archbishop of Trier, whose illustrious name he makes more illustrious by his talent and prudence, under Emperor Maximilian, in the year of the Lord in which we write these things, 1495, indiction 13.

*Heinrich [Euticus?]*, an easterner from Mount Noricus, otherwise Nuremberg, a most skilled doctor of the arts, philosophy, and medicine, who for a long time practised his art in Augsburg and now practises it in Frankfurt, a man certainly most learned in every respect, subtle in talent, eloquent in speech, excellent in verse and prose. He wrote, in a varied kind of meter, a polished and very bright work which he entitled *Scommata, or the Urbane and Witty Jests of Young Men*, one book; also a satire against the Sophist Dialecticians, enemies of the study of humanity, one book; *In Praise of Blessed Mary Ever-Virgin*, one book; also various epigrams, and many most ornate letters to various people, and several other things unknown to us. He is still living in the imperial [unclear], also a philosopher and a very celebrated rhetorician, ready in talent, eloquent in speech, mature in life and conduct. He wrote certain distinguished treatises, with which he profitably occupies his talent and commends his memory to posterity. Yet he conceals the things he writes, either to avoid the [unclear] of vain glory, or so that he may correct what he has written with the file of mature examination. For few of his works have become known to us: *On the Method of Single Combat*, one book; also *On War Machines*, [unclear]; learned and studious in [unclear], and outstandingly learned in secular letters, professor of both laws; *On the Care of Soldiers' Horses*, one book; elegant orations delivered on other occasions in synods. [unclear] he adorns in [unclear] fashion. He wrote many distinguished little works both in verse and in prose, and in addition published many letters, both to me and to others, full of every charm; from these it is easily apparent to readers how much he is worth in learning, in eloquence, and in experience of many things. He is still living in the church of Speyer, thirty-five years of age, under Emperor Maximilian, in the year of the Lord in which we have written these things, 1495, indiction 13.

*Sebastian Titio, otherwise Brant*, citizen of Strasbourg, distinguished doctor of both laws, and very learned both in the divine scriptures and in other humane letters, no mean master of poetry, subtle in talent, eloquent in speech, outstanding in counsel and action, who has spread his name far and wide. Among his works the following are extant: *On the Titles of Both [Laws?]* and [unclear] to be recovered, one book; to the same, an epilogue, [The Kingdom?] of Jerusalem, in elegiac verse, one book; *In Praise of the Glorious Virgin Mary* and of many saints, many poems of various kinds, one book; *Of Various Epigrams*, one book; a Sapphic poem in our book *On the Misery of Prelates*; *Against Slanderous Advocates*; *On the Captivity of King Maximilian*; commendatory poems for various printings. Furthermore, with wondrous skill and industry, though in the common vernacular tongue, he compiled a certain little book which he called the *Ship of Narragonia*, in which he so elegantly expressed the cause and root of all follies, censures the morals of fools, and gives certain remedies for each, that it is [unclear] called not a book of fools, but [unclear]. For he weaves together various things under Emperor Maximilian, whom he singularly loves, and composed about him and to him several very charming poems, even secret ones, as they say, in the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1495, indiction 13.

*Conrad Summenhart*, eminent professor of sacred theology, studious and learned in the holy scriptures, not ignorant of secular philosophy, and outstandingly learned in canon law, subtle in talent, composed in speech, who ordinarily reads and teaches divine letters in the school of Tübingen. He wrote several distinguished little works, by which [Blank page in the source scan.]

*Catalogue of Illustrious Men.*

On matters and pleasant novelties, a dialogue, one book; a dialogue on kinds of meters, two books; a dialogue on the accents of Latin words, two books; a panegyric addressed to me, two books; a dialogue on the brotherhood of the Rosary, two books; also a book of epigrams, one book; a consolatory dialogue addressed to me concerning his tribulations and the calamities of these times, in which he consoles himself in turn with words once exchanged with us; on the love of the monastery, zeal for letters, and why studious and learned brothers are hated by the prelates of monks, one book; likewise a dialogue addressed to me on the exposition of his melodies in the hymns of Mary, Mother of God, where he introduces and explains fifty-two kinds of meters, one book; to lord Johannes Dalburg, bishop of Worms, a heroic Sapphic poem, one book; letters, both to me and to others, almost innumerable. Against the above-mentioned brother “weighing hands,” of the Order of Preachers, who attacked the most pure conception of the Mother of God, he produced many letters and verses. And certain other works which are still unfinished in his hands. He is still living, having almost forty-four years of age, in the monastery of Heyn in the diocese of Worms, under King Maximilian, in the year of the Lord in which we write these things, 1495, indiction XIII.

Jacobus Vimpfeling of Schlettstadt, priest in the church of Speyer, a man most learned in the divine scriptures, exceptionally learned in secular letters, theologian, philosopher, orator, and very celebrated poet, who first at Erfurt and then at Heidelberg publicly taught philosophy and sacred letters, and acquired great glory for his learning; a man, I say, most learned in every respect, subtle in intellect, [unclear] in eloquence. From [unclear] still unfinished in his hands. He is still living, years [unclear]; still unfinished in his hands. And from whatever [unclear] he published many and explains, one book; to lord Johannes Dalburg, bishop of Worms, [unclear] of the Order of Preachers, attacking the above-mentioned most pure conception of the Mother of God, he published many letters and explains, one book; to lord Johannes Dalburg, bishop of Worms, [unclear] of the Order of Preachers, attacking the most pure conception of the Mother of God, many letters [unclear] and explains, one book; to lord Johannes Dalburg, bishop of the diocese of Worms, under King Maximilian, in the year of the Lord in which we write these things, 1495, indiction XIII.

He wrote in both kinds many outstanding volumes, by which he spread his name far and wide; a man most learned in every respect, subtle in intellect, [unclear] in eloquence. Of these the following are extant. To lord Berthold, archbishop of Mainz, he wrote a very celebrated volume in hexameter and pentameter, most elegantly, on the threefold whiteness of blessed Mary ever virgin, against those attacking her most pure conception, one book. Likewise to Theodicius Gresmund the younger of Mainz, Precepts of Rhetoric, one book; Praises of the distinguished Church of Speyer, one book; a brief postil on the Creed of Athanasius, one book. At the urging of Ludwig, bishop of Speyer, he composed the legend and office of the Compassion of blessed Mary ever virgin, which the same bishop established to be sung publicly in his diocese. He also produced a useful treatise on the poetic art, which was printed, very corruptly, at the end of the New Grammar without the author’s name. A History of a certain idiot Stylpho, one book; also a poem on the angelic message, one book; Prothymologia on the good method of preaching, a work well furnished from the sources of the orators, one book; Isodonius Germanicus on the easier instruction of boys, one book; an oration against the invaders of priests; an oration for ecclesiastical immunity; an oration to the Cardinal of Tournai; an oration to Raymond, nuncio of indulgences; an oration to the Heidelberg Gymnosophists on Saint Catherine; an oration to the same on the Holy Spirit; an oration to the same on the assumption of the divine Virgin; an oration to the synod of Worms; an oration to the synod of Speyer; an oration to the rural synod of Schlettstadt, and also various [others]. A heroic poem to Eberhard, duke of Württemberg; a book of epigrams, one book; against the brother “weighing hands,” who attacked the conception of the Mother of God [unclear], and also various questions. A heroic poem to Eberhard, duke of Württemberg; a book of epigrams, one book; against the brother “weighing hands,” attacking and rejecting the conception of the Mother of God, he wrote elegant and well-furnished letters. He is still living in the city of Speyer, having forty-five years of age, under Maximilian the Emperor, in the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1495, indiction XIII.

Philippus Alberti, from the town of Neuss in the diocese of Cologne, of the order of the brothers of blessed Mary ever virgin of Mount Carmel, of the Frankfurt convent, bachelor formed in sacred theology, a man studious and learned in the divine writings, and exceptionally learned in Aristotelian philosophy, subtle in intellect and distinguished in speech; who first in the Gymnasium of [Parthenice?], and now in the school of Cologne, by his learning and uprightness of morals, [unclear]. He publicly reads at Cologne a notable lecture on the Song of Songs, one book; also many and various sermons preached at Frankfurt, two books. Now he writes and publicly reads in the Cologne convent a singular and beautiful work on the Sentences, four books. He also wrote a lengthy letter, supported by very firm authority and reason, against Wigand of the Order of Preachers, [unclear].

*Jacobus Vimpfeling of Schlettstadt.*

*Philippus Alberti de Nussia.* 176 *Of Johannes Trithemius* [unclear], thinking otherwise concerning the most pure conception of the Mother of God than the Church has determined; in it he checked all his barkings by keen disputation. But he also composed other letters to various persons, not inelegant. He is still living in the University of Cologne, diligently applying himself to sacred letters, under Emperor Maximilian, in the year of the Lord in which we write these things, 1495, in the thirteenth indiction.

*Theodericus Gresemundus the Younger*, of Mainz, born of his father Theodericus Gresemundus of Meschede, a very distinguished doctor of arts and medicine, a youth of excellent talent, who writes much, in verse and prose, has written remarkable little works, most ornate whatever their subject, displaying Ciceronian eloquence. He offers so great a marvel that, like another Adeodatus, once Augustine’s son, by his native ability and readiness in writing and arguing, he is an object of wonder and astonishment to many, even very learned men. For his talent far outruns his age, since there is in him such learning and eloquence together that he has had few or no equals of his own age. He wrote to me a distinguished dialogue on the seven liberal disciplines, in which he defends, explains, and commends these same arts no less elegantly than learnedly, one book. Also a most ornate oration in the name of Philosophy the orator, to the governors of commonwealths. Likewise he composed an elegant dialogue on the madness of the Germans, by which at carnival time children [unclear], one book. Against a brother [unclear] of the Order of Preachers, stupidly attacking the most pure conception of the Mother of God, he wrote a poem, and many letters. He has also produced many poems of different kinds and epigrams. He has also written most ornate letters, both to me and to others, almost countless, from which the liveliness and vein of his most noble talent are gathered. He is still living at Mainz in his father’s house, being about eighteen years of age, under Emperor Maximilian, in the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1495, in the fourteenth indiction. Let no one be angry with me because I have placed this boy, young in age, among illustrious writers, since by his talent he excels many older men; for from the mouth of infants and sucklings the Most High has perfected praise, and we require not age but talent.

He is said to have written some commendable volumes, by which he commended the memory of himself to posterity. But I do not remember that any of them have come into our hands, except that very celebrated work which he composed with great labor: On the year, day, and weekday of the Lord’s Passion, in three volumes. The other things which he wrote and writes are wholly unknown to me. He is still living, as I hear, in the University of Louvain, composing various works, under King Maximilian, in the year of the Lord in which we write this, 1495, in the thirteenth indiction.

*Theodericus of Osenbruck*, of the Order of Friars Minor of the province of Cologne, a man whose talent is exercised in the divine Scriptures, a very famous declaimer of popular sermons, whose life all who have known him proclaim to be holy and most religious. For in making sermons to the people he is illumined by so great a grace from God, speaks with so great an eloquence, and finally affects his hearers with so great a compunction and sweetness, that he has had no equal among the Germans; hence he was appointed general preacher throughout the whole province. Recently, when he was with me at Cologne in the monastery of Saint Martin, he read to me a beautiful little work, suited to devotion: On the Passion of the Lord, [unclear] for simple devout persons, one book; On daily interior exercise, one book; and various sermons. He wrote certain other things unknown to us. He is still living in the province of Cologne, instructing many by word and example in the discipline of God. Under Emperor Maximilian, in the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1495, in the thirteenth indiction.

*Theodericus Ullenius*, by homeland a Frisian, a man most learned in every respect, a philosopher, physician, orator, and famous poet, subtle in talent, eloquent in speech, excellent in verse as well as prose. He wrote certain well-constructed little works, by which, exercising his talent, he commended the memory of himself to posterity. Among these there survives a volume of elegies, one book; of epigrams *Catalogue of Illustrious Men.*

[unclear] also, one book, and he wrote various letters to various persons. He is still living, composing various things, under Emperor Maximilian, in the year of the Lord in which we write these things, 1495, indiction 13.

Arnold Bostius, of the Order of the Brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin, of Mount Carmel, of the convent of Ghent, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, and not ignorant of secular literature, subtle in intellect, composed in speech, devout in life and conduct, practiced in verse and prose. He wrote several little works of reading not to be despised, of which the following survive: a prose volume, with poems sometimes inserted, on the fact that the Blessed Virgin Mary is the special patroness of the Carmelite Order, whence he wished to entitle it *On Patronage*, one book; *On the Illustrious Men of His Own [Order]*, one book; *On the Illustrious Men of the Carthusian Order*, one book; against Vincent of Newcastle, of the Order of Preachers, who attacked the most pure conception of the Mother of God, one book; *On the Four Last Things*, one book; many poems and epigrams. He wrote almost innumerable letters both to me and to others. And certain other things unknown to me. He is still living in the new convent of nuns near Bruges, having passed forty-five years of age, under King Maximilian, in the year in which we write these things, 1495, indiction 13.

Jodocus Beysselius, the unique ornament among the patricians of the royal city of Aachen, a man most learned both in the holy Scriptures and in secular letters, a philosopher, orator, distinguished poet, most celebrated professor and interpreter of both laws, subtle in intellect, eloquent in speech. Although he is necessarily occupied with the affairs of his commonwealth, nevertheless with incredible fervor of love for the Scriptures he writes much, forges much, and composes much in verse and in prose, by which his name is spread abroad with great glory. Of these the following have become known to us: a very fine dialogue, *On the Best Kind of Musicians*, one book; *On Christian Ambition*, one book; an epitome of *The Goad of Love*, one book; *On the Rosaceous Crown of Mary*, one book; a metrical rosary on the Blessed Virgin; a poem on the Sacrament of the altar. He wrote to me an elegiac rosary on the most holy mother Anna. He also began the deeds of the Flemings, but, hindered by various occupations, has so far been unable to finish them. He is also said to have written various most elegant orations. He also wrote many epigrams and a considerable number of poems of different kinds. He gave almost innumerable, most ornate letters both to me and to others. And other things. He is still living at Aachen, under King Maximilian, in the year of the Lord in which we write these things, 1495, indiction 13.

Jodocus Badius Ascensius, originally from Ghent, a man most learned in secular letters, not ignorant of the divine Scriptures, a most learned philosopher, rhetorician, and poet, excellent in intellect and eloquent in speech, who once at Ferrara heard Baptista Guarino teaching Greek letters. He also became skilled in that language. He wrote in verse on the Blessed Virgin, one book; also very many epigrams, almost innumerable, on vices and virtues, which, lucidly explaining them with his own commentaries, he entitled *Moral Woods*, twelve books. Also of epigrams of various kinds [unclear]. [unclear] still illuminating Lyons, a city of Gaul, with his learning, [unclear] one book of [unclear]; he also published most ornate letters, both to me and to others, in meter and prose, almost innumerable. He is said to have written certain other things too, which have by no means come into our hands. He is still living at Lyons, instructor of the same [unclear], one book in Sapphic meter. He brought together from various authors a notable volume on vices and virtues, which with his own [unclear], residing in his convent at Cologne, under Emperor Maximilian, in the year of the Lord in which we write these things, 1495, indiction 12.

Jacob Sprenger, of the Order of the Brothers Preachers, provincial of Cologne, professor and learned interpreter of the divine Scriptures, and excellently learned in Aristotelian philosophy, distinguished in intellect, scholastic in speech, when formerly he had been appointed inquisitor of heretical depravity by Pope Innocent VIII, together with Heinrich Institoris, theologian of the same order. He wrote, for the precaution and instruction of the simple, against little women who are witches, one book. If he wrote anything further, it has not come to my knowledge. He is still living [unclear]. *Of Witches*, one book. If he wrote anything further, it has not come to my knowledge. Also letters [unclear] in his convent at Cologne, under Emperor Maximilian, in the year of the Lord in which we write these things, 1495, indiction 13.

Johannes Tholafus, originally from Franconia, canon of Regensburg, provost of Forchheim, a man studious and learned in the holy Scriptures, and excellently learned in secular letters, a distinguished philosopher and cosmographer, an excellent doctor of pontifical law, subtle in intellect and eloquent in speech. He wrote some little works in mathematics and astronomy, by which he clearly shows the liveliness of his intellect to all who read them. Also letters [Blank page in the source scan.]

many [letters?] to various persons. He also wrote some other things unknown to us. He is still living in the city of Regensburg, under King Maximilian, in the year of the Lord in which we write these things, 1495, in the thirteenth indiction.

Hartmann Schedel of Nuremberg, doctor of arts and medicine, and not ignorant of the divine Scriptures, outstanding in talent and distinguished in eloquence, compiled and wrote, among other small works of his talent, with Sebald Schreyer and Sebastian Kammermeister, citizens of Nuremberg, providing the costs and expenses, a great volume of histories from the beginning of the world down to these times of King Maximilian. Whether he wrote anything more I do not know. He is still living in the city of Nuremberg, in the year of the Lord in which these things are being written, 1495, in the thirteenth indiction.

Jacob Philippi, parish priest of the church of Basel, formed bachelor of sacred theology, studious and learned in the holy Scriptures, and not ignorant of secular philosophy, excellent in talent, clear in speech, honorable in life and conduct, wrote certain very distinguished little works, the reading of which is judged especially necessary for the devout. Among these there is said to be a little book entitled *The Precordial of Priests*, one book; also *A Reformer of the Life and Conduct of Clerics and Priests*, one book. There are also said to be several sermons of his to the people, and many other things unknown to us. He is still living in the city of Basel, under King Maximilian, in the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1495.

Bernard, a monk of the Carthusian order, of the house of the Passion of Jesus Christ near the city of Liegnitz, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, and not ignorant of secular literature, ready in talent and distinguished in eloquence, is said to have written many excellent volumes; but I have seen none of them except that most beautiful dialogue which he elegantly composed on the praises and miracles of blessed Mary ever virgin, one book. He flourished in the year of the Lord 1480, under Frederick III, emperor, and I believe that he is still living.

Johannes Gerbrandi of Leiden, of the order of the brothers of blessed Mary ever virgin of Mount Carmel, subprior of the Haarlem convent, a very studious and learned man, outstanding in talent, scholastic in speech, an excellent preacher of popular sermons, is said to have written a notable history of his order, [unclear] books; also sermons on the season and on the saints, not to be rejected, and several other things unknown to us. He is still living in his Haarlem convent, under Emperor Maximilian, in the year of the Lord in which we write these things, 1495, in the thirteenth indiction.

Bohuslaus of Hassenstein, a noble man and most learned in every respect, an excellent philosopher, orator, and poet, subtle in talent, and therefore eloquent in speech, illustrating the preeminence of his family by learning and erudition, is said to be writing various works both in verse and in prose, in which no less probity than knowledge is said to shine forth. Among these there exists an instructed work, *On the Particular Inventions of the Germans and Italians*, one book; also a book of epigrammatic poems, [unclear] book; and several very ornate letters of his to various persons are reported. And certain other works are to be published from day to day. He is still living in his castle of Hassenstein and writing various things, under Emperor Maximilian, in the year of the Lord in which these things are being written, 1495, in the thirteenth indiction.

Aegidius Fabri of Brussels, native of a town of Brabant, of the order of the brothers of blessed Mary ever virgin of Mount Carmel, prior of his Brussels convent, doctor of sacred theology and a distinguished interpreter of scholastic philosophy, ready in talent, composed in speech, mature in life and conduct, is said by those who knew him closely to have composed a work not to be despised on the *Sentences*, four books; also various disputed questions, many elegant sermons to the people, and therefore certain other things. He is still living in his Brussels convent in Brabant, under Emperor Maximilian, in the year of the Lord 1495.

Haryngus Sifridi Sinnama, from Hage in Frisia, who is commonly called Hermann, doctor of both laws, properly instructed both in the divine Scriptures and in scholastic philosophy, lively in talent, ready in counsel, who adorns Cologne by teaching, writing, and giving counsel, wrote a very celebrated work on the titles of both laws, no less useful than pleasant to all who wish to be initiated in canons or laws. He once promised me, when at Cologne we were speaking together at some time about writings, that he would also write certain other things; whether he has done so I do not know with sufficient certainty. He is still living in manly age, under Emperor Maximilian, in the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1495.

Conrad Leontorius, commonly Leonberg, monk of the Cistercian order, of the monastery of Maulbronn in Swabia, a man studious and learned, a philosopher, orator, and poet not to be rejected, both in the divine Scriptures and in secular letters, ready in talent and therefore also *Catalogue of Illustrious Men.*

has not yet allowed to come to light. There are extant his most ornate sermons, on the Temporal and on the Saints, in 2 books. Also various orations to the clergy. Several elegant letters, both to me and to others. I hear that he has composed a prepared oration for the coronation of the Queen, soon to be delivered, at the request of a friend appointed to speak on the occasion. The rest that he wrote is unknown to me. He is still living in his own convent at Aachen, writing various things, under King Maximilian. In the year of the Lord 1495, indiction 13.

Jodocus Gallus Rubiacensis, a man zealous and learned in the holy Scriptures, and excellently instructed in secular letters, a theologian and orator, distinguished in talent, eloquent in speech, excelling in verse and prose, diligently teaching the youth of the Heidelberg academy in humane letters. He is said to have composed many treatises still unknown to us, by which he commended his memory to posterity. There are extant several of his most ornate orations to the university and clergy, of which I have found only: an oration on Saint Catherine; an oration on the Purification of the holy Virgin Mother; an oration on the Nativity of the Lord; an oration on the Annunciation of the Lord; two orations to the Synod of Speyer; an oration on Saint John the Baptist; two orations on the Holy Spirit; an oration on Epiphany; a dialogue, in the manner of an oration, on the Purification; an oration to the clergy of Worms, delivered by another; two dialogues on those to be promoted to the mastership; several orations for bachelors; and many other most ornate works. He is still living in the Heidelberg academy, having passed 35 years of age, under King Maximilian, in the year of the Lord in which we write these things, 1495, indiction 13.

Eitelwolf von Stein, a Swabian by country, a noble man and most learned in humane letters, especially in philosophy and oratory, subtle in talent, and a very great lover and emulator of Roman eloquence, who, because of his learning and natural wisdom, is held in no small esteem by the Margrave of Brandenburg. He wrote to Georg von Stein, his maternal uncle, a lover of letters as much as he himself, *On the Praises of Heroes and Illustrious Men*, 1 book. Also most ornate letters to various persons, 1 book. And many other things unknown to us. He was once a pupil of Master Craftho, the excellent and most watchful instructor of the youth of Schlettstadt, who is himself also said to have composed some works that are unknown to us. He is still living, steadfastly persisting in the study he has begun, and writes various things. Under King Maximilian, in the year of the Lord in which we write these things, 1495, indiction 13.

Johannes, from the town of Brussels in Brabant, of the order of the regular canons of Saint Augustine, of the monastery of Saint Agnes near Zwolle, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, and not unacquainted with secular literature, distinguished in talent and polished in speech. He wrote a large and not unuseful volume for the instruction of all Christians, which he entitled *Rose-Garden of Spiritual Exercises and Sacred Meditations*, in 2 books. Likewise *On the Illustrious Men of His Order*, 1 book. And certain other things unknown to us. He is still living, as I understand, a young man in the town [unclear], companion of the confessor of the nuns, and writes various things, under Maximilian, most excellent King of the Romans. In the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1495, indiction 13.

Johannes Tinctoris, a Brabanter by country, from the city of Nivelles, and a canon in the church of that same city, doctor of both laws, formerly arch-chaplain and singer of King Ferdinand of Naples, most learned in every respect, a very great mathematician, an outstanding musician, subtle in talent, eloquent in speech, wrote and writes many excellent little works, by which he renders himself useful to those now living and memorable to posterity. Of these I have found only: in music, *On the Art of Counterpoint*, 3 books. Likewise *On the Tones*, 1 book. Also *On the Origin of Music*, 1 book. He gave several most ornate letters to various persons; he depicted one figure in which he included all the most ancient musicians, and called Jesus Christ the supreme singer. He is still living in Italy, writing various things, being about 60 years of age. Under King Maximilian, in the year of the Lord in which we write these things, 1495, indiction 15.

*Thilmannus Dulmauiensis.*

[unclear] canon in Böddeken, formerly prior in Drübeck, a man zealous in the divine Scriptures, and [unclear] have not come to my knowledge. He is still living today under King Maximilian, in the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1495.

*Catalogue of Illustrious Men.*

179 and eloquent in speech, not ignorant of the Hebrew and Greek languages. He wrote, in verse and in prose, certain distinguished works, by which he commended his memory to posterity. Of these there survive several very ornate letters to various persons, one book; also various orations; one book of poems and epigrams of various kinds. The commentaries begun by Sebastian Murrho of Colmar on Baptista the Carmelite of Mantua, but left unfinished when death pressed upon him, he completed and perfected. He still lives in his monastery of Maulbronn, being about forty-five years old, and writes various things under Emperor Maximilian, in the year of the Lord in which we write these things, 1495, in the fourteenth indiction.

Engelhard Funck, otherwise Scintilla, an East Franconian, native of Suobach, a learned man and skilled in every respect, a philosopher and distinguished poet, not ignorant also of the divine Scriptures and pontifical law, outstanding in talent and eloquent in speech. He is said to have fashioned certain little works in verse and prose, by which he made his name known far and wide. Among these is: an elegiac poem in praise of his homeland, Franconia; a poem on the ring; a poem on the death of the Cardinal of San Marco; also one book of epigrams in various kinds of meter. He also composed very ornate letters to various persons, and certain other things unknown to us. He still lives, as I hear, in the city of Rome, an advocate in legal cases, under Emperor Maximilian, in the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1495, in the thirteenth indiction.

Johannes Langer of Bolekenhan, priest of the Church of Wroclaw, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, and not ignorant of secular literature, excellent in talent, composed in speech, practiced in verse and prose. He wrote, in a double style, certain little works worthy of commendation, by which he made his name known. To Georgius de Lapide, lord of Steynaura, he wrote a distinguished volume on rents and redemptions, one book; also many letters to various persons; many poems; and certain other things. He still lives in Wroclaw and will compose various things, under King Maximilian, in the year of the Lord 1495, in the thirteenth indiction.

Paulus Niavis, commonly Schneevogel, a man learned in humane letters, especially in rhetoric, and not ignorant of the divine Scriptures, outstanding in talent and eloquent in speech, who by teaching and writing in the gymnasium of Leipzig acquired great fame for erudition for his name. He wrote for religious novices on the implanting of Latin speech, one book; a life of a certain hermit, one book; on the colors of rhetoric, one book; formal letters for the instruction of young men, [unclear]; [unclear] and a learned Gymnosophist, one book; [unclear] letters to various persons, three books; also familiar letters to various persons, and certain other things unknown to us. I believe the things that came into our hands are not all. He still lives in the margraviate of Meissen and composes various things, under Emperor Maximilian, in the year of the Lord 1495, in the thirteenth indiction.

Heinrich, native of the town of Northeim in Saxony, a man studious and learned in secular letters, and not ignorant of the divine Scriptures, subtle in talent and clear in speech, magnificently practiced in verse and prose. He wrote to Frederick, margrave of Meissen, duke of Saxony, the Dymetromachia on the conflict of virtues and vices, one book; also many poems and various letters to various persons; and certain other things unknown to us. I believe that he is still living, under Emperor Maximilian, in the year of the Lord in which we write these things, 1495, in the fourteenth indiction.

Nicolaus of Alsenz, of the order of the brothers of blessed Mary ever virgin, of Mount Carmel, of the convent of Kreuznach in the county of Sponheim, lector of sacred theology; studious and learned in the holy Scriptures, and not ignorant of secular philosophy; ready in talent, scholastic in speech, and practiced by long habit as a preacher of popular sermons. He wrote on Exodus, one book; also on the Apocalypse of John, one book; on the office of the Mass and the canon, a long and extensive volume, one book; sermons for the season and on the saints, two books; and certain things still hidden with him. He lives to this day in his convent of Kreuznach, about forty years old, under Emperor Maximilian, in the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1495, in the fourteenth indiction.

Bartholomaeus of Cologne, a man studious in secular letters and [unclear] of Carmel, clear in talent and eloquent in speech, a distinguished philosopher and poet, who in the school at Deventer shone with no small distinction by teaching and writing. He wrote in verse and prose several little works worthy of commendation, by which he spread abroad his name. A poem on the praises of philosophy, which he entitled Sylva of Poems, one book; a poem on the feast of Diogenes the philosopher, one book. The rest that he composed have by no means come into our hands. He still lives at Deventer, a town of the diocese of Utrecht, under King Maximilian, in the year of the Lord 1495.

Nicolaus, son of Simon, from the town of Haarlem in Holland, of the order of the brothers of blessed Mary...

*Catalogue of Illustrious Men.*

[unclear], following the example of the sainted fathers, I shall append the titles of my works. First, at the command of our General Chapter, I made an abridgement of the statutes of the order, one book. Then I wrote The Manner of Celebrating the Provincial Chapter itself, one book; also On the Visitation of Monks, one book. These three little works, by command of that General Chapter, have recently been printed at Nuremberg in one volume.

I also wrote On the Rule of our holy father Benedict, two books; Exhortations to Monks, two books; On the Temptations of Religious, two books; To Nicholas, priest of [Mernic?], On Priestly Life and Formation, one book; On the Vice of Private Possession among Monks, one book; On the Vanity and Misery of This Life, one book; A Lament on the Ruin of Our Order, one book; On the Illustrious Men of Our Order, four books; Praises of the Order of Carmelites, two books; to Lord Johann Kämmerer Dalberg, bishop of Worms, On Ecclesiastical Writers from the time of the apostles down to the last year of Emperor Frederick III, one book; to Rumold, prior of the Carmelites of Frankfurt, On the Praises of Saint Anne, one book; to Rutger the Sicamber, canon of [Dumetum?], On Greek Questions in the Gospel of John, one book; On the Misery of Claustral Prelates, one book; A Chronicle of our monastery of Spanheim, one book.

At the request of Lord Blasius, abbot of the monastery of Hirsau, I wrote the Chronicle of that monastery of his, Hirsau, one book; the History of the Virgin Daughter of Dagobert, whose head is among us, one book; On the Praises of Saint Andrew the Apostle, one book; Praises of Saint Joseph, Spouse of Mary, one book; Praises of Saint Benedict the Abbot, one book; Praises of the Coenobitic Life, one book; On the Praise of Penitence, one book; A Man’s Soliloquy to the Soul, one book; On the Praise, Love, and Study of Scripture, one book; On the Miracles of Saint Anne, one book; also various sermons, delivered both to the brothers and sometimes to the people on the highest feasts, one book; Letters to Various Persons, one book. Orations delivered in chapters or elsewhere are without a fixed number.

From Greek I translated the dialogue of Maximus the Abbot, On the Incarnation of the Lord; the Anathemas of Saint Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, against the heretics, promulgated in the third synod of Ephesus; and certain letters of the same synod. These are the things that at present I recall having written.

Under Emperor Maximilian, in the year of the Lord 1495, indiction 13, on the last day of the month of July, I corrected, enlarged, and completed for the second time, after the first edition, this Catalogue of Illustrious Germans. To the honor of almighty God, the benefit of those who do not despise our works, and the adornment and praise of our German nation, to which we owe whatever we can do.

Here, most beloved Jakob Wimpfeling of Sélestat, you have from me the work long requested, in which, according to your desire, I have arranged in order the illustrious men of Germany and those excellent in talent, and have indicated, as far as I was able, what so venerable a cohort wrote. Yet you should not think that I have written up all who by their talent and writings have made our nation illustrious, but rather that I have included a few from among many, and those who readily occurred to me. I have also inserted into this little work not a few, both from among the living and from those departed from life, of whom no mention is made in the larger catalogue, because their works were formerly unknown to me, but in the meantime they have been brought to light, not without labor.

Nor indeed am I unaware how many today illuminate our Germany by writing various things, who have obtained no remembrance either in this catalogue or in the larger one; not because I judged them unworthy, but because nothing at all about their little works became known to me. Indeed I call God as witness, who knows the hidden things of the heart, that I have never knowingly omitted anyone whose works, even a few, I had known. Therefore, if any of the living who write anything have been passed over by me, let them charge it not to my will but to necessity and the shortness of time. For no opportunity was given to search out those who are lacking.

Meanwhile, sweetest Wimpfeling, see that you fare well, and accept as commended to you the little work destined for you, together with its author and friend. From our monastery of Spanheim, on the last day of the month of July, in the year of the Lord 1495.

*Here ends the book of Trithemius, abbot of Spanheim, On the Illustrious Men of Germany.*

*The End.* of the ever-Virgin of Mount Carmel, lector of the Haarlem convent, and at times prior in various places, certainly a studious man, practiced in the divine scriptures, ready in talent and an excellent declaimer of sermons. He wrote sermons not to be rejected, on the temporal cycle and on the saints, which he entitled *Sermones vade mecum*, two books. The rest that he composed has not come to my knowledge. He is still living in the Haarlem convent in the year of the Lord in which we write these things, 1495, in the thirteenth indiction.

Adam Werner of Themar, a man excellently learned in secular letters and not ignorant of the divine scriptures, a student and interpreter of imperial laws, no less learned than eloquent, subtle in talent and distinguished in speech, practiced in verse and prose. He wrote little works not to be despised, by which he entrusted his name to posterity and memory. Among these there is extant in my possession a volume of various poems and epigrams, one book. He wrote many poems of different kinds to me concerning Saint Anne. Besides this he gave many letters, both to me and to several others, of singular learning and eloquence. He also wrote some other things, to be brought to light in their own time. His pupil is Johannes Herbst of Luterburg, chaplain in the castle at Heidelberg, a man equally learned and erudite, who himself also wrote to me many poems about Saint Anne and most ornate letters. But also certain other things are shortly to be published. Both are still living in the gymnasium of the city of Heidelberg, under Emperor Maximilian, in the year in which we write these things, 1495.

Johannes of Lamsheim, born in a village situated not far from Worms, of the order of the regular canons of Saint Augustine, of the monastery of the Garden of Blessed Mary, which is otherwise called Kyrsgarten, outside the walls of the city of the Wangiones, a studious man and practiced by continual reading of the scriptures, gifted in talent and open in speech; worthy indeed that he should devote himself only to letters and not also to the cares of temporal affairs, for he is steward, he would compose many things worthy of reading. He wrote *On the Institution and Utility of the Fraternity of the Rosary of the Virgin Mary*, one book; *The Mirror of the Mass*, one book; *The Mirror of the Last Things*, one book; another is entitled *The [unclear] of Eternal Salvation*, one book; and certain other things. He is still living in the aforesaid monastery near Worms, under King Maximilian, in the year of the Lord 1495, in the fourteenth indiction.

Franciscus Wyler, of the order of the Friars Minor of the Observance, a man studious and learned in the divine scriptures, and not ignorant of secular literature, ready in talent and distinguished in speech, an excellent declaimer of sermons, when about three years ago he was living in the convent of the town of Kreuznach, wrote at the instance of Albert Latro, professor of the same order, an outstanding *Repertory of the Letters of Saint Jerome the Priest*, one book; to the same man, *On Remedies for Scruples of Conscience*, one book; against a certain man attacking the most pure conception of the Mother of God, a lengthy letter in the manner of a little book; also many sermons to the people. There are extant many letters of his, both to me and to several others. Likewise, on the Passion of the Lord, on vices and virtues, on music and its praises, a varied and not-to-be-rejected compilation. And certain other things. He is still living under Emperor Maximilian, in the year of the Lord in which we write these things, 1495, in the fourteenth indiction.

Thomas of Strasbourg, of the order of the Friars Preachers, first a secular priest, parish priest of Saint Thomas at Strasbourg, then curate of Saint Andrew in Andlau; soon, after taking up the religion of the Friars Preachers, he was made confessor of the nuns of his order in the upper Steiga and in Rentyngen, who had been expelled from Klingental at Basel. For the love of God and of devout sisters he has sustained many labors with a brave spirit, and sustains them up to the present. A man of most elegant sermons, so suited to devotion and compunction that he never seems to me to speak superficially, but from the heart, so learnedly, so eloquently, so devoutly that he seems able to move hearts of stone. For he does not spend time on superfluous citations, but, after the example of the ancients, proceeds in rhetorical fashion. He wrote in the same spirit and fervor most beautiful *Meditations*, one book; letters to various persons, both many and ornate. Questions of the scriptures, profound ones, put to him by friends, he unraveled so appropriately, so catholically, so eloquently, that nothing more apt could have been answered to the matter proposed. He is still living in Steiga, a monastery of nuns in the diocese of Strasbourg, under Emperor Maximilian, in the year of the Lord in which we write these things, 1495, in the eighteenth indiction.

Godefridus Candelarij, prior of the convent of the friars of the order of Blessed Mary ever-Virgin of Mount Carmel, in the royal city of Aachen, a man studious and learned in the divine scriptures, and not moderately learned in secular letters, acute in talent and eloquent in speech, an excellent declaimer of sermons, is said to have fashioned certain distinguished little works, which not yet *Johannes Trithemius*

Matthew Herbenus, a native of Maastricht, a man studious in every respect and very learned, an excellent philosopher and a musician of singular erudition, subtle in talent, eloquent in speech, practiced in verse and prose. He wrote certain distinguished volumes, of which the following are extant: *On the Nature of the Voice and the Theory of Music*, a very beautiful work, 5 books; *On Scholastic Institutions*, 2 books; *Diasynthetica*, 1 book; *On the Capture of Negroponte*, 1 book; *On the Restoration of His Native Soil, namely the town of Maastricht*, 1 book; *Against Wigand [Cauponis?], of the Order of Preachers, on the Most Pure Conception of Blessed Mary Ever Virgin*, 1 book, which he entitled *Antilogion*. Also orations of various kinds and poems. He also wrote many very ornate letters, both to me and to others, and certain other things. He is still living in Maastricht, writing various works, being 44 years of age, under King Maximilian, in the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1495, indiction 13.

Gerard of Marbais, born in the town of Maastricht, canon there in the church of Blessed Mary Ever Virgin, a man excellently learned both in the divine scriptures and in secular letters, skilled in both laws, a philosopher and eloquent rhetorician, who greatly adorns the nobility of his family by his erudition and by the study of the good arts, a great lover of books and cultivator of discipline. He wrote, in a very fine dialogue, *On Prime Matter*, 1 book. He also composed another dialogue, *On the Capture of the City of Tongeren Made Last Winter*, 1 book, where he neatly mocks the people of Tongeren, who, by sleeping, so wretchedly lost their city. In these he introduces as speakers Andrew Kanharus the Frisian, Matthew Herbenus of Maastricht mentioned above, and Aegidius de Holy of Tongeren. But he is said to have written some other things which have not come into our hands. He is still living in the city of Maastricht, firmly persisting in the study he began above, about 28 years old, under King Maximilian, in the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1495, indiction 13.

Matthias Mynnecomius, of the order of those whom people commonly call Crosiers, a native of upper Maastricht, once a hearer and disciple of Matthew Herbenus, a man studious and learned both in the divine scriptures and in secular letters, skilled in mathematics, very learned in the art of music, subtle in talent, clear in speech. With remarkable zeal he abbreviated the music of Boethius in one volume. Likewise, with similar industrious compression, he reduced the *Natural Theology* of Raymond Sebeidi into one volume. He is reported to be writing some other works, soon to be made public. He still lives [unclear] of the monastery of Saint Jerome in Ghent, a man studious and learned in divine writing and rich in reading of the ancients, also not ignorant of secular literature, subtle in talent, clear in speech. Among the other little works of his talent he wrote a treatise *On the Titles of the Psalms according to the Ancients*, furnished with eloquence and erudition; several letters, both to me and to others, of nectar-like eloquence. He is still living in Ghent, a young man who gives us hope of a larger work of study, under King Maximilian, in the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1495, indiction 13.

Christian Masseen, priest of the order of the monastery of Saint Jerome in Ghent, a man studious and learned in the divine scriptures and rich in reading of the ancients, also not ignorant of secular literature, subtle in talent, clear in speech. Among the other little works of his talent he wrote [unclear], subtle in talent, eloquent in speech, strong in verse and prose. He is said to be writing many things, of which I have read only a long Sapphic poem and various epigrams. The rest of what he wrote has not come to my knowledge. He is still living in Gyßlingen, a village of Swabia, writing various things, under King Maximilian, in the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1495, indiction 13.

Johannes Trithemius, abbot, although unworthy, of the monastery of the holy bishop Martin in Sponheim, of the Order of Saint Benedict, in the diocese of Mainz, a Mosellan by homeland, native of the village of Trittenheim in the diocese of Trier. I do not think myself worthy to occupy a place among the illustrious writers, men of Germany, because of the poverty of my talent. But lest there befall me what I have read has happened to many, who omitted the titles of their works. But in the *Apology* to which we write: in these matters let the testimony of conscience suffice for each person; let no one seek more outside himself. Let others, out of humility, conceal the little works which they have published; the things that I have written I have resolved, rather out of humility and charity, to bring to light. For I prefer, if error appears anywhere, to be corrected while living rather than when dead, since, just as confession ceases from the dead, so correction benefits the living. For I am not so insolent as to demand, as the reward for my labor, the memory of a name subject to vanity. Therefore, lest I seem to have composed the works of others, or to have concealed 184

*[unclear]*

*Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers, or Illustrious Men, with an appendix of those who have also flourished as very learned men in our own age.*

*Most judiciously compiled by the venerable man, Lord Johannes, Abbot of Spanheim.*

*In praise of this most noble work, an epigram by D. Sebastian Brant.*

Whoever you are who wish to know the approved writers of the Church, and whatever distinction each one has, read this epitome of Johannes, Abbot of Spanheim, whom his learned life commends.

As he restores the ancient teachings of the fathers of the order, and renews the sacred laws of Benedict, so he takes care to gather together the scattered names of the ancient writers and collect them into one book.

He sets forth a catalogue in which he reckons the times, and what that venerable company of authors wrote. He rescues from decay so many names of worthy men, whom devouring time now tramples underfoot.

And it is wonderful that one man could, in order, either read or recall such many worthy men. Indeed, I should hardly doubt that, if perhaps he did not read them all, still a large part of all of them was seen by him.

Hence it comes about that I rightly place this magnanimous and distinguished man also among the number of the learned.

*Letter of the venerable and eminent father in Christ, Lord Johannes of Trittenheim, Abbot of Sponheim, to the most reverend father in Christ, Lord Johannes de Dalberg, Bishop of Worms.*

To the most reverend father and lord in Christ, Johannes de Dalberg, by divine providence Bishop of Worms: Brother Johannes, called abbot in Sponheim, of the Order of Saint Benedict, the little that he is.

In former times the ancients were accustomed, most reverend father, if they had fashioned any new work, to dedicate it to distinguished men, so that it might receive enduring strength and firmness, and so that the venomous tongue of rivals, beaten back by the light of majesty, would nowhere be able to set the tooth of a wicked bite. Nor did the opinion that proceeded from humility deceive them, since in learned prelates there is always a kindness toward their subjects, to be raised up with praises, by which it rewards the studies of the good and restrains those of the wicked.

Our men too, imitating as far as they can this example of antiquity, are accustomed to submit the works they write, dedicated to prelates of churches, to learned men, so that, approved by their authority, they may safely go forth in public. For those things come forth into the light without fear which are supported by the testimony of a bishop. Indeed no one, unless he is foolish, readily accuses what he knows has been approved by the judgment of his superiors. The innocence of the sheep rests safely when the compassion of the good shepherd watches over it.

Since, therefore, the examples of the ancients are incentives to virtue for us, it is fitting that we imitate the sacred customs of those whose praises we sing, so that, while we profit from them and others from us, the order of the ecclesiastical hierarchy may remain inviolate. And although I am too insignificant to trust that anyone will take pleasure in my little works, yet I have resolved humbly to offer what I have into the Lord’s treasury, in which the widow’s two [coins?] are rightly preferred to riches.

And so, when recently, at the urging of friends, I had gathered together with much labor a book on ecclesiastical writers, as the matter itself bears witness, I resolved, so as not to stray from the tracks of the ancients, to submit this labor of mine to some very learned man, a prelate of ecclesiastical dignity, by whose authority and benevolence it might pass the teeth of the envious without a bite. And when much thought arose in me as to whom I might more acceptably entrust this same little night-work, many presented themselves to me as I hesitated, concerning whose learning and benevolence no small promised hope was strong. Among them you, most reverend father, came to my mind as the more powerful, more eminent, and more learned man, you who surpass all in learning and exceed everyone in erudition.

In you the nobility of lofty lineage shines forth; episcopal authority stands out; uprightness of morals is seen; knowledge of every kind of good art is praised. For where shall we be able to find, apart from you, such a man in whom all these things come together at once? Among the Germans, most reverend father, no one has appeared equal to you, in whom lineage, dignity, and erudition shine so greatly. I do not speak in flattery; may the Almighty be witness, that we do not hesitate to compare [you?] with those of whom we have made mention in the catalogue. The most lucid orations which you are said to have delivered bear witness to this; letters bear witness; many epigrams bear witness. Indeed the very famous renown of your name has become known with praise not only to our Germans, but to Italians and Frenchmen.

Hence it came into my mind that I should inscribe the work on ecclesiastical writers, submitted to so great a bishop as you, and dedicate it to your name, so that I might rest secure under the shadow of the pontifical height. But while I behold in you the flashing splendor of light, I am dazzled, I draw back, and I am wholly shaken by fear of your so great majesty, lest perhaps I, wholly inferior in learning, merit, and dignity, should displease you, an exalted and most learned father, in that very thing by which I presumed to please you. For I know your many occupations, and I am not unaware of your sacred studies; I ought not to have troubled them with my trifles. But your learning gives me courage, which your kindness and humanity render lovable to all, since it shrinks from no one’s letters and judges no one unworthy of its address.

Therefore I approach your highness, although I am very lowly, and to you I humbly submit this present little work; I appoint you its judge and defender. Receive, I pray, most reverend and most learned father, this poor lucubration of ours, examine it, judge it, and defend it; and if you shall judge it worthy, follow it with kindly favor. And you, who in continual reading turn over the writings of the ancients, may you deign also, if ever there is leisure, to inspect their catalogue. But I have not yet communicated this present little work to anyone, until I know it approved by the testimony of your authority. Friends are awaiting it; printers are expecting it. But I judge that the opinion of your fatherhood must be preferred to all.

May your most gracious fatherhood, I pray, pardon me for having presumed to disclose my follies to ears occupied with weighty matters, because I have such confidence in your humanity, gentleness, and kindness that it is in no way permitted to doubt the benevolent reception of our catalogue. And I shall count it among the greatest delights if I learn that you take pleasure in my little lucubrations. Farewell, most reverend father, and hold me, your most devoted servant, commended to you together with the destined volume. From Spanheim, 26 April, in the year of the Lord 1492.

*A reply-letter of the Reverend Father Lord Johannes de Trittenheim, Abbot of Sponheim, to the venerable and most learned man Father Albert Morderer, giving the reason why he placed many teachers of secular letters among the ecclesiastical writers.*

Brother Johannes de Trittenheim, abbot in Sponheim, of the order of Saint Benedict, sends greeting to Brother Albert Morderer, of the Observant Order of Minors, his friend. You say, most beloved Albert, that you wonder that I have placed teachers of secular letters, who wrote nothing ecclesiastical, among illustrious men and ecclesiastical writers, since Jerome, Gennadius, Isidore, Sigebert, and the remaining assessors of doctors are found not to have done this at all; you judge it unworthy that men intent on secular disciplines, who did no labor for the edification of the universal Church, should obtain a place among ecclesiastical writers.
