I do not wonder that you wonder; others wonder too. Therefore, by answering you I shall satisfy all who hold the same opinion.

And first, indeed, why others did not do what you wonder that I have done is no concern of mine; but why I have done what they did not, I shall briefly relate. Indeed, teachers of the good arts who remain in the Catholic faith, philosophers, orators, and poets, who have written anything useful and honorable in their faculty, I by no means judge unworthy of the catalogue of illustrious men, since I know that they adorn the Church by their studies. For I think that no one can be called sufficiently learned in the divine Scriptures if he is ignorant of the discipline of secular letters. But how shall the theologian learn it, if there is no one who has handed it down? Who will not know how much a Christian and faithful philosopher benefits the Church, who destroys the errors of the gentiles, lays bare arguments and fallacious syllogisms, and confounds the doctrines of unbelievers? Read the histories of the ancients, and you will find [unclear] establishing the faith by words. How often have orthodox philosophers destroyed the cunning of heretics by disputing, overcome the gentiles, and conquered schismatics? Why say many things? Every school of theologians now takes its beginning, for the student, from philosophy, so much so that one cannot be a theologian who has not first been a philosopher among them.

What shall I say of orators, without whose instruction antiquity used to judge a theologian unfruitful, since he could not persuade others of the good things he had learned? For the rhetorician unlocks the figures of the Scriptures, clarifies tropes, dissolves knots, shows colors, unravels doubtful matters, and makes clear what is in the shadows of words. When he assumes the office of an orator, he will easily destroy the allegations of heretics and convict their errors. Finally, who can worthily pursue the praises of good orators, if he carefully weighs how much power there is in persuasion? O if only all the theologians of our time had the coloring of orators, how much fruit they could produce in the Church of God by their exhortations. A theologian-orator is said to have the minds of his hearers in his power; by his persuasions they are easily moved to those things which are holy and just.

Nor do we cast aside Christian poets, whom we do not doubt come closer to our theory, who under the shadow of a thing done, or, that is, show us briefly what must be done or avoided. Nor are we ignorant how great an injury poets today suffer from certain undigested and crude theologians, who condemn all poets in one sentence, asserting that they are liars and foul-speakers, as though those who imitate the poems of the ancient poets could not be truthful and good. Far be it that a good and modest poet cannot exist, who in this art had the holy fathers Augustine, Jerome, Prudentius, Bede, and innumerable others as predecessors. But it is not my office, nor is this the time, to refute their sloth.

Therefore, to close the letter, I have judged that philosophers, orators, and cultivators of the other good arts who are faithful and Christian, and who have written something useful, should be counted among ecclesiastical writers for three reasons. The first is that I thought their little works could contribute not a little to the knowledge of the holy Scriptures. The second is that it seemed likely to me that they wrote some ecclesiastical things which escape my notice. The last is that, by an occasion given them through us, they may understand that henceforth, as they are to write ecclesiastically, they should adorn the place they have received with worthy labors. Do you therefore think that such great men, so useful to the Catholic Church, should be rejected? Far be it from us that we should inflict upon her that now rash injury, by which we might be thought provoked by zeal for rivalry, not by reason of piety. Finally, that proverb commonly tossed about belongs to us: Knowledge has no enemy except the ignorant man.

These things, then, I wished to answer briefly in this book, so that you might know that what you previously wondered had been done was not done without cause. Farewell, remembering us before God in your prayers. From Sponheim, the fourth [unclear] of April. In the year of the Lord 1492.

Q 183

*Prologue of the Author.*

Often, at the insistence of many people, I have been asked that the book which I had formerly begun on ecclesiastical writers, for the sake of obtaining knowledge of books, I should at some time, when opportunity was found, bring to completion. I confess that I put it off for a long time, lest, if I presumed rashly to undertake so arduous a matter, I should provoke the hatred of rivals through my own levity. But now, when to the petition of learned friends there was added the counsel of those who by their arguments encouraged me to undertake this province, I could no longer resist their requests, especially since this little work of ours is supported by the patronage of such great men. For why should I fear the hatred of detractors, when I see that a refuge among the learned lies open to me? There will be, I do not doubt, some who will judge this labor of ours worthy of praise; there will also be some who, from a zeal of rivalry, will disparage it. What then? Are we therefore to abandon the exercises of good works, lest we provoke the hatred of rivals? Far from it. Everyone who does not imitate the wicked offends them; but [unclear]. And indeed to have displeased the wicked is praiseworthy, since they are accustomed to love nothing unless it is compared with their own morals.

Now therefore, importunate friends and exactors, receive the book composed on ecclesiastical writers, which with diligent prayers you so greatly desired to be brought to an end. I have done what I could, and have spent my ready strength on this work, although in many matters the capacity itself is less than the desire. For I, after the manner of those who see dimly, entered this forest under the guidance of the fathers who went before, and, gathering from their little works individual things suitable to my purpose, I carried them together into this bundle. I have also inserted into our catalogue many writers found by long investigation, with great toil and expense. Do not wonder, excellent reader, if in the annotations and titles of books my opinion does not always agree with yours. Who, in so manifold a variety of books, could enumerate the opinions of individuals, not to say harmonize them? You will therefore grant pardon if at times you find a volume marked in one way or another differently from what your opinion takes it to be. For it was not possible for me everywhere to express the diversities of individuals. For, as I have already said, I have followed the footsteps of the fathers, and where they disagreed I embraced what I believed to be truer. But if you find something else established by more solid truth, I shall gladly yield to your judgment.

It pleased me, moreover, to proceed by a new manner of writing, so that the reader himself might more easily find knowledge of the books from their beginnings. Beginning, therefore, from the disciples of the apostles, down to the last year of Emperor Frederick III, that is, the year of the Lord one thousand four hundred and ninety, I have drawn up a catalogue of illustrious men, in which I have recorded not the names of all, but only of those whom I found, their dignities, writings, and times, adding opposite the titles the beginnings of the volumes; but those things not seen I passed over for lack of space. The times in which certain men flourished I could not readily find; nevertheless I placed them, as seemed to me fitting, in an appropriate place. And in each defect let the knowledge of one who knows supply what is lacking, namely that he compute the times of individuals and restore those transposed to their proper places.

I confess that I have also deliberately passed over many whose writings are not easily found, nor their times. I also know at present many very learned men living, who are said to be publishing various little works; since I do not have certain knowledge about them, I prefer to pass by in silence rather than to think uncertain things. And, to use the words of Jerome, if any of those still living who write have been omitted by me in this catalogue, let them impute it not to me but to themselves, since they preferred to hide their writings rather than have them come into the light. But I believe that, content with their own writings and talent, they will not trouble themselves over the losses caused by my silence. For of those also whom I found, I wished to depict not their praises, but their books. For that study would require a rather lengthy volume.

Go now, therefore, into the city, work completed by our labor; go, and display to lovers of books the treasure which you contain. What do you fear? Why do you tremble? Why do you delay? Do not be afraid to come forth in public; do not fear the hatred of rivals, supported by the patronage of so many saints. Come then, book, of slender talent indeed, but displayer of great things. What is it that you dread, as if sluggish and useless? Go forth confidently; a thousand will praise you, while scarcely one disparages you. The love of God, for which you were written, may it, I pray, mercifully excuse you together with your author always and everywhere. Yours.

*COM-* *Of the Most Commended Man and Reverend Father in Christ, Lord Johannes de Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim. Book on Ecclesiastical Writers.*

Clement, fourth bishop of the holy Roman Church from blessed Peter, as some hold, a Roman by nation, a holy man and beloved of God, adorned also with comeliness of morals, whose life and passion are found in ecclesiastical writings, sat in the pontificate for nine years and ten days, banished into exile for the faith of Christ with steadfast spirit. He died in the third year of Trajan Caesar, and in the one hundred third year of the Lord. This most blessed martyr is said to have written, in the person of the Roman Church, some letters full of faith and learning, of which the principal ones are extant:

To the Church of the Corinthians.
Also to James the Apostle.
Moreover, of the itinerary of his life.
Likewise, of the disputation of Peter.

These last two volumes, however, are counted among the apocrypha, as is clear in distinction 15, *Sancta Romana*. Other letters of his are also reported, but they are apocryphal.

Dionysius the Areopagite, an Athenian, a distinguished philosopher, converted to the faith by blessed Paul the Apostle, was ordained the first bishop of Athens, as some hold, a man of outstanding holiness and incomparable learning. After the death of the Apostles, blessed Clement, bishop of the city of Rome, sent him with Rusticus the priest and Eleutherius the deacon into France to preach the word of God to the nations, another having been ordained bishop in [unclear] place. He wrote many excellent little works in the Greek language. Of these I have found among the Latins only the following:

On the Celestial Hierarchy, one book.
On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy, one book.
On the Divine Names, one book.
On Mystical Theology, one book.
On Symbolic Theology, one book.
To Gaius, four letters.
To Dorotheus the minister, one letter.
To Sosipater the priest, one letter.
To Polycarp, one letter.
To Demophilus, one letter.
To Saint John the Evangelist, one letter.
To Apollophanes the philosopher, one letter.
On the death of Paul, to Timothy, one letter.

Every best gift, etc.
Our priest indeed.
Now already the man of God after.
Of the supersubstantial Trinity.
Saint Timothy indeed.
Darknesses are hidden.
The divine darkness is in.
Do not suppose here [unclear].
I indeed did not know to.
Of the history of the Hebrews.
I greet you, holy soul.
To Apollophanes [unclear].
Farewell, divine disciple.

These are the things that I find among the Latins concerning the writings of blessed Dionysius; if he published anything further, it has remained among the Greeks. But since the aforesaid works were covered with great obscurity, they were made clear by the explanation of the following fathers. The first of these, John Scotus, monk of our order, translated and expounded them; then Hugh of Saint-Victor, Rupert of Lincoln, Albert the Great, Dionysius the Carthusian, and many others whose *On Ecclesiastical Writers*

He wrote, among other things:

An Apologetic for our faith, one book.

When he had recited it in order before the senate, he was beheaded. He flourished at Rome under the emperors Commodus and Severus, in the year of the Lord 190.

TERTULLIAN, a priest, by origin a Carthaginian of the African province, his father a centurion and a man of proconsular rank, was a man of keen and vehement intellect, most learned in both divine and secular writings, since at Carthage he taught rhetoric with distinction for many years. He wrote in Latin almost innumerable small works, in which he powerfully crushed the errors of the heretics. The most blessed martyr Cyprian held this man’s writings in such veneration that he let no day pass without reading them. For he was accustomed to say to his secretary, “Give me the master,” meaning Tertullian. At last he is said to have slipped into the error of Montanus; for this reason his works are counted among the apocrypha, Distinction 15, *Sancta Romana*. And although he erred in some things, nevertheless in many things he wrote well, as his volumes bear witness. Of these I have seen:

On the Patience of God, one book. “I confess to the Lord God.”

One book. “Various [unclear] the devil.”

Five books. “If anything was done before.”

One book. “Instruction comes very near.”

One book. “The condition of present things.”

One book. “We are accustomed to [unclear] heretics.”

One book.

He also wrote many other things, and various treatises, which have not yet come into our hands, and he lived studious until old age and senescence. He flourished in the times of the emperor Severus, in the year of the Lord 200.

ORIGEN, who is also Adamantius, a priest, by nation an Alexandrian, son of the martyr Leonides, once a disciple of Clement of Alexandria, was a man of great and excellent intellect, so that he never had an equal in zeal and learning. In the tenth year of Severus Pertinax, when a persecution was stirred up against the Christians and his father Leonides was crowned with martyrdom for the faith of Christ, he was left poor with his widowed mother and six brothers, being about seventeen years old. For the treasury had seized all their substance because of their confession of Christ, so that they no longer had anything from which they might live. And although the number of years reckoned in the young man was rather small, nevertheless his learning was already wonderful, and the constancy of his Christian faith admirable. For he had resolved to fall bravely with his father Leonides for the faith of Christ, had it not happened that, through his mother’s stratagem, he was preserved for the advantage of the Church, since he was to become a great teacher. For when he had decided early in the morning to hasten to his father at the place of contest on the day before, his clothes were taken away by his mother during the night and the doors of the lodging were locked, and he was forced to remain at home. But when he grew into a man, he resolved to lead a most ample life, and, proclaiming the word of God round about him, he went barefoot for many years. Finally, he never slept on a bed spread with feathers; he abstained altogether from wine and meat, except in illness; and he was intent on serving God devoutly with fasts, vigils, prayers, and continual studies and expositions of the divine Scriptures.

On the instruction of morals, one book.

These are the writings of Seneca that I have been able to find up to the present. He is said, however, to have written some other little works, which have not yet come into our hands. He was indeed a most ardent lover of wisdom, a zealous investigator of it, and of so tenacious a memory that he immediately recited from memory two thousand names read in his presence. Moreover, when a certain poet had produced two hundred verses and was reciting them in order before Nero, gathered together on a sheet, Seneca at once, using his memory in place of a volume, repeated those same verses one by one in reverse order, beginning from the last, back to the first. He is also read to have held in memory the names of all his fellow citizens. He flourished at Rome in the times of the apostle Paul under the emperor Nero, in the year of the Lord 50.

Marcellus, son of Marcus, prefect of the city of Rome, once a disciple of Simon Magus, sufficiently instructed in secular letters, converted to the faith of Jesus Christ by the preaching of blessed Peter the Apostle, composed many things for the usefulness of the Church of God. For he wrote, at the request of Christians:

On the conflict of Peter and Simon, one book.
To the saints Nereus and Achilleus, one book.
On the acts of Peter and Paul, one book.
On the arts of Simon, one book.
On the death of Saint Petronella, one book.
On the passion of Saint Felicula, one book.
On the passion of Saint Nicomedes, one book.

He also published other works concerning the deeds of the saints, which have not come to our knowledge. He flourished at Rome in the times of Saint Peter the Apostle, in the year of the Lord 50.

Linus I, after blessed Peter bishop of the city of Rome, a Tuscan by nationality, a man of most holy conduct, shining with many miracles in life and after death, sat in the pontificate eleven years, three months, twelve days. Since he was a most learned man, beloved of God, he wrote in the Greek language concerning the holy apostles Peter and Paul, who suffered on one day:

The martyrdom, one book.
And certain letters.

At length he was punished with capital sentence by the prefect Saturnius, whose daughter he had freed from a demon, and was made a martyr, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of October. He flourished at Rome under the emperor Galba, in the year of the Lord 70.

Philo, a Jew by nationality, an Alexandrian, of priestly stock, is placed by blessed Jerome among the ecclesiastical writers for this reason, because in his little works he very often in Chri*On Ecclesiastical Writers*

is occupied with praise of the Christians. When this man had been sent to Rome as ambassador of his people, he is recorded to have had the friendship of the blessed apostle Peter; and for this reason he also adorned with his praises at Alexandria the followers of Saint Mark, his disciple. He was a man most learned in every respect, and was regarded as a second Plato, so that it was commonly said: either Plato imitates Philo, or Philo imitates Plato. For so great a likeness of thought and eloquence is reported in them both. He wrote many very elegant books, of which the following are related.

*On the Life of the Wise Man*, one book.
*On the Heir of Divine Things*, one book.
*On the Conduct of Life*, one book.
*On the Division of Unequal Things*, one book.
*On the Confusion of Languages*, three books.
*On the Three Virtues*, one book.
*On the Nature of Quadrupeds*, one book.
*On the Nature of Discovery*, one book.
*On Those Things Which We Testify by Sense*, one book.
*On Covenants*, one book.
*On Instruction*, one book.

*On the Course of Generation*, one book.
*On Drunkenness*, two books.
*On the Change of Names*, one book.
*On Victims and Promises*, one book.

He is also read to have written many other things, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under the emperor Nero, in the year of the Lord 50.

Josephus, a Jew by nation, a Jerusalemite, a priest by religion, son of the priest Matthias, a philosopher, rhetorician, and distinguished writer of the times, whom I would not place in our catalogue unless the Church read his writings and blessed Jerome had done this before: after the destruction of Jerusalem, he was captured by the emperors Vespasian and Titus and brought to Rome; because of the excellence of his talent he was magnificently honored by the senate and people of Rome. Although he remained a Jew, nevertheless he often praised the race of Christians, and in the eighteenth book of the *Antiquities* he wrote a notable testimony concerning our Lord Jesus Christ. His volumes were held in such authority among the Romans while he was still living that they were entrusted to the public library; after his death, moreover, he was presented by the senate and people with a bronze statue. Of his works I have seen only the following.

*On the Jewish War*, seven books. “Since the war which.”
*Antiquities of the World*, twenty-four books. “To write a history.”
*Against Apion*, one book. “Sufficiently, as I think.”
*On the Power of Speaking*, one book. “To the holy elder John.”

He flourished at Rome under the emperors Vespasian and Titus, and remained among men until the times of the emperor Trajan, in the year of the Lord 100.

Ignatius, third bishop of the church of Antioch after blessed Peter, a man of exceptional holiness and a singular, most fervent lover of our Lord Jesus Christ, was accustomed to say, as Dionysius testifies: “My love has been crucified.” Since this most blessed prelate was a learned and zealous preacher of the divine word, he wrote several elegant letters full of fervor, in which he showed that he was a lover of holy martyrdom. Of these, the following are considered the more important.

To the Church of the Ephesians, one letter.
To the Magnesians, one letter.
To the Trojans, one letter.
To the Romans, one letter.
To Saint John, one letter.
To the blessed Virgin, one letter.
To the Philadelphians, one letter.
To Polycarp, one letter.

He suffered martyrdom at Rome under the emperor Trajan, in the year of the Lord 111.

Papias, hearer and disciple of Saint John, bishop of Hierosolyma in Asia, a most steadfast propagator and defender of the Christian faith, a disciple and devoted imitator of the holy apostles, wrote works of no contemptible authority. Of these there survives an outstanding work, divided into five volumes, which he entitled thus: *Explanation of the Sayings of the Lord*, five books. The other things that he wrote we have not seen. This man, the novelty of a thousand ye*The Abbot of Sponheim*

... was the first to invent [unclear], after whom he dreamed that Christ would reign again in the flesh with the elect upon the earth; others later enlarged this error and were called Chiliasts, from the thousand.

He flourished in the times of Trajan Caesar, about the year of the Lord 100.

Hegesippus, a Jew by nation, converted to the faith of Christ, shone forth in the Church of God as admirable in learning and holiness; his feast, with those of the other saints, obtained a place in the martyrology. He wrote several little works of excellent talent, of which I have found only: an outstanding work, from the time of the Lord’s Passion down to his own age; A History of Ecclesiastical Acts, five books, “In the Parthian war which between...” I have seen no other of his works.

He flourished near the apostolic times under Antoninus Pius, in the year of the Lord 160.

Justin, converted from being a philosopher to the catholic faith, an eminent Christian and worshipper, when in the city of Rome he was refuting Crescens the Cynic, who was blaspheming Christians, as gluttonous, fearful of death, and a follower of luxury and lusts, was accused before the senate through that man’s plots because he was a Christian, and was crowned with martyrdom for Christ. He wrote many distinguished little works in defense of our faith, of which these are reported:

Against the Gentiles, to Antoninus, one book. On the Soul, one book.
To Aurelius, Against the Gentiles, one book. [The Psalmist?] so entitled, one book.
Likewise Against the Gentiles, one book. Against Trypho the Jew, one book.
Corrections Against the Gentiles, one book. Against Marcion, one book.
On the Monarchy of God, one book. Against All Heresies, one book.

He also composed many other works which have not come to our knowledge.

He flourished under Antoninus Pius, in the year of the Lord 150.

Quadratus the Athenian, bishop after Publius the martyr, formerly a hearer and disciple of the holy apostles, a man steadfast and of incomparable learning, labored and advanced much for the advantage of the Christian faith, and gathered into the unity of faith the Church that had been dispersed by fear of persecution. Since he was an eminent teacher, he wrote, among other things, for the Christians to the emperor Hadrian an Apologetic full of instruction, one book, and other things unknown to us. At last he suffered for the defense of the catholic faith on the seventh day before the Kalends of June. He flourished under the emperor Hadrian, in the year of the Lord 120.

Aristides the Athenian philosopher, a man most learned in secular letters and very devoted to the divine Scriptures, shone forth distinguished by such eloquence that he presented a marvel of himself to the gentiles; under the garb of a philosopher he bore Christian faith and conduct, and shone forth famous, not without a reputation for holiness. He wrote an Apologetic for the Christians, to the emperor Hadrian, one book, and certain other things. He flourished under the emperor Hadrian, in the year of the Lord 120.

Melito the Asian, bishop of Sardis, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and venerable no less for holiness than for doctrine, shone forth famous among catholic preachers. He wrote many excellent volumes for the advantage of the Church of the faithful. Of these, the following are listed:

On Easter, one book. On the Life of the Prophets.
On the Fallen, one book. [On the Fallen?]
On the Body and the Soul, one book. On the Senses.
On Baptism, one book. On Faith.
On Truth, one book. Philoxenia.
one book. The work that is entitled [The Key?].
On the Generation of Christ, one book. On the Devil.
Eclogues, one book. On the Apocalypse of John,
one book. “Melito, servant of Christ.”
On the Passing of Saint Mary, one book.

He also published other little works which antiquity has not permitted to come to our memory. Tertullian, mentioning in a certain place his elegant and declamatory talent, asserts that he was regarded by our people as a prophet. It should indeed be noted that the book On the Passing of Saint Mary written by him is reckoned among the apocrypha, 15 dist., Sancta Romana.

He flourished under the emperor Marcus Antoninus Verus, in the year of the Lord 160.

Theophilus, sixth bishop of the church of Antioch, a man very devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, famous in talent and speech, and an excellent declaimer, wrote many volumes for the advantage of the faithful and shone forth as an excellent expounder of the Lord’s sayings. Of his little works the following are reported:

Con*On Ecclesiastical Writers*

Against Marcion, book 1. Commentaries on the Gospels, four books.
Against Hermogenes, book 1.
To Autolycus, 3 books. On the Proverbs of Solomon, book 1.

He also composed many other short treatises pertaining to the edification of the Catholic Church, which among the Latins are seldom found together. He was ordained bishop in the year of the Lord 173, in the eleventh indiction.

APOLLINARIS of Hierapolis, bishop in Asia, a learned man, an outstanding defender of the Christian faith, brilliant in intellect, eloquent in speech, wrote little works of no contemptible reading, in which he showed himself a man not so much learned as zealous. Of these the following are reported:

Apology for the Christians, book 1. Against the Nations, 5 books.
On Truth, 3 books. Against the Cataphrygians, 2 books.

But he published some other works, knowledge of which antiquity has taken from us. He flourished under Marcus Antoninus Verus, in the year of the Lord 165.

DIONYSIUS, bishop of the church of the Corinthians, a most eloquent man, very learned in the divine Scriptures, a most watchful shepherd of Christ’s sheepfold, was of such solicitude and diligence that he instructed not only the people of his own city with saving teachings, but also urged the congregations of foreign cities, through letters, to constancy in the faith. These epistles are said to be so useful and lengthy that they may not improperly be called books. Of these, the following are reckoned:

To the Lacedaemonians, epistle 1. To the Athenians, epistle 1.
To the Nicomedians, epistle 1. To the Cretans, epistle 1.
To the [Gnossians?], epistle 1. To the Roman pope, epistle 1.
To the [Amastrians?], epistle 1. To Chrysophora, a woman, epistle 1.

He flourished under the rulers Marcus Antoninus Verus and Lucius Aurelius, in the year of the Lord 170. Not without a reputation for sanctity, he wrote various things.

TATIAN, a heresiarch, was a hearer and follower of Justin Martyr so long as he did not depart from his side. But afterward, when Saint Justin had been crowned, puffed up with the swelling of eloquence, he founded a new heresy, which is called that of the Encratites; Severus later increased it, from whom the heretics of the same party were called Severians. They abominate meats, do not drink wine, do not receive the Old Testament, and do not believe in the resurrection. Tatian wrote volumes, which nevertheless have not come to my knowledge. For because of [unclear], countless volumes, indeed [unclear] volumes, perished. There survives of his, according to Jerome, an outstanding [volume?], which he entitled:

Against the Nations, book 1.

He flourished under Marcus Antoninus Verus, in the year of the Lord 170.

PHILIP, bishop of Crete, that is, of the city of [Gortyna?], whom Dionysius, bishop of the Corinthians set above, mentions in his letter which he had written to the church of the same city, was a noble and learned man. For the benefit of believers he published works sufficiently learned, as they say, which by no means came into our hands. There survives of his:

Against Marcion, book 1. The rest is unknown to us.

He also wrote certain letters to various persons and various treatises, which to our [unclear]; in them the abundant vein of his talent is visible. Of these there survives a notable volume:

Against Marcion.

He flourished in the year of the Lord 170, in the times of Marcus Antoninus Verus, emperor.

MODESTUS, indeed a man of flourishing talent, although what dignity or rank he held is unknown to us, wrote, as blessed Jerome bears witness, little works of no contemptible reading, in which the abundant vein of his talent is visible. Of these there survive volumes; of these the following are reported:

Against the Nations, book 1. On the Monarchy of God, book 1.
On Discipline, book 1. On the Ogdoad, book 1.
To Blastus on Schism, book 1. On Easter, to Pope Victor, book 2.
Against Heresies, 5 books. On the Apostolic Preaching, book 1.

Va*The Abbot of Sponheim*

[unclear]. Seven books of various treatises.

He wrote many other things which have so far come to my knowledge. At last, when persecution was raging against the Christians, together with almost all the people of his city he was crowned with martyrdom for the Catholic faith on the fourth day before the Kalends of June. He flourished under Marcus Antoninus, in the year of the Lord 175.

Theodotion, by birth an Ephesian, once a disciple of Tatian while he was still a faithful philosopher, certainly a man most learned in every respect, was the third translator of the divine Scriptures. Besides the translation of the Scriptures, which he made from Hebrew into Latin, he also composed certain other little works, which, however, have not yet come into our hands. He flourished in the times of the emperor Commodus, in the year of the Lord 180.

Rhodon, an Asian by race, once a hearer and disciple of Tatian, a man most learned both in the divine Scriptures and also in secular letters, is said to have written many things in Greek speech, copies of which are rarely found among our people. Of these, however, the more important are said to be those which we have set down below:

Against Marcion, three books. To Callistion, one book.
Against the Cataphrygians, one book. On the Hexaemeron, six books.

He flourished under the rulers Commodus and Severus, in the year of the Lord 200.

Clement, presbyter of the church of Alexandria, once a hearer and disciple of Pantaenus, a Stoic philosopher and Christian, who after him held the ecclesiastical school at Alexandria for many years, was a devout, learned, and most eloquent man. He wrote many excellent volumes:

Stromata, that is, Miscellanies, eight books. On Disputation, one book.
Against the Gentiles, one book. On the Salvation of the Rich Man, one book.
The Paedagogue, three books. On Detraction, one book.
On Easter, one book. Against the Judaizers, one book.
On Fasting, one book. On Ecclesiastical Canons, one book.

He also published many letters and various treatises, whose titles we do not know. He flourished in the times of the rulers Commodus and Severus, in the year of the Lord 200.

Melciades, whom Rhodon recalled in his work which he composed against the Cataphrygians, Montanus, Prisca, and Maximilla, the mad prophets, was a man most learned in secular letters and trained by constant study in the divine Scriptures. He wrote no few little works for the edification of the faithful. Of these the following are reported:

Against Montanus, one book. Against the Jews, one book.
Against the Gentiles, one book. An Apologetic for Our Faith, one book.

He is also said to have written many other things which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished in the times of Marcus Antoninus Commodus, in the year of the Lord 170.

Apollonius, a certain learned and most eloquent man, distinguished no less in life than in eloquence, a most valiant destroyer of heretical depravity, composed many things on behalf of our faith. He often refuted the madness of Montanus in words and writings, as is clear to those who read that notable volume which he is said to have composed with the greatest charms of eloquence:

Against Montanus, one book.

But he published several other things which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under the rulers Commodus and Severus, in the year of the Lord 180.

Serapion, formerly an anchorite, the eighth bishop of the church of Antioch, a man of keen intellect, very zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, venerable no less for his life than for his knowledge, is said to have forged several little works for the benefit of believers, in which he showed himself a learned man and a most keen defender of the Christian faith. Among their number are held:

To Carinus on Montanus, one book.
On the Gospel under the Name of Peter, one book.
Short but Numerous Letters, one book.

He was ordained bishop of the aforesaid city under Commodus, ruler of the Romans, in the year of the Lord 193, in the first indiction.

Apollonius, a senator of the city of Rome, a man most learned both in the divine Scriptures and in secular letters, venerable no less for holiness than for knowledge, when he had been denounced before the senate because he was a Christian and would not deny Christ, received sentence of capital punishment, since the ancient law among them held that Christians, who had once been brought before their judgment, were not to be released without denial.

He wrote:

[unclear], one book.
[unclear], one book.

*On Ecclesiastical Writers*

He wrote, among other things:

*An Apology for Our Faith*, one book, which, when he had recited it in order before the senate, he was beheaded. He flourished at Rome under the emperors Commodus and Severus, in the year of the Lord 190.

TERTULLIAN, priest, by homeland a Carthaginian of the province of Africa, his father a proconsular centurion, a man of sharp and vehement talent, most learned both in divine and in secular writings, since indeed he taught rhetoric gloriously at Carthage for many years. He wrote in the Latin language almost countless little works, in which he vigorously crushed the errors of the heretics. The most blessed martyr Cyprian held this man’s writings in such veneration that he let no day pass without reading them. For he was accustomed to say to his secretary, “Give me the master,” meaning Tertullian. At last he is said to have slipped into the error of Montanus; on account of this his little works are counted among the apocrypha. 15, distinction, *Sancta Romana*. And although he erred in some matters, nevertheless in many he wrote well, as his volumes testify. Of these I have seen:

*On the Patience of God*, one book. “I confess to the Lord God.”

One book. “Various [unclear] the devil.”

Five books. “If anything was done previously.”

One book. “Next comes [unclear].”

*Against All Heresies*, one book. “Of the heretics of [unclear].”

One book. “The condition of present things.”

One book. “We are accustomed to [unclear] heretics.”

One book. “The Valentinians often.”

One book. “Those who [hold] the faith of the resurrection.”

*On the Prescriptions of the Heretics*, one book. “The confidence of Christians.”

One book. “Most beloved in the Lord.”

One book. “Recently it happened [unclear].”

One book. “Among the foods of the flesh.”

One book. “Repentance, this kind.”

One book. “Now a proper matter.”

One book. “Set on earth, delay.”

One book. “Handmaids of the living God, [unclear].”

One book. “Heretics forbid marriages.”

One book. “The chiefs, always Africans.”

One book. “Sought recently, Fab[ius?].”

*On the Veiling of Virgins*.

*On the Dress of Women*.

*On the Adornment of Women*.

*To His Wife*.

*On Persecution, to Fabius*.

*To Scapula*.

*Exhortation to Chastity*.

*On Monogamy*.

*On the Pallium*.

*On Spectacles*.

*On Ecstasy*.

*On Modesty*.

One book. “We indeed neither [unclear].”

One book. “I do not doubt, brother, that you.”

One book. “Heretics forbid marriages.”

One book. “The chiefs, always Africans.”

One book. *On Fasts*.

One book. *Against Apollonius*.

One book.

He also wrote many other things, and various treatises, which have not yet come into our hands at all; and he lived studious until old age and advanced years. He flourished in the times of the emperor Severus, in the year of the Lord 200.

ORIGEN, also called Adamantius, priest, an Alexandrian by nationality, son of the martyr Leonides, once a disciple of Clement of Alexandria, was a man of great and excellent talent, so that in zeal and learning he never had an equal. In the tenth year of Severus Pertinax, when a persecution was stirred up against the Christians, and when his father Leonides had been crowned with martyrdom for the faith of Christ, he was left poor with his widowed mother and six brothers, being about seventeen years old. The treasury had seized all their substance because of confession of Christ, so that they had nothing more from which they might live. And although the number of years was reckoned small in the young man, nevertheless his learning was already wonderful, and the constancy of his Christian faith admirable. For he had determined to fall bravely with his father Leonides for the faith of Christ, if, through his mother’s stratagem, it had not happened that he, destined to be a great teacher for the usefulness of the Church, was preserved. For when early in the morning he had resolved to go to the place of contest to his father, his clothing having been taken away by his mother during the night and the doors of the chamber locked, he was compelled to remain at home. But when he had grown into manhood, he resolved to lead a more ample life, and, announcing the word of God round about him, he walked barefoot for many years. Finally, he never slept on a bed spread with feathers; he entirely abstained from wine and meats, except in infirmity; and he was intent on serving God devotedly with fasts, vigils, prayers, and continual studies and expositions of the divine Scriptures.

*196. ABBOT OF SPONHEIM.*

…was. By Christ's counsel, too, he was wont to put on only one tunic, and, made a contemner of all worldly [things], thought nothing of the morrow. For love of chastity, that he might dare to preach to the women who followed [him], he had himself castrated—although in this deed zeal remained without knowledge. On account of his doctrine, eloquence, and apostolic life, Mammaea, the most Christian mother of the emperor Alexander, seized with desire of hearing him, came from Alexandria to Antioch, and heard his mellifluous teaching with great admiration. He was so intent on the study of the divine Scriptures that he never took food or sleep unless one of the brothers had first set forth a reading of the Scriptures, with all listening. The New and Old Testament, like another Esdras, he knew by heart; and now an old man, against his age, he learned the Hebrew tongue, and gathered the editions of all the interpreters except the Septuagint into one, by wonderful study. In dictating editions of the Scriptures he was of such admirable memory and subtlety that he wearied seven notaries, and as many girls most swift in writing, besides other young men, writing diverse [things] at once from his mouth, by an incredible agility of pronouncing. And although he was held, and was, so great a doctor, distinguished among all ecclesiastics, yet he is noted for great errors, by which either he himself was foolish, or was depraved by others inserting false [things] into [his] writings. For there was always a varied opinion of the doctors concerning Origen, some asserting [him] a heretic, others affirming that fraud was imposed on him. [It is] not to be wondered at if the first [man], without example, erred, who unfolded so many volumes without a preceding master. Yet it is ours, not only concerning Origen but concerning whatever writers, to think with the holy Roman Church, and to despise superfluous opinions. He published almost infinite volumes, of which I have seen, rendered into Latin, only the following: [a long list of homilies and commentaries follows—On Genesis hom. 16; On Exodus hom. 13; On Leviticus hom. 16; On Numbers; On Joshua hom. 26; On Matthew hom. 26; On Isaiah; On Jeremiah; On Ezekiel hom. 14; On the Song of Songs; On Luke hom. 26; On Romans, 4 books; On the martyrs, 1 book; Against Celsus the philosopher, 8 books; Peri Archon (On First Principles), 15 books; and others—rendered as printed]. He composed, besides, many others, which have not come into our hands. There are [those] who write that they have read six thousand treatises of Origen—which number is both great and unknown to the Latins. Nor [is there] doubt that many of his little works have been newly translated, which by no means came to the notice of our reading. He dies an old man and poor, buried at Tyre, under the princes Valerian and Gallienus, in the year of the Lord 261, in the ninth indiction, in the 70th year of his age.

AMMONIUS of Alexandria, a man erudite in the divine Scriptures and most learned in secular letters, the most celebrated philosopher and rhetorician of all his time, subtle in talent and eloquent in speech, wrote in the Greek tongue certain illustrious volumes, by which he left the memory of himself to posterity. Of whose number the following are extant:
On the consonance of Jesus and Moses: 1 book.
Of the Gospel Canons: 1 book. ["In the first canon, four…"]
"One out of four": 1 book. ["Since indeed many…"]
And certain others. Him the most impious Porphyry, most bitter enemy of the Christians, a gentile philosopher, falsely accuses of having—the faith being denied—become a heathen; [him] who, it is agreed, remained a devout Christian up to death. He flourished under Alexander, son of Mammaea, in the year 250.

*On Ecclesiastical Writers*

Ambrosius, a hearer of Origen, at first a Marcionite and afterward corrected by Origen himself, was a distinguished confessor of the Christian faith; he also deserved to be promoted to the office of deacon. He was certainly a very learned man and a devoted lover of books; by supplying funds, shorthand-writers, and scribes, he enabled our Adamantius to compose almost infinite volumes. He was so great a promoter of Origen’s nightly labors that by day and night he urged him, by words and writings, to write something new, so much so that in a certain familiar letter he is named by Origen as “the taskmaster of the work.” He used to say that he had never gone to bed or taken food in Origen’s presence unless first one of the brethren, who were always at hand, had sounded forth the sacred writings. He wrote to Origen, giving thanks for his conversion.

Letters, 1 book. And certain other works. He flourished with Origen, in the year of the Lord 230.

Tryphon, a hearer and disciple of Origen, to whom some of Origen’s letters are extant, was a man most learned both in the divine Scriptures and in secular letters, subtle in intellect and eloquent in speech. He wrote in Greek certain excellent little works, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these the following are extant:

On the Red Cow in Deuteronomy, 1 book. On the Quality of Sacrifices, 1 book.
On the Dove and the Turtledove, 1 book.

He flourished in the times of the emperor Alexander, in the year of the Lord 240.

Minucius Felix, an advocate, Roman by birth, a man most learned in secular letters and devoted to the divine readings, excellent in intellect and eloquent in speech, wrote in Latin certain excellent little works, by which he commended the memory of himself to posterity. Of these there is extant a dialogue between a Christian and a heretic, which is entitled:

Octavius, 1 book. On Fate, against the Mathematicians, 1 book.

He flourished at Rome under the emperor Alexander, in the year of the Lord 35.

Beryllus, bishop of Bostra in Arabia, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and excellently instructed in secular matters, after he had ruled the church gloriously for some time, at last fell into the heresy of the Paulianists, who denied that Christ existed before Mary; but, corrected by Origen, he wrote many things. Of these there is extant between them:

A Dialogue Held, 1 book. Letters to Various Persons, 1 book.

And certain other works. He flourished under the emperor Alexander, in the year of the Lord 245.

Hippolytus, bishop of a certain city whose name Jerome did not state, was certainly a man both devoted to and learned in the divine writings. He wrote many and almost incredible volumes, so that Ambrosius, of whom we have already made mention above, used to exhort Origen to imitate him and strongly persuaded him to expound the divine Scriptures, providing him, as we have said, with seven shorthand-writers, and as many very swift girls for writing, and an equal number of copyists, with their costs and expenses. One could see a beautiful and delightful contest, in which each greatly desired to surpass the other in the publication of books.

Concerning the works of Hippolytus, the following are reported:

On the Hexaemeron, 1 book. On the Apocalypse, 1 book.
On Genesis, 1 book. On the Proverbs of Solomon, 1 book.
On Exodus, 1 book. On Ecclesiastes, 1 book.
On Numbers, 1 book. On Saul and the Pythoness, 1 book.
On the Song of Songs, 1 book. On Antichrist, 1 book.
On the Prophet Zechariah, 1 book. Against Marcion, 1 book.
On Daniel, 1 book. Against All Heresies, 2 books.

He also published many and various treatises on the Psalms, and almost innumerable homilies and sermons, and many other works still unknown to us. He flourished under the emperor Alexander, in the year of the Lord 250.

Alexander, bishop of Cappadocia, when he was going to Jerusalem out of desire for the holy places, was ordained bishop there by divine revelation after Saint Narcissus. He shone forth not only as famous for sanctity and learning, and at last, under Decius, [unclear] for the faith of Christ, he consummated many [unclear] and martyrdom. He wrote many elegant letters to various persons serving the most impious tyrant. Of these the following are especially reported:

On the Peace of the Church, to the Aaronites, 1 letter. To the Antiochenes, 1 letter.
For Origen against Demetrius, 1 letter. To Origen, several letters.

He suffered at Caesarea under Decius, in the year of the Lord 253, indiction 1.

Julius Africanus, a man most learned in every respect, a philosopher, historian, and distinguished theologian, and a most ardent lover of the divine Scriptures and of books, by his studies *The Abbot of Sponheim*

by his studies and at his own expense founded at Caesarea in Palestine a notable library, in which he gathered many volumes, both of secular and of divine writings. He also wrote several works of great usefulness. Of these the following are reported:

Chronicles, 5 books. On Easter, 1 book.
On the Holy Trinity, 1 book. On the Sabbath, 1 book.
On Circumcision, 1 book. To Origen on Susanna, 1 book.
On Attalus, 1 book. To Aristides the Philosopher, 1 book.

And he is said to have composed many other works, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under Marcus Aurelius, in the year of the Lord 220.

Gregory, bishop of Neocaesarea in Pontus, hearer and disciple of Origen, was a learned and holy man; he both wrote many things and, while living, shone with miracles. While still a young man, seeking the study of secular philosophy with his brother Athenodorus, he placed himself under the school of Origen, by whom he was gradually and almost imperceptibly converted to the faith of Christ together with his brother, and became a most learned and most holy man. Among his writings there survives:

A Panegyric to Origen, 1 book.
Interpretations on Ecclesiastes, 1 book.

And several letters. He flourished under the emperor Gordian, in the year of the Lord 240.

Cornelius, the twenty-second bishop of the city of Rome after Peter, a Roman by country, son of Castinus, was made pope after the glorious martyrdom of Fabian. He sat in the chair of Peter for two years, a learned and most holy man, until at last he too, crowned with martyrdom, passed, released from the flesh, to those above. He wrote several letters for the benefit of the Church. Of these I have found only the following:

To Fabius, bishop of Antioch.
On Synods, 1 letter. On Novatian, 1 letter.
To the same, on the Novatians, 1 book. On the Acts of the Synod, 1 letter.

He wrote several letters to Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, and others to other persons. He flourished under the tyrant emperor Decius, in the year of the Lord 255.

Cyprian, bishop of the church of Carthage in Africa, a learned and most holy man, taught rhetoric gloriously for many years, and was a magnificent teacher in every secular literature. Then, by the persuasion of the priest Caecilius, from whom he received his surname, he was converted to the faith of Christ and distributed all his property to the poor. Not long after, having been chosen priest, he was also ordained bishop. Since he was zealous in the divine Scriptures, he usefully published many works for the edification of the faithful. And he wrote the following volumes in the Latin language, namely:

On the Grace of God, to Donatus, 1 book. “You advise well, Donatus.”
Against Demetrianus, 1 book. “You bark at and against.”
1 book. “Many and great are they.”
On Piety and Almsgiving, 1 book. “You desired, Fortunatus.”
On the Praise of Martyrdom, 1 book. “Be zealous for what seems good.”
On Jealousy and Envy, 1 book. “About to speak of patience.”
On the Good of Patience, 1 book. “Even if among very many of you.”
On Mortality, 1 book. “The guardian of discipline, of hope.”
On Virginity, 1 book. “Peace, behold, most beloved.”
On the Lapsed, 1 book. “Cyprian to brother Caecilius.”
On the Sacrament of the Chalice, 1 book. “Since the Lord warns and [unclear].”
On the Unity of the Church, 1 book. “The evangelical precepts.”
On the Lord’s Prayer, 1 book. “That idols are not gods.”
On the Vanity of Idols, 1 book. “I had indeed promised you.”
To Antonianus on Novatus, 1 book. “The proof of the chapters.”
On the Two Mountains, 1 book. “We have received the first letters.”
To Quirinus, against the Jews, 1 book. “The Jews into offence.”
To Pope Cornelius, 8 letters. “We have learned, brother [unclear].”
On Gamblers, 1 book. Letters to Various Persons, 1 book.
To Julianus, his friend.

But he is said to have composed many other works, which have not come into our hands. The little book On the Twelve Abuses of the World, ascribed by many to Cyprian, does not have the scent of his style. At last he suffered under Valerian, on the same day on which Cornelius did at Rome, but not in the same year, namely in the year of the Lord 249, in the twelfth indiction, on the eighth day before the Kalends of October.

Pontius, priest, hearer and disciple of blessed Cyprian, a learned and holy man, and *On Ecclesiastical Writers*

and a distinguished declaimer; coming into Gaul after the glorious triumph of his master, he obtained the palm of martyrdom for the faith of Christ at the city of Cimella. This Pontius, by his honey-sweet preaching and zeal, converted the two Philips, emperors, to Christ, and persuaded them to be the first among the Roman rulers to renounce idols. He also wrote, in an elegant style, a notable volume, which contains:

The Life of Saint Cyprian, one book.

He flourished under Emperor Philip, in the year of the Lord 240.

Dionysius, the thirteenth bishop of the city of Alexandria, formerly a hearer and disciple of Origen, while he was still a presbyter held the public school under Heraclas and acquired great glory for his learning. For he was a man most learned in every science, a philosopher, rhetorician, and distinguished theologian, who, agreeing with the doctrine of Cyprian and the African synod on rebaptizing heretics, wrote very many letters on that matter to various persons. Among them these are counted:

On repentance, to Fabius, one letter. On the Sabbath, one book.
To the Romans, one letter. To Hermonion [Hermammon?], one book.
To Saint Sixtus, pope, two letters. On the persecution of Decius, one book.
To Philemon and Dionysius, presbyters, two letters. Against Nepos, the Chiliast, one book.
To Dionysius after he became pope, two letters. Against Sabellius, one book.
To Novatian the heretic, one letter. To Ammon, bishop of [Berenice?], one letter.
[unclear: Dionysius Novatianus]. To Pope Dionysius, one book.
To Dionysius and Didymus, one letter. To Thelephorus, one letter.
To the Laodiceans, on repentance, one letter. To Euphranon, one letter.
To Origen, on martyrdom, one letter. A canon on repentance, one book.
On the order of offences, one letter. On nature, to Timothy, one book.
To the Alexandrians, on exile, one letter. On temptations, one book.
On Easter, one book. Commentaries on Ecclesiastes, one book.
To Bishop Heraclas in Egypt, one book. On Jewish foods, one book.

Several letters of his to Basilides are also reported. A distinguished letter of his Against Paul of Samosata is extant, which he had written a few days before his death. He also composed many other things for ecclesiastical use, which are unknown to us. He flourished under the rulers Gallus and Volusianus, in the year of the Lord 255.

Novatian, presbyter of the Roman church, having attempted to usurp the episcopal chair against Cornelius, and being unable to do so, stirred up the first schism in the church and established the heresy of the Novatians, refusing to receive apostates who repented, and rebaptizing those duly baptized. The author of this error was Novatus, Cyprian’s presbyter. He wrote:

On Easter, one book. On Jewish foods, one book.
On the Sabbath, one book. On earnestness, one book.
On Circumcision, one book. On Attalus, one book.
On the Priest, one book. On the Holy Trinity, one book.
On Prayer, one book. Several letters to various persons.

He is also said to have written some other things besides, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished in the times of Emperor Philip, in the year of the Lord 260.

Malchion, presbyter of the church of Antioch, a learned and most eloquent man, since indeed he taught rhetoric in that same city for many years with the greatest distinction, published some excellent little works which in his own time seemed to contribute greatly to the defense of the Christian faith against heretics. Of these there is extant a notable work of dialogues:

Against Paul of Samosata, one book.
To Pope Dionysius from the synod, one letter.

He flourished under the rulers Claudius and Aurelian, in the year of the Lord 270.

Victorinus, bishop of Pictavium, a man very learned in the divine Scriptures and trained in Greek and Latin eloquence, wrote many excellent little works, in which he splendidly exercised his talent. He was also a distinguished preacher of the divine word, and it is recorded that at last he was crowned with martyrdom for the faith of Christ. Of his writings the following are reported:

On Genesis, one book. On Habakkuk, one book.
On Exodus, one book. On Ecclesiastes, one book.
On Leviticus, one book. On the Song of Songs, one book.
On the prophet Isaiah, one book. On the Apocalypse, one book.
On Ezek202 *The Abbot of Sponheim*

On Ezekiel, one book.
And many other things. He flourished in the times of the emperors Valerian and Gallienus, in the year of the Lord 270.

Pamphilus, priest of Eusebius of Caesarea, out of love for the Scriptures gathered so many books at Caesarea that at that time no library in all the earth was more celebrated. Indeed, he copied out with his own hand a great part of the books of Origen and placed them in that same Caesarean library. From him Eusebius obtained the surname Pamphili. But before Eusebius began to write, he wrote some little works of no contemptible authority. Of these I have found only:

Against the Mathematicians, one book.
An Apology for Origen, one book.

He is also said to have written certain letters full of faith and learning. At last, after blessed studies and many labors for the Church of God, he was crowned with martyrdom for the faith of Christ at Caesarea in Palestine, under the persecution of Maximian, who ruled around the year of the Lord 240.

Anatolius of Alexandria, bishop of Laodicea in Syria, a man skilled in the divine Scriptures and second to none in secular letters in his time, a distinguished rhetorician, astronomer, and geometer, left many splendid little works of his genius; yet very few of them have come to our knowledge. There survives his notable volume entitled:

On Easter, one book.
On Arithmetical Instruction, ten books.

He flourished under the emperors Probus and Carus, in the year 285.

Archelaus, bishop of Mesopotamia in Syria, a learned man and acute disputant, wrote some little works in the Syriac language, which are rarely found among the Latins. He vigorously disputed against Mani, the heresiarch coming out of Persia, and confounded all his arguments, although he was unable to recall him from error. He wrote that same disputation:

Against Mani, one book.

Other works are unknown to us. He flourished under the emperors Aurelian and Probus, in the year of the Lord 280.

Lucian, priest of the church of Antioch, a man of such learning and eloquence that, learned and eloquent, he was of excellent ability in delivering homilies to the people, and venerable no less for his life than for his knowledge of the Scriptures, was crowned with martyrdom for the faith of Christ under the persecution of Maximian. He was buried at Helenopolis in Bithynia. Among other things he wrote:

On Our Faith, one book.

And various other treatises, sermons, homilies, and letters. He flourished under the emperor Maximian, in the year of the Lord 240.

Pierius, priest of the church of Alexandria, a noble and most learned man, was called the younger Origen; he was most excellent in delivering homilies to the people. Under Theonas, bishop of the Alexandrians, shining forth as most renowned in life and doctrine, he was a distinguished cultivator of voluntary poverty for love of Christ and an admirable teacher of the people. He wrote countless treatises, which nevertheless have not come to our knowledge. There survives his very long discourse delivered to the people on the vigil of Easter:

On the Prophet Hosea, one book.

He flourished under the emperor Diocletian, in the year of the Lord 290.

Phileas, bishop of the city of Thebaid in Egypt, a noble and most learned man, distinguished no less in character than in knowledge of the Scriptures, after many labors and various treatises published for the benefit of the faithful, at last under the emperor Maximian flew away to heaven as a martyr for the faith of Christ. Of his writings there survives a disputation held:

Against an Unjust Judge, one book.
On the Praise of Martyrs.

The other things he wrote are unknown to us, although many are reported by the fathers. He flourished under the emperor Maximian, in the year of the Lord 240.

Arnobius, priest, philosopher, and distinguished rhetorician, while he was still a pagan teaching rhetoric, was called by divine mercy and began to profess himself a Christian. And when, going to the bishops, he sought to be baptized, they did not believe him, fearing that a man then swollen with secular eloquence was attempting to mock the sacraments of the faith; and therefore they deferred their judgment. But Arnobius, seeing that no trust was being placed in him, as proof of his sincerity wrote and offered to the bishops a notable volume:

Against the Nations, seven books.
Also On the Psalter, one book.

*On Ecclesiastical Writers*

*On Rhetorical Instruction*, one book.

He also published many other works which have not come to my knowledge.

He taught rhetoric in Africa under the emperor Diocletian, and had many excellent and noble pupils, who became very learned men. He therefore flourished in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 300.

John Climacus, which in Latin means Scholasticus, abbot of Mount Sinai, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, outstanding in talent, gentle and humble, devout and most holy in life and conduct, when he was still sixteen years old, abandoned the world with its delights, and most earnestly sought and obtained permission to become a monk in the said monastery. Then after nineteen years, when he had already learned, according to the rule of monks, to fight and conquer as a solitary, with the permission of his abbot he sought the wilderness, in which for many years he lived alone with God in all holiness. Finally, when his most holy life had become known to all, by the unanimous consent of all he was elected abbot and, though resisting, was called back to the monastery. He wrote to John, abbot of Raithu, a very celebrated work, very suitable for the instruction of monks, containing thirty sermons, which is entitled:

*On the Thirty Steps*, one book. “From the good and above the good.”

*To the Shepherd*, one sermon, one book. “In the lower book indeed.”

Several letters to monks, one book.

And certain other things.

In certain places, especially where he treats of the impassibility of the mortified spiritual man, he is criticized by modern theologians, as may be seen in certain treatises in John Gerson. He flourished around the times of Constantine, Constantius, and Constans, brother emperors, who reigned in the year of the Lord 346.

Ildephonsus, bishop of the see of Toledo after Saint Eugenius, a man very learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular literature either, excellent in meter and subtle in talent in prose, eloquent in speech, and above all the bishops of his time fluent and eloquent, worthy of God and most holy in life and conduct. For he was endowed with constant fear of God, devout in religion, overflowing with compunction, grave in his gait, praiseworthy in integrity, singular in pastoral patience, distinguished in talent for disputation, supreme in wisdom. When he was still a boy, touched by the divine spirit, despising the things of the world and the affections of his parents, he sought the Agaliense monastery, and for many years conducted himself fittingly in it as a monk. He also built a convent of virgins in the little estate of Dehbia, which he endowed from his parents’ resources. Then, having been made abbot of the Agaliense monastery, he trained the morals of the monks, managed the property, and preserved the life. After this, by royal violence, he was brought back to Toledo, and there, after the death of his predecessor, was appointed bishop. He wrote many distinguished little works. Of these the following are reported:

*On the Holy Trinity*, one book. *On the Knowledge of Baptism*, one book.

*On His Own Weakness*, one book. *On the Progress of the Spiritual Desert*, one book.

*On the Virginity of Saint Mary*, one book. Hymns of various kinds, one book.

Annotations on the daily office, one book. Various sermons, one book.

Annotations on sacred matters, one book. Many epigrams, one book.

Annotations on the sacraments, one book. Also *On the Mass*, one book.

And many other things. When this most blessed bishop Ildephonsus had completed to the end the book on the virginity of Mary, the most pure Mother of God, whom he was always accustomed to serve most devoutly with all the zeal he could, the most sacred Lady of the world appeared to him and affirmed [unclear]. But he, wishing to honor her more highly, established that her solemnity should be celebrated each year on the eighth day before the Nativity of the Lord; this solemnity has now prevailed, so that throughout the whole Church of the faithful it is celebrated in honor of her most pure conception, on the sixth day before the Ides of December. Hence again the blessed Mother of God appeared to him and brought him a priestly vestment, which we call an alb, and that cathedral [unclear], concerning which many wondrous and glorious things are told. He flourished.

Firmianus Lactantius, once a hearer and disciple of Arnobius the rhetor, a man abundantly learned in secular letters and nobly instructed in the divine Scriptures, so that in the art of speaking he easily obtained first place after Cicero: he first taught rhetoric gloriously at Nicomedia, then at Rome under Diocletian, after being summoned by him. There, when through lack of pupils he had fallen into poverty, at last, already an old man, he was made in Gaul the tutor of Caesar Crispus, son of Constantine.

He wrote *The Abbot of Spanheim*

He wrote many excellent volumes. Of these the following are reported:

On the Divine Institutes, one book. It begins: “Great and excellent.”
On the Origin of Error, one book. It begins: “Although in the first book.”
On False Wisdom, one book. It begins: “I should wish it to be declared to me.”
On True Wisdom, one book. It begins: “As I was thinking, and with my mind.”
On Justice, to Constantine, one book. It begins: “There is no doubt with me.”
On True Worship, one book. It begins: “That was its duty.”
On the Blessed Life, one book. It begins: “It is well.”
On the Anger of God, to Donatus, one book. It begins: “I have often observed, Do[natus].”
On the Workmanship of God, one book. It begins: “How very little at rest I am.”
To Asclepiades, one book.
Letters to Probus, four books.
On Persecution, one book.
Symposium, in hexameter verse, one book.
Letters to Severus, two books.
Entitled The Grammarian, one book.
An Epitome against the Gentiles, one book. It begins: “There is a happy place in the first.”
On Paradise, in hexameter, one book.

He is said to have written not a few other works besides, but they have not come into our hands. He flourished under the emperor Constantine, to whom he was very dear, in the year 320.

Eusebius, bishop of the church of Caesarea in Palestine, surnamed Pamphilus, formerly a disciple of the eunuch Dorotheus, a most learned man, very devoted to the divine Scriptures, and, together with the martyr Pamphilus, a most diligent restorer of the ecclesiastical library: although he was an Arian, when he came to the first council of the fathers held at Nicaea, he put aside his error and, following the opinion of the fathers, at their command composed the creed which is called Nicene, and offered it to them to be read and confirmed as testimony of his own most pure faith. In it he powerfully crushed the errors of the Arians, and nothing has been either added to or taken from his edition, but it is sung publicly in the Church of God down to the present day. After this, persevering in the orthodox faith, he was most holily brought to his end. He wrote many excellent volumes in Greek. Of these the following are reported among the Latins, namely:

Against Porphyry, thirty books.
Explanations of the Gospel, twenty books.
On Isaiah the Prophet, [fourteen?] books. It begins: “Since what is for Christians.”
On the Preparation of the Gospel, ten books.
Successions of the Saints.
Ecclesiastical History, one book. It begins: “Moses of the Hebrew people.”
Epitome of the Chronicle, one book.
On the Disagreement of the Evangelists, one book.
Theophany, one book.
Apology for Origen, six books.
Topics, three books.
On the Whole Psalter, one book.
On the Life of Pamphilus, one book.
Martyrology, one book.

He also composed many other works which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under the great emperor Constantine, to whom he was very dear because of his distinguished learning and the holiness of his life, in the year of the Lord 320.

Rheticus, bishop of the Aedui at Autun, a man devoted to the divine Scriptures and, in his time, a teacher of renowned reputation. He is said to have written not a few little works, and especially commentaries on the divine books, but I recall that few have come to our knowledge, namely:

On the Song of Songs, one book.
Against Novatian, one book.

Saint Jerome censures his exposition on the Song of Songs as foolish. He flourished in Gaul under Constantine the Great, in the year of the Lord 320.

Jacob, surnamed the Wise, bishop of the city of Nisibis of the Persians, a man of great learning and incomparable holiness, one of the number of the confessors who were victorious under the persecutor Maximian, was present at the Council of Nicaea and condemned the most impious Arius by the addition of homoousion. This man of most holy conduct often freed the city entrusted to him from many dangers by his prayers. For the edification of the faithful he wrote not a few little works in the Syrian tongue, of which the following are reported:

On Faith, one book.
On Love of Neighbor, one book.
On General Charity, one book.
On Prayer, one book.
On Fasting, one book.
On Life after Death, one book.
On the Resurrection, one book.
On Patience, one book.
On Humility, one book.
On Satisfaction, one book.
On Penance, one book.
On *On Ecclesiastical Writers*

On Virginity, one book. On the Sense of the Soul, one book.
On Circumcision, one book. On the Blessing of Unleavened Bread, one book.
On Christ, That He Is the Son of God, one book. On Chastity, one book.
Against the Nations, one book. On the Construction of the Tabernacle, one book.
On the Conversion of the Nations, one book. On the Kingdom of the Persians, one book.
On the Persecution of Christians, one book. A Chronicle of the Times, one book.
On the Words of Isaiah, one book.
Thus the whole work just designated comprises 25 books. He flourished under the great emperor Constantine, in the year of the Lord 330.

Methodius, bishop of Olympus in Lycia, and afterward of Tyre, learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, a confessor and distinguished defender of the Christian faith, and a diligent emulator of evangelical perfection, after the publication of many volumes, was crowned with martyrdom for the faith of Christ under the last persecution, or, as others affirm, under Decius and Valerian, at Chalcis in Greece. He wrote, in a polished and well-ordered style, not a few volumes, of which the following are reported:

Against Porphyry, two books. The Symposium on the Ten Virgins, one book.
On the Resurrection, one book. On the Pythoness, one book.
On the Departure of the Soul, one book. On Genesis, one book.
On the Song of Songs, one book. “For it must be known, brothers,” one book.
On the Last Times, one book. Also a Chronicle, one book.

He flourished under the great emperor Constantine, or, as others prefer, under Decius and Valerian, in the year of the Lord 355.

Antonius, monk and abbot, Egyptian by nation, a most holy man and distinguished cultivator of the desert, whose praises the whole world proclaims, furnished to many a rule of religious and blessed life. Although he had not learned letters, he was nevertheless so learned in the divine Scriptures that none of the doctors of his age would presume to put himself before him. He had memory in place of books, understanding and sense in place of letters, grace in place of the study of reading. In the Egyptian language he dictated various letters, of apostolic sense and speech, to different monasteries. Of these, that distinguished one is extant:

To the Arsenoites, one letter. To other monasteries, six letters.

Blessed Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, described his life in an outstanding volume in the Greek language. He flourished under Constantine the Great and during the reigns of his sons, in the year of the Lord 330, shining with many miracles.

Juvencus, priest, Spanish by nation, a noble man and a most learned philosopher, distinguished poet, rhetorician, and theologian, and venerable to the Church no less for his conduct than for his knowledge of the Scriptures, published for the edification of readers many excellent volumes, both in meter and in prose; but few of them have come to my knowledge. I have read the distinguished work which he composed in hexameter and pentameter verses:

On the Four Gospels, four books. “Nothing immortal [unclear].”
On the Sacraments, one book.

The rest which he is said to have composed have not come into our hands. He flourished under Constantine the Great and his sons, in the year of the Lord 350.

Against the Arians, three books. On the Soul, one book.
Almost innumerable Letters, one book.
Against Origen, one book.

He flourished in the times of Constantine and his sons, in the year of the Lord 350.

Athanasius, nineteenth bishop of the city of Alexandria, a holy man and most learned in the divine Scriptures, endured many persecutions from the Arians on behalf of the catholic faith. Indeed the whole world was narrow for him, with the Arians persecuting him everywhere; they nowhere seemed to be wholly secure. For a man’s enemies were those of his own household. Therefore, fleeing from the face of the emperor and of the Arians, he came to the city of Trier in Gaul, and, honorably received by Saint Maximianus the archbishop, for [unclear] years hid with him in a cistern without water, which to this day is shown in the crypt at the monastery of Saint Maximinus in Trier. While lying hidden in this place for many years, as we have said, he did not see the sun, and there the creed “Whoever wishes to be saved” *Abbot of Sponheim* he composed, until at last, betrayed by a certain girl, by the will of God he escaped by flight. If anyone wishes to know his deeds more fully, let him read the Tripartite History. He wrote in the Greek language almost innumerable little works, of which I have found the following among the Latins.

On the Unity of the Trinity, one book. “You, one God, God the Father.”
On the proper persons of the Trinity, one book. “Now through each [unclear].”
On the Assumption of Man, one book. “Just as in one.”
On the Names of the Trinity, one book. “Here now concerning the names of each.”
On the One Substance of the Trinity, one book. “Here, contradicting, the person.”
On the Blessedness of Faith, one book. “I ask of you concerning the one.”
One book. “For which reason most earnestly.”
On the Profession of the Catholic Rule, one book. “Before the beginning of times, above.”
On the Unity of Faith, one book. “When you have read this faith.”
On the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, one book. “To those who say that the Son of God was created.”
On the Trinity and the Holy Spirit, one book. “To the most blessed lord and.”
To Lucifer the Bishop, one book. “The first objection of these men is.”
Against the Objections of the Arians, one book. “When at Nicaea [unclear].”
A Disputation against Arius, etc., one book. “The Arians, behaving childishly.”
Against Valens and Ursatius, one book.
On the Titles of the Psalms, one book. “All things whatsoever our Lord.”
One book. “The letters of holy charity.”
One book. “Of divine worship and of [unclear].”
Book 2. “Even if I have boasted of anything.”
Against the Arians, one book. “Heresies, as many as he himself.”
One book. “Whoever wishes for salvation.”
Against the same, fourteen books. “Paul, and [unclear]. Nor Moy[ses?].”
One book. “The Arians, behaving childishly.”
On the Homoousion of the Father and the Son, one book. “Those who maliciously [treat] divine things.”
Dialogue with an Arian, one book. “It was brought about by the providence of God.”
An Exhortation to Monks, one book. “Even if someone boasts in.”
Life of Saint Antony, one book. “Excellent, in these matters, brothers.”
Symbol of His Faith, one book. “Whoever wishes to be saved.”
On All the Epistles of Paul, fourteen books.
Sermons to the People.
On the Persecution of the Arians, two books. He flourished when Constantine and his brothers were reigning, in the year of the Lord 350.
On His Flight and Exile, one book.
On the Gospel of John, one book.
Many Homilies.
He published several letters to various persons, and also sermons and various treatises, which either have not yet been translated into Latin or have not come to my knowledge. He died in the time of the emperors Valentinian and Valens, in the year of the Lord 379, the forty-sixth year of his priesthood, on the sixth day before the Nones of May, in the seventh indiction.

Theodorus, bishop of Heraclea in Thrace, devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, an outstanding declaimer and a man of polished speech, published commentaries on the sacred volumes that are not to be despised in reading. Of these the following are reported.

On the Psalter, one book.
On the Epistles of Paul, fourteen books.
He is also said to have written some other works, but they have not come to my knowledge. He flourished in the times of Constantine II, in the year of the Lord 340.

Eusebius, bishop of Emesa, a man most learned in the divine writings, and, in delivering homilies to the people, second to none in his own time, a rhetorician and theologian most celebrated in the opinion of all. He is said to have written many, indeed almost countless, little works, but we have been able to find the titles and numbers of only a few, namely:

Against the Gentiles, one book.
Sermons to the People, ten books.
Against the Jews, one book.
Many Homilies, one book.
He flourished when Constantine and his brothers were reigning, in the year of the Lord 350.

Triphilius, bishop of Cyprus or of Leucontheon, a man most learned in both divine and secular writings, and easily the most eloquent prelate of his age, is said to have written not a few volumes and to have expounded the divine Scriptures in many ways, but I do not recall that any of his works have come into our hands. His exposition is reported:

On the Song of Songs, one book.
He flourished in the times of the emperor Constantius, in the year of the Lord 340.
