He was a man most learned in the divine scriptures and distinguished by the adornment of many virtues; being continually devoted to almsgiving and holy works, he shone with no small reputation for sanctity. At Rome, after holding a synod of fifty bishops, he established certain measures for ecclesiastical propriety. He also wrote certain necessary works. Of these I have found only the following:

A synodal decree, one book: “Since the more religious Holy Spirit.”
To the bishops of the province of Tarragona, one letter: “After your letters.”
To Ascanius, bishop of Tarragona, one letter: “The grace of God toward us.”
Concerning the Council of Nicaea, one letter.
Concerning the Council of Ephesus, one letter.
Concerning the Council of Chalcedon, one letter.
Letters to various persons, one book.

He died under Emperor Leo, in the year of the Lord 468, in the sixth indiction, on the ninth day before the Kalends of March; Simplicius succeeded him.

Eusebius, bishop of Milan, very learned in the holy scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, was both familiar and dear to the most blessed pontiff Leo. Fighting and writing bravely for the holy Catholic faith against heretics, he is said to have published some works for the edification of the faithful, but they have not come to my knowledge. For I have seen only one letter of his, which he is said to have written in matters of faith:

To Saint Pope Leo, one letter: “Having returned, with the Lord granting it.”

He flourished under Emperor Marcian, in the year of the Lord 450.

Asclepius the African, bishop of the territory of Vaga, a studious and learned man:

Innumerable homilies to the people, one book.
Many homilies unknown to us.
And many other things unknown to us.

He flourished under Theodosius the Younger, in the year of the Lord 440.

Prosper, bishop of Reggio after Faventius, an Aquitanian by nation, a man in [unclear], one book.
Against the Arians, one book.
V2 232 *The Abbot of Sponheim* was most learned in the divine Scriptures, and trained in secular letters, excellent in verse and prose, eloquent in speech, deep in understanding, subtle in intellect, vigorous in assertion, and most holy in life and conduct. He was once notary of blessed Pope Leo the Great, and composed many letters in his person. He also wrote many distinguished little works from his own vein. Of these I have found only the following.

From the Sentences of blessed Augustine the bishop, in hexameter and pentameter verses, mixed with prose, a very beautiful work which he wished to entitle:

Epigrams, one book. “While it pleases [unclear].”
On the Contemplative Life, three books. “The contemplative life in …”
On Free Choice, one book. “To the lord brother, most beloved, Ru…”
Responses to the Chapters of the Gauls, one book. “The doctrine which holy …”
To the Objections of the Vincentians, one book. “Certain Christian and …”
To the Excerpts of the Genoese, one book. “In the books of blessed memory …”
A large Sum of 330 propositions, one book. “True knowledge is that which …”
Against Cassian on Free Choice, one book.
A Chronicle of Histories, one book.
Letters to Various Persons, one book.
On Illustrious Men, one book.
On the Captivity of Rome, one book.

He is said besides to have written some other works, but they have not come into our hands. He flourished in the time of the great emperor Leo, in the year of the Lord 460. His feast is celebrated on the seventh day before the Kalends of July.

VICTOR, bishop of the Mauretanian city of Cartenna, learned in the holy Scriptures and an outstanding declaimer of sermons, a notable persecutor of heretics, is said to have composed many volumes, in which he both instructed the devout people and vigorously crushed those erring about the faith. Of these, the following are reported:

Against the Arians, one book.
Against the Donatists, one book.
A Consolatory Work to Basil, one book.
On Penance also, one book.
Homilies to the People, one book.

He also published not a few other works, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under Marcian Augustus, in the year of the Lord 450.

VICTORINUS, an Aquitanian by nation, a man very studious in the divine Scriptures and most learned in secular letters, is said to have left certain little works, which have not yet come to my knowledge at all. At the command of Pope Hilary he wrote, for finding the date of Easter:

The Great Cycle of 532 Years, one book.

This is called the great cycle of 532 years; when they have elapsed, all the calculations of the luminaries return to the same point. Dionysius the abbot later corrected it, and it has endured down to our own age, although in some points it has failed. That Victorinus also wrote certain letters. He flourished under the emperor Leo, in the year of the Lord 460, and wrote his cycle under Pope Hilary, in the third year of his pontificate.

PETER, priest of the church of Edessa, learned and practiced in the holy Scriptures, obtained an altogether excellent power and talent for declaiming homilies to the people, so much so that in his times he had no equal. He wrote many distinguished volumes in the Syrian language. Of these, only a very few titles have come to my knowledge:

Commentaries on the Psalms, one book.
He also played in meter on the Psalms, one book.

He composed and delivered almost infinite homilies to the people, which are rarely found among us. Nor is the number of his treatises certain to us. He flourished under the emperor Marcian, in the year of the Lord 459.

SABATIUS, bishop of a Gallic province, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and sufficiently trained in secular letters, subtle and keen in intellect, often fought against the poison of heretics, both by writing and by disputing. Hence, asked by a certain Secunda, a virgin dedicated to Christ, he wrote a notable and memorable volume:

Against Marcion and Valentinus, one book.
Against Eunomius and Aetius, one book.

He also published some other works, but they have not yet come to my knowledge. He flourished under Theodosius the Younger, around the year of the Lord 440.

URSINUS, a monk, learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of humane letters, subtle in intellect and cautious in speech, [unclear] many treatises for the benefit of the faithful *On Ecclesiastical Writers*

He is said to have composed [them], but I do not recall that any of them has ever come into our hands. His work against those who rebaptize persons once duly baptized is reported; its title is:

*On the Manner of Rebaptizing Heretics*, one book.

He flourished, as I have found, under Theodosius the Younger, in the year of the Lord 440.

Julian, bishop of the church of Toledo in Spain, a Moor by nation, to whom Saint Prosper is said to have written three books *On Contemplation*, was a man very learned in the divine Scriptures and sufficiently instructed in secular studies, scholastic in speech, clear in understanding. He wrote many notable volumes, of which the following are reported:

Eight books.

*On Holy Virginity*, one book. *On the Nature of the Soul*, one book.

*Questions on the Resurrection*, one book. *On Contempt of the World*, one book.

*Prognosticon of the Future Age*, three books. “The faith of the nascent Church.”

*On Vices and Virtues*, one book. *Letters to Various Persons*, one book.

He is also said to have composed some other works which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under the emperor Marcian, in the year of the Lord 450.

Victorianus Buconius, bishop of the city of Castelliana in Mauretania, a man exercised by constant study in the divine Scriptures and not moderately learned in the disciplines of secular letters, a most powerful hammer of heretics and an outstanding [unclear] of the faithful peoples, is said to have written many treatises in defense of the Catholic faith. Of these the principal ones are reported as follows:

One book. *Against the Arians*, two books.

*Against All Heretics*, three books. Also *On the Sacraments*, one book.

He flourished under the emperor Marcian, in the year of the Lord 460.

Musaeus, priest of the church of Marseilles, being most learned in the divine Scriptures and refined by most subtle exercise in their meanings, scholastic and polished in language, at the exhortation of Saint Venerius the bishop excerpted from the holy Scriptures readings and responsories suited to the individual feast days of the whole year, and arranged psalms suited to each season to be sung in the Church. He also wrote an excellent little work to Eustasius the bishop.

Seven books. Several homilies to the people.

*Of Sacraments* [unclear]

And certain other things. He flourished under the rulers Marcian and Leo, in the year of the Lord 480.

Vincentius, a priest, a Gaul by nation, much exercised in the divine writings, made [unclear] by love, a man very learned in secular letters, distinguished in skill of speaking. In his writings, using syllogisms more than the authorities of the divine readings, while he inveighs too much against Nestorius, he is said to favor the dogma of Timothy, and by his ambiguities he suspends the mind from agreement with the Council of Chalcedon; nor does he think one should acquiesce in the view that the Son of God, after the incarnation, consists of two natures. Of his writings, however, there is reported:

One book. *Against Heretics*, one book.

Commentaries on the Psalms, and certain other things.

He flourished under the emperor Marcian, in the year of the Lord 510.

Cyrus, Alexandrian by origin, a physician by art, from a philosopher made a monk for love of Christ, a man very learned in secular letters, distinguished in skill of speaking. In his writings, using syllogisms more than the authority of the divine readings, while he inveighs too much against Nestorius, he is said to favor the dogma of Timothy, and by his ambiguities he suspends the mind from agreement with the Council of Chalcedon; nor does he think one should acquiesce in the view that the Son of God, after the incarnation, consists of two natures. He wrote letters [unclear] of wisdom [unclear]. To Claudius, bishop of Vienne, he wrote several letters composed with [unclear] wisdom. To Marcellus the priest.

One book. *Against Heretics*, one book.

He flourished under Leo Augustus, in the year of the Lord 490.

Salvianus, priest of the church of Marseilles, a man very learned in the divine writings and sufficiently instructed in secular letters, teacher of the bishops of his time, wrote in scholastic and clear language many and various treatises; of these the following [unclear]:

Homilies made to bishops, one book. Also *On the Sacraments*, one book.

Several homilies to the people, one book. He flourished under Ze[unclear]

He also published many other works which have by no means come to my knowledge. He flourished under the emperor Zeno, in the year of the Lord 680.

Samuel, priest of the church of Edessa, by constant exercise in the divine Scriptures *Abbot of Sponheim*

[unclear], an outstanding preacher of homilies to the people, skilled in the Greek and Syriac languages, flourished first at Edessa; afterwards, coming to Constantinople, he was held there in great esteem and ended his last day. He wrote, in both Greek and Syriac, almost innumerable small works. Of these very few have come to my knowledge. For I have found only:

Against the Nestorians, one book. Against the Eutychians, one book.
Against the Timotheans, one book.

He flourished under the emperor Zeno, in the year of the Lord 480.

Gennadius, bishop of the city of Constantinople, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, subtle in intellect and eloquent in speech, wrote in Greek a number of small works on the sacred volumes, but they have by no means come into our hands. For he was an outstanding preacher of homilies, and distinguished no less for his life than for his knowledge of the Scriptures. Among other things, however, a work of his commentaries is reported:

On Daniel the prophet, one book.

Many homilies to the people, one book. He died under Leo, the first emperor who reigned, in the year of the Lord 460.

Claudius, bishop of Vienne, to whom Salvian the priest composed one book, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and most highly trained in secular letters, famous no less for holiness than for knowledge, shone forth in his own times. Because of frequent earthquakes, he first instituted the litanies, which the Roman Church thereafter undertook to continue. He also wrote letters. He wrote:

On the State of the Soul, three books.

And certain other things. He flourished under the emperor Zeno, in the year of the Lord 480. And lest the name Claudius offend anyone who is unaware, let him know that the same man is called Mamertus.

Sidonius, bishop of the Auverni, learned in the divine Scriptures and, in the judgement of all, the most learned man of his time in the disciplines of secular letters, excellent in verse and prose, subtle in intellect and eloquent in speech, wrote many distinguished little works both in meter and in unbound discourse. Of these I have been able to find only those which are set down below, namely:

Panegyric to the emperor Anthemius, one book. Auspicio et numero.
Panegyric to Julius Valerius, one book. Concepe praeteritos.
Panegyric to his father-in-law, one book. Phoebe peragrato tam.
To Felix, one book. Dic dic quod petoma.
Epithalamium for Ruricius and Hiberix, one book. Inter cyaneas epieram.
Epithalamium for Polemius, one book. Forte procellosi reme.
Eucharisticon to Faustus, one book. Phebum et ter ternas.
Also of epigrams, one book. Quatuor ante dies.
To Pontius Leontius Burgus, one book. Bistonii regis stabulum.
In Praise of the City of Narbonne, one book. Salve Narbo potens.
Letters to various persons, nine books. Diu precipis domine ma.

He also wrote many other compositions, brief indeed, but sufficiently learned; for the sake of brevity I have passed over their titles. He flourished in the times of the emperor Zeno, in the year of the Lord 480.

Simplicius, pope, by nation a Tiburtine, after Saint Hilary presided over the Roman and universal Church for [unclear] years. He was a learned and holy man, who appeared not only simple according to his name, but also upright, turning away from evil and fearing God. He restored many churches that had fallen down from extreme age, issued decrees necessary for the Christian commonwealth, and wrote some things for the edification of the faithful. Of these I have read only:

To John, bishop of Ravenna, one letter. Si quis esse intuitus Eccle.
To Florentius and Equitius, bishops, one letter. Relatio nominis vestrae.
To Severus, bishop, one letter.

But he also wrote many other very useful letters, which I have not yet seen.

He died under the emperor Zeno, in the year of the Lord 483, in the sixth indiction, on the sixth Nones of March, and was numbered among the saints.

Servusdei, bishop of a certain church whose city-name I have not been able to find, a man learned in the divine Scriptures by constant exercise and rich in the reading of the ancients, subtle in intellect, clear in speech, is said to have fashioned a number of little works. Of these there exists a volume furnished with sacred Scriptures, against those who say that Christ, while living in this life, did not see the Father with his bodily eyes. The heading of this work is:

That the Son Saw the Father, one book.

He also wrote certain other things.

In this *On Ecclesiastical Writers*

In this work he shows that the Son of God, even from the hour of his conception in the womb of the Virgin Mary by the Holy Spirit, always saw God the Father with his bodily eyes, and thereafter, now clothed in human flesh. He is said to have flourished under Emperor Leo, in the year of the Lord 480.

VICTOR, bishop of Capua, learned in the Holy Scriptures, sufficiently imbued with secular letters, an outstanding theologian and computist, keen in intellect, renowned in eloquence, is said to have written some little works on the sacred volumes, but very few of them have come to my knowledge. He refuted the error of Victorius of Aquitaine, who, at the order of Pope Hilary, writing Paschal cycles, taught that Easter was to be celebrated on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May in the year of the Lord 455, whereas it was more correctly to be celebrated that year on the seventh day before the Kalends of May. Therefore, when this occasion arose, he wrote:

On Easter, one book. One Gospel from Four, one book.

He flourished under Zeno Augustus, in the year of the Lord 480.

CEREALIS, an African bishop, a man very skilled in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular disciplines, was asked by Maximinus, bishop of the Arians, whether he could establish the consubstantiality of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit by a few testimonies of divine Scripture, without, at least, the assertion of disputation. He replied, not with a few testimonies, as that man mockingly had requested, but with many testimonies from both Testaments, composing a distinguished work:

Against the Arians, one book. He also wrote other works:
Against the Timotheans, one book. Several Homilies to the People, one book.
And many other things.

He flourished in the times of Emperor Leo, in the year of the Lord 460.

JOHN, priest of the church of Antioch, rich in his reading of the ancient Scriptures, after he had taught grammar at Antioch for some years, began to wish to profess himself a cleric; and, made a priest by legitimate succession, he applied himself to divine readings. Having become a teacher through these, he was so powerful in delivering homilies that he had no equal in his time. He wrote a sufficiently learned volume:

Eclogues, one book. The lands of the Ethiopians.
On the Harmony of the Scriptures, one book. Concerning the rest I have found nothing.

He flourished in the year of the Lord 480, under Zeno Augustus, under whom he died.

THEODULUS, priest, an Italian by nation, a man learned in the divine writings and nobly instructed in secular letters, coming from Italy into [Caelesyria?], is recorded to have been ordained there first priest, then bishop; and by writing and composing much he transmitted his name to posterity. Of his little works I have found only a metrical work on the miracles of the Old Testament, [unclear] with the fables of the poets.

The lands of the Ethiopians.
Concerning the rest I have found nothing.

EUGENIUS, bishop of Carthage in Africa, a learned man, public confessor of the undivided Holy Trinity, suffered many injuries from the Arians under Huneric, king of the Vandals, who after his father Genseric was persecuting Christians in Africa. For with many other bishops, their tongues having been cut out, he was sent into exile. He wrote some little works full of faith and learning. Of these the following are reported:

Exposition of the Catholic Faith, one book. A Debate Held with the Arians.
Apologetic for the Faith, one book. To His Church, when he was going into exile, one letter.

He is said nonetheless to have written other things, but they have not come to my knowledge.

He flourished in the times of Augustus Zeno, in the year of the Lord 480.

FELIX, the third pope, Roman by nation, after the pontiff Saint Simplicius sat in the chair of Peter for eight years. He was a good, learned, and holy man, who, inflamed with zeal for the faith, condemned Peter and Acacius, Eutychian bishops, relegating them into exile. For this reason, holding a synod at Rome, he established many things for ecclesiastical usefulness and wrote:

Synodal Decree, one book. To Flavius Poetius, [unclear].
Several Decretal Letters, one book.

He died under Emperor Anastasius, in the year of the Lord 493, the first indiction.

GENNADIUS, priest of the church of Marseilles, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, perfectly instructed in Greek as well as Latin eloquence, wrote many little works and translated not a few volumes of the ancient fathers from Greek into the Latin language. Concerning his own writings, however, he himself, at the end of [On Illustrious Men?], [unclear]:

On His Faith, to Pope Gelasius, one book. Against Nestorius, six books.

*The Abbot of Spanheim*

Against Eutyches, 9 books.
Against Pelagius, 3 books.
Against all heresies, 8 books.
On Illustrious Men, 1 book. “James, by surname.”
On the Heresy of the Thousand Years, 1 book.
He wrote these and certain other works, but they have not yet come to my knowledge. He flourished under the emperor Anastasius, in the year of the Lord 490.

Gelasius, Pope the First, an African by nation, sat after Felix in the pontificate for four years. He was a holy man and very learned in the divine scriptures. Soon at the beginning of his pontifical office he sent into exile the Manichaeans whom he found in the city, and publicly burned their books at the basilica of Saint Mary Major. He established many things for ecclesiastical utility and wrote very many works against heretics. Among his works the following are cited:

Synodal Decree, 1 book. “A necessary distinction of things.”
Against the Arians, 2 books.
Against Eutyches and Nestorius, 5 books.
Hymns in the manner of Ambrose, 1 book.
Letters to various persons, 1 book.
Several weighty prayers.
And he arranged certain other graduals, alleluias, and tracts, with prefaces suitable for the Mass, and separated the authentic books of the holy fathers from the apocryphal, as is found in Distinction 13, “Sancta Rom.” He died while Anastasius Augustus was emperor, in the year of the Lord 496.

Faustus, formerly abbot of the monastery of Lerins, bishop of Riez in Gaul, was indeed a learned and eloquent man, but stained by the Pelagian error; hence his little works are counted among the apocrypha, as is clear in Distinction 15, “Sancta Rom.” At length, corrected and amended by blessed Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe, he abandoned the error and returned to the truth of the catholic faith. As proof of this matter he published an excellent volume against his former errors, which he entitled On the Grace of God. Of his works the following are cited. The same volume:

On the Grace of God, 1 book.
Against the Arians, 1 book.
Against the Anthropomorphites, 1 book. “The catholic faith in one...”
On the Holy Spirit, [unclear].
To Felix the prefect, 1 book.
To Gratus the deacon, against Nesto[rius?].
Several homilies to the people.
He flourished under the emperor Anastasius, in the year of the Lord 480.

Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe in Africa, a man most learned in the divine scriptures and nobly instructed in secular letters, was subtle in intellect, deep in understanding, sweet in speech, eloquent and polished, very ready for teaching, sharp for arguing, fit and most gentle for persuading. He shone forth most brightly no less by holiness of life than by knowledge of the scriptures. He wrote many excellent volumes, of which the following are cited:

On the Grace of God and Free Will, 7 books.
On the Holy Trinity, 1 book.
Disputation with King Thrasamund, 1 book.
On the Remission of Sins, 1 book.
On Predestination, to Monimus, 3 books. “[unclear] of a very dear son.”
To Ferrandus the deacon, 1 book. “Your letter, holy brother and [unclear].”
On Conjugal Continence, 1 book. “Your letter, holy [unclear].”
On Virginity, to Proba, 1 book. “With spiritual desire and...”
On Prayer, to the same, 1 book. “Lord, in Christ, very many...”
On Charity, to Abbot Eugipius, 1 book. “Would that, holy brother, such great...”
On Penitence, to Venantia, 1 book. “As the true light in no way...”
“Some months ago,” 1 book.
To Theodore the senator, 1 book.
“Adam without a, Abel without b,” etc., 1 book.
On the Mystery of the Mediator, 3 books.
On Faith, to Donatus.
Letters to various persons, 1 book.
On the Sacrament of the Incarnation.
Also innumerable homilies, 1 book.
Moralizations of Virgilian [unclear]. “He was indeed awaiting with gentle...”
On the Passion of the Lord, 1 book.
On the Immensity of the Son of God, 1 book.
But it should be noted that the title of the book On Adam without a *On Ecclesiastical Writers*

is the title. A book without letters [unclear]: on Adam without b, on Cain without c, and so with the rest according to the sequence of the letters. But in the book whose title is *Exposition of the Virgilian Content According to the Moral Philosophers*, with marvelous industry he sought gold in the mud, so to speak, and found it, when he bent the poet’s work toward a physical interpretation. He wrote this work to a certain deacon; another, on mythologies, to Catus, a priest of Carthage; and *On the Obscure Expressions of the Ancients* to Calcidius the grammarian, already an old man, while he himself was still young and a teacher and director in a school of humane letters. He flourished in the time of Thrasamund, king of the Vandals, persecutor of the Catholic churches, under the emperor Anastasius. A.D. 500.

Ferrandus, deacon of the Church of Carthage, to whom some little works of the above-mentioned Saint Fulgentius are extant, was a man both zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, and venerable no less for the holiness of his conduct than for his doctrine. He is said to have forged certain volumes of lively talent, of which only the following have come to my knowledge.

To Reginus the count.

*On the Seven Rules of Innocence*, one book. “For the toil of social life.”

To Saint Fulgentius, one epistle.

*Letters to Various Persons*, one book.

He flourished with Fulgentius under the emperor Anastasius. A.D. 500.

Anastasius II, pope, a Roman by nation, sat after the holy pontiff Gelasius for one year and ten months. He was indeed a learned man, but, seduced by Acacius, bishop of Constantinople, not long afterward paid the deserved penalties of his error. For when he wished to obey the necessity of nature, wretchedly struck by God, he poured out his intestines together with his excrement, as is clear in Distinction 19, “Anastasius.” And he was the second infamous pope. He wrote to the emperor Anastasius:

One epistle. “The beginning of the pontificate.”

*On the Peace of the Church*.

He is also said to have written other letters, but they have not come into our hands. He died, struck by divine judgment, when he had secretly wished to recall from exile Acacius, bishop of Constantinople, condemned and cast out by the Church, under Anastasius Augustus. A.D. 498.

Paschasius, deacon of the Roman Church, a learned and holy man, father of the poor, wholly intent on the distribution of alms, was of such virtue and holiness that Pope Gregory writes in the fourth book of the *Dialogues* that a demoniac was cured after his death by the touch of his dalmatic. Saint Germanus, bishop of Capua, saw his soul in the pains of purgatory, tormented for nothing other than that in the election of Pope Symmachus he himself had rather chosen Laurentius, and had persevered in this opinion until death, although peacefully. He wrote, as Gregory attests, a notable volume against the errors of the Greeks:

*On the Holy Spirit*, one book.

And certain other things.

He flourished under the emperor Anastasius. A.D. 500.

Symmachus, pope, a Sardinian by nation, a learned and holy man, obtained the pontificate after Anastasius, not without discord from the party of Laurentius, and sat for fifteen years and six months. A man merciful and munificent toward the poor, he loved the clergy, enriched churches, and drove heretics from the city. In a synod held at Rome of one hundred and twenty bishops, he canonically cleared himself of the crimes charged against him, and thrust Peter, bishop of Ravenna, with his accomplices into exile. He wrote certain letters and little works not to be despised. Of these I have found:

One book. “Because of the frequent [unclear].”

*Decree of the First Synod*, one book. “When together at blessed...”

*Decree of the Roman Synod*.

*The Fourth Synod Held*.

*Acts of Another Synod*, one book. “Indeed well, brotherly...”

*On the [unclear] of Clerics*.

*Letters to Various Persons*.

He died under the emperor Anastasius. A.D. 515, in the [unclear] indiction, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of August. Pope Hormisdas succeeded him.

Symmachus the patrician, Roman senator and consul, father-in-law of Boethius, a distinguished philosopher and rhetorician and a magnificent worshipper of the Christian faith, was banished into exile at Pavia together with Boethius by Theoderic, king of Italy, on suspicion of aiming at liberty; and not much later he cruelly had him slain. Since he was a learned and most eloquent man, he is said to have composed some little works, of which I was able to find only one volume, brief indeed, but elegant:

*Letters to Various Persons*, one book. “Surely you laugh because concerning...”

238 *The Abbot of Sponheim*

Concerning the rest I have seen nothing. He died under the emperor Anastasius, killed by Theodoric, king of Italy, at Ravenna, in the year of the Lord 524, indiction 2.

AVITUS, bishop of Vienne, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and most skilled in secular letters, a very distinguished theologian, rhetorician, and poet, who in his time was held in esteem no less for holiness of life than for learning in the Scriptures. He wrote not a few small works, both in verse and in prose, but very few have come to my knowledge. Of these, the following are said to have been composed in heroic and elegant meter:

On the Origin of the World, one book.
On Original Sin, one book.
On the Sentence of God, one book.
On the Flood of the World, one book.
On the Crossing of the Red Sea, one book.
On Virginity, to Fuscina his sister, one book.
Letters to various persons, nine books.
Many Homilies, one book.
And many other things. He flourished under the emperors Zeno and Anastasius, in the year of the Lord 500.

GODELBERTUS, priest, learned in the divine Scriptures by continual exercise, rich in the reading of the ancients, and most learned in secular letters; a profound theologian, a renowned orator and notable poet, subtle in talent and ornate in eloquence. He wrote in heroic meter a most polished work, proceeding most elegantly through histories and allegories from the beginning of the world to the birth from the Virgin. The title of this work is:

Allegories of the Scriptures, four books.

But he also wrote many other things. He flourished, as they say, in the times of the emperor Anastasius, in the year of the Lord 500.

EUGIPPIUS, priest and abbot, learned in the holy Scriptures, singularly devoted to the reading of the books of Saint Augustine, and sufficiently instructed in the letters of the secular arts; also distinguished in life and conduct according to monastic institution. Some letters of Saint Fulgentius of Ruspe are said to have been addressed to him. He wrote certain necessary little works. Of these I have found only the following. He excerpted, from the books of the blessed bishop Augustine, a large volume having three hundred chapters, addressed to Proba. It begins thus:

Prologue, Letter 1: “To the lady deservedly venerable.”
The book itself thus, book 1: “That [unclear] wrote [unclear].”
The Life of Saint Severinus the Monk, one book.
His Rule of Monks, one book.

He flourished under the emperor Anastasius, according to Honorius the priest. But according to Sigebert, he flourished then under Tiberius Constantine, in the times of Pope Pelagius II, in the year of the Lord 580.

BENEDICT, first abbot and founder of Cassino, by homeland a man of Nursia, founder and chief of the monks of the West, a man of most holy conduct and illumined by the prophetic spirit; from whose order many men, both most learned and most holy, afterwards became famous. By word and example he converted countless peoples from iniquity to Christ. From his order the Roman see has had eighteen pontiffs; more than two hundred cardinals; sixteen hundred archbishops in various churches; nearly four thousand bishops; fifteen thousand seven hundred notable abbots who became famous for learning and writings or for life. And those canonized and entered in the catalogue of saints, as we are instructed by the monuments of the ancients, number fifteen thousand six hundred, apart from those whose names in all these categories have not come down to us. And concerning these illustrious men of our order we have already written four special books, in which we have recorded the names of some of them, though not of all.

Saint Benedict wrote, in lucid language and with excellent discretion:

The Rule of Monks, one book. “Listen, O son, to the precepts.”

It has seventy-three chapters.

Under this rule twenty orders serve, which we have set forth one by one in the first book On the Illustrious Men of Our Order, although among us some are rare. He flourished under Justin the Elder, in the year of the Lord 530. And he died, as some maintain, in the year of the Lord 542, indiction 5, on the twenty-first day of the month of March, when he was sixty-two years old, on the Saturday of holy Easter. But Marianus Scotus, the excellent computist, writes otherwise, saying thus: “If the holy father Benedict, abbot, as some write, died on 12 Kalends of April, on the Saturday of holy Easter, in the year of the Lord 601, there seems to be an obelus. For unless it was in the ninety-sixth year before this year, his death is not found, because then, if he was born, he was very small.” Therefore the holy father Benedict died, according to this calculation of Marianus, in the last year of the emperor Maurice, namely in the year of the Lord 601, at more or less his ninetieth year of age, indiction 4, 12 Kalends of April.

BOETHIUS Manlius Severinus, Roman ordinary consul, philosopher, orator, and poet *On Ecclesiastical Writers*

an outstanding poet, learned in the divine Scriptures, and the most learned of all men of his time in secular letters; he was the son-in-law of Symmachus the patrician. A man most abundantly furnished with Greek and Latin eloquence, since he translated many volumes both of Aristotle and of other philosophers from the Attic tongue into Latin; subtle in intellect, ready and Catholic in judgment, in speech not inferior even to Tully. It is known that Saint Benedict had friendship with him, and that on Monte Cassino, with Tertullus, senator and father of Placidus the monk, he ate at his table. He wrote many excellent volumes, of which I have found the following.

To Symmachus, his father-in-law, patrician of the city of Rome.

*On the Holy Trinity*, book 1. After it had been investigated for a very long time.
*On the Unity of the Trinity*, book 1. I ask whether the Father, the Son.
*On the Two Natures in Christ*, book 1. Indeed anxiously for you [unclear].
*On Faith, to John the Deacon*, book 1. The Christian faith I know.
*On Unity and the One*, book 1. Unity is that by which one.
*On Porphyry's Isagoge*, books 2. In the season of the wintering year in.
*On the Second Edition of the Same*, book 1. This second [unclear].
*On Aristotle's Categories*, books 2. These matters having been set forth, which pertain to.
*On the Same Author's Perihermenias*, book 1. Great indeed the books.
*On the Second Edition of the Same*, books 6. Alexander in the commentary.
*On Divisions*, book 1. How great for students.
*On Definitions*, book 1. Of speaking and disputing.
*Introduction to Categorical Syllogisms*, book 1. Many things the ancient philosophers.
*On Cicero's Topics*, books 6. By your exhortation, pa[unclear].
*On Topical Differences*, books 4. Every method of arguing.
*On the Categorical Syllogism*, books 2. Many ancient Greeks.
*On the Hypothetical Syllogism*, book 1. Since in all philoso[unclear].
*On the Hebdomads*, book 1. You ask that from the hebdo[unclear].
*On Arithmetic*, books 2. Among all the ancient authorities.
*On Music*, books 5. Indeed the perception of all things.
*On Philosophical Consolation*, books 3. Songs which once.
*On the Geometry of Euclid*, book 1. But he who, my Patricius.
*On the Discipline of Scholars, as some think*, book 1. Your intention knows.
*On Rhetorical Places*, book 1. Concerning the predication of power [unclear].
*Letters to Various Persons*, book 1.

He is also said to have written some other things, but they have not come to my knowledge. He died in the same year as Symmachus the patrician, under Pope John, under Emperor Anastasius, [unclear], in the year of the Lord 524, indiction 2. And under the name of Severinus he is said to have been inserted in the catalogue of saints.

Hormisdas the pope, a Campanian by nation, after the pontiff Symmachus presided over the Church for nine years; a good, learned, and vigorous man, who, when a synod had been gathered at Rome, condemned the Eutychian heresy, and, when the Manichaeans were again sprouting up, burned the books of their errors and banished them into exile.

Among the other little works of his talent he wrote:
book 1. Meanwhile the things which pertain to unity.
To Justin Augustus, letter 1. Having read the letters of your affection.
Letter 1. the [Eutychi]an heresy he condemned, and, when the Manichaeans were again sprouting up, burned the books of their errors and banished them into exile.
Several letters to various persons, book 1.
He died under Justin the Elder Augustus, in the year 521, indiction 14, on the eighth ides of August. John succeeded him.
*On the Catholic Faith*, book 1.

Evodius, bishop of Pavia, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular letters, of singular eloquence both in Greek and in Latin, was sent by Pope Hormisdas to Constantinople in matters of faith to Anastasius, the heretical emperor. After receiving many insults, he was expelled from the city together with his companions, Anastasius saying: Why do you present commands to us, who are under the sway of no one? The Roman pontiff ought to obey us, not also to command. Evodius, however, wrote to Pope Symmachus, book 1, and certain other things. He flourished under Emperor Anastasius, in the year of the Lord 510.

Jordan, from a monk bishop of the Goths, a man zealous in the divine Scriptures, competently learned in secular letters, gentle in character, open in speech, an outstanding investigator of times and writer of deeds. He is said to have composed certain excellent *The Abbot of Spanheim*

there were volumes, of which very few have come to my knowledge. For I have found only two books of *Histories*. In the first of these he reviewed the deeds of the Romans, and in the second the origin and deeds of the Goths down to the end of their kingdom. He flourished under the emperor Justinian, in the year of the Lord 530.

Faustus, a monk and disciple of our most holy father Benedict, Italian by nation, a man venerable in learning and character, when he was seven years old was offered by his parents to the divine father Benedict. By him, at length, after the completion of his instruction in the regular profession, he was sent with blessed Maurus into Gaul to build a monastery; there, after living for many years in great holiness, when Saint Maurus had died, he returned to Monte Cassino. At the brothers’ request, he wrote, in a very clear style, to Boniface II, pontiff of the city of Rome:

*The Life of Saint Maurus the Abbot*, 1 book.

He flourished under the emperor Phocas, in the year of the Lord 600.

Justinian the Great, emperor, nephew by his sister of the elder Justin, reigned after him for 38 years. A man of great and excellent talent, he rightly acquired a place among ecclesiastical writers; he both published a very famous volume against the heretics and, through the hands of John the patrician and the consuls Theophilus and Dorotheus, corrected with marvellous brevity the Roman laws, which lay scattered in more than two thousand books. For he reduced all the constitutions of the princes, which were contained in many volumes, to twelve books and called them the Code. Again, reducing the laws of the individual magistrates and judges, which, as we have said, extended to almost two thousand books, to the number of fifty books in three volumes, he named them the Code of the Digest or Pandects. He also composed four books of Institutes, in which the kernel of the laws is contained and explained. The new laws too, which he himself had established, he reduced into one volume. Therefore the order of all the books of the emperor Justinian that have come down to us is the following, namely:

*The Code of Justinian*, 12 books. “These things which are necessary.”

*The Digest or Pandects*, 50 books.

*Institutes*, 4 books. “The Imperial Majesty.”

*Epitome of the Laws*, 1 book.

*On the Incarnation of the Lord, against Eutyches*, 3 books.

*Against the African Bishops*, 1 book. “Who would doubt that he also wrote other things, especially many elegant letters, which have not come into our hands?” He at last, in his old age, became deranged and foolish and died, in the year of the Lord 565, in the thirteenth indiction. Justin the Younger succeeded him.

Dionysius, a Roman abbot, surnamed, as is reported, Exiguus, a man certainly great and most renowned in talent and learning, trained in the holy scriptures and nobly learned in the discipline of secular letters, was distinguished in Greek and Latin eloquence. Of these I have found only the following:

*The Great Paschal Cycle*, 1 book, of 532 years.

*On the Calculation of the Paschal Feast*, 1 book. “The calculation of the paschal feast.”

Concerning the rest I have found nothing. He translated from Greek into Latin the life of Saint Pachomius the abbot, also the book of Gregory of Emesa *On the Creation of Man*, and the writings of Proterius, bishop of Alexandria, to Pope Leo, and certain other things. He began his cycle in the year of the Lord 532, which was the last year of the great paschal cycle; once it has been completed, it always returns to the same point.

He therefore flourished under the great emperor Justinian, in the year of the Lord 540.

Fecundus, bishop of Valencia, a man learned in the divine scriptures and not ignorant of humane letters, had three brothers by one mother who were bishops, namely Justus, Nebridius, and Elpidius, learned and erudite men, who wrote various little works, which nevertheless have by no means come into our hands. He himself, among other things, composed for a certain man named Rusticus:

*On Five* *On Ecclesiastical Writers*

On the Five Questions, 1 book. And certain other works. He flourished in Spain under the emperor Justinian, in the year of the Lord 540.

Justus, bishop of the church of Urgell, brother of the aforesaid prelate Justinian, was himself also a man practiced and learned in the holy Scriptures, of excellent talent in expounding the divine and canonical books. He wrote a sufficiently elegant and commendable volume in scholastic style: On the Song of Songs, 1 book. And many other things. He flourished with his brother under the emperor Justinian, in the year of the Lord 540.

Aprigius, bishop of the Pacensian church, learned in the divine Scriptures and most highly instructed in secular letters, subtle in intellect and eloquent in speech, expounded the sacred Scriptures so gloriously and profoundly that, in comparison with him, the ancient writers seemed not to have expounded them. Among his little works there survives a distinguished volume, subtle in meaning and brilliant in expression: On the Apocalypse of John, 1 book. On the Song of Songs, 1 book. He also published many other works which have not come into our hands. He flourished in the times of Theodotus, king of the Goths, under the great emperor Justinian, in the year of the Lord 530.

Cassiodorus, monk and abbot of a monastery near the city of Ravenna, a man very learned in the divine Scriptures and easily the most learned of all in his time in secular letters, shone forth most brilliantly no less in holiness than in knowledge. He was first chancellor of Theoderic, king of Italy, and a senator of Ravenna, and consul of the city of Rome; afterward, despising the empty honors of the world, he became a monk for the love of God. From then on, applying the study of humane letters to the exposition of the holy Scriptures, he composed many very elegant treatises. Of his little works the following are reported. In the person both of himself and of King Theoderic he wrote: Letters to Various Persons, 28 books. On the Nature of the Soul, 1 book, “Since now, having undertaken...” On the whole Psalter, 1 book, “Blessed is the man,” etc.; “Exceedingly...” On the Song of Songs, 2 books, “Since the studies of secular men...” Instruction in Divine Readings, 9 books, “Solomon, inspired...” He also published many other works which have not come into our hands. Complexiones on the Apocalypse, “Our purpose is concerning...” Instruction in Secular Letters, 9 books, “Very usefully in the beginning...” He compiled the Tripartite History, 12 books. On Etymologies, 7 books. A Catalogue of the Roman Consuls, 1 book. On Figures and Tropes, 1 book. The Priest Foretitled, 1 book. A Memorial of the Scriptures, 1 book. On Orthography. A Memorial of the Scriptures, 1 book. On the Canonical Epistles, 1 book. Complexiones on the Apocalypse [unclear], 1 book. On the Acts of the Apostles. He also composed many other works which have not come to the knowledge of our reading. He flourished from the times of the elder Justin almost to the end of the reign of the younger Justinian, having more than 95 years of age, in the year of the Lord 575.

Arator, subdeacon of the most holy Roman Church, a man practiced in the divine Scriptures and nobly learned in the letters of secular disciplines, strong in verse and prose, offered it in the presence of bishops and men of learning, and, at the pope’s command, recited a large part of it publicly before everyone. As the hour was passing, Pope Vigilius handed the codex to the venerable Surgentius, primicerius, to be placed in the archive, so that he might complete the reading of it at a free time. His works: Acts of the Apostles, 2 books, “As judge of his own crime...” To Abbot Florianus, 1 letter, “He who by merits the flower...” To Pope Vigilius, 1 letter, “With watery walls...” And certain other things which I have not seen.

This Arator, a most illustrious poet and distinguished theologian, composed in elegant meter a codex on the Acts of the Apostles and offered it to Pope Vigilius before the confession of St. Peter on the seventh Ides of April, in the presence of many bishops and men of learning. Since only half of the book was read in one day, [unclear] he recited it before everyone. As the hour was passing, Pope Vigilius handed the codex to the venerable Surgentius, primicerius, to be placed in the archive, so that he, when free, might complete the reading of it in due time. When he had ordered this to be done in the church of St. Peter in Chains, a great crowd of religious persons and noble laymen assembled, and, with Arator himself reciting in distinct words, both books were heard four times, since only half of the book was read in one day because of the constant repetitions which the listeners demanded with manifold favor. Where now in these times is such zeal for letters? Where is love of saving knowledge? Our religious nobles and clerical pontiffs too heap up not books but revenues; they cultivate not letters but greed. Now *The Abbot of Sponheim*

Antimachus wrote many poems, and [unclear]; among individual [unclear] scarcely a single Plato is found and remains. But we are now speaking of these things out of season. Arator flourished under the emperor Justinian, in the year of the Lord 540.

Victor, bishop of the [Tunnunensian?] church in Africa, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly trained in secular letters, for his defense of the Three Chapters against the emperor Justinian and Eutychius, bishop of the city of Constantinople, when he resisted the emperor and bishop as detractors of those same chapters, was sent to a monastery of that same city to be kept under guard, and, as they say, died remaining under the same condemnation. Among other little works of his talent he wrote, from the beginning of the world down to the first year of Justin the Younger’s empire, a very useful history On Deeds and Ecclesiastical Wars, one book; For the Defense of the Three Chapters, one book; and certain other things.

He flourished under the emperor Justinian, in the year of the Lord 510.

Gregory, the first pope from the monastic order of St. Benedict, a Roman by birth, sat after Pope Pelagius in the chair of Peter for 13 years and 6 months. He was a man most learned in divine Scripture and likewise most learned in secular letters, the prince of theologians, the splendor of philosophers, and the light of rhetoricians, upright and most holy in life and conduct. As he was expounding the divine Scriptures, the Holy Spirit sometimes appeared to him in visible form, and is reported to have revealed to him the hidden mysteries of those same four bishops. At Rome, in a synod of twenty-four bishops held at St. Peter’s, he established many things for the benefit of the Church and promulgated a decree concerning the immunity of monasteries. He wrote many necessary volumes, of which the following are given:

To Leander, bishop of Seville.
Moralia on the Book of Job, 35 books. “Among many, often...”
On Pastoral Care, 2 books. “The care of the pastoral office...”
Dialogues on the Miracles of the Saints, 4 books. “One day, when exceedingly...”
On the Song of Songs, 4 books. “After from paradise...”
Homilies on the Gospels, 40 homilies, 2 books. “By the inspiration of almighty God...”
A brief Explanation of the Four Gospels, 1 book. “Our Lord and Redeemer...”
On the Seven Penitential Psalms, 4 books. “Matthew, as in...”
Letters to various persons, 10 books. “Gregory, bishop, servant...” or otherwise “Very necessary...”
Rationale of Divine Things, 1 book.
Proems to the New and Old Testament, 1 book.
On the Sacraments, 1 book.

When he was still a deacon, in the person of Pope Pelagius, he composed a very notable letter to Elias, bishop of Aquileia, who was unwilling to accept the Three Chapters of the Council of Chalcedon; it is not found among his letters. He is also said to have written many other works, namely on the prophets, on the books of Kings, also on the books of Moses, and on other holy Scriptures, which after his death, before they had yet been multiplied, his most wicked rivals, envying his glory and holiness, burned with fire, as John the Deacon complains in the book of his life. The most blessed Pope Gregory died in the second year of the emperor Phocas, which was the year of the Lord 605, in the eighth indiction, on the fourth day before the Ides of March, shining with many miracles.

Leander, bishop of Seville, formerly a monk, a Carthaginian by birth, from the province of Spain, born of his father Severianus, was a most studious man, nobly learned both in divine Scripture and in secular letters, sweet in eloquence, most outstanding in talent, and also holy in life and conduct and beloved by God. By his preaching and effort Hermenegild, son of Leovigild, the Arian king of the Goths, was brought back to the confession of the orthodox faith and, killed by his heretical father on the vigil of Easter, received the crown of martyrdom. His brother Reccared, as soon as he had received the kingdom after his father’s death, at Leander’s urging and preaching, renounced heresy and converted the whole people of the Visigoths subject to him to the Catholic faith. To this Leander blessed Gregory dedicated the volumes of his commentaries on Job. He himself also wrote several little works, of which the following are given. When he had been driven into exile by the Arians because of the Catholic faith, he wrote:

Against the Heretics, one book.
Against the Institutions of the Arians, one book.
On Virginity, to Florentina, one book.
Prayers, in a double edition, on the Psalms, one book.
Letters to His Brother, one book.
On the Praise of Sacrifices, one book.

He also published several other works which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished in the year of the Lord 590, under the emperor Maurice. He died under Reccared, the most devout prince of the Goths, shining with miracles.

Priscu*On Ecclesiastical Writers*

PRISCIAN the grammarian, a native of Caesarea, a man most learned in secular letters, skilled in Greek and Latin eloquence, was held in great esteem with Chosroes, king of the Persians. He wrote certain distinguished volumes on the art of grammar, which among the ancients were held in great authority. Of these the following are reported: To Julian the patrician. *On the Parts of Speech*, 2 books. *On Construction*, 1 book. *On Accents*, 1 book. *On Cosmography*, 1 book. *On Natural Questions*, to [him?], 1 book.

He is also said to have written several other works, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished, as some think, in the times of Chosroes king of the Persians and of the emperor Heraclius, in the year of the Lord 620.

MARCUS, a monk, disciple of the holy father Benedict, most affectionately loved by him, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, most skilled in secular letters, a distinguished orator and poet, outstanding in character and manner of life. After the blessed Pope Gregory he wrote, adding certain things in a heroic verse running most elegantly: *The Life of Saint Benedict*, 1 book, and certain other works.

He flourished down to the reign of Heraclius Augustus, in the year of the Lord 610.

FORTUNATUS, bishop of Poitiers, an Italian by nation, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, most erudite in secular letters, subtle in intellect, eloquent and polished in speech, excelling in verse and prose, shone brightly among all the teachers of his age, renowned no less for holiness of life than for knowledge and learning. Freed from pain in his eyes by the power of Saint Martin, he came to Tours to his tomb to give thanks; then going on to Poitiers, he was ordained there first priest and then bishop, and was renowned for great learning and religion. He wrote in elegant verse many useful and devout little works. Of these I have seen only the following. To Saint Radegund, daughter of the last king of the Thuringians, captive of the king of the Franks, afterwards abbess of the monastery of Poitiers, in hexameter verse: *The Destruction of the Kingdom of the Thuringians*, 1 book. “Conditio belli tristis.”

To Jovinus, *On Radegund*, 1 book. “Aonias avido qui [unclear].”
To Justin the Younger, 1 book. “Gloria summi patris natique.”
To Sophia Augusta, 1 book. “Cui meritis compar [unclear].”
In the person of Radegund, 1 book. “Post patriae cineres.”
*In Praise of Martin the Bishop*, 1 book. “Lumen Apostolicum cum spar[unclear].”
*On Leontius, the Venerable Bishop*, 1 book. “Inter quos genuit radi[unclear].”
On the same, a praise, 1 book. “Agnoscat omne saeculum.”
*Seventy-seven Hymns*, 1 book. “Agnoscat omne saeculum.”
*The Life of Saint Hilary of Poitiers*, 1 book. *To Oporicus on His Life*, 1 book.
*The Life of Saint Maurilius the Bishop*, 1 book. *Letters to Various Persons*, 1 book.
*Poems to Friends*, 1 book. “Rex regionis apex.”

He also composed many other works, which, since they are short, I did not wish to record under the title of books; for he wrote many epitaphs and short verses, which I have seen. He flourished under Justin the Younger Augustus, in the year of the Lord 570.

GREGORY, bishop of Tours, formerly a monk and once a disciple of Saint Avitus, bishop of the Auvergne, a learned, noble, gentle, and humble man, was of such holiness and purity that even in life he shone with miracles. Visiting the thresholds of the apostles Peter and Paul, he was received by the blessed Pope Gregory with the greatest reverence and love, as a truly holy man, a singular friend uniquely beloved by him. He wrote several volumes in a simple and clear style. Of these there survive:

*On the Praise of the Holy Martyrs*, 1 book. “Hieronymus presbyter.”
*On the Life of Certain Confessors*, 1 book. “Statueram illa tantum seri[unclear].”
*On the Miracles of Saint Julian the Martyr*, 1 book. “Magnum in nobis quo.”
*On the Miracles of Saint Martin*, 1 book. “Omnibus sanctis in Christi.”
*History of the Franks*, 10 books. “Scripturus bella regum.”
*Epitome of the Same*, 1 book. *Chronicle of Ecclesiastical History*, 1 book.

The other works which he composed have not yet come to the knowledge of our reading. He flourished in the times of the emperor Maurice, in the year of the Lord 600.

MARTIN, bishop of Dumium, once rector and abbot of the monastery, a man learned both in the divine Scriptures and in secular letters, coming from the regions of the East into Gaul, converted the people of the Suevi by teaching and miracles from Arian impiety to the right faith, *Abbot of Sponheim*

... converted, established rules of the orthodox faith, founded monasteries, reformed churches. He wrote to Miro, king of Galicia, on the four virtues which they call cardinal, an instructive volume which he wished to title *The Pattern of an Honorable Life*, one book, beginning: “To the most glorious and serene ...” *Moral Letters*, two books. And certain other things which I have not seen. He flourished under Theudemir, king of the Suevi, while Justinian Augustus governed the Constantinopolitan empire. In the year of the Lord 540.

Paterius, notary and secundicerius of the Roman church, a man continually exercised in the study of the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, collecting all the testimonies of divine Scripture by which the blessed Pope Gregory clarified the obscure points of his exposition, produced three books: two, namely, on the testimonies of the Old Testament, and one on the testimonies of the New Testament. He titled that volume *Testimonies*, three books, beginning: “Since the most blessed and apostolic ...” Of the rest I have seen nothing. He flourished at Rome at the same time when Pope Gregory presided over the universal church, and at his urging compiled the aforesaid volume, while Maurice Augustus held the empire, and after him Phocas. In the year of the Lord 600.

Columbanus, first founder and abbot of the monastery of Luxeuil, a Scot by nation, a man of outstanding holiness, merit, and learning, father of many thousands of monks and founder of several monasteries, an excellent sower of the divine word, coming from Ireland into Gaul and Germany, increased divine worship, monasteries, and servants, like a prince of the Druids of old. When he was still rather young he devoted great study to sacred letters, so that he wrote in an elegant style. *Commentaries on the Whole Psalter*, two books. And certain letters to the brothers. He died under the emperor Maurice, in the year of the Lord 598, in the first indiction, on the second day before the Kalends of December.

John, bishop of Constantinople, a Cappadocian by nation, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, of inestimable abstinence and holiness, so intent on almsgiving and works of piety that the emperor Maurice, moved against him by zeal for avarice, ordered all poor beggars to be expelled from the city of Constantinople. He wrote in the Greek language to St Leander, bishop of Seville, of whom we spoke above: *On the Sacrament of Baptism*, one book; *Letters to Various Persons* [unclear]. And certain other things. He flourished under the emperor Maurice, in the year of the Lord 600.

Licinianus, bishop of Cartagena, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, after many exercises of study was killed near Constantinople by his rivals with a cup of poison under the emperor Maurice. Sudden death did not harm him, for Scripture says: “The just man, by whatever death he may be overtaken, will be in refreshment.” For then he truly begins to live when, adorned with good works, he goes through death to Christ, never to die. He wrote certain little works of reading not to be despised, of which I have not yet been worthy to see any. His little work is reported, however: *On the Sacrament of Baptism*, one book; *Letters to Abbot Eutropius* [unclear]; also *Letters to Various Persons* [unclear]. And certain other things.

Severus, bishop of the city of Malaga, once the companion and colleague of the aforesaid Bishop Licinianus, a man learned in the holy Scriptures and nobly instructed in the disciplines of secular letters, keen in talent, distinguished in speech. He wrote against Vincentius, bishop of the city of Zaragoza, who had slipped from the Catholic faith into Arian depravity: *Correctorium*, one book; *On Virginity*, to his sister [unclear]; *Letters to Various Persons*, one book. He flourished in the year of the Lord 580, under the emperor Maurice, under whom he also died.

Eutropius, bishop of the church of Valencia, formerly abbot of the monastery of Servitanus of the order of St Benedict, to whom Bishop Licinianus, while still residing in the aforesaid monastery, wrote many letters, a man splendidly learned both in the divine Scriptures and in secular letters, and very well imbued with monastic disciplines. While he was still abbot, he wrote to Bishop Licinianus why, after this, chrismatic anointing is given to baptized infants: *Chrismatic Anointing*, one book; *On the Exhortation of Monks* [unclear]; and several letters to various persons. He flourished in the times of the emperor Maurice, in the year of the Lord 600.

John, bishop of Girona, from a monk of our order, a Goth by nation, from the province of Lusitania, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, and also in morals *Description of Ecclesiastical Writers*

also illustrious in life and conduct, learned and renowned in Greek and Latin speech, who, when as a young man he went to Constantinople out of love of learning, after seven years had passed returned to Spain. When King Leovigild wished to lead him over to the Arian impiety and could not, he condemned him to a rather harsh exile for ten years. Thereafter, recalled by the most Christian King Reccared, he founded a monastery, where by word and example he showed his brothers the path of regular discipline. He wrote:

An Exhortation to Monks, book 1. Additions to the Chronicle, book 1.

He also composed many other things, which have not come to my knowledge.

He flourished under Reccared, most Christian king of the Visigoths in Spain, in the times of the emperors Maurice and Phocas, in the year of the Lord 600.

Maximus, bishop of the city of Caesaraugusta, learned in the divine Scriptures, not moderately instructed in secular letters, ready in intellect, polished in eloquence, excellent in verse and prose, published sufficiently distinguished volumes of both kinds, which as yet have by no means come to the knowledge of our reading. But a notable volume of his is reported, a pleasing work:

On the Deeds of the Goths in Spain, book 1.

He flourished in the times of the emperor Phocas, in the year of the Lord 610.

Jonas, a monk, disciple of St. Columbanus the abbot and companion of his pilgrimage, a Scot by nation, a studious man, learned, distinguished in knowledge, venerable no less for religion than for doctrine, at the request of many wrote in composed discourse for their edification:

The Life of Saint Columbanus, book 1. The Life of Saint Attala the Monk, book 1.

The Life of Saint Eustasius the Abbot, book 1.

He flourished under the emperor Heraclius, in the year of the Lord 630.

Leontius, bishop of the Neapolitan city on the island of Cyprus, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular letters, and also most distinguished in life and conduct, a prelate worthy of God. Among the other little works of his talent he wrote a notable volume on the acts and conduct of that most admirable Alexandrian patriarch, who because of his incredible piety and compassion toward the poor was surnamed:

John the Almsgiver, book 1. I have found nothing about the rest.

He flourished in the times of the emperor Phocas, in the year of the Lord 640.

Isidore the Younger, bishop of Seville after Leander, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, second to none in his time in secular letters, subtle in intellect, clear in understanding, composed in eloquence, excellent in verse and prose, shone out no less eminent in sanctity than in doctrine. He is called the Younger to distinguish him from the elder Isidore, bishop of Cordoba, of whom we made mention above, or also from another who preceded him as bishop of Seville. This Isidore the Younger wrote many distinguished little works. Of these I have found only the following. To Bishop Braulio:

Etymologies, books 20. Discipline from learning.

On Genesis, allegorically, book 1. The history of the sacred law.

On Exodus, book 1. Certain mysteries.

On Numbers, book 1. Therefore this one book.

On Leviticus, book 1. The following Leviticus [unclear].

On Deuteronomy, book 1. The book of Deuteronomy.

On Joshua, book 1. After the death of Moses.

On Judges, book 1. The history of Judges.

On Kings, books 4. After the book of Judges follows.

On Ezra and Nehemiah, book 1. On Tobit.

On Judith, book 1. On Esther, book 1.

On Job, book 1. On the Psalter, book 1.

On the Proverbs of Solomon, book 1. On Ecclesiastes, book 1.

On the Song of Songs, book 1. On the prophet Isaiah, book 1.

On Ecclesiasticus, book 1. On Ezekiel, book 1.

On Jeremiah, book 1. On the Twelve Minor Prophets, books 2.

On the prophet Daniel, books 2.

On the Four Gospels, books 7. On the canonical epistles.

On the Epistles of Paul [unclear]. On the Apocalypse.

*The Abbot of Sponheim*

On the Acts of the Apostles, 1 book.
Of the Interpretation of the New and Old Testament, 2 books.
Of Prefaces, 1 book.
Of Differences, 1 book.
On the Birth and Death of the Saints, 1 book.
To His Sister, Against the Jews, 2 books.
Of Synonyms or Soliloquies, 2 books.
On Illustrious Men, 1 book.
Of Sentences on the Highest Good, 3 books.
On the Origin of the Offices, 2 books.
On the Holy Trinity, 1 book.
On the Office of the Mass, 1 book.
On Computation and the Nature of Things, 1 book.
Of Sermons, 1 book.
The Lament of a Penitent, 1 book.
On Astronomy, 1 book.
A History or Chronicle, 3 books.
On Grammar and Words, 1 book.
Also of Allegories, 1 book.
On Heresies, 1 book.
He is said also to have written many other things, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under the emperor Heraclonas, son of Heraclius, in the year of the Lord 630, in the times of Sisebut, king of the Goths in Spain; and on account of his most holy life and conduct he was inserted in the catalogue of the saints. His feast is celebrated on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of February.

Caesarius, from a monk of the monastery of Lerins bishop of Arles, a man very learned in the divine Scriptures, gentle in mind, sweet and adorned in speech, and distinguished by a wondrous brevity of sentences, most holy in life and conduct, since from his youth he had been trained in monastic disciplines and was for a long time abbot of Lerins, wrote certain excellent little works of no contemptible reading, which are very necessary and useful for monastic and religious persons dedicated to God. Of these there are extant:

On Grace and Free Will, 1 book.
Of Sermons to Monks, 1 book.
The Decree of the Three Councils of Arles, 3 books. I have found nothing concerning the rest.

In the third sermon, which is on the monk's battle against the vices, he acknowledges both himself and those to whom he speaks as professed men and monks of the order and rule of our most holy father Benedict.

He flourished in the times of the emperor Constantine, son of Heraclius, and of his sons, in the year of the Lord 670; under them he gloriously presided over the Synod of Arles.

Audoenus, who is Dado, bishop of Rouen, a Gaul by nation, brother of the monk Saint Ado, a learned and most holy man, founder of the monastery of Rebais, since he was instructed both in the holy Scriptures and also in secular letters, wrote in a most elegant style to Rupert, bishop of Paris:

The Life of Saint Eligius, bishop of Noyon, 3 books. And certain other things.

He was renowned for great holiness, virtues, and signs, in the times of the above-named emperor Constantine, in the year of the Lord 660.

Theodore, seventh archbishop of Canterbury, consecrated by Pope Vitalian, a Greek by nation, from Tarsus of Cilicia, a monk of our order in the city of Rome, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, second to none in his time in secular letters, highly skilled in Greek and Latin speech, excellent also in verse and prose, no less renowned for knowledge, after holding a synod in England made many provisions for the benefit of the English Church. Among the other monuments of his talent he wrote an excellent work on the quality of penance to be imposed on those who had sinned in many and enormous ways. The title of this work is:

The Penitential of Theodore, 1 book. Some letters to various persons.

He died, not without a reputation for holiness, under Justinian the Younger, in the year of the Lord 690, in the third indiction, in the seventy-eighth year of his age and the twenty-second of his episcopate.

Leo, the second pope, a Sicilian by nation, sat in the chair of Peter after Agatho for only eleven months. A man most learned in divine and secular writings, sufficiently instructed in the Greek and Latin language, subtle, eloquent, no less holy than learned, he translated from Greek into Latin the sixth Synod, which in the time of Pope Agatho had [unclear]

[unclear]
1 book.
1 book.
[unclear]
1 book.
Of Letters to Various Persons, 1 book.
I fear in Christ [unclear].
I have found nothing concerning the rest.
And certain other things.
Some letters to various persons.
In the year 690, in the third indiction, in the seventy-eighth year of his age and the twenty-second of his episcopate.

*On Ecclesiastical Writers*

...of my predecessor was held in the city of Constantinople, in which Macarius, bishop of Antioch, was condemned with his accomplices, the bishops Cyrus, Sergius, Honorius, Pyrrhus, Paul, and Peter, who taught as doctrine one will and only one operation in our Lord Jesus Christ. He also wrote:

Many letters to various persons, one book. And certain similar things.

He died under the emperor Constantine, son of Constantine, in the year of the Lord 677, in the fifth indiction, on the fifth Nones of July.

Adamannus, priest and abbot of the monastery of Iona, which St. Columbanus once built on an island of Scotland, a man very devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant also of secular letters, careful in intellect, sweet in speech, outstanding in life and conduct, not without a reputation for holiness, was the father of many monks. Among other things he wrote, in sufficiently well-composed style, a volume:

On the places of the Holy Land, one book. And certain letters.

He flourished under Justinian the Younger Augustus, in the year of the Lord 690.

Benedict, abbot in Britain, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, and an outstanding preserver and expounder of regular discipline, wrote a distinguished little work for monks, in which, comparing all the rules of the holy fathers with the rule of our most blessed father Benedict, he shows that the rules of all the others harmonize with it, and that it disagrees with none at all. For this reason he entitled his book:

The Concord of the Rules, one book. He wrote other things.

He flourished under the emperor Constantine, in the year of the Lord 670.

Adelmus, bishop of the West Saxons, formerly abbot of the monastery of Maildub in Scotland, of the Order of St. Benedict, a devout man of exceptional holiness, devoted to and learned in the holy Scriptures, and in secular letters the most learned of all in England in his time, excellent in verse and prose, a most fervent preacher of the divine word. He wrote certain instructive volumes in a twofold style. Of these I have found only the following. While he was still abbot, at the command of the synod of his people, he wrote against the error of the Britons a distinguished and useful work:

On the Celebration of Easter, one book. “Almighty Father of the world...”

On the Virginity of the Saints, in verse, one book. “Most reverend man of Christ...”

On the same subject, in prose, one book. Several letters to various persons, one book.

He is also read to have written many other things, which have not come to the notice of our reading.

He flourished under Justinian the Younger, in the year of the Lord 680.

Ceolfrid, after Benedict the second abbot of the monastery of the holy apostles Peter and Paul in England, of the Order of St. Benedict, teacher and nurturer of Bede the priest, a devout and learned man, and a vigorous governor of regular discipline. He wrote to the king of the Picts, who had requested it, a fairly lengthy letter in the manner of a little book:

On the Observance of Easter, one book.

He flourished in England in the times of Justinian the Younger, emperor, in the year of the Lord 690. At length, when he was returning after visiting the thresholds of the Apostles, he died in the city of Langres, in the seventy-fourth year of his age.

Egidius, a monk of the Order of St. Benedict, Greek by nation, learned in the divine Scriptures, most skilled in secular letters, a physician, philosopher, and distinguished poet, venerable no less in his way of life than in knowledge. He wrote certain little works of no negligible usefulness, of which I have found only the following: a distinguished work composed in meter:

On Pulses, one book. “The powers of genius with modest...”

On Veins also, one book. “From here a vein is led when it becomes...”

Bede, monk and priest of the monastery of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, which is in England, of the Order of St. Benedict, a man most devoted to the divine writings, very learned, and most skilled in secular letters, a philosopher, astronomer, calculator, [unclear], not ignorant of the Greek language, outstanding in intellect, not over-elaborate in speech, and a distinguished poet. He wrote many volumes, in which the sharpness of his intellect [unclear]. When he was seven years old, by the care of his relatives he was given to be educated by Abbot Benedict, and thereafter by Ceolfrid of the said monastery of Wearmouth, and all from that time...

*248. ABBOT OF SPONHEIM.*

…passing the time of [his] life in the dwelling of the same monastery, he gave all [his] effort to meditating on the Scriptures; and, amid the observance of regular discipline and the daily care of singing in church, he always held [it] sweet either to learn, or to teach, or to write. In the nineteenth year of his age he received the diaconate, in the thirtieth the grade of the presbyterate, each through the ministry of bishop John, Ceolfrid the abbot commanding [it]. [There follows his works-list—On Genesis up to Isaac, 4 books; On Exodus; On Numbers; On Leviticus; On Deuteronomy; On the tabernacle and vessels, 3 books; On Kings; On the building of the temple; On Judges; On Joshua, 2 books; On Paralipomenon, 3 books; thirty questions on Kings, 6 books; On Proverbs; On Ecclesiastes, 3 books; On Jeremiah; On the Song of Songs; On Daniel; On Ezra and Nehemiah, 2 books; On Tobias, 4 books; On Isaiah; On Ezekiel, 12 books; On the twelve minor prophets, 7 books; On Luke, 6 books; On the canonical Epistles, 2 books; On the Acts of the Apostles; the Chronicle of his own monastery, 2 books; On the nature of things and [its] reckoning; Hymns in diverse meter, 2 books; On the holy places, 1 book; Epigrams in heroic meter, 1 book; Lessons of the New Testament; Lessons on the Old Testament; Distinctions on Job; Distinctions on Jeremiah, 2 books; On the canticle of Habakkuk; the Life of Saint Albert the bishop; a Martyrology; On the art of meter; Of letters to various [persons]; On figures; On orthography—rendered as printed]. He published, besides, many others, which have not come to the notice of our reading. His little works, even while he yet lived and was always writing new [ones], were of such great authority that, by the ordinance of the prelates of England, they were publicly read in the churches. And since, in the heading of [his] homilies, they wrote by custom the name of "the venerable author Bede the presbyter"—not being able, while he lived, to call him otherwise—the title attributed once from the beginning has prevailed up to the present day, that he is called Bede the Venerable rather than Saint. For while [he was] living it was not permitted to name [him] otherwise (even if he were a saint). There are [those] who invent other reasons for this title "Venerable"—some from the inscription of [his] epitaph, others dreaming that Bede was blind. But they err, since Bede was neither blind, nor do we know such an epitaph inscribed on his tomb. And indeed, were I not consulting brevity, I would most easily refute these ravings. He dies under the emperor Leo, in the year of the Lord 732, in the 15th indiction, in the 72nd year of his age, the day before the Kalends of June.

GREGORY, pope, the second, a Roman by country, sat in the chair of Peter after Constan[tine]… *249. ON ECCLESIASTICAL WRITERS.*

[Gregory II] …Constantine the pontiff, for 16 years [and] 9 months, a man otherwise learned and most holy, who ordained Boniface—an English monk, a Mainzer by nation—bishop. He wrote certain little works full of erudition, of which the following are reported: To the questions of Justinian, of Responses, 1 book; Against Leo Augustus, 1 book; To John, bishop of Constantinople, 1 book; Of letters to various [persons], 1 book. He dies under the emperor Leo, in the year of the Lord 731, in the 14th indiction, the 3rd [day before] the Ides of February. To whom Gregory III succeeded.

BONIFACE, the first archbishop of Mainz, a Scot by nation, a monk of the order of Saint Benedict, when he was a boy of five years, was offered by his parents to a monastery in England which is called Michael's; in which, devoting [his] study to letters and morals, he turned out a man both learned and most holy. Ordained presbyter, for love of pilgrimage for Christ, he came to Germany, and there, preaching the word of God, was ordained bishop of Mainz by Pope Gregory [II], and by his successor Gregory III was raised to archbishop and primate of Germany. Who, being an erudite man, taught the people committed to him not only by word but also by writings. Of his little works I have found only: Of letters to various [persons], 1 book; the Life of certain saints, 1 book. He dies preaching in Frisia, crowned with martyrdom, in the times of Pippin the emperor, in the year of the Lord 755, in the eighth indiction, in the 36th year of his episcopate, on the Nones of June. Whose body blessed Lullus—whom he had ordained archbishop after himself—caused to be brought back to the monastery of Fulda, situated in Buchonia, and honorably buried.

VERUS, bishop of Seville, of the province of Baetica, where Isidore once held the prelacy, a man erudite in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, [subtle] in talent, [wrote]: Of letters to various [persons], 1 book; the Life of Saint Gallus in prose, 1 book; the same afterward in meter, 1 book. [He flourished under the same period.]

*The Abbot of Spanheim* ... of the Church for ten years, a most learned man, who, because of his learning and holiness of life, is rightly judged comparable to the best pontiffs.
