Franco, scholasticus of the church of Liège, a German by nation, a man magnificently learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular literature, also outstanding as an astronomer and computist, and venerable no less for religion than for knowledge. He is said to have composed some treatises on the sacred Scriptures, which have not yet come to my knowledge. He wrote to Hermann II, archbishop of Cologne, a subtle and excellent work, a volume in mixed prose and verse, composed with fine variety, on the marriage of Christ and the Church:

[unclear], one book.
*On the Squaring of the Circle*, one book.
And many other works.

He flourished under Emperor Henry III, in the year of the Lord [unclear].

Bernard, a monk of Cluny, of the order of St. Benedict, a man practiced in the holy Scriptures by constant meditation, and not ignorant of secular literature, also in religion and [unclear].

*The Customs of Cluny*, one book.

Bernard, a monk of Corbie in Saxony, of the order of St. Benedict, a German by nation, a man nobly learned in the divine writings and very skilled in secular letters, excellent in verse and prose, subtle in talent and eloquent in speech. He wrote to Hartwin, archbishop of Magdeburg, in a clear indeed but bitter discourse, a volume:

*Against Henry IV*, one book.
And other works which I have not seen.

He also wrote other things. He flourished under Emperor Henry III, in the year of the Lord 1050.

Ivo, bishop of Chartres, formerly provost of St. Quentin of Beauvais, of the order of regular canons of the divine father Augustine, a man practiced in the divine Scriptures and a most careful interpreter of the canons of the holy fathers and general councils, and revered no less for holiness than for knowledge, magnificently reformed his order, which had long since collapsed. After Burchard, bishop of Worms, he wrote from the canons of the saints a concise decretal collection, which jurists used before the time of Gratian, and which he entitled:

*Panormia*, ten books.
*Excerptiones ecclesi[asticae?]* [unclear].
*Letters to Various Persons*, one book.
[unclear] the Church of Chartres. And 268 *The Abbot of Sponheim* And certain other things. He flourished under Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1090.

*Hildebert*, bishop of Le Mans and afterwards archbishop of Tours, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, and in secular learning second to none in his time; sharp in intellect and very eloquent in speech; formerly a disciple of Berengar of Tours, but a persecutor of his error; who endured many persecutions and tribulations, even to imprisonment, for ecclesiastical liberty. He wrote in both styles, namely verse and prose, certain excellent little works, of which as yet only a few have come to our knowledge for reading. He wrote, in elegant meter, a very beautiful and useful exposition:

*On the Whole Office of the Mass*, one book: “I have proposed to write what...”
*On His Exile*, one book: “Recently I was wealthy in...”
*On the Misery of This Life*, one book: “We are taken from the midst [unclear]...”
*On the Sacrament of the Altar*, one book.
*Of Hymns and Prayers in Diverse Meter*, one book.
*Letters to Various Persons*, one book: “If anyone [says] one nature...”

He comprised the epitaph of Berengar, once his teacher, in fifty-two verses. He wrote also many other things still unknown to us. He flourished under Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1090.

*Anselm*, archbishop of Canterbury in England, formerly abbot of the monastery of Bec in Normandy, of the Order of St Benedict, once a hearer and disciple of Lanfranc; a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, second to none in his time in knowledge of secular letters; upright and most holy in life and conduct; devout in mind, eloquent in speech, continual in action, angelic in countenance, mature in bearing, exemplary in progress, in the study of the Scriptures:

*Against the Gentiles, Why God Became Man*, one book: “Often, earnestly, by many...”
*On the Incarnation of the Word, against the Jews*, one book: “To the lord father of the whole...”
*On the Virginal Conception*, one book: “Since in all things, religious...”
*Proslogion*, one book: “Come now, little man...”
*Monologion*, one book: “Anselm, servant, etc.”
*On the Holy Spirit, against the Greeks*, one book: “It is denied by the Greeks that the Spirit...”
*On the Fall of the Devil*, one book: “That saying of the Apostle, ‘What have you...’”
*On the Diversity of the Sacraments*, one book: “To the lord and friend Waltram...”
*On Leavened and Unleavened Bread*, one book.
*On the Song of Songs*.
*On the Will of God*, one book: “Human reason, when concerning...”
*On the Holy Trinity*, one book.
*Dialogue of a Christian and a Gentile*.
*On Peace and Concord*, one book: “Wherever sacred Scripture...”
*On Grace and Free Will*, one book.
*On Blessed Sufficiency*.
*Dialogue on Truth*, one book: “Since God is truth...”
*On Similitudes*, one book: “The will in three ways...”
*Measurement of the Cross*, one book: “Jesus of Nazareth, by [unclear]...”
*Meditations*, one book: “[unclear] whether it is...”
*Against the Fool*, one book: “Since he does not rebuke me...”
*On the Misery of Man*, one book: “My life terrifies me...”
*On Antichrist*, one book.
*To Lanfranc the Archbishop*.
*On the Eight Beatitudes*, one book.
*On St John the Baptist*.
*On the Members Attributed to God*, one book: “Since your probity...”
*On the Sacraments and Divine Offices*, one book: “Servant of the servants of God, in...”
*Proverbs*, that is, *On the House of Conscience*, one book: “[Jesus] entered; what...”
*On the Hexaemeron*, one book.
*Letters to Various Persons*, one book.
*On the Grammarian*, one book: “A desertory, on account of the second place, whatever is...”
*On the Assumption of St Mary*, one book.
*On Servitude, on account of the second place, whatever is...*
*To William of Hirsau*, one book.
*On Sin:* *On Ecclesiastical Writers*

On original sin, one book. Also some sermons. But he is said to have written many other works also, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under Emperor Henry III, in the year of the Lord 1080.

Wilhelm, abbot of the monastery of Hirsau, in the diocese of Speyer, of the Order of St. Benedict, a German by nation, to whom blessed Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, wrote several letters, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and, in secular letters, inferior to no one among the Germans in his time, a philosopher, astronomer, and distinguished musician, most holy in life and conduct, since he is read to have shone with many miracles, reformed regular discipline, which had already collapsed, in many monasteries of Germany. Therefore, for the conversation of monastic observance, from the statutes of the ancients, he wrote:

Constitutions of monks, two books. “Since I, brother Wilhelm.”
On music and tones, one book. “After, by God’s gift, [unclear].”
One book. “Whoever [is] most truthful.”
On the clock, one book. “If anyone in this necessary [matter].”
On the correction of the Psalter, one book.
Letters to various persons, one book.
To St. Anselm of Canterbury, three letters.
And certain other works.

He also published several other works, which through the negligence of the ancients have fallen into oblivion. He died under Emperor Henry III, but as king of the Romans the fourth, in the year of the Lord 1091, indiction 14, on the fourth Nones of July. He was buried in the middle of the church of the Apostles, with a great reputation for holiness.

Giselbert, provost of the monastery of Weltin in England, of the Order of St. Benedict, hearer and disciple of Anselm of Canterbury, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and skilled in the practice of secular [learning], and nobly taught in the disciplines of secular letters, a clear theologian and poet, ready in talent and cautious in speech, not ignorant of philosophy, sufficiently endowed in talent, made his name known to posterity by writing, while he composed certain necessary works, in which he exercised his talent magnificently. Of these are reported the following; [he wrote] splendid volumes, of which few have come to my knowledge. There exists his volume, written in elegant meter; the following are reported:

On the Passion of St. Cyriacus, one book.
Life of Saint Bavo, one book.
On the prophet Isaiah.
And certain other works.

He flourished under Henry IV, with Anselm, in the year of the Lord [1090?].

Gunther, monk of Elno, of the Order of St. Benedict, skilled in the practice of the divine writings, and nobly taught in the disciplines of secular letters, a theologian and clear poet, sufficiently instructed by talent, excelling in verse and prose. Not ignorant of philosophy, ready in talent and cautious in speech, he wrote his name; he made [it] known to posterity by writing, while he magnificently exercised his talent in certain works. Of these splendid volumes, of which few have come to my knowledge, there exists his volume written in elegant meter; the following are reported:

Life of Saint Trudo, one book. “To the one and eternal first [one].”
Life of Saint Remaclus.
And certain other works.

And many other works. He flourished in the times of Henry IV, in the year of the Lord [1090?].

Theoderic, abbot of the diocese of Canterbury, of the Order of the divine father Benedict, a German by nation, a man studious and learned in the sacred writings, and sufficiently instructed in secular letters, excelling in counsel and [unclear]. Nobly taught in philosophy, in proof of his sincere faith, he wrote in both styles. He wrote, under the name of Moses, what he had been as a Jew, and of Peter, what he had begun to be as a Christian, a distinguished dialogue, necessary concerning Christ, concerning the Church, and concerning the future life, which he entitled:

Against the Jews, one book.
On free will, one book.
On knowledge and philosophy. “You are said to wonder.”
One book.
Offense concerning priests, one book.
Seal of St. Mary.
Summary of histories, one book. “The army in the camps of the eternal [one].”
Twin-spotted [unclear] of the soul, on the divine offices, three books. On the ima*270 The Abbot of Spanheim*

On the Image of the World, one book. “The world, therefore, is so called.”
On the Song of Songs, one book. “At the beginnings of books.”
On the Luminaries of the Church, one book. “Gelasius of the city of Rome.”
On the Body of the Lord, one book. On the Hexaemeron, one book.
On God and Eternal Life, one book. On the Soul, two books.
The Ladder of Heaven, on the degrees of visions, one book. The Key of Physics, on the natures of things, one book.
On the Whole Psalter, one book. Homilies on the Gospels, one book.
On the Pope and Emperor, one book. A Dialogue from the little works of Augustine, one book.
A Refutation of [unclear] on feasts, one book. Food of Life, on the saints, one book.
Letters to various persons, one book.

He also published many other things, whose titles I have not been able to find. He flourished under Henry V, in the year of the Lord 1120.

Sigebert, a monk of Gembloux, of the Order of St. Benedict, a Gaul by nation, a man from his youth most devoted to the divine Scriptures and very learned, and in secular letters second to none in his time in the territory of Liege, practiced in verse and prose. He wrote many volumes in both styles, by which he transmitted his name to posterity. He is reproached, however, for this: that, adhering to Henry, persecutor and rebel against the Roman Church, he wrote letters and little works against Hildebrand, Pope Gregory VII, which did not befit his purpose. What he wrote, indeed, he openly declared at the end of On Illustrious Men. When he had been placed in the monastery of St. Vincent at Metz to instruct boys, he wrote in heroic meter:

The Life of St. Theodoric the Bishop, one book. The Passion of St. Lucy, in meter, one book.
On the Translation of the same, one book. The Life of King Sigebert, one book.
The Passion of the Thebans, one book. The Life of St. Guibert, one book.
The Deeds of the Abbots of Gembloux, one book. The Life of St. Maclou, one book.
The Life of St. Theobald, one book. Against Pope Gregory, one book.
An Apology to the Emperor, one book. Against the Letter of Pope Paschal, one book.
On Ecclesiastes, in heroic meter, one book. Histories after Eusebius, one book.
On Illustrious Lives, one book. “Marcellus Marcivr.”
Letters to various persons, one book.

He also published other things after these, which he did not mark together with the little works written above. He flourished in the times of Emperor Henry III, King Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1070. He brought his Chronicle down to the year [unclear].

Calixtus II, pope, a Burgundian by nation, brother of the duke of Burgundy, formerly archbishop of Vienne, sat in the pontificate after Gelasius for six years. He was a man learned in the divine writings and not ignorant of secular letters, a special lover of St. James the Apostle; in his honor he raised the church of Compostela to an archbishopric. He wrote, in well-composed speech and with the greatest diligence:

On the Miracles of St. James, one book. “Calixtus, bishop, servant.”
Letters to various persons, one book.

And certain other things. He flourished under Henry V, in the year of the Lord 1120.

Stephen, also called Herrand, the fourteenth bishop of the church of Halberstadt, formerly abbot of the monastery of Ilsenburg, of the Benedictine Order, a German by nation, was a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, subtle in intellect and eloquent in speech. He wrote little works not of contemptible reading, but few have come into our hands. In the person of Count Louis he wrote a very elegant and useful letter to Waltram, bishop of the church of Naumburg, defending Henry, rebel against the Roman Church.

A Defense of the Pope, one book. “As a good man from the good.”
And several letters to various persons, one book.

And certain other things. He died under Henry V, in 1107, in the fifteenth indiction. And he was honorably buried in Reinsburg.

Bernard, the first abbot of Clairvaux, of the Cistercian Order, a Burgundian by nation, a noble and holy man, who was renowned for many miracles both in life and after death, learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, subtle in intellect and adorned in speech, since he neglected nothing in his writings that could serve to adorn discourse. He published many distinguished little works, of which the following are reported.

On con*On Ecclesiastical Writers*

On Consideration, to Eugenius, five books. “It comes into the mind to dictate [unclear].”
Of his Meditations, one book. “Many know many things,” and On the Soul of Christ.
On Contempt of the World, to clerics, one book. “To hear that it may be believed.”
On the Degrees of Humility, one book. “You have asked me, brother Gotfrid.”
One book. “As he was speaking [unclear].”
On Grace and Free Will, one book. “To Hugh, soldier of Christ.”
To the Knights of the Temple, one book. “If anyone among you [unclear].”
The Mirror of the Religious Life, one book. “When on a certain day [unclear].”
On the Monastic Ladder, one book. “To the brothers of the Mountain of God.”
To the Carthusians, one book. “The conscience in which [unclear].”
On Conscience, one book. “He indeed exhorts the timid [unclear].”
On the Order of Life, one book. On Confession of Sins, one book.
On the Two Eyes of the Soul, one book. “To the lord abbot of Coulombs.”
On Precept and Dispensation, one book. “It has pleased your excellency.”
To Henry of Sens, one book. “I seem to you too slow.”
To Hugh of Saint-Victor, one book. “Virtue is acquired in peace.”
Against Gerard, one book. “Dangerous matters of every kind,” and [unclear].
On the Misery of This Life, one book. “The days of man are as [unclear].”
On Temptations and Leisure, one book. “The servant of God freely for God.”
On the Will, one book. “All kinds of vices.”
An Apology to the Cluniacs, one book. “Until now, if any [unclear].”
On the Degrees of Charity, one book. “To the illustrious man, lord Au[unclear].”
On the Passion of the Lord, one book. On the Magnificat, one book.
On Loving God, one book. “Come, let us ascend.”
On the Psalm ‘He who dwells,’ one book. “I consider various labors.”
On the Song of Songs, 86 homilies, one book. “To you, brothers, otherwise than to others.”
On ‘The angel was sent,’ one book. “That I should write something.”
To his sister, on the manner of living, one book. “Most dear to me in Christ.”
The Life of Malachy the Bishop, one book. “Enough, more than enough.”
Of Letters to various persons, one book. “Today, brothers, we celebrate.”
Many sermons, one book.
And certain other things.
He died under Conrad, the third emperor, in the year of the Lord 1140.

Anselm of Laon, scholasticus, very devoted to the divine Scriptures, skilled through long practice, and in the disciplines of secular letters a notably acute teacher, scholastic in speech, distinguished no less in life than in knowledge, explained the Scriptures of both Testaments with an interlinear and marginal gloss, from the writings of the Fathers, in a new kind of exposition. He also wrote certain other little works which have come to me. It is reported.
Commentaries on the Psalter, one book. And certain letters.
He flourished under Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1110.

Hugh, priest and monk of Saint-Victor at Paris, of the order of the regular canons of Augustine, abbot there, as they say, a Saxon by nation, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, inferior to none of the ancients in secular philosophy, who, like a second Augustine, was regarded as a most celebrated teacher in his time, subtle in intellect, adorned in eloquence, and venerable no less in conduct than in learning. He wrote many, almost countless, little works, of which few have so far come into our hands.
A Summary of His Sentences, one book. On the Soul of Christ, one book.
On the Sacraments, two books. “The profession [unclear] difficult [unclear].”
One book. “Of all things to be expected, first [unclear].”
Didascalicon, one book. “Let the soul speak in secret.”
One book. “With what zeal, with what [unclear].”
On the Manner of Praying, one book. “So many already praised [unclear].”
On the Praise of Charity, one book. “Because, brothers, with God granting [unclear].”
On the Rule of Saint Augustine, one book. “These precepts which [unclear].”
On the Mystical Ark of Noah, five books. “When I was once sitting in [unclear].”
On Ecclesiastes, sixteen homilies, one book. “Those things from the book of Solomon.”
On the Song of Songs, one book. “At the beginning of the labor.”
On the Lamentations of Jeremiah, one book. “How sits, with respect to [unclear].”
On Je[unclear].

*The Abbot of Sponheim*

On the Hierarchies of Dionysius, 14 books.
On the Praise of the Fathers, 1 book.
On the Perpetual Virginity of Saint Mary, 1 book.
On the Magnificat, 1 book.
On the Love of the Bridegroom and the Bride, 1 book.
On the Medicine of the Soul, 1 book.
On Meditation, 1 book.
On the Incarnation of the Word, 1 book.
On the Wisdom of Christ, 1 book.
On the Vanity of the World, 1 book.
On the Substance of Love, 1 book.
On Discipline, 1 book.
On the Mysteries of the Church, 1 book.
On Spirit and Soul, 1 book.
On the Lord’s Prayer, 1 book.
On Confession, 1 book.
On the Prophet Ezekiel, 1 book.
On Certain Psalms, 1 book.
On the Simple Nature of God, 1 book.
On the Threefold Will in Christ, 1 book.
On the Power and Will of God, 1 book.
On Sacred Scripture, 1 book.
On the Nature of Animals, 1 book.
On Contemplation, 1 book.
Letters to Various Persons, 1 book.

He also composed many sermons and various other treatises. He flourished under Emperor Henry V, in the year of the Lord 1130.

Rupert, abbot of the monastery of Deutz near Cologne, of the Order of Saint Benedict, German by nation, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, enlightened by the Holy Spirit through vision, not ignorant of secular letters, a monk of Saint Lawrence of [Traiectum], was taken from there by Frederick, archbishop of Cologne, on account of his incredible learning, and raised to be abbot of the monastery of Deutz. He composed many distinguished little works. For from the time when in his youth he entered the monastery, he had exercised himself so much in the holy Scriptures that not even when sleeping did he seem able to rest from those meditations, but his tongue and lips were moved as if in reading. Of his works I have found only the following at present. To Cuno, abbot of Siegburg and afterwards bishop of Regensburg.

On the Victory of the Word of God, 13 books. It begins: “Recently, when you as a guest...”
On Genesis, 1 book. It begins: “Whoever to a faithful soul, while...”
On the Song of Songs, 1 book. It begins: “He who against a man like...”
On the books of Saint Job, 10 books.
On the books of Kings, concerning David, 15 books.
On the Holy Trinity in the Old Testament, 12 books. It begins: “That you also, venerable...”
On the Apocalypse of John, 11 books. It begins: “Those things which through the cycle of the year...”
Meditations on the Fire at Deutz, 3 books. It begins: “Behold how the accuser...”
On the Twelve Minor Prophets, 14 books.
On the Rule of Saint Benedict, 1 book.
On the Gospel of John, 1 book.
Letters to Various Persons, 1 book.
An Apology for the Same Work, 1 book. It begins: “He was made...”

He wrote, moreover, works not contemptible in reading, of which I have only [unclear]. Finally, he is said to have written many other works, and to have explained the greater part of the New and Old Testament in many books; of these, up to the present, we have seen nothing except those which we have marked. He flourished in great holiness, gleaming with doctrine and miracles, under Henry V, in the year of the Lord 1124. And he died under Lothar III.

Rupert, abbot of the monastery of Limburg in the diocese of Speyer, of the Order of Saint Benedict, German by nation, magnificently learned both in the divine Scriptures and in secular letters, distinguished in life and conduct, so much so that he deserved to be visited by frequent divine revelations. For many years he applied himself to secular philosophy in the school of Paris and became a noble philosopher. But, considering that the philosophy of the present life was empty, he abandoned the study of vanity; returning to his homeland, he became a monk in the said monastery, and finally abbot. He wrote works not contemptible in reading, of which I have found only the following.

On the Can*On Ecclesiastical Writers*

On the Song of Songs, 4 books. “Whoever [unclear] of his own matters.”
On contempt of the world, 2 books. “The world by an undeserved name.”
On St. John the Baptist, 1 book. “The evangelical historian relates.”
Of his revelations, 1 book. “In the year of the Lord’s incarnation.”
He wrote certain sermons on the saints whose bodies or patronages were held in the same monastery of Limburg. He flourished under Emperor Henry V, not without a reputation for holiness, in the year of the Lord 1124.

Rudolph, abbot of St. Trond in the diocese of Liège, of the order of the divine father Benedict, a German by nation, a man skilled in the divine Scriptures through constant practice, and not meanly learned in secular letters, strong in verse and prose, and an excellent musician, no less distinguished in work than in knowledge, wrote in both styles some little works not to be despised, of which there are reported: 7 books. Also a chronicle.
Against the simoniacs, 1 book.
Many poems.
He also composed many chants in praise of the saints, in sweet and regular melody. He flourished under Henry V, in the year of the Lord [unclear].

Franco, the second abbot of the monastery of Affligem, of the order of St. Benedict, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and sufficiently instructed in secular doctrine, strong in talent and distinguished in eloquence, wrote both in meter and in prose certain commendable little works, by which he transmitted his name with glory to posterity. While he was still a simple monk in the aforesaid monastery, at the command of Fulgentius his abbot he began an outstanding work, 1 book, which, after he had been made abbot, he later completed, adorned with learning and eloquence.
On the grace of God, 7 books.
On the state of future glory, in verse, 1 book.
Letters to various persons, 1 book.
Sermons on the Blessed Virgin, 1 book.
And certain other things. He was elected abbot of the aforesaid monastery of Affligem under Emperor Henry V, in the year of the Lord [unclear], indiction 13.

Gilbert, bishop of Poitiers, formerly a scholastic of Paris, surnamed Porretanus, a Frenchman by nation, a man much practiced in the divine Scriptures and magnificently learned in secular letters, subtle in talent and confused in eloquence by novelty of terms, was accused in certain matters of heresy by blessed Bernard, and, convicted in the council of Reims celebrated by Eugenius, is said to have renounced his error. There are those who excuse him, saying that the authorities introduced in his expositions were understood by some persons in a less sound way. But we, thinking with the Roman Church, confess that what has once been concluded by it may be infringed by no one. Gilbert wrote many little works, of which the following are reported:
On the whole Psalter, 7 books.
On all the epistles of Paul, 14 books.
On the Gospel of John, 7 books.
Books of Questions, etc.
On Boethius, On the Trinity, 7 books.
And certain other things.
Several sermons.
He flourished under Emperor Conrad III, in the year of the Lord [unclear].

Lucas, abbot of the mount of St. Cornelius, of the order of the divine father Benedict, learned in the holy Scriptures by continual practice and sufficiently instructed in secular letters for his state, having obtained a noble talent for expounding the divine volumes, transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity by writing various treatises. But I do not recall that any of them have come into my hands. There is reported an outstanding work of his, addressed to Milo, bishop of the church of Thérouanne, likewise a very learned man, which I have not yet seen.
On the Song of Songs, 1 book.
Several sermons and letters.
And certain other things.
He flourished in the times of Lothar, the last emperor, in the year of the Lord 1130.

Wilbert, bishop of Chartres, studious and very skilled in the divine Scriptures, and inferior to none of the doctors of his time in the disciplines of secular letters, of talent and sufficiently adorned eloquence, notable in morals and life, and a special lover and worshipper of the most blessed Mary, Mother of God, wrote an outstanding little work on this prophecy: “The scepter shall not be taken away from Judah,” 7 books.
Against the Jews, 1 book.
On the nativity of St. Mary, 1 sermon.
Approved customs.
Various sermons, 1 book.
He is also said to have written a number of other things, which have not come to my knowledge. I believe that he flourished under Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1100.

Odo, bishop of Cambrai, a man learned in the holy Scriptures and nobly taught in humane letters, subtle in talent and distinguished in eloquence, in composing and declaiming ho*Abbot of Sponheim*

[unclear] in homilies to the people, according to the custom, by no means undistinguished. He wrote a disputation which he had held with a certain Jew concerning the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation, in dialogue form, with the first letter of his own name and that of the Jew disputing with him noted.

To Wilbodo the monk, one book. On the Canon of the Mass, one book.
On the steward of iniquity, one book: “There was a certain rich man.”
Several homilies and letters.
And he composed not a few other things, which have not come to my knowledge.

Emondus, a monk of Canterbury in England, of the Order of St. Benedict, formerly a hearer and disciple of Archbishop Anselm, a man learned in the divine Scriptures through long practice, and not ignorant of secular letters, wrote little works not unworthy of reading, by which he benefited the edification of the faithful and made his name known to posterity. Of these there is extant one volume on the discord which existed between William, king of the English, and the aforesaid St. Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury.

On ecclesiastical liberty, one book. The life of the same Anselm, one book.
And certain other things. He flourished in the time of Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1120.

Gratian, a monk of Bologna or of Classe, of the Order of St. Benedict, by country, as some think, an Etruscan, a man most learned in the divine writings, burning with marvelous zeal, ready in talent, distinguished in eloquence, and notable also in life and conduct. After Ivo, bishop of Chartres, he wrote a distinguished volume of Decrees from the statutes, sanctions, and writings of the ancients, which professors of canon law use in the schools down to the present, approved by Pope Eugene III. Its title is:

The Concord of Discordant Canons, four books: “The human race by two.”

He composed certain other things. He flourished under Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1120.

Hugh, a monk of Corbie, of the Order of St. Benedict, called “of Fouilloy,” a man rich and learned in the holy Scriptures through the reading of the ancients, distinguished in talent, sweet in eloquence, and no less venerable in conduct than in knowledge, made his name known to posterity by his writings. For he wrote a notable volume, for all religious persons fearing God not so much useful as delightful, divided into four little books, entitled as follows:

On the material cloister, one book: “On the ordering of the cloister.”
On the spiritual cloister, one book.
On the cloister of the soul, one book: “The cloister of the soul contem[unclear].”
On the cloister of paradise, one book: “In the heavenly Jerusalem cloi[unclear].”
And certain other things. He flourished in the time of Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1120.

Richard, a monk of St. Victor at Paris, of the order of regular canons of St. Augustine, a man most learned in the divine writings and nobly instructed in secular philosophy, outstanding in talent, scholastic in eloquence, and excellent in morals and conduct. He wrote many, almost innumerable, little works, by which he greatly benefited the usefulness of believers and consecrated his name to immortality. Among these the following are reported:

On the Holy Trinity, one book: “I have established my [unclear] from faith,” etc.
On contemplation, one book: “Arise, O Lord, into thy rest.”
On the twelve patriarchs, one book: “Benjamin the youth.”
On the mystical ark, one book: “That mystical ark of Moses.”
On the Song of Songs, one book: “In the little bed,” etc., “the soul which.”
On the extermination of evil, one book: “What is it to thee, O sea, that.”
On the advancement of good, one book: “Every head is sick.”
Against the Judaizers, one book: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive.”
On the tabernacle of the covenant, one book. On the forty-two stopping-places.
On the four degrees of charity, one book. On the priesthood of Melchizedek.
On the twelve apparitors, one book. On the study of wisdom.
On the progress of monks, one book: “Since to thy question,” etc.
On the threefold holocaust, one book: “Bring to the Lord, O sons of God.”
On the authority of Peter, one book: “The things which in the Gospel.”
On judicial power, one book. On diverse affections.
On the difference of sins, one book: “In Da-”
On the instruction of novices, one book. On the Apocalypse of John.

*On Ecclesiastical Writers*

one book. *A Chronicle from the beginning of the world*, one book.
[unclear] Daniel the prophet.
*On the double Passover*, one book.
24 books. “O God supremely good,” etc.
*Of divisions or exceptions*.
*On the vision of Nebuchadnezzar*, one book. *On the sacrifice of Abraham*, one book.
*On the four winds*.
*On the words of Isaiah*, one book. “On that day a man will nourish.”
*On the words of the Apostle*, one book. “You ask how,” etc.
*On the Acts of the Apostles*, one book. “King Herod sent [unclear].”
*On violent charity*, one book. “Purge out the old leaven.”
*On newness of life*, one book.

He also composed many other things besides: letters, sermons, various treatises. He flourished under Conrad III, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1140.

Guido, the fifth prior of the Carthusians, a man skilled through long study in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular letters, gentle in disposition, clear in speech, and venerable no less in his way of life than in his learning, is reported to have composed several little works, by which his name has been bestowed upon immortality. Of these there survives an excellent work written in lucid style:

*On the life of Hugh, bishop of Grenoble*, one book. *On the institutions of the Carthusians*, one book.

And certain other things. With diligent study he corrected, according to the rule of truth, the letters of the most blessed father Jerome, corrupted by the excessive fault of scribes, and brought them together into one. He died under the younger emperor Lothar, in the year of the Lord 1137, in the fifteenth indiction, on the sixth day before the Kalends of August.

Peter Lombard, bishop of Paris after being a scholastic, a man most devoted to the divine Scriptures and nobly learned, subtle in intellect and clear in speech, transmitted his name to posterity by writing with such great glory that, down to the present day, the school of theologians everywhere, exercised in his little works, names and holds him as Master with singular veneration. For with sagacious study he wrote, from the sayings of the holy fathers, a commendable work:

*Sentences*, one book. “Desiring something concerning.”
*On all the Epistles of Paul*, fourteen books. “Since all the prophecies of the Spirit.”
*Various sermons*, one book. “The beginning of things require [unclear].”

He also composed not a few other things, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under Conrad III, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1140.

Eckard, first abbot of the monastery of St. Lawrence, which is called [Vraugia], in the diocese of Würzburg in the Hercynian forest, of the order of St. Benedict, a German by nation, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, and, in secular letters, inferior in learning to no one among the Germans in his time, excelling in verse and prose, wrote little works not to be scorned for reading, by which he made clear the liveliness of his talent. Of these I have seen only an excellent work, composed in a double style in imitation of Boethius, very useful and necessary for the instruction and consolation of monks and of all the faithful who fear God, which he entitled:

*The Lantern of Monks*, one book. “Concerning lives and virtues.”
*Elegant sermons*, one book. He was buried in the middle of the church of the aforesaid monastery.

Engelbert, abbot of the monastery of Admont, of the order of St. Benedict, a German by nation, a man very studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, and sufficiently instructed in the disciplines of secular letters, clear in intellect and speech, and no less [unclear] in way of life than [unclear], in verse and prose, wrote in both styles certain excellent little works, whose authority has already long been approved by use in the Church. He was called Comestor, or Manducator, for this reason: because, by more frequently citing the authorities of the Scriptures in his sermons and little works, he as it were [unclear] the volumes into the belly of his memory and talent,

an excellent work addressed to William, archbishop of Sens, briefly and usefully explaining all the historical books of the Bible, which now by usage is entitled:

*Scholastic History*, twenty books. “Of the imperial majesty.”

*The Abbot of Sponheim*

On the praises of Saint Mary, one book.
Sermons on the season, one book.
Sermons on the saints, one book.
And several other works, one book.

He flourished under Frederick, the first emperor, in the year of the Lord 1160.

PETER the Dialectician of Paris, called Abelard, a Gaul by nation, a man most learned in secular philosophy and learned in the divine Scriptures, delighting in novelty of terms and attempting to examine things too lofty for himself, was overwhelmed by glory, fell into several errors, and, through the action of the holy abbot Bernard, was condemned with his depraved teachings at the council of Sens. From this time secular philosophy began to defile sacred theology with its useless curiosity. This Peter wrote some little works which, if he had not mixed errors into them, could have served the utility of posterity. Among them there exists a volume, shadowed over with dialectical obscurity and varied with many opinions, which he wished to entitle:

His Theology, one book. Know Thyself, one book.
And certain other works.

He flourished under Conrad, the third emperor, in the year of the Lord 1140.

ADELPHUS, abbot of the order of Saint Benedict, a man skilled in the divine Scriptures by long practice and not ignorant of secular letters, an indefatigable cultivator of regular observance, so that by word and example he might show himself a good shepherd to the sheep of Christ entrusted to him. He is said to have forged several little works for their utility, in which a rich vein of talent commends ornate eloquence. Of these there survive elegant works:

Sermons to the brothers, one book. Against the Saracens, one book.

The other things which he is said to have composed have not come to my knowledge.

WILLIAM, abbot of Saint-Thierry and afterward, as is said, a monk of Clairvaux under the divine father Bernard of the Cistercian order, a man zealous and learned in the divine writings, distinguished also by his life and by the holiness of his conduct, and for that reason singularly beloved by him, published little works not to be despised in reading. Of these only a few have come to my knowledge. He began to write, but, overtaken by death, did not complete:

The Life of Saint Bernard the Abbot, one book. Incipit: “About to write a life for the service.”
The Mirror of Faith, one book. The Enigma of Faith, one book.
Sentences of Faith, one book. To Theophilus on the Nature of the Soul, one book.
On Contemplating God, one book. On the Nature and Dignity of Love, one book.
On the Sacrament of the Altar, one book. Meditations for Novices, one book.
Against Peter Abelard, one book. On the Song of Songs, unfinished, one book.
On Paul’s Epistle to the Romans, one book. And certain other works.

There are some who say that this William, while he was still abbot of Saint-Thierry, wrote that well-known letter to the Carthusians whose beginning is “To the brothers of Mont-Dieu, an eastern light,” which is ascribed by many to blessed Bernard. He flourished under Conrad, the third emperor, in the year of the Lord [1140?]. And before Bernard, when he had completed one book on his life, he died; Arnold, abbot of Bonneval, added four other books to it.

CONRAD, a monk of the monastery of Hirsau on the borders of the Swabians, of the order of Saint Benedict, a German by nation, of the diocese of Speyer, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and very skilled in secular letters, a philosopher, rhetorician, musician, and distinguished poet, composed many very excellent little works under the name of the Pilgrim. In these the ornate arrangement of the opinions and the cultivation of graceful speech declare their author inferior to none of the ancients. Of these only the following have come to my knowledge: a distinguished work of dialogues under the name of the pilgrim priest and Theodora, a virgin consecrated to God, which he entitled:

The Mirror of Virgins, one book. Incipit: “When I am about to confer with you, O Theo-.”
On the Gospels throughout the Year, one book. Incipit: “Because in the letter of the Old Testament.”
On the Life of the Spirit and the Fruit of Death, one book. Incipit: “Since every page of divine.”
The Matricularius, one book. Incipit: “Since it is manifest [unclear].”
On the Praises of Saint Benedict, in verse, one book. Incipit: “Like light the sun.”
Didascalon, one book. Incipit: “Because I see myself for a long [unclear].”
On Music and the Tones, one book. Incipit: “Music is, according to someone’s [unclear].”

Of the rest I have seen nothing. There was another declaimer of the order of preachers who, according to the custom of the moderns, composed sermons to the people under the name of Peregrinus, much inferior to our man in eloquence and also later in time. Whatever this Conrad wrote resounds with Ciceronian eloquence, which the other could not achieve. He flourished under Conrad, the third emperor, in the year of the Lord [1140?].

ARNOLD, abbot of Bonneval, of the Cistercian order, once of blessed Bernard the abbot *On Ecclesiastical Writers*

...a close friend, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant also of secular letters, ready in intellect and distinguished in eloquence, conspicuous no less in conduct than in learning, made his name known to posterity by writing. For when William, abbot of Saint-Thierry, had died and left unfinished the work on the life of Saint Bernard, while that saint himself was already holding the heavenly realms, he wrote and composed:

*The Deeds of Illustrious Men*, one book.
*The Life of Saint Bernard*.
And certain letters.

He flourished under Frederick, the first emperor, in the year of the Lord 1160.

Richard, a monk of Cluny, of the Order of Saint Benedict, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, and in secular letters the most learned of all men of his time, subtle in intellect, eloquent in speech, who by writing and composing various treatises transmitted his name with great glory to the knowledge of posterity. Yet I do not recall that any of them has so far come into our hands. His notable and distinguished work is reported, however:

*Histories of the Times*, one book.
*Letters to Various Persons*, one book.

He flourished in the times of Frederick, the first emperor, in the year of the Lord 1160.

Ganfred of Auxerre, a monk of the Cistercian order, formerly a hearer and disciple of Peter Abelard; but lest he should also become an imitator of his error, he betook himself to the teaching of Saint Bernard of Clairvaux. Under his discipleship, distinguished in learning and religion, he composed little works not contemptible for reading, by which he made his name known also to posterity.

*Against Peter Abelard*, one book.
*On the Apocalypse of John*, one book.
*Letters to Various Persons*, one book.

He flourished in the times of Frederick, the first emperor, in the year of the Lord 1160.

Peter, cleric of the church of Reims, called de Riga, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, and in secular letters most learned among all the doctors of his time; a grammarian and an outstanding philosopher, excelling in verse and prose. He wrote not a few volumes in both styles, by which he made his name known to posterity. Of these I have seen only the notable metrical work on the Bible, which he entitled *Aurora*, as follows:

*On Genesis*, one book. It begins: “The beginning of the world, what sort...”
“The twelfth of the fathers...”
One book. “But the voice of the Lord Moses [unclear]”
“God addresses Moses.”
One book. “These are the words of God.”
“After Moses, Joshua.”
One book. “The Hebrew sins, he says.”
“Solomon reigned.”
“To Ruth [unclear] quickly...”
“Dwelling on Mount Ephraim...”
“Origen alone with [unclear].”
One book. “After [unclear] and [unclear] for himself...”
“You who read the history...”
“Certain persons [ascribe] the book of Job to Moses.”
“To Eustochium and Paula...”
“As far as under the Ethiopians...”
“Great Alexander.”
“Herod flourished [unclear].”
“In the nineteenth year of Tiberius.”
One book. “These things concerning the new law...”
*On Grammar*.

Joachim, abbot of the monastery of Fiore, of the Order of Saint Benedict, born in Calabria, a man devoted to and practiced in the divine Scriptures, who, since he was regarded as a prophet in his own time, even attempted to foretell future things. But he seems to me, if I may speak without prejudice to his own opinion or that of his followers, to have spoken more from conjectures of the Scriptures than to have prophesied. For, to be silent for the moment about the rest, he dreamed that Emperor Frederick would be a future enemy of the Church, whom all [unclear]. He wrote, however, in plain speech, a number of little works, in almost all of which, as though foreknowing the future, he wove in mystical prognostications.

*On Hie-* *The Abbot of Sponheim*

On Jeremiah the prophet, one book.
On the Gospel of John, two books. On the Apocalypse of John, three books.
To Henry the Sixth, three books. “You piously ask something from ...”
On the seven seals, four books. “The first time ...”
The Psalter of ten strings, five books. “Of concord ...”
On the fifteen pontiffs, one book. “Go up, bald man, that [unclear] ...”
On future times, one book. “Since the general [unclear] of the world ...”
Letters to various persons, one book. “Among all historians ...”
He also published many other works, especially against the Jews and other adversaries of the Catholic faith, which have not come into our hands. But the treatise which he wrote against Peter Lombard, bishop of Paris, was condemned in a general council, as is clear at the beginning of the Decretals, “We condemn.”
He flourished under Henry the Sixth, in the year of the Lord 1100.

Rupert, monk of the monastery of St. Remigius in the diocese of Reims, of the order of the divine father Benedict, a Frenchman by nation, a man trained by constant study in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular disciplines, distinguished in talent and clear in speech, wrote several small works of his intellect, by which his name became known to posterity. Of these I have seen only the deeds done by the Christians in the Holy Land in the time of Urban the Second against the infidels.
A distinguished history, ten books. “Among all historians ...”
Of the others I have seen nothing. He flourished under Henry the Fifth, in the year of the Lord 1120.

Roswitha, a noble woman born in Saxony, a nun in the monastery of Gandersheim, which is not far distant from Hildesheim, was distinguished by marvelous talent and learning, and admirable in both kinds of writing. For, exhorting consecrated virgins to chastity and continence, she wrote six comedies in the Latin language. On the deeds of the Ottos, a panegyric in verse, one book. “The sole hope ...” Also the passion of St. Dionysius in elegiac verse. Also several works on St. Gangolphus and other saints. She also had knowledge of the Greek language. She was a contemporary of John the Englishman, who by his learning deserved the papacy.

Dudechinus, priest of the church in Logenstein, a German by nation, a man learned through long practice in the holy Scriptures and sufficiently instructed in the disciplines of secular letters, went to Jerusalem, in hope of eternal recompense, with many others under the emperor Conrad the Third; when they fought with the Saracens in a naval battle, [unclear]. Great in subtlety and distinguished in speech, he transmitted his name with glory to posterity by writing many and varied works. Of his small works few have come into our hands. These, however, are reported:
A Summa of Theology, one book. “On the books of Dionysius ...”
The Summa which is called Numerical, one book. “Those who rule well, pref. ...”
On the celestial sphere, one book. “Our intention in this treatise ...”
On ecclesiastical computation, one book. “Computation is the science of nume...”
A beautiful calendar, one book.
He furthermore published many other works, which have not come to my knowledge.

John, bishop of Chartres, by native place of Salisbury, formerly clerk and disciple of blessed Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, a man learned in the divine writings and nobly instructed in secular letters, subtle in talent, eloquent in speech, and composed with beautiful grace, excellent in verse and prose, and venerable no less for religion than for knowledge, wrote many distinguished volumes, by which he made his name known to posterity; but few of them have come into our hands. I have read his distinguished work on the trifles of courtiers and philosophers, which he wished to title:
Polycraticon, eight books. “Most delightful then among many ...”
A Penitential, one book. “Since the mercies of the Lord ...”
The Life of St. Thomas the archbishop, one book.
Letters to various persons, one book.
He flourished under Frederick, the first emperor, in the year of the Lord 1140.

Peter *Ecclesiastical Description*

Peter of Blois, archdeacon of Bath, the close friend of the above-mentioned bishop John of Chartres, to whom he dictated some letters, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures and exceptionally instructed in secular letters, acute and forceful in talent, who knew not how to flatter the vices of princes and prelates but to rebuke them, held in esteem among kings, princes, and bishops for his learning and the uprightness of his life, wrote many little works. Of these the following are reported:

*On Christian Friendship*, 1 book. “For they have been diminished.”

*On Salutary Penitence*, 1 book. “You asked me that for you [unclear].”

1 book. “Who will give to my head...”

*On Hastening the Passage*, 1 book. “Your excessive [austerity?] of severity...”

1 book. “You are divided [unclear].”

*On the Quality of Penitence*, 1 book. “Your little exhortation.”

1 book. *Against the Depraver*, 2 books. “You have been chosen by your own.”

*Exhortation to an Abbot*, 2 books.

*On the Office of a Bishop*, 1 book. “You ask more urgently, reverend father.”

1 book. “Whenever I recall the words.”

1 book. “I give thanks to your grace.”

*Letters*, 194 in number, 1 book. “Asked by you, [unclear].”

2 books. He wrote many other works.

*On the Danger of Prelates*, 2 books.

*On the Life of Court Clerics*.

*On the Deceptions of Fortune*.

He flourished under Frederick the First, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1160.

Alexander, the third pope, a Sienese by homeland, after Adrian the Fourth sat in the chair of Peter for twenty-one years; a learned and vigorous man, who endured many injuries from Emperor Frederick, while he stoutly crushed the three antipopes raised up by him against himself, and at last, overcoming the emperor himself, trampled his neck with his foot as a sign of his subjection, saying: “It is written: You shall walk upon the asp and the basilisk; you shall trample the lion and the dragon.” He wrote elegant works:

*Letters to Various Persons*, 1 book; and *On Ecclesiastical Power*, 1 book.

And certain other works. He died in the time of Frederick the First, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1181, in the fourteenth indiction.

Crisolanus, archbishop of the church of Milan, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, nobly instructed in secular letters, distinguished in Greek and Latin eloquence, published certain little works of great authority, by which he transmitted his name with glory to the knowledge of posterity; none of these has come into our hands. His work is reported:

*On the Holy Spirit, Against the Greeks*, 1 book. *On the Holy Trinity*, 1 book.

Letters, sermons, and various other treatises, which are unknown to me.

Hugh Eterianus, a Tuscan by nation, easily the most learned in the holy Scriptures of all the learned men of his time, exceptionally instructed in secular letters, a philosopher and most eloquent rhetorician, perfectly equipped in Greek and Latin speech, whom all Greece admired as he wrote, most subtle in talent, a disputant second to none. He wrote many distinguished volumes, both in Greek and in Latin, by which he transmits his name with glory to posterity. Of these I have found only one work, brief indeed, but not to be despised, on the heresies which the Greeks lay upon the Latins:

*To Cardinal Ardoinus*, 1 book. “Careful prudence.”

*On the Immortal God*, 1 book. I have found nothing about the rest.

He flourished in the times of Manuel, emperor of Constantinople, with whom he was of great authority, under Frederick the First, emperor of the Romans, and Pope Alexander III, in the year of the Lord 1160.

Christian, archchancellor of Frederick the First, emperor, a Teuton by nation, a man most learned in secular literature, eloquent and industrious, whom the Italians in his time admired when he spoke, not ignorant also of the divine Scriptures, whom Leo the Tuscan, notary of Manuel, emperor of the Greeks, extols with praises. He wrote certain distinguished little works of his talent, of which there are extant:

*The Deeds of the Life of Frederick the First, Emperor*, 1 book. Various letters, or speeches, and certain other works.

He flourished under the same Frederick the First, in the year of the Lord 1170.

Leo, a Tuscan by nation, interpreter of imperial letters under Manuel, the great prince of the Greeks, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, an excellent cultivator of secular letters, skilled in Greek and Latin speech, whose office it was [to handle] letters sent to the emperor *The Abbot of Sponheim*

or to be sent to others, from one language into another. He published certain distinguished volumes, by which he transmitted his name even to the knowledge of posterity. Of these I have read only the excellent work which he entitled:

*On the Prevarications of the Greeks*, 2 books. “The intolerable [unclear] of the Greeks.”
*Against the Errors of the Greeks*, 1 book.

He flourished at Constantinople in the times of Emperor Frederick I and Pope Alexander III, in the year of the Lord 1170.

JOHANNES, archdeacon of a certain church of Horit., a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular literature, skilled in Greek and Latin speech, outstanding in talent and distinguished in eloquence, wrote certain little works, not to be despised, for the edification of the faithful, by which he made his name known. Of these there is an excellent and distinguished work, addressed to a certain royal notary Stephanus, against the Greeks.

Also various letters, 1 book. “[unclear] Greek.”
*On the Procession of the Holy Spirit*.

But he is also said to have written certain other works, which have not come into our hands.

GODEFRIDUS of Viterbo, priest, a man zealous and learned in the divine writings, and not ignorant of secular literature, outstanding and distinguished in talent, practiced in verse and prose, wrote little works of reading not to be despised, by which he left his memory to posterity. Of these there is a large volume addressed to Urban III, mixed in verse and prose, on the beginning of the world, on the whole Old and New Testament, and on the ages of the world, the deeds of the times, and all the histories of kings, which he entitled:

*Pantheon*, 15 books. “On the beginning of the world.”

Of the others I have seen nothing.

He flourished under Emperor Frederick I and his son Henry, in the year of the Lord 1185.

ECKEBERTUS, second abbot of the monastery of Saint Florinus, of the order of the divine father Benedict, in the diocese of Trier, a German by nation, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, and no less venerable in conduct than in knowledge, was the brother of the blessed virgin Helizabet, abbess of Schonau. He had previously been a canon of the church of Bonn; summoned by his holy sister to Schonau, he was first made a monk, and then abbot. He wrote little works of reading not to be despised, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these I found the following:

*Against Heresies*, 1 book. “Prophesied long ago [unclear].”
*On the Beginning of the Gospel of John*, 1 book. “The mysteries of divine [unclear].”
*On the Magnificat*, 1 book. “The Spirit of the Lord upon you [unclear].”
*On ‘The Angel Was Sent’*, 1 book. “The Gospel sermon [unclear].”
*On the Death of His Sister*, 1 book. “To virgins consecrated to God.”
*Meditations*, 1 book. “I have a word for you.”
*Sermons through the Year*, 15 books. “There will be signs,” etc., “of Advent.”
*Praises of the Savior*, 1 book.
*Letters to Various Persons*, 1 book. “It happened in the beginning.”

He also published some other works which have not come to my knowledge. For he was an excellent, learned, and eloquent declaimer, so much so that by a single disputation he overcame a certain heretic whom no one was able to refute. He flourished in the aforesaid monastery of Saint Florinus, which is called Schonau, in the diocese of Trier, under Emperor Frederick I, in the year of the Lord 1160, and was held in esteem because of his religious life and learning.

HELIZABET, nun and abbess of the sisters’ monastery of Schonau, of the order of Saint Benedict (for there are two monasteries, one of monks and the other of nuns, situated at the end of the diocese of Trier not far from the Rhine in the Hercynian forest), sister of the aforesaid abbot Eckebertus, a virgin of most holy conduct, received many revelations from God, which she committed to writing for the edification of posterity. Of these I have read the following:

*The Ways of God*, a useful work, 1 book. “It happened in the beginning.”
*On the 11,000 Virgins of Cologne*, 15 books. “To us who [unclear] pious [unclear].”
*Of Various Revelations*, 1 book. “All who are going to read.”
*To Her Brother Eckebertus*, 15 books. “You ask of me, brother.”
*Letters to Various Persons*, 1 book. “From the bishopric of Metz [unclear].”
*To Saint Hildegard*, 15 books. And certain other works.

She died under Emperor Frederick I, in the year of the Lord 1165, in the thirteenth indiction, in the thirty-sixth year of her age.

*On Ecclesiastical Writers*

Of her conversion, the twenty-fourth; but of the visitation of the heavenly splendor, the thirteenth. On the fourteenth day before the Kalends of July. Buried in the church of the monks of Saint Florin, in the middle of the choir.

Hildegard, abbess of the monastery of Saint Rupert the Confessor, opposite the town of Bingen on the other side of the river Nahe, in the diocese of Mainz, of the order of the holy father Benedict, German by birth, from the county of Sponheim, once a disciple of the blessed virgin Jutta, sister of Megenhard, count of Sponheim, our founder, a virgin of most holy conduct and enlightened from her childhood by divine revelations, whose life, approved by many miracles, spread the fragrance of her holiness into far distant regions, so much so that Eugene III, Anastasius IV, and Hadrian III, Roman pontiffs, visiting her very frequently by letters, commended themselves and the Roman Church to her prayers. And Eugene III, in the council of Trier, with Saint Bernard present, publicly approved her writings and small works when they had been read before all, and again strengthened her by letters to persist in the undertaking she had received. All the things that she committed to writing she learned by divine revelation.

Among these are the following:

On the Rule of Saint Benedict, one book. “And I, a poor little woman...”

Thirty Questions, one book. “Charity, which with abstinence...”

Life of Saint Rupert the Confessor, one book. “For, as in a true vision...”

Life of Saint Disibod the Bishop, one book. “In a mystical vision,” etc.

Fifty-eight Homilies on the Gospels, one book. “A certain man who...”

On the Sacrament of the Altar, one book. “In a vision which of the soul...”

Scivias, a large volume, one book. “And it came to pass in the ninth year...”

Life of Merits, one book. “O crowd of men being born...”

Compound Medicine, one book. Simple Medicine, one book.

Divine Works, one book. “And it came to pass in the sixth year...”

To the People of Cologne, one book. “He who was, and who is...”

To the People of Trier, one book. “I, a poor little woman...”

Exhortation for Secular Persons, one book. “O crowd of men being born...”

To Her Sisters, one book. “O daughter, who the footsteps...”

To the Gray Monks, one book. “I, a poor little woman, in...”

Various Songs, one book. “Who are these who, as...”

And to Saint Bernard, one letter. “In the spirit of mysteries...”

Letters to various persons, 135, one book. “Every father, I, poor...”

She also wrote other things. In all her small works Catholic doctrine shines forth, which either confirms faith or instructs morals; nor did she ever say or write anything that could be called into doubt. And although she was ignorant of Latin speech, nevertheless, as the Spirit of God revealed it, she dictated everything in Latin and fittingly, with notaries taking it down. We have seen many letters of Conrad III and Frederick I, emperors, and of the bishops of Mainz, Trier, Cologne, Bremen, Jerusalem, and of others almost innumerable, who, stirred by the fame of her holiness and revelations from various regions of the world, commended themselves in writing to her prayers and sought solutions. She died under Emperor Frederick I, in the year of the Lord 1180, at the age of 82, in the thirteenth indiction, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October.

Albert, patriarch of Jerusalem, a learned and most holy man, who gave a rule to the Carmelite brothers while they were still dwelling in the Holy Land, which those same brothers, now established in Europe, profess everywhere after it had been modified and approved by the Apostolic See, at the urging of Pope Innocent III described in a clear and truthful discourse:

The State of the Holy Land, one book. The Rule of the Carmelites.

He flourished under Emperor Henry VI, in the year of the Lord 1190.

Innocent III, pope, Campanian by birth, previously called Lotharius, after Pope Celestine III presided over the Church for eighteen years. He was very learned in the divine Scriptures, since from his childhood he had devoted himself to letters in the school at Paris, and he became a man no less upright than learned. He left not a few small works of his genius, of which the following are circulated under the name of Lotharius the Levite, or also of Pope Innocent:

On the Usefulness of the Human Condition, two books. “Why from the womb of the mother...”

On the Seven Penitential Psalms, one book. “There are three things especially in which...”

On the Office of the Mass, one book. On the Cloister of the Soul, one book.

On the Sacrament of Baptism, one book. Many Sermons. Let*282 The Abbot of Spanheim, book I.*

Letters to various persons, one book.

He flourished at the time of the discord which was between Philip, brother of Henry, and Otto, duke of Saxony, in the year of the Lord 1200.

William of Auxerre, as they report a bishop, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly instructed in secular philosophy, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, ascending the theological chair in the school of Paris, shone forth with distinction for a long time, and among all the doctors of that time was celebrated with the greatest reputation and esteem. He wrote a very notable and useful volume, or

A Summa of Theology, "As the Apostle says, Faith," one book.
On the divine offices, "On the divine offices," one book.

He is also said to have written many other things, which have not come to my knowledge.

Cyril, priest and monk of Mount Carmel, and third prior general of the same order, by nation, as they report, a Greek, a holy man and illuminated with a prophetic spirit, to whom almighty God is said to have revealed his will by angelic ministry, when he was honored with silver tablets written by the finger of God. Among the other little works of his talent he wrote, to Abbot Joachim, On the Angelic Oracle.

The prologue begins thus, one epistle: "To the house of the whole divine..."
But the Oracle thus, one book: "In the time of the years of Christ..."
On the progress of his order.
Several letters to various persons, one book.

He flourished under Philip and Otto, in the year of the Lord 1200.

Helinand, monk of Froidmont, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures through long practice, and nobly instructed in secular letters, keen in intellect and eloquent in speech, because of the excellence of his learning and the integrity of his life appeared not least among the ecclesiastical doctors of his time. For he wrote many things by which he gave his name to immortality. Of these the following are reported: from the beginning of the world down to his own age, a great and notable volume,

Histories, 48 books.
On the restoration of the fallen, one book: "G. Lamentations and ve..."
Several sermons, one book.
Letters to various persons, one book.

And many other things. He flourished under Henry VI, in the year of the Lord [unclear].

Gilbert, monk of the Cistercian order, and afterward abbot of a certain monastery, a man studious in the divine writings and excellently learned, subtle in intellect and clear in speech. After the death of St. Bernard the abbot, he wrote, where he had left off, namely from that place, "On my bed by night," down to the end, 46 subtle and most elegant sermons.

On the Song of Songs, one book: "There are different kinds of lovers..."

And certain other things.

He flourished under Henry VI, in the year of the Lord 1200.

Aelred, abbot of a certain monastery of the Cistercian order, as one practiced by continual study in the holy Scriptures and not ignorant of secular philosophy, gentle in intellect, sweet in speech, outstanding in devotion. He wrote for the benefit of his brothers several little works, by which he both profited them and transmitted knowledge of his name to posterity. Of these there is extant a little work of great usefulness for religious men, filled with spiritual sayings, which he entitled

The Mirror of Charity, one book.
On Luke, one homily: "When Jesus was of the years..."

And other things which I have not seen.

He flourished in the times of Henry VI, around the years of the Lord 1209.

Maurice, bishop of Paris, very studious and learned in the divine writings, and nobly instructed in secular philosophy, as one who before his episcopate taught theology gloriously for many years at Paris, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, was of excellent application in declaiming sermons to the people. He is reported to have composed certain excellent little works, by which he made his name known to posterity. Of these there are reported, through the course of the whole year, both on Sundays and on feast days,

Sermons to the people, one book.
On the care of souls, to priests.

But the rest which he is said to have written have not come to my knowledge.

He flourished in the times of Henry VI, in the year of the Lord 1190.

Papias, by nation a Lombard, a man most learned in secular letters, the most distinguished grammarian of all in his time, fully instructed in Greek and Latin speech, and also not moderately practiced in the divine Scriptures. He wrote in a twofold style in both literatures *On Ecclesiastical Writers*

[unclear] certain excellent little works. Of these a few have come to my notice.

On the order of speaking, one book.

On the words of the Latin language, one book. It begins: “Of all things in this book [unclear].”

Letters to various persons, one book. About the rest I have found nothing.

He flourished in the time of Henry VI, in the year of the Lord 1200.

John Beleth, once a distinguished theologian of the University of Paris, learned in the divine Scriptures and sufficiently instructed in secular philosophy, ready in intellect, scholastic in speech, not undistinguished among the doctors of his time, by writing and disputation brought his name with glory to the knowledge of posterity. For he wrote the not unprofitable work:

A summa on the divine offices, one book. It begins: “In the primitive Church.”

Also various sermons, one book.

He is said besides to have written not a few other things, but they have not come to my notice.

Theoderic, abbot of the order of St. Benedict, German by nation, a man devoted to the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, no less renowned for his manner of life than for his knowledge. He is reported to have composed several little works, of which I have seen only, addressed to certain abbots:

The life of Saint Hildegard, four books. It begins: “In the Roman commonwealth.”

And certain letters. He flourished under Henry VI, in the year of the Lord 1200.

Werner, otherwise Hirnerius, an illustrious and notable man, professor of civil law and a most distinguished interpreter, and an exceptional cultivator of humane letters, who was deservedly called the lamp of law, because he was the first to expound civil law with little glosses, and gave to others after him an unparalleled example of illuminating the law. And from this time professors of both laws have always flourished in abundance, and began to explain the volumes of his instruction down to the present day. He taught in both places, both at Rome and at Bologna, for a long time, where he had many distinguished pupils, who by their learning spread the fame and glory of their master. His glosses and splendid memorials on the laws are extant, very well known among professors of this field. He flourished in the time of Henry VI, in the year of the Lord 1200.

Peter, abbot of Cluny, of the order of St. Benedict, a man learned in the divine Scriptures through constant exercise, gentle in intellect, sweet and composed in speech, and quite fit for persuasion, devout and praiseworthy in manner of life, and a distinguished zealot for regular observance, making his name known to posterity by writing, composed certain devout little works for the benefit of readers. Of these the following are reported:

Accounts of many things, one book.

On the eremitical life, one book. It begins: “I have received the letters of love.”

Letters to various persons, one book.

He also published several other things, which have not come to my notice.

Peter Cantor of Paris, and afterward, as they report, bishop, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly instructed in secular philosophy, gloriously presided for many years over the theological school at Paris and trained many distinguished pupils. He also wrote certain excellent [unclear], transmitted with glory to the knowledge of posterity. Among his little works there is found a certain notable and by no means contemptible summa, which he entitled:

The Abridged Word, one book. It begins: “The abridged word.”

Another book of distinctions, one book. It begins: “Abel is called the beginning.”

The Grammar of Theologians, one book. Various sermons.

On certain miracles, one book.

Also On the Sacraments, three books. It begins: “The people went about.”

He flourished in the time of Henry VI, in the year of the Lord 1200.

Pileus of Modena, professor of both laws, very celebrated in intellect, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, renowned for knowledge and cautious in counsel, held in the highest esteem among the older jurists, by writing and teaching various things in that faculty [unclear]. His name [unclear] appeared first among the expositors of law, and by his example gave many both the spirit and the form of studying. He is reported to have written in that faculty certain splendid little works, by which he gave his name to immortality. Of these there is extant a brief summa on the Pandects, which is entitled:

*Vento-* *The Abbot of Sponheim, book I.*

“Ventosa,” and certain other things. He flourished under Henry VI, in the year of the Lord 1200. Book 9.

Stephen the Englishman, once the ornament and rector of the school of Paris, studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, and second to none in his time in Aristotelian philosophy, taught theology gloriously for many years, and was the first to begin expounding Sacred Scripture inwardly and morally. And from this the custom grew up among us that masters of theology should explain the divine books more clearly to their pupils in their lectures in the schools. This Stephen, as I have learned, wrote the following little works:

On the five books of Moses, 5 books. A lecture on the hundred [unclear]. On Joshua, 1 book.

Also on the book of Judges, 1 book. Also on Kings, 4 books. [unclear]

On the twelve minor prophets, 12 books. He also published many other works, which have not yet come to my knowledge. He flourished about the times of the rule of King Henry VI, but the fifth emperor crowned by the pope, in the year of the Lord 1200.

Bagorotus, distinguished professor of both laws and a very celebrated interpreter, not ignorant also of other secular letters, whose authority among the ancient jurists was not small, on account of his excellent talent for teaching, also made his name known to posterity by his zeal in writing. Of his little works there survives a noteworthy summa, which he entitled:

Of Cavillations, 1 book. “Since his danger is [unclear].”

On the Order of Judgments, 1 book. “By the prayers and insistence.”

He is said besides to have written several other works, but they have not come to my knowledge.

Placentinus, an Italian by nation, a most celebrated cultivator and expounder of both laws, attained great glory by teaching and writing on Mount Pestilanus. He once held a place among the principal doctors among the professors of this art, on account of certain most commendable volumes which he composed. Of these, among others, there is said to survive:

A Summa of Judgments, 1 book. “When I was at Mantua.”

Also on the Code, 1 book. I have found nothing concerning the others.

He flourished in the times of Henry VI, in the year of the Lord 1200.

Rofredus, Beneventan by homeland, a most renowned doctor in both laws, subtle in intellect, composed in scholastic fashion in speech, sufficiently fit, by long practice, for resolving doubts and questions of law, wrote little works not to be despised by students in that faculty, by which he consecrated his name and reputation to immortality. Of these, however, we have been able to find only a few, which we have set down below, a very useful volume containing:

Questions of Civil Law, 1 book. “If I were considering the talent.”

Questions of Canon Law, 1 book. “On all actions.”

A Summa of Law, 1 book.

Whatever more he published has not yet come to my knowledge at all.

Peter, archbishop of Sens, learned in the divine Scriptures by continual study and rich from reading the ancients, and also learned in secular letters, subtle in intellect and clear in speech, wrote little works of no small utility, by which he both cultivated his own talent and prepared material for the edification of others. He wrote very subtly, with sayings of the fathers added:

On all the epistles of Paul, 1 book. Also various sermons.

He also diligently expounded various books of the Bible, and is said to have written other treatises, both various and useful, which have not come to my knowledge.

Azo, an Italian by nation, took the origin of his life from the city of Bologna; formerly the hearer and disciple of Johannes Bosianus of Cremona, a very learned man; a most famous interpreter of civil law, a fountain of laws, an abundance of words, a lamp of law, who by his learning and knowledge easily surpassed all the jurists who had preceded him, published many little works pertaining to civil law, by which he acquired immortal praise and glory:

A noteworthy Summa of Law, 1 book. On the Old Digest, [unclear] books.

Also on the Code, 9 books.

In addition, he produced excellent apparatuses on the laws, and added additions to several summae, and wrote various things which are not unknown to learned jurists. He flourished in the times of Emperor Frederick II, in the year of the Lord 1230. And he left after him many distinguished disciples, nobly learned in the imperial laws as well as in other disciplines of humane letters, subtle in intellect and clear in speech, a doctor of great authority among the old professors of this faculty. He wrote certain excellent volumes in that discipline, of which I have seen only:

On the Order of Judgments, 1 book. “In the name of our Lord Jesus.” On [unclear].

*On Ecclesiastical Writers, book I.* It remains now that concerning the office.

*On the Office of a Notary*

Various questions of law.

The other things which he composed have not yet at all come into our hands.

FRANCIS, founder and head of the Order of Minors, an Italian by nation, sprung from the city of Assisi in Italy, a man of most holy conduct and a most ardent follower of evangelical poverty, who by word and example converted many from iniquity and directed them into the way of Catholic justice, was so great a lover of Christ that in contempt of the world and of transitory consolation he scarcely had an equal. In his order many very learned men have already flourished, who for the usefulness of the faithful have composed almost innumerable little works. Francis himself, however, wrote a brief work:

The Rule of the Minors, book I, "The rule and life of the Minors."

A brief Testament, book I, "The Lord gave to me, brother."

He flourished under Emperor Frederick II, in the year of the Lord 1220.

CAESARIUS, a monk in Heisterbach, of the Cistercian order, a German by nation, of the diocese of Cologne Agrippina, a devout man, outstanding in regular discipline, and by long practice devoted to the divine scriptures, composed for the instruction of the novices, whose instructor he was, some little works in a simple and open style, the reading of which is not to be despised by more simple devout brothers. Of these I have found only the following.

A lengthy work on miracles and diverse visions made in Germany in his own time, which he entitled in imitation of the holy Pope Gregory.

Dialogues on various matters, 12 books, "Gather up the fragments, lest."

On the Sunday Gospels, book I, "The cluster of Cyprus, beloved."

On the Gospels for saints, book I, "Our Lord and Savior Jesus."

Sermons to novices, book I.

Besides these he published several other works, which have not come to my knowledge.

WILLIAM, monk of the monastery of the divine martyr Dionysius of Paris, of the Order of St. Benedict, a Frenchman by nation, a man skilled in the divine scriptures by constant study and excellently learned in the disciplines of secular letters, clear in talent and eloquence, and a distinguished knower of times, not ignorant, notable in morals and life, was of excellent talent in declaiming sermons to the people; gloriously preaching the cross against the Albigensian heretics, by apostolic authority he signed many of the faithful against them. He wrote little works of reading not to be despised, by which, writing and teaching various things, he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Among these there is extant:

A volume of Histories, 3 books. And many letters to various persons, book I.

He is said, moreover, to have published commentaries on the divine scriptures, which I have not yet seen.

JACOBUS de Vitriaco, bishop of Acre, afterward cardinal of the most holy Roman Church, bishop of Tusculum, a man learned in the divine scriptures, not ignorant of secular letters, notable in morals and life, was of excellent talent in declaiming sermons to the people; gloriously preaching the cross against the Albigensian heretics, by apostolic authority he signed many of the faithful against them. He wrote little works of reading not to be despised, by which he made his name known to posterity.

The Eastern History, book I. The Life of Mary of Oignies, 3 books.
